# Bezel Language Specification

**Version 0.248 — August 2026**

Bezel is a compiled language for services and tools, with ownership-based memory management and no garbage collector. The compiler tracks ownership of every heap object and ensures that each one is disposed exactly once. Borrowing lets you pass references without transferring ownership, with lifetimes checked at compile time rather than enforced by a runtime. The result aims to give you the safety of a managed language and the predictability of a manual one, without the ceremony of either.

This document is the normative reference for the language. It defines syntax, type system, ownership rules, and the semantics of every construct. The specification is partitioned into a Core level and a set of Extended features; Appendix D defines the levels and what a conformance claim at each means. It is intentionally dense — written to be precise rather than introductory — and is best read alongside its companion documents: the design rationale, which explains *why* each decision was made and records the alternatives considered; the standard library, which catalogs the types and methods the language ships with; and the revision changelog, which carries the per-revision narrative history.

If this is your first encounter with Bezel, the rationale's opening section is a gentler starting point: it sketches the goals of the language and the shape of its memory model before the spec's formal definitions begin. If you want concrete code first, the short companion guides (memory and ownership; errors and nullability; modeling data) work from worked examples. Once you know what you are looking for, this document is the place to look it up.

<a id="sec-lexical-structure"></a>
## 1. Lexical Structure

<a id="sec-source-files"></a>
### 1.1 Source files

A Bezel source file is a sequence of Unicode code points, encoded in UTF-8. Source files use the `.bzl` extension. Line endings are LF, CR, or CRLF.

<a id="sec-tokens"></a>
### 1.2 Tokens

A token is a keyword, identifier, literal, operator, or punctuation symbol. Whitespace and comments separate tokens but are not themselves tokens.

<a id="sec-identifiers"></a>
### 1.3 Identifiers

An identifier begins with a Unicode letter or underscore (`_`) and continues with letters, digits, or underscores. Identifiers are case-sensitive: `Foo`, `foo`, and `FOO` are distinct. The bare underscore `_` is **not** an identifier: it is a reserved token (Appendix [B.1](#sec-reserved-keywords)) — the discard, whose sanctioned forms and rejected positions are [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_) — never declarable and never readable as a name. Identifiers merely *containing* underscores (`_camelCase`, `snake_case`, `_f`) are ordinary identifiers; only the bare single-character token is reserved.

The convention is `PascalCase` for types, methods, properties, and other public members; `_camelCase` for private fields; `camelCase` for parameters and locals. The compiler does not enforce these conventions. The lowercase keyword `string` and the standard-library type name `String` (`System.String`) name the same type — they are interchangeable in source — but the lexer treats them as different tokens: `string` is a reserved keyword (Appendix B) producing a primitive type token; `String` is an ordinary PascalCase identifier whose meaning is established by name resolution against the auto-imported standard library. The same dual-form rule applies to the other primitive-keyword aliases listed in [§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types).

<a id="sec-keywords"></a>
### 1.4 Keywords

Reserved words may not be used as identifiers, except for the contextual keywords listed in Appendix B which have meaning only in specific syntactic positions.

All keywords are lowercase. Type identifiers like `Object`, `Array`, and `Exception` are not keywords; they are PascalCase names defined in the standard library or compiler intrinsics.

<a id="sec-comments"></a>
### 1.5 Comments

Three forms:

- `// ...` — line comment, extends to end of line
- `/* ... */` — block comment, does not nest
- `/// ...` — documentation comment, attached to the immediately following declaration

Documentation comments use XML element syntax. See [§34](#sec-comments-and-documentation) for the recognized tag set and details. The compiler preserves the comments for documentation generators but does not interpret their content.

<a id="sec-statements-and-termination"></a>
### 1.6 Statements and termination

Every statement terminates with a semicolon. Block-bodied constructs terminate with `end`, optionally followed by a label, then a semicolon. **One uniform rule: `end` may be followed by the construct's name if it has one, or by its introducing keyword otherwise; when a label is present, it must match.** Concretely:

- **Named constructs** — class, interface, record, enum bodies; method bodies; property accessor blocks; labeled loop statements ([§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue)) — the loop label is the construct's name: `end scan;`. The optional label is the *identifier*: `end ClassName;`, `end methodName;`. A mismatch is a compile error.
- **Keyword-labelled constructs** — everything else, labelled by the keyword that introduced the block: `end constructor;`, `end destructor;`, `end operator +;` (the operator token must also match), and the statement-level and container blocks: `end if;`, `end while;`, `end for;`, `end do;`, `end try;`, `end case;`, `end when;`, `end extension;`, `end extern;`. (`end while;`/`end for;` apply to **unlabeled** loops; a loop carrying a loop label is a named construct — previous bullet — per the umbrella rule's "otherwise".) A label that does not match the construct's introducing keyword is a compile error.

The unlabelled form `end;` is always valid everywhere — the label is for readability across long bodies and carries no semantic weight beyond compile-time verification that it matches.

---

**Trailing commas.** Every comma-separated list admits one optional trailing comma before its closer — argument, parameter, and generic lists, positional fields, enum constants, choice cases, inheritance and constraint lists, lambda parameters and destructuring slots, positional patterns, extern parameters, and the literal/arm/assignment lists that always allowed it. One rule, no exceptions; `|`-separated pattern alternatives are not comma lists.

<a id="sec-modules-and-compilation"></a>
## 2. Modules and Compilation

<a id="sec-module-declarations"></a>
### 2.1 Module declarations

Every source file declares its module on its first non-comment line; any `import` declarations follow the module declaration:

```bezel
module BankingApp.Transactions;
```

A module name is a single identifier or a sequence of identifiers separated by dots. The dotted form is a single name; it does not establish nesting. `BankingApp` and `BankingApp.Transactions` are unrelated modules.

Multiple files with identical `module` declarations **presented to the module's one compilation ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure))** belong to the same module. Files in the same module share `internal` access ([§13](#sec-visibility)).

<a id="sec-imports"></a>
### 2.2 Imports

```bezel
import System.Collections.Generic;
```

`import` makes the public names of the named module visible in the current file. Imports are file-scoped: an import in one file has no effect on other files in the same module. Public `extern` methods ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)) are **not** among the bare names an import makes visible: they are reachable only through a qualifier — the module name or an alias ([§32.2](#sec-scoping), stated explicitly).

**Aliases.** An import may bind a file-scoped alias: `import BankingApp.Transactions as Tx;` — thereafter `Tx.Ledger` names that module's public `Ledger`. The alias is an additional *qualifier*, not a rename: the module's publics are still visible by bare name (subject to the collision rule below), and the full dotted module name also remains usable as a qualifier (`BankingApp.Transactions.Ledger`). An alias may not collide with another alias, an imported module's name segment in qualifier position, a type declared in the file's module, or an **unambiguously imported public bare name**: [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) rule 1 resolves imported bare names before aliases with no backtracking, so a same-named alias would be unreachable in every chain-head position — the collision is an error at the alias declaration rather than a silently dead alias.

**Collisions.** When two imported modules export the same public name, the **bare** name is ambiguous: using it unqualified is a compile error citing both origins; the fix is qualification (full module name or alias). Imports never shadow one another, and import order is immaterial. A declaration in the *current module* shadows any same-named import for bare-name purposes (the import stays reachable by qualifier) — the same shadowing already specified for auto-imported names ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)).

A duplicate plain `import` of a module already imported in the same file is idempotent: the later occurrence adds nothing and is not diagnosed — an import is a visibility effect, not a declaration, so there is no name to collide (the same deduplicate-not-diagnose posture as [§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) rule 3's repeated artifact presentation). Alias declarations are the exception, because each *is* a declaration: a repeated `import A as X;` is the alias-collision error above.

**Qualified access.** `SomeModule.Name.Type` and `Alias.Type` are admissible wherever a type or static-member root is expected; resolution order for dotted names is defined in [§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order).

<a id="sec-always-available-names"></a>
### 2.3 Always-available names

The following names are visible in every source file without import.

**Language primitives.** `bool`, `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `char`, `string`. The unit type `()`. `Object`, `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`. Inline arrays `[N]T` (with size N as part of the type). `Type`. `IDisposable`, `IAsyncDisposable`. `IEnumerable<out T>`, `IEnumerator<out T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<out T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<out T>`. `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`. `IReadOnlyCollection<out T>`, `IReadOnlyList<out T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IList<T>`, `IOwningCollection<T>`, `IOwningList<T>`. `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`. `Subscription`. `CancellationToken`. `IEvent<out T>`, `IAsyncEvent<out T>`, `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, `ISharedEvent<out T>`, `SharedEventSource<T>`. The exception types listed in [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types).

`Subscription` is declared in `System` (standard library [§2.11](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-subscription)) and is auto-imported. It is the return type of event `.Subscribe()` methods and `CancellationToken.Register()` — operations that pervade idiomatic Bezel code. `CancellationToken` is also auto-imported (despite living in `System.Threading`) because it appears in the `await for ... with` desugaring ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)), in default parameter values on standard async methods, and in `IAsyncEnumerable<T>.GetAsyncEnumerator` — making it a de-facto language-level type. The six event types of stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) are auto-imported: `IEvent<T>`/`IAsyncEvent<T>`/`ISharedEvent<T>` because they are the public property types of the standard event pattern — requiring an import to subscribe to any event would defeat the design — and the source types `EventSource<T>`/`AsyncEventSource<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` because they appear in the declaration of every event in the program (the same reasoning that auto-imports `CancellationToken` despite its `System.Threading` home). Importing `System.Threading` is not required to use `Subscription`, `CancellationToken`, or any of the six event types; it is required for `CancellationTokenSource`, `Mutex`, and the other threading types.

The iteration-interface family — `IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IList<T>`, plus the owning variants `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningCollection<T>`, `IOwningList<T>` — is auto-imported because these interfaces participate in core language constructs: `IEnumerable<T>` and the async variant in the `for` and `await for` desugarings ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)); the read-only and mutating interfaces in standard-library types' inheritance clauses (`Array<T>: IList<T>`, `OwningArray<T>: IOwningList<T>`, etc.) and in pattern-frequent variable type ascriptions. The stdlib documents their full declarations in [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic); the language treats them as primitives for visibility purposes, in the same way it treats `Array<T>` and `Object` (also documented in stdlib but always visible).

**Auto-imported standard library.** `System` (for `Console`, `Math`, `Convert`, `Environment`, `DateTime`, `TimeSpan`, `Guid`, `Random`, `IComparable<T>`, `IEquatable<T>`, `IDisposable`, `IAsyncDisposable`, `ISerializer`, `IDeserializer`, `ISerializable`, `IDeserializable`, and the FFI-boundary types `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `CString`, `WString`, `RawBytes` — stdlib [§10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ffi-boundary-types), whose module home is `System`; the parenthetical is representative, not exhaustive — stdlib §2 is `System`'s full catalog, including `DateOnly`/`TimeOnly`, `BitConverter`, `Type`, `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>`, `IFormattable`, and the stdlib §2.19 static abstractions) and `System.Text` (for `StringBuilder`, `Encoding`, and `ReadOnlyStringSpan` — stdlib §3). `System.Interop` — `Ptr<T>` and the `Interop` intrinsics ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)) — is deliberately **not** auto-imported: the `import System.Interop;` line is the audit marker that a file performs foreign-memory access.

All other library modules require explicit `import`.

Only the primitive value-type keywords and their reserved PascalCase aliases (and `string`/`String`) cannot be shadowed ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)). The other always-available names — the auto-imported library types such as `Object`, `Array<T>`, `Task`, `Subscription`, and the iteration interfaces — may be shadowed by local declarations under the normal name-resolution rules.

<a id="sec-compilation-unit"></a>
### 2.4 Compilation unit

The compilation unit — a module, or an import-cycle SCC of modules ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)) — is the unit of compilation. The compiler takes all source files belonging to the compilation unit and, reading its dependencies' artifacts ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution), [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)), produces one native artifact per member module:

- An **executable** is a native binary requiring no language-runtime installation; whether its dependency artifacts are embedded in it or accompany it is the [§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) link-mode choice. An executable build requires exactly one qualifying `Main` method as defined in [§33](#sec-program-entry-point) in the root compilation, selected per [§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) and [§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution).
- A **library** is a non-executable artifact; whether it takes the form of a shared native library (`.so`, `.dylib`, `.dll`), an object embedded statically by its consumers, or both, is the [§2.8.4](#sec-program-assembly) link-mode choice. It exposes its `public` types and methods.

<a id="sec-dependency-resolution"></a>
### 2.5 Dependency resolution

Dependencies are declared through `import` statements. In the acyclic case the compiler resolves each dependency by reading the imported module's compiled artifact, which embeds the module's interface ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)).

Circular imports compile as one unit. Modules whose imports form a cycle constitute a **strongly-connected component**, and an SCC is the unit of compilation: the build supplies the sources of all SCC members to one compiler invocation, which resolves their types against each other directly (no artifacts consumed within the SCC) and still emits one artifact per member module. A build that presents only part of an SCC is an error naming the missing members. Between SCCs, resolution is artifact-based as above; the module dependency graph condensed by SCCs is processed in topological order. Circular *static-initialization* dependencies are checked per [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s two-part rule regardless of compilation grouping: the compile-time approximation rejects the cycles it can see, and the runtime re-entrancy backstop converts the rest into `TypeInitializationException` — never silent observation of partially-initialized statics.

<a id="sec-build-phases"></a>
### 2.6 Build phases

1. Parse all source files of the compilation unit (module or SCC, [§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)).
2. Resolve all type declarations across the module and its dependencies.
3. Type-check method bodies, field initializers, and expressions.
4. Generate native code; emit the artifact with embedded interface metadata.

Build-tool integration and project-file format are implementation-defined.

<a id="sec-name-resolution-order"></a>
### 2.7 Name resolution for dotted names

A dotted name `A.B` (and longer chains) can in principle read as a module-qualified type, a nested type ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)), an enum constant or named `const` ([A.8](#sec-constants-and-literals)), or a static-member access ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)). Resolution is **leftmost-first and type-wins**, with no backtracking:

1. **Resolve the leftmost segment `A` as a bare name**: local scope, then the enclosing type's accessible members **in the position given below**, then the current module's declarations, then unambiguous imported bare names (per [§2.2](#sec-imports)'s collision rule), then import **aliases**. If `A` resolves to a *type*, the rest of the chain resolves against that type (nested type, enum constant, static member — each segment in turn). If it resolves to a *value* (a local, field, or property), the chain is member access.
2. **Otherwise, match the longest dotted prefix of the chain against an imported module's full name** (or the current module's). The remainder then resolves against that module's public declarations, continuing as in rule 1. A prefix matching *no* import is an error at `A` (naming the unresolved segment, and — when a non-imported module of that name is known to the build — suggesting the missing `import`).

**Enclosing-type members.** Inside a type's bodies, the enclosing type's accessible members (inherited included; instance and static, under [§11](#sec-classes-and-interfaces)'s accessibility rules and the static-context restriction — a static body has no `this`, the premise of [§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)'s clause-typing rule and [§28](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)'s no-receiver rule for static calls) participate in rule 1's bare-name lookup at a position fixed by the name's syntactic shape, decided before any lookup. The decision, tabulated (the prose that follows is the normative statement; the table is its case analysis):

| Head shape (decided from tokens, before any lookup) | Example | Enclosing-type members rank | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chain head** — name followed by `.` (directly, or with a balanced generic-argument group: [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s scan) | `Color.Red;` `Registry<int>.M()` | **last, after aliases** | a reachable type outranks a same-named member; `property Color: Color` still lets `Color.Red` reach the choice type |
| Bare value read | `Data` | **between local scope and module declarations** | member outranks same-named top-level/imported type |
| Assignment target | `C := c;` | same | a field write is never preempted (a type cannot occupy value position) |
| Bare callee (incl. explicit method type args) | `Helper();` `Method<int>(x)` | same | a callee is not a receiver |
| Head continued by `?.` or postfix `!` | `Color?.ToString()` | same | these operators demand a nullable *value*; static access is spelled with `.` alone |
| **Warning row:** chain head resolves to a type while a same-named accessible member exists | — | — | warn, *unless* the member's declared type is the resolved type (or an instantiation of the resolved generic) — the `property Color: Color` idiom; qualify `this.` to reach the member |

A **chain head** — a name followed by `.`, either directly or with a generic-argument group between per [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s balanced-scan rule (`Color.Red`; `Registry<int>.M()`, the static-access form on a generic type) — consults members **last, after aliases**: a type reachable at the head outranks a same-named member, so `Color.Red` inside a type declaring `property Color: Color` resolves through the choice type, and `Registry<int>.M()` beside a member named `Registry` reaches the generic type's static. **Every other head is a one-segment name** and consults members **between local scope and the current module's declarations**: a member outranks a same-named top-level or imported type. One-segment shapes include a bare value read; an assignment target (`C := c;` — a field write is never preempted by a type, which cannot occupy value position); a bare callee, explicit method type arguments included (`Helper()`; `Method<int>(x)` — a callee is not a receiver, even though [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s scan commits its generic reading); and a head continued by `?.` or postfix `!`, operators that demand a nullable *value*, which no type can be (static access is spelled with `.` alone), so `property Color: Color?` … `Color?.ToString()` resolves the member. There is no C#-style dual-meaning rule (recorded decline): the winner is fixed by position, decided from tokens alone, never by whether the losing candidate could have hosted the next segment — resolution still never backtracks. A member shadowed at a chain head stays reachable by qualifying (`this.Data.W()`; the enclosing type's name for statics); a type shadowed by a member or local stays reachable via rule 2's module qualification. Because the chain-head member fallback ranks below imports, it is the one rule-1 source a later-added import or type declaration can preempt — loudly in practice, since the preempting type must itself host the accessed member — and the compiler **warns** when a chain head resolves to a type while a same-named accessible enclosing-type member exists, *unless* the member's declared type is the resolved type itself or, for a generic head, an instantiation of the resolved generic (the `property Color: Color` and `property Buffer: Buffer<int>` idioms; qualify with `this.` to reach the member). Nested types ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)) and [§19.8](#sec-inside-enum-scrutinees)'s scrutinee-driven pattern prefix-omission are not reordered by this paragraph.

Consequences worth stating: a type named `A` in scope **shadows** a module-name prefix `A.…` for chain purposes (the compiler warns when both readings exist — qualify via an alias to reach the module); two module prefixes cannot be ambiguous (module names are exact); and because resolution never backtracks, the meaning of a chain is determined by its shortest resolvable head — adding an unrelated import can make a previously-erroring chain resolve, but can never silently *change* a chain that already resolved (rule 1 outranks rule 2, and rule-1 resolutions are collision-checked) — with the one warned exception of the chain-head member fallback above.

<a id="sec-module-identity"></a>
### 2.8 Module identity, artifact interface, and program assembly

Sections [§2.1](#sec-module-declarations)–[§2.7](#sec-name-resolution-order) define a single compilation's view of modules: declarations, imports, name resolution, and the unit of compilation. This section defines everything downstream of one compilation: what makes a module *one* module across separately-compiled artifacts, what a compiled artifact must carry, who supplies the artifacts of transitive dependencies, and how a program is assembled. Terminology, consistent with [§2.4](#sec-compilation-unit)/[§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution):

- A **compilation** (**unit**) is one compiler invocation over the sources of one module, or of one import-cycle SCC ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)); it emits one artifact per member module.
- The **root compilation** is the compilation a build is currently performing: the sources presented directly, as opposed to the dependency artifacts supplied alongside them.
- A **build** (**program assembly**) presents a root compilation plus a set of dependency artifacts to produce a final artifact.
- A **program** is an executable together with the dependency artifacts assembled into its process.

<a id="sec-module-identity-and-closure"></a>
#### 2.8.1 Module identity and closure

1. **One module, one compilation, one artifact.** Every module in a program is the product of exactly one compilation. A module's membership is fixed by the source files presented to that compilation; no other source file becomes part of the module by declaring its name. An SCC compilation ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)) is one compilation producing one artifact per member module; each member module is still produced exactly once.

2. **`internal` is closed by compilation, not by name.** `internal` ([§13.1](#sec-levels)) grants access only among the source files compiled together as the declaring module ([§13.4](#sec-modules-and-internal)). Co-compilation does not widen it: within an SCC unit, each member module's internals remain invisible to the other members — the SCC is a compilation-order grouping, not an access grant.

3. **Duplicate module names are a build error.** A build whose artifact set — the root compilation plus the dependency closure ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)) — contains two **distinct** artifacts declaring the same module name, or a dependency artifact declaring a module name that the root compilation also declares, is ill-formed; the diagnostic names both origins. The intended diagnostic point is artifact-set load (metadata time); an implementation that discovers the duplication only at native linking conforms, but the metadata-time diagnostic naming both artifacts is the standard. Presenting the *same* artifact more than once (the same file, or bit-identical content — as when a build tool concatenates per-dependency closures that share a diamond base, [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)) is idempotent: duplicates are deduplicated, not diagnosed. Within one process there is exactly one artifact per module name (runtime dynamic loading is out of scope, [§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)).

4. **Self-import is a compile error.** An `import` naming the enclosing file's own module is rejected ("a module cannot import itself"). Import *cycles between distinct modules* remain legal and compile as an SCC ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)); the self-loop is not a cycle, it is a mistake.

5. **Implementation-provided modules.** The standard-library modules — the [§2.3](#sec-always-available-names) always-available set and the other explicitly-imported modules the standard-library document defines — are provided by the implementation, not by any presented artifact. They are implicit members of every build's artifact set: exempt from the presentation requirement of [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 1, resolvable by `import` with no artifact supplied. They **do** participate in duplicate-name detection: a root compilation or dependency artifact declaring a module name the implementation provides (`module System;`, `module System.Threading;`, …) is the rule-3 build error.

<a id="sec-artifact-interface"></a>
#### 2.8.2 The artifact interface is a semantic requirement

A compiled artifact embeds its module's **interface** ([§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution)). The interface's required capability is semantic; its format is implementation-defined (source text, serialized AST, IR, or any mix). It must be sufficient for a consumer, given only the artifact (and the artifacts of its dependencies, [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)), to:

1. **Type-check** every well-formed use of the module's public surface: public (and, for cross-module derivation, `protected`) types and members, with full signatures — ownership modifiers (`owned` returns and parameters, `ref`/`out`, `scoped`), default argument values, generic parameters with variance and constraints, base types and implemented interfaces, enum constants, `const` values, serialization conformances, the purity modifier ([§22.15](#sec-pure-members)), and the contract clauses and `invariant` members ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses); carried as **contract records** per the paragraph below) — and the **derived type properties** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)): carried as computed verdicts for non-generic public types, and as the structural facts needed for per-instantiation evaluation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2) for public generics. (These properties are computed from structure the public surface does not show — private fields, destructor presence — yet [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3 makes them part of the public contract, and rules dispatch on them at the consumer: sendability at domain boundaries ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)), trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), element category ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)). An interface that omitted them would force the consumer to either reject imported types at those rules or guess.)

2. **Instantiate** every public generic type and generic method at arbitrary module-external type arguments satisfying the declared constraints. An external instantiation behaves identically to a same-module instantiation of the same generic at the same arguments.

3. **Identify and describe dependencies**: the interface of every dependency type referenced from the module's public surface *or from any declaration body carried in the interface* (the definition-site clause below), keyed by program-wide type identity ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)), sufficient for the consumer to use such types without holding their declaring module's artifact *at type-check time* (the artifact itself is still required in the build's closure).

**Definition-site visibility.** Visibility inside a generic body is judged at the *definition site*: a public generic's body may reference its own module's `internal` declarations, and an external instantiation binds to them. The interface must therefore carry whatever internal machinery its exported generic bodies reach; internal declarations so carried do not become visible to the consumer's *source* (visibility is unchanged — only the instantiation may bind to them). Carried bodies may equally reach *other modules'* declarations that appear nowhere on the exporting module's public signatures; clause 3's "or from any declaration body carried in the interface" makes those modules describable and puts them in the build's closure ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 1).

Cost: definition-site visibility makes a module's `internal` declarations reached by exported generic bodies part of its **binary** interface even though they are absent from its *source* interface — changing one invalidates dependents exactly as a signature change does (a [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3 staleness error until they recompile). Under the recompile-the-world model ([§2.8.5](#sec-module-system-non-goals)'s ABI non-goal) that is a build-time inconvenience, not a compatibility trap; it is the price of monomorphizing generics across artifact boundaries.

**No restrictions beyond visibility.** Cross-module use of a public generic is not restricted relative to same-module use. An implementation unable to carry some body shape in its interface format must reject the export, or the import, with a diagnostic naming the shape; it must not alter the instantiation's semantics.

**Contract records.** For every member the interface describes, it carries the member's purity modifier ([§22.15](#sec-pure-members)) and, in declaration order, one **contract record** per contract clause; for every class it describes, one record per `invariant` member, base classes' records first ([§22.16](#sec-class-invariants)). A contract record is: the clause **kind** (`requires`, `ensures`, or `invariant`), the presence of the **`static` qualifier**, the **canonical clause text**, and the **recorded enforcement tier**. The canonical clause text is the clause expression's token sequence with comments removed and token spellings as written, except that each reference to a parameter of the member is replaced by its zero-based parameter position and each reference to a type parameter of the member or of its enclosing type declarations is replaced by its zero-based position; all other names are recorded as resolved at the declaration (module-qualified). Two clauses are **the same clause** exactly when their kinds, qualifiers, and canonical texts are identical — a parameter or type-parameter rename changes no record; any other re-spelling is a different clause. The recorded tier is the clause's [§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers) tier, which is itself a declaration fact: **proven** for a `static`-qualified clause — including the [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) nullability postconditions, which are `static ensures` clauses; each demands discharge, so an artifact that compiled has discharged it — and for a clause whose expression as written is a constant expression folding to `true` ([§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers)'s prover floor: the fold depends on the clause text and the `const` values it names, never on the member's body or call sites); **assumed** where [§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers) admits stated-unverified clauses (reserved; unpopulated in this revision); and **checked** otherwise. A per-call-site discharge of a checked clause is never recorded: it is an as-if optimization ([§22.16](#sec-contract-violation)), not a promise — the clause's recorded tier stays checked, exactly as §22.16 states — and recording it would make the interface depend on particular bodies and call sites. The matching consumption rule: downstream *static* consumption of a clause's proof — a consumer's own `static` clause discharged against it under the contract-proving feature (Appendix [D.2](#sec-extended-features)) — requires the recorded proven tier; an opportunistic per-site discharge is not consumable, being a fact no interface promises. Contract records are part of a type's description for [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3: every embedded copy must agree, and disagreement is that rule's staleness error. As everywhere in this subsection, the byte format is implementation-defined; what is normative is the *capability* (a consumer can recover each member's records) and the *equivalence* (what counts as the same clause), which rule 3's agreement check and the [§2.8.6](#sec-interface-delta-classification) classification both need. An implementation may additionally carry each clause's display text (original names) for diagnostics; display text never participates in identity. One consequence is stated rather than hidden: a clause over non-public state (legal for checked clauses, [§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers)) carries that state's names and expression text into the interface — the same disclosure the definition-site clause above already makes for internals reached by exported generic bodies, with the same recompile-the-world cost profile.

<a id="sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity"></a>
#### 2.8.3 Transitive dependencies and cross-artifact type identity

1. **The build supplies the transitive closure.** A build must present the artifacts of the root compilation's direct imports *and, transitively, of every module those artifacts' interfaces reference* — where an interface's references include those made by the declaration bodies it carries ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface), definition-site clause), not only its public signatures. A missing member of the closure is a build error naming the missing module and the artifact(s) that reference it; diagnosis quality is implementation-defined — a conforming implementation may discover the omission as late as native linking, but a metadata-time diagnostic naming the module is the intended standard. Implementation-provided modules ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) rule 5) are implicit members of every closure and are never required to be presented.

2. **Use without import; naming requires import.** A file that imports module `A` may freely **use** values of any public type reachable through `A`'s public surface — receive them (including into `var`/`using var` bindings with inferred types), call their public members, pass them as arguments, return them, and dispose them — without importing the type's declaring module. **Naming** the type in source — in a type ascription, parameter or return type, `new` expression, cast, `is`/pattern type test, `catch` clause, explicit (source-spelled) generic type argument, or extension declaration — requires importing its declaring module (which then also puts the name under [§2.2](#sec-imports)'s collision discipline). An instantiation the compiler *infers* at a transitive type (a call `Util.Process(pay)` inferring `Process<Money>`; a call returning `Box<Money>` bound with `var`) spells no name and remains **use**.

3. **Program-wide type identity.** A type is identified program-wide by its **declaring module name, its qualified type name (including any enclosing-type path, [§11.6](#sec-nested-types)), and its generic arity**; a constructed generic type is identified by its generic's identity plus the identities of its arguments. Two modules each declaring a public type of the same name declare two unrelated types (distinguished in diagnostics by module qualification). All descriptions of one type — the declaring artifact's own and every copy embedded in dependents' interfaces ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) clause 3) — denote the same type and **must agree**; a build whose closure contains disagreeing descriptions (a stale artifact) is ill-formed, with a diagnostic naming the artifacts and recommending recompilation of the dependents. A type's identity never includes its members' contract records or purity ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)): two descriptions of one type that differ in clauses, tiers, or purity are the *same type described inconsistently* — the staleness error above — not two types; identity stays nominal because it is the unit of runtime oneness (rule 4), while contracts are obligations revised across revisions of one module.

4. **Identity is one type at runtime, too.** A type — in particular a constructed generic type, whose monomorphized code may be emitted by several consumers' compilations — is one type *in the running process*: exactly **one copy of its static state** and **one recorded initialization** ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1: a type's static initializer runs exactly once process-wide; [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)), and **one runtime type identity** — `is` tests, `catch` clauses, and [§19](#sec-the-case-construct) patterns over values of the instantiation match identically regardless of which artifact produced the value or performs the test. Duplicate *code* copies of a monomorphization are permitted only where observationally indistinguishable from one copy.

**The diamond, worked.** `App` imports `Lib1` and `Lib2`; both import `Base`; `App` never imports `Base`.

```bezel
// base.bzl
module Base;

public class Money
  private _cents: long;

  public constructor(cents: long)
    _cents := cents;
  end constructor;

  public property Cents: long => _cents;

  public method Format(): string
    return $"{_cents} cents";
  end Format;
end Money;
```

```bezel
// lib1.bzl
module Lib1;
import Base;

public class Payroll
  public static method Net(hours: int, centsPerHour: int): owned Money
    return new Money(hours * centsPerHour);   // fresh owned Base.Money, crossing Lib1's surface
  end Net;
end Payroll;
```

```bezel
// lib2.bzl
module Lib2;
import Base;

public class Invoices
  public static method Total(m: Money): long   // borrows a Base.Money
    return m.Cents;
  end Total;
end Invoices;
```

```bezel
// app.bzl
module App;
import Lib1;
import Lib2;
// no `import Base;` — and none is needed for anything below

class Program
  public static method Main()
    using var pay := Payroll.Net(40, 2500);      // USE: inferred binding of a transitive type (rule 2)
    Console.WriteLine(Invoices.Total(pay));      // USE: passing the value across module surfaces
    Console.WriteLine(pay.Format());             // USE: member access
  end Main;                                      // USE: `using var` disposal of a transitive type
end Program;

// Each of the following would be NAMING, and each requires `import Base;` first:
//   var m: Money := Payroll.Net(1, 1);           — type ascription
//   using var m2 := new Money(500);              — `new`
//   if pay is Money then … end;                  — type test
//   var box := new OwningArray<Money>();         — generic type argument
```

The build compiles `Base` first, then `Lib1` and `Lib2` against `Base`'s artifact, and finally compiles `App` presenting the artifacts of `Lib1`, `Lib2`, **and `Base`** — the closure of rule 1 — even though `app.bzl` never writes `import Base;`; omitting `Base`'s artifact is the rule-1 build error naming `Base` and the artifacts that reference it. `Money` arrives in `App`'s compilation three ways — embedded in `Lib1`'s interface, embedded in `Lib2`'s, and directly from `Base`'s artifact — and all three descriptions are `(Base, Money, arity 0)`: **one type** (rule 3); `pay` flows from `Lib1`'s surface into `Lib2`'s parameter with no conversion. Had `Lib1` been compiled against an older, different `Base.Money`, the descriptions would disagree and the build fails naming the stale artifact — and supplying both an old and a new artifact for `Base` is two distinct artifacts declaring one module name, the [§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) rule 3 error. (`Money` is trivial-dispose — no destructor, no owned fields ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — so the disposal the `using var` inserts runs no user code here; the legality of the binding is the point. A `Base` type with an owned field behaves identically under rule 2 — disposal of the transitive value is still use, not naming.)

When the root compilation is an SCC of several modules, the rules of this section and [§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure) interact as follows: each member module is still produced by exactly one compilation — the same one (rule 1); co-compilation grants no `internal` access between members (rule 2); imports between members along the cycle are legal while self-import stays an error (rule 4); and a consumer importing any one member must still present every member's artifact in its closure — [§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution) already requires an SCC's artifacts to have been produced together.

<a id="sec-program-assembly"></a>
#### 2.8.4 Program assembly: artifact kind, entry point, one copy per process

1. **Artifact kind is chosen by the build request.** Whether a compilation produces an executable or a library ([§2.4](#sec-compilation-unit)) is a property of the *build request*, not of the source text; how the request is spelled is part of [§2.6](#sec-build-phases)'s implementation-defined build-tool surface. An **executable** build requires exactly one qualifying `Main` ([§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)) in the root compilation, or a `--main-class` selection among several ([§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution)); zero qualifying `Main`s is an error citing [§33.1](#sec-the-main-method)/[§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures). A **library** build has no entry point; a qualifying `Main` in a library compilation is an ordinary method. (An implementation may additionally *offer* kind inference from `Main`-presence as a tooling convenience; the normative rules above are stated for explicit kinds — chosen over inference because deleting the last `Main` from an application must be the zero-`Main` error above, never a silent flip of artifact kind.)

2. **The main module, defined.** The **main module** is the module containing the selected entry point ([§33.1](#sec-the-main-method)).

3. **Entry-point search scope is the root compilation only.** Only classes of the root compilation are searched for qualifying `Main`s; a qualifying `Main` in a dependency artifact is **inert** — it is never selected, never conflicts under [§33.5](#sec-program-entry-point-resolution), and must not perturb the consumer's build. Consequence: adding a dependency can never break, change, or steal a program's entry point. `--main-class` disambiguates *within the root compilation*; it cannot reach into a dependency.

4. **Dependency artifacts are library-kind.** Presenting an executable artifact as a dependency is a build error naming the artifact and its kind. (An executable carries a native entry symbol; admitting it as a dependency re-opens rule 3's perturbation hole from the other side, for no use case a library-kind artifact doesn't serve.)

5. **One copy per process.** How a dependency artifact joins a consuming program — statically embedded in the executable or dynamically loaded alongside it — is implementation-defined, under one normative guarantee: **a process contains exactly one copy of each module's code and, for each type — including each generic instantiation ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 4) — exactly one static state and one runtime identity**, regardless of link mode and regardless of how many compilations emitted code for the type.

6. **Static initialization across artifacts: same rules, one new obligation.** Initialization order is a property of the running program, not of the artifact graph: statics initialize lazily on first use with the runtime recording the single process-wide order ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1), and exit disposal runs in reverse of that recorded order. What the artifact dimension adds is the obligation rule 5 states: the one-copy guarantee is *not* free where monomorphized instantiations are emitted by several compilations, and [§22.12](#sec-static-members)/[§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) are well-defined across artifacts only once it holds. The *compile-time* rejection of cross-type initialization cycles ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); [§2.5](#sec-dependency-resolution): "regardless of compilation grouping") additionally requires cross-unit dependency edges the artifact interface does not yet carry; pinning that dependency relation and its interface metadata is deferred, and [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)'s interface requirement gains the corresponding clause when it lands.

<a id="sec-module-system-non-goals"></a>
#### 2.8.5 Non-goals of this section

The following are deliberately absent from this revision's module system; each absence is decided, not forgotten. Revisiting one requires new evidence — real programs hitting real walls — against the stated reason.

- **Package management, versioning, registries.** This chapter identifies modules within one build; *which* artifact provides a module is the build tool's input ([§2.6](#sec-build-phases): implementation-defined), and version arbitration is a package-manager design question for a later stage of the language's life.
- **ABI stability across recompilation.** The model is recompile-the-world: an artifact's interface is a compile-time contract for *this* build ([§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3 makes staleness an error, not a compatibility negotiation); a stable binary ABI is a separate commitment nothing yet motivates.
- **Conditional compilation (`#if`, feature flags).** One source text, one meaning: a file that means different things under different flag sets defeats spec-derived testing; platform variance belongs in the build tool selecting *which files* compile, not in files that change meaning.
- **Selective imports (`import M.{X}`).** `import` is file-scoped and [§2.2](#sec-imports)'s collision rule already keeps bare-name pollution diagnosed and fixable (qualify or alias); a selective form adds a second place where a file's name set is edited, for no capability qualification doesn't already give.
- **Re-exports (`public import`).** A module's public surface is what it declares; forwarding another module's names would break [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity)'s naming rule (naming requires importing the *declaring* module) for zero expressiveness — consumers can always import the declaring module.
- **Wildcard imports.** Nothing to add: `import M;` already makes all of `M`'s public names visible; there is no narrower form for a wildcard to generalize.

<a id="sec-interface-delta-classification"></a>
#### 2.8.6 Interface delta classification

The records of [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) make deltas between two interfaces of one module *classifiable*. This subsection fixes the classification — the vocabulary in which a change to a module's contract surface is reported. Computing and reporting it is tooling surface, but the verdicts are normative, so that no two conforming tools classify one delta differently.

**Verdicts.** An interface delta between two interfaces of one module is classified **identical**, **preserving**, **widening**, or **breaking**, in that severity order. *Preserving*: every use and every implementation conforming to the old interface remains conforming, and every fact a consumer could soundly rely on still holds (guarantees may grow). *Widening*: existing uses remain conforming; new surface exists (new members, types, overloads). *Breaking*: some conforming use, implementation, or soundly-consumed fact does not survive. The whole-artifact verdict is the maximum over all per-member and per-type deltas. Verdicts are computed per conformance level (the layered verdict below); at the Core level the classification consults only Core-consumable facts.

**Member matching.** Members of the old and new interface are matched by overload identity ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)): declaring type, name, arity, parameter types, and `ref`/`out` modifiers. Facts that never distinguish overloads — `owned`, `scoped`, contract clauses, purity, return type — are compared *within* a match; a change to a matching fact (a parameter type, a `ref`/`out` modifier) reports as removal plus addition.

**Audiences.** A delta on an **overridable slot** — a `virtual` or `abstract` member, or an interface member — is classified for both audiences, callers and implementors, and takes the **stricter** verdict: inherited clauses and required purity bind implementors through the slot ([§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance), [§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch)), so a change that is caller-preserving can still be implementor-breaking.

Contract deltas, per matched member ("slot" = overridable as above):

| Delta | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `requires` clause removed | preserving; **breaking on a slot** | A weaker precondition admits every old caller. On a slot, implementor bodies assumed the inherited clause ([§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance)) and are now reachable with arguments they excluded. |
| `requires` clause added | **breaking** | Narrows every caller, through every face of every slot ([§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance)). |
| `ensures` clause added | preserving *(slot note: binds every implementor's next checked run — behavior-revealing, not compile-breaking; a clause of the [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) `when`-family shape — detectable from the record alone — classifies under the `when`-added row below instead, whose stricter slot verdict wins per this section's audience rule)* | A strengthened postcondition; callers were promised no less. |
| `ensures` clause removed | **breaking** | Callers consumed the promise — runtime reliance at every level, proof consumption at the contract-proving level. |
| clause text changed (either kind) | **breaking** | Removal plus addition under textual identity; at least one direction breaks. |
| clause list reordered, same record set | preserving | Order changes only which violation is blamed first ([§22.16](#sec-clause-evaluation)); no conforming execution differs. |
| tier upgraded (checked → proven: `static` added and discharged) | preserving | The ratchet direction ([§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers)): strictly more guarantee, zero new obligation. |
| tier demoted (proven → checked: `static` dropped) | **layered** — below | |
| any tier → assumed (when that tier is populated) | **breaking** at every level that consumed the enforcement | Enforcement withdrawn, statement retained: a checked-to-assumed `requires` stops faulting violating callers in every mode. |
| purity added | preserving; **breaking on a slot** | More admitting contexts for callers; on a slot every override and implementation must restate `pure` ([§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch)) — a compile break. |
| purity removed | **breaking** | Pure-context callers stop compiling ([§22.15](#sec-pure-members)). |
| `invariant` added | preserving *(subclasser note as for ensures-added)* | A strengthened observable guarantee. |
| `invariant` removed or text changed | **breaking** | As ensures-removed, for observers of the class ([§22.16](#sec-class-invariants)). |

Signature and type-level deltas — the facts [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) already carries, classified so the whole-artifact verdict is meaningful:

| Delta | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| member added (including a new overload) | widening | *Recorded caveat:* an added overload can re-route existing calls under [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s ranking (adding a non-generic beside an applicable generic re-routes by the non-generic preference; the defaulted-arity tie-break keeps *optional-parameter* overloads from re-routing). Re-routed calls stay well-typed; the classification names added overloads so the audit is possible. |
| member removed, or visibility narrowed below the carried surface | **breaking** | |
| parameter or return type changed; `owned`/`scoped`/`ref`/`out` changed; `when` clause removed | **breaking** | Ownership and modifier surface is contract ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)); `when`-removed is ensures-removed ([§22.16](#sec-when-clause-unification)). `when`-*added*: preserving; **breaking on a slot** (overrides must repeat it exactly, [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)). |
| default value added to a trailing parameter | widening | New legal call shapes; existing calls unchanged ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s tie-break). |
| default value changed or removed | **breaking** | Omitting call sites change meaning, or stop compiling ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)). |
| generic constraint removed; variance added (`in`/`out` where invariant) | widening | More instantiations and assignments admitted ([§12.9](#sec-variance)). |
| generic constraint added; variance removed or flipped | **breaking** | |
| public type added | widening | Except the closed-world rows below. |
| public type removed; base class changed; implemented interface removed | **breaking** | An interface *added* to a type: widening. |
| derived-property verdict gained (sendable, trivial-dispose, hashable, C-compatible) | preserving | More admitting contexts ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)). |
| derived-property verdict lost; element category changed | **breaking** | [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3: a breaking change for clients relying on it, exactly as a signature change is. |
| enum constant or choice case added or removed; enum constant value changed | **breaking** | [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) and [§35.6](#sec-choice-exhaustiveness): coverage is by declared constants and cases — an addition turns dependents' statically-exhaustive `case` expressions partial. The new-member-is-widening intuition inverts under closed-world constructs. |
| new leaf added to a closed (`closed`-rooted) hierarchy | **breaking** | The same [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) inversion, hierarchy form — detected structurally: a new public type whose base chain reaches a carried closed root. |
| public `const` value changed | **breaking** | Consumers fold the value ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)). A `const` added: widening; removed: breaking. |
| carried generic bodies or carried internal machinery changed, contract records unchanged | preserving — **informational** | The regenerable interior: no declared contract changed. The classification's claims stop at declared contracts; it never compares the behavior of bodies. |

**Layered verdict.** A tier demotion — dropping `static` from a clause whose text is unchanged — changes no runtime semantics for any conforming execution: a proven clause never evaluates, a checked clause evaluates and passes, `requires` stays always-on in both ([§22.16](#sec-contract-tiers)); the only executions that differ are violating ones (caught at runtime instead of rejected at compile time) and a checked clause's own evaluation fault ([§22.16](#sec-clause-evaluation)). But the demotion **withdraws a static fact**, and consumption of that fact is level-gated, so the verdict is computed per conformance level. At the **Core** level a demotion is *preserving*, **except** for a clause whose proof Core machinery itself consumes — at this revision exactly the [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) nullability-postcondition family, whose demotion disables caller-side narrowing and is therefore *breaking* at Core (dependents' narrowed reads stop compiling). At the **contract-proving** level (Appendix [D.2](#sec-extended-features)) every demotion is *breaking*: a downstream `static` clause discharged against the demoted clause's recorded proof no longer discharges. A verdict at a level consults exactly the facts consumable at that level; classification requires no prover (tiers are recorded), so a Core-only toolchain reports both levels correctly, and conforming tooling reports both. The §22.4 family is detectable from the record alone — kind, qualifier, and the canonical §22.4 shape — so no dedicated carriage marker exists.

**Degradation.** An input interface that carries no contract records (an artifact of an implementation without carriage) is *contract-opaque*: classification against it runs at the signature level and is reported as such; an implementation must not treat absent records as empty record sets — that would classify the first record-carrying rebuild as a wall of clause additions. The [§2.8.3](#sec-transitive-closure-and-type-identity) rule 3 agreement check likewise treats an artifact without records as making no record claim, not as claiming an empty set.

---

<a id="sec-type-system"></a>
## 3. Type System

<a id="sec-type-kinds"></a>
### 3.1 Type kinds

Bezel types fall into these kinds:

- **Primitive value types** — `bool`, the integer types, `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `char`. ([§4](#sec-built-in-types))
- **`string`** — a reference type with content equality and runtime-managed lifetime. ([§4.6](#sec-string))
- **Records** — user-defined value types with positional or body declarations. ([§9](#sec-records))
- **Enums** — user-defined value types backed by an integer constant. ([§10](#sec-enums))
- **Choices** — user-defined value types whose values carry one of a fixed set of named cases, each with optional payloads. ([§35](#sec-choices))
- **Classes** — user-defined reference types with inheritance and disposal. ([§11](#sec-classes-and-interfaces)–[§12](#sec-inheritance-and-dispatch))
- **Interfaces** — user-defined contracts. An interface variable is a reference; its underlying value may be a class instance, a boxed record, a boxed enum, or a boxed primitive ([§3.2](#sec-reference-vs-value-types), [§8.6](#sec-boxing)). ([§11](#sec-classes-and-interfaces))
- **Arrays** — `[N]T` (inline, value-typed, fixed compile-time size) and `Array<T>` / `OwningArray<T>` (heap-allocated, class types, may be used resizably or fixed). ([§15](#sec-arrays))
- **Function types** — `(T1, ..., Tn) -> R`, reference types. ([§27](#sec-lambdas-and-function-types))
- **The unit type `()`** — exactly one value, also written `()`.

Additionally, *type aliases* ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)) may be declared at module level. An alias is not a separate kind of type; it is a naming convenience for an existing one. Identity, equality, and method dispatch all see through the alias.

Every type derives from `Object`. Primitives, records, enums, inline arrays, the unit type, and value-typed instances generally derive via boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)); classes, interfaces, `string`, heap arrays (`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`), and function types are reference types whose values are already heap-allocated and reach `Object` directly through the inheritance chain.

<a id="sec-reference-vs-value-types"></a>
### 3.2 Reference vs. value types

Every type is exactly one of two storage classes. The classification is total and disjoint.

A **value type** is copied on assignment; each variable holds an independent value. Records, enums, choices ([§35](#sec-choices)), primitives, inline arrays (`[N]T`, including `[N]T?` and `[N owned]T?`/`[N owned]T`), and the unit type are value types. (Owning inline arrays and owning-classified choices are a special sub-category — *move-only value types* — that transfer rather than copy on assignment; see [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types).)

A **reference type** is shared on assignment; multiple variables may refer to the same heap-allocated object. Classes (including heap-array classes `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>`), interfaces, `string`, and function types are reference types.

An interface-typed variable holds a reference: to a class instance directly, to a record value boxed at assignment ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)), to an enum value boxed at assignment, or to a primitive value boxed at assignment. Interfaces play two roles simultaneously — as **contracts** (specifying the operations a conforming type must provide) and as **reference types** (variables of interface type are heap references with the standard reference semantics). The roles compose rather than conflict: the contract aspect determines which types satisfy a given interface; the reference-type aspect determines what an interface-typed variable holds and how it is shared.

The classification has direct consequences in three places:

- **Assignment.** Value-typed `:=` copies; reference-typed `:=` aliases.
- **Ownership and disposal.** Only class types and class-implementing interface variables carry a disposal obligation ([§28](#sec-resource-management)); value types and runtime-managed reference types ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) do not.
- **Generic constraints.** `where T: value` admits value types only; `where T: class` admits non-nullable reference types of any kind. See [§14.2](#sec-constraints).

<a id="sec-nullability"></a>
### 3.3 Nullability

A reference type is non-nullable by default. A trailing `?` produces its nullable form. Value types may also be wrapped in `?` to produce an optional. See [§7](#sec-nullability-2).

<a id="sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types"></a>
### 3.4 Keyword aliases for built-in types

Each primitive keyword aliases a standard library type. `string`, though a reference type rather than a primitive value type ([§3.1](#sec-type-kinds), [§3.2](#sec-reference-vs-value-types)), is included in this table because its lowercase keyword follows the same aliasing convention. The two forms are interchangeable:

| Keyword | Standard library name |
|---|---|
| `bool` | `System.Boolean` |
| `byte` | `System.Byte` |
| `sbyte` | `System.SByte` |
| `short` | `System.Int16` |
| `ushort` | `System.UInt16` |
| `int` | `System.Int32` |
| `uint` | `System.UInt32` |
| `long` | `System.Int64` |
| `ulong` | `System.UInt64` |
| `float` | `System.Float` |
| `double` | `System.Double` |
| `decimal` | `System.Decimal` |
| `char` | `System.Char` |
| `string` | `System.String` |

Static members of the standard library type are accessible through either form: `int.Parse`, `int.MaxValue`, `double.IsNaN`, `string.IsNullOrEmpty`.

`Object` has no lowercase keyword alias. Keyword aliases are reserved for primitive value types; `Object` is a class and is referenced as `Object` unconditionally — there is no `object` spelling.

The PascalCase standard-library names in the table above (`Boolean`, `Byte`, `SByte`, `Int16`, `UInt16`, `Int32`, `UInt32`, `Int64`, `UInt64`, `Float`, `Double`, `Decimal`, `Char`, `String`) are **reserved type names**: a program may not declare a user type (class, record, enum, interface, or type alias) whose name is one of them. Each names a compiler-known primitive (or `string`) through its lowercase keyword alias, and the dual-form rule above makes the PascalCase form interchangeable with the keyword everywhere a type is named — except the enum underlying-type position, which requires the keyword form ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type), Appendix A.3 EnumInheritance); allowing a user type to take one of these names would let a declaration silently shadow the primitive at some use sites and not others, producing a different value than the author intended. Declaring such a type is a compile error directing the author to choose a different name. (This does not reserve other standard-library type names — only the PascalCase aliases of the primitive value types and `String`; an ordinary library type such as `Array` or `Stream` may still be shadowed by a user type under the normal name-resolution rules.)

<a id="sec-operators-on-primitive-types"></a>
### 3.5 Operators on primitive types

The arithmetic, comparison, bitwise, and shift operators on primitive numeric types are **compiler intrinsics**. They are not declared as `operator` methods on the primitives' record-syntax standard-library declarations (`Int32`, `Double`, `Boolean`, etc.); the compiler translates them directly to machine-level operations rather than calling user-visible methods.

The intrinsic operators are:

- **Arithmetic** on `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, unary `-`, and unary `+` (unary `+` is the identity, yielding its operand's value at its operand's type, defined exactly where a numeric operand is; invalid on `bool`, `char`, and `string`). Plus `mod` on integer types and `decimal` ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)).
- **Equality** on every primitive (including `bool`, `char`, `string`): `=`, `<>`. **Ordering** (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) on every primitive **except `bool`**: the ordering operators on `bool` operands are a compile error (the stdlib `Boolean` wrapper deliberately declares no `IComparable`, and an ordering would be truthiness-shaped, [§4.1](#sec-bool); to order by a flag, convert explicitly — `int(b)`, [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)).
- **Bitwise** on `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~` (unary). Not valid on `bool`, `char`, or floating-point types ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)). Boolean operations use `and`/`or`/`not` (next bullet), which short-circuit and have boolean-only semantics.
- **Shift** on the integer types: `<<`, `>>`.
- **Logical** on `bool`: `and`, `or`, `not` (with short-circuit evaluation, [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)).

Operand-type combinations follow the numeric-promotion rules in [§6](#sec-arithmetic-and-overflow) — for example, `int + long` promotes the `int` to `long` and uses the `long + long` intrinsic. The set of admitted combinations is fixed; primitives do not declare cross-type `operator +` methods that user code could inspect.

By contrast, operators declared on user-defined record and class types are regular `operator` method declarations subject to [§25](#sec-operator-overloading)'s overload-declaration rules. `String.operator +` (concatenation) is one such regular declaration: the compiler may constant-fold it for string-literal operands, but the method is real and could in principle have been written by user code. The same applies to user-defined operator overloads on records and classes.

`string` straddles the two categories: it is a reference type (and not listed among the primitive value types in [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)), but its comparison operators (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) are intrinsics, not declared overloads. Two reasons: classes — which `string` is — cannot overload `=` and `<>` per [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) (they are reserved for reference equality on most classes; `string` overrides this with content equality through compiler intrinsics); and the ordering operators on `string` are defined uniformly as ordinal lexicographic comparison ([§4.6](#sec-string)), which the compiler implements directly rather than dispatching to a method. The asymmetry — `string`'s `+` is a declared overload while its `=` is intrinsic — reflects this rule about classes and equality, not a categorical statement that `string` is "primitive."

This split — intrinsics for primitive numeric operators and class-typed equality, declared methods for user-defined and string-concatenation operators — keeps the std lib's record-syntax primitive declarations short (they exist mainly to host static methods like `Parse` and `MaxValue`, not to enumerate every operator) while preserving the regular operator-overload mechanism for user types.

<a id="sec-derived-type-properties"></a>
### 3.6 Derived type properties

Several rules in this specification classify types by a predicate computed from the type's *structure* — its declaration and, for a generic type, its type arguments — rather than by anything the programmer declares. Such a predicate is a **derived type property**. This section defines the mechanism once; the individual properties are defined where their subject matter lives and obey the common rules below.

The derived type properties of this revision:

| Property | Defined in | Classifies |
|---|---|---|
| **trivial-dispose** | [§28](#sec-resource-management) intro, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) | classes whose disposal provably runs no user code and releases only memory: no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no owning-inline-array fields, trivial-dispose base |
| **borrow-bearing** | [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) | records (and inline arrays, [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays); choices, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) carrying at least one borrow of a non-runtime-managed reference type |
| **choice classification** | [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) | every choice type, as value-like, borrow-bearing, or owning — the classification on which a choice's copyability, lifetime tracking, and disposal obligation depend |
| **auto-hashable** (formerly *auto-equality-bearing*) | [§9.2](#sec-body-records) | records and value-like choices for which `=`, `GetHashCode`, and `ToString` are synthesized ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)); membership is computed after `equality skip` exclusions ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) |
| **serialization-eligible** | [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) | records, enums, and value-like choices for which `Serialize`/`Deserialize` are synthesized ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)) |
| **hashable** (formerly *equality-bearing*) | [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode), [§9.2](#sec-body-records) | types usable where consistent `Equals`/`GetHashCode` are required (hash-container keys/elements): every type except (a) a record that is neither auto-hashable nor declares user equality, and (b) a choice that is not value-like auto-hashable ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) — owning and borrow-bearing choices are not hashable); *declaring user equality* means (`operator =`/`<>` with `Equals(T)`/`GetHashCode` per the [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) co-declaration rule) |
| **element category** | [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership), stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) | every type, as collection-element: value, runtime-managed reference, class/interface, or move-only value — the classification on which collection and buffer slot semantics dispatch |
| **sendable** | [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) | types whose values may cross an execution-domain boundary (spawn arguments and results, channel elements) |
| **C-compatible** | [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) | records passable across the FFI boundary by address: fixed field order, FFI-pointee field types, target-C-ABI layout |

Common rules, normative for every derived type property:

1. **Computed, never declared.** A derived type property cannot be asserted, opted into, or waived by annotation. It follows from structure; the only way to change it is to change the structure.
2. **Per-instantiation evaluation for generics.** For a generic type or member, the property is evaluated at each instantiation, after substituting the type arguments. A generic body type-checks under the weakest assumption its constraints establish; an instantiation that violates a property-dependent requirement is rejected *at the instantiation site*, with a diagnostic naming the property, the offending type argument, and the structural reason ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s generic-owned-field check and the owning-collection element restriction of [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument) follow this pattern).
3. **Part of the public contract.** A declaration change that flips a derived type property of a public type — adding a destructor flips trivial-dispose; adding a computed property in the wrong form flips auto-hashable; adding or removing `equality skip` on a member ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) flips comparison results and hash values for clients and can flip auto-hashable/hashable — is a breaking change for clients relying on it, exactly as a signature change is (the artifact interface carries the clause as it carries `serialized` clauses, [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)). Library documentation should state the properties a type's clients are expected to rely on.
4. **Named in diagnostics.** A diagnostic produced by a property-dependent rule names the property in the words of the table above, so the reader can find the defining section.

Dispatch of *behavior* (not merely admissibility) on a derived type property — as the element category does for buffer and collection slot semantics ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership), stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) — is reserved to compiler-known standard-library types; it is not a user-available mechanism in this revision; two scoped exceptions are recorded. The **C-compatible** classification ([§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records)) — whose consequence is a static representation guarantee, compile-time-visible and constant, never behavior dispatch — was ratified with the FFI's structured-data design (rationale §16.5). The **choice classification** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) does flip per-instantiation behavior (copy vs. move on assignment, disposal vs. none at scope end), and is admitted because the dispatch is performed by the language on a language construct — derived from structure, identical for every user, with no user-programmable hook — the recorded generalization path of the compiler-known specializations (rationale §5.15); users still cannot write code conditioned on a type parameter's category.

New rules added to this specification that need a structural classification of types must define it as a derived type property under the rules of this section, rather than introducing a parallel mechanism.

---

<a id="sec-built-in-types"></a>
## 4. Built-in Types

<a id="sec-bool"></a>
### 4.1 `bool`

Two values: `true` and `false`. No implicit conversion to or from any other type. Conditions of `if`, `while`, and the `when` construct ([§19.1](#sec-forms)), as well as a `case`/`catch` arm's `when` guard, require `bool`.

<a id="sec-integer-types"></a>
### 4.2 Integer types

| Type | Width | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `byte` | 8, unsigned | 0 to 255 |
| `sbyte` | 8, signed | −128 to 127 |
| `short` | 16, signed | −32 768 to 32 767 |
| `ushort` | 16, unsigned | 0 to 65 535 |
| `int` | 32, signed | −2 147 483 648 to 2 147 483 647 |
| `uint` | 32, unsigned | 0 to 4 294 967 295 |
| `long` | 64, signed | −2⁶³ to 2⁶³ − 1 |
| `ulong` | 64, unsigned | 0 to 2⁶⁴ − 1 |

An integer literal without a suffix has type `int` if it fits in `int`'s range; otherwise the literal requires a suffix or a typed context (below). Suffixes are case-insensitive: `L` (long), `U` (uint), `UL` or `LU` (ulong — both orderings accepted). A **suffixed** integer literal whose value does not fit the suffix's type is a **compile error** (`5000000000U` exceeds `uint`'s range — write `5000000000UL`), except as the boundary carve-out below admits: literal formation is range-checked, uniformly with the typed-context rule's check against a declared target.

**Boundary carve-out.** The decimal literal of magnitude 2³¹ (unsuffixed) or 2⁶³ (`L`-suffixed) is admitted **only** as the immediate operand of unary `-`, denoting `int.MinValue` / `long.MinValue` respectively (`-2147483648`, `-9223372036854775808L`); anywhere else those magnitudes remain errors. Without this carve-out the most negative values would be unwritable as literals (the magnitude alone overflows before the `-` applies).

**Typed-context widening.** In a context whose target integer type is declared — a typed variable declaration (`var x: long := 3_000_000_000;`), a typed field initializer, a parameter with a declared integer type, an **assignment target** whose declared type is an integer type (`x := 3_000_000_000;` for `x: long`), or a **`return`** in a method with a declared integer return type — an unsuffixed integer literal (decimal, hexadecimal, or binary spelling alike) that exceeds `int`'s range but fits the declared target is admitted at the target type. The suffix discipline's purpose (no *accidental* width) is preserved: the wider type is taken only from a declared target, and the value is range-checked against it. In an **untyped** context (`var x := 3_000_000_000;`) the literal remains a compile error directing to a suffix.

<a id="sec-floating-point-types"></a>
### 4.3 Floating-point types

| Type | Width | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `float` | 32 | IEEE 754 single-precision |
| `double` | 64 | IEEE 754 double-precision |

A floating-point literal (one with a decimal point or exponent) has type `double` by default. The `f` suffix produces `float`. IEEE 754 values `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` are valid; floating-point division by zero produces one of these rather than raising an exception.
