A floating-point literal denotes the nearest representable value of its type; a literal whose magnitude exceeds its type's largest finite value (`1e999`, or `1e40f` against `float`) is a **compile error** — literal formation is range-checked like the integer literals of [§4.2](#sec-integer-types), and never rounds to `±Infinity` ([§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic)'s overflow-to-infinity governs arithmetic operations, not literals; spell an infinity explicitly via `double.PositiveInfinity`). The same rule bounds `decimal` literals ([§4.4](#sec-decimal)) against `decimal`'s range.

<a id="sec-equality-semantics-for-floating-point-types"></a>
### 4.3.1 Equality semantics for floating-point types

The equality operators `=` and `<>` ([§17.3](#sec-the-=-and-operators)) follow reflexive-equality semantics rather than IEEE 754:

- `NaN = NaN` is **true**. Any non-NaN value compared with NaN by `=` is **false**.
- `-0.0 = +0.0` is **true**.
- For all other pairs, `=` agrees with IEEE 754 equality.

The relational operators `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` follow IEEE 754: any comparison involving `NaN` is false, including `NaN < NaN`, `NaN > NaN`, `NaN <= NaN`, and `NaN >= NaN`.

The asymmetry is deliberate. Equality is the operation used by hash tables, sets, and `case` patterns; programmers expect a value to be equal to itself, and an irreflexive `=` makes `Set<double>` and `Dictionary<double, V>` misbehave when NaN is inserted. The relational operators retain IEEE semantics so numeric algorithms continue to work as published.

For strict IEEE comparison (where `NaN` is unequal to itself), use `Double.IeeeEquals(a, b)` and `Float.IeeeEquals(a, b)` from the standard library. For bitwise comparison (which distinguishes the bit patterns of `+0.0` and `-0.0` and of distinct NaN payloads), use `Double.BitwiseEquals`/`Float.BitwiseEquals`.

`decimal` has no `Infinity`, `NaN`, or signed zero, so the question does not arise: `=` on `decimal` is straightforward value equality.

<a id="sec-decimal"></a>
### 4.4 `decimal`

High-precision decimal floating-point. 28–29 significant decimal digits. Exact representation of finite decimal fractions. The `m` suffix produces a `decimal` literal: `1.50m`. Division by zero raises `DivideByZeroException`. `decimal` has no `Infinity` or `NaN`.

<a id="sec-char"></a>
### 4.5 `char`

A single Unicode scalar value, 32 bits wide. Surrogate code points (U+D800 to U+DFFF) are not valid `char` values.

Character literals: `'a'`, `'\n'`, `'\u0041'`, `'\U0001F600'`. Character values compare by code-point value: `'A' < 'B'`.

<a id="sec-string"></a>
### 4.6 `string`

An immutable sequence of `char` (Unicode scalar values). A reference type with content-based equality. `string` implements `IEnumerable<char>`, so strings may be iterated with `for`:

```bezel
for var c in "hello" do Console.WriteLine(c); end;
```

Operations:

- `s.Length` returns the number of code points in `s`. O(1).
- `s[i]` returns the `char` at code-point position `i`, zero-indexed. O(1). Out-of-range raises `IndexOutOfRangeException`.
- `s[r]` for a `Range<int>` value `r` returns the substring spanning `r`. O(k) for a result of length `k`. Endpoints follow the standard rules for `Range<int>` over `s`'s indices: a closed `s[a..b]` includes both ends, a half-open `s[a..<b]` excludes the upper, and the open-ended forms (`s[..b]`, `s[a..]`, `s[..]`) extend to the start or end of the string. Out-of-range endpoints raise `IndexOutOfRangeException`; an empty range produces the empty string. The result is a fresh `string`; mutating one does not affect the other (strings are immutable, so this is observably true regardless of representation).
- `s = t` and `s <> t` compare by code-point sequence. O(min(|s|, |t|)).
- `s < t`, `s > t`, `s <= t`, `s >= t` perform ordinal lexicographic comparison of the code-point sequence. Locale-aware comparison is provided by standard library methods. Ordering requires **non-nullable** operands: an operand of static type `string?` is a compile error — narrow first ([§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)) — the same use-requires-narrowing discipline as every other operation on a nullable reference; equality stays null-safe per [§8.4](#sec-=-and), and [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators)'s relational lifting is a nullable-*value*-type rule that does not extend here.
- `s + t` concatenates two strings. The compiler does not implicitly convert other types to `string`; use interpolation or `.ToString()`.
- `c in s` tests whether the character `c` appears in `s` (equivalent to `s.Contains(c)`, [§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)).

The user-visible model is "a sequence of code points indexed in O(1)." The internal representation is implementation-defined: an implementation is expected to choose a per-string storage width — typically 1, 2, or 4 bytes per code point, selected at construction based on the largest code point in the value — to keep the common case (predominantly-ASCII text) compact while preserving O(1) indexing for every string. The choice of width is invisible at the language level; programs observe only the `char` sequence and its length.

A pure-ASCII string (every code point in U+0000–U+007F) is identical in memory layout to a UTF-8 byte sequence. Implementations expose this through the runtime predicate `s.IsAscii: bool` (standard library [§9.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-string)). Byte access to a string's contents goes through `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes` (standard library [§3.2](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-encoding)) in one of two forms: `GetBytes(s)` produces a fresh owned `Array<byte>` — `O(n)` and always correct — and the span-destination form `GetBytes(s, destination: Span<byte>)`, paired with `GetByteCount(s)`, encodes into a caller-reused buffer — the allocation-conscious path for repeated encoding: zero per-call allocation, for every string, not only ASCII ones. (`ReadOnlyAsciiByteSpan` is retired, stdlib §3.4.)

`string` is **runtime-managed**: its memory is reclaimed automatically. `Dispose()` on a string is a no-op. String fields cannot be marked `owned`. See [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types).

Whether the runtime interns strings (shares storage for identical string values) is implementation-defined. String literals appearing in source code may be interned at compile time. The `=` operator on strings always performs content comparison ([§4.6](#sec-string) above); implementations may short-circuit via reference equality when both operands refer to the same object, but this optimization is invisible to programs.

<a id="sec-the-unit-type"></a>
### 4.7 The unit type

`()` is the type with exactly one value, also written `()`. It is the return type of methods declared without an explicit return type.

Wrapping the unit type with `?` (yielding `()?`) is permitted by the grammar and produces an optional with two values, `null` and `()`. It is rarely useful; the natural representation of "presence or absence" for a procedure-shaped result is `bool`.

The unit type is a value type and can in principle be boxed via the `Object` derivation chain ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — `var o: Object := ();` is grammatically valid and produces a boxed `()`. The result is rarely meaningful; treat the unit value as a sentinel that you don't store in `Object`-typed variables. The interface-substitution description in [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds) omits boxed unit for the same reason.

<a id="sec-ffi-only-primitive-types"></a>
### 4.8 FFI-only primitive types

The standard library defines `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `CString`, `WString`, and `RawBytes` for use at the FFI boundary. `IntPtr` and `UIntPtr` are compiler intrinsics. The `CString`, `WString`, and `RawBytes` APIs are documented in standard library [§10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ffi-boundary-types). See [§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface) for FFI-side usage. These types live in the auto-imported `System` module ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)). The typed foreign-memory family — `Ptr<T>` and the `Interop` intrinsics — lives in the explicitly-imported `System.Interop` module (stdlib [§10.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-ptr)–[§10.6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-interop-interop); language rules in [§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)).

---

<a id="sec-type-conversions"></a>
## 5. Type Conversions

<a id="sec-implicit-conversions"></a>
### 5.1 Implicit conversions

A value of one type implicitly converts to another when no programmer-visible information is lost — or, for the floating-point cases noted below, when the operation is universally safe enough that explicit casts would create unjustified noise.

| From | Implicitly converts to |
|---|---|
| `sbyte` | `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `byte` | `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `short` | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `ushort` | `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `int` | `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `uint` | `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `long` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `ulong` | `float`, `double`, `decimal` |
| `float` | `double` |
| `char` | `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal` |

Implicit conversions to `float` from integers wider than 24 bits, and to `double` from integers wider than 53 bits, may lose precision but never overflow.

The following are **never implicit**:

- Between signed and unsigned types of the same or narrower width (e.g. `int → uint`, `uint → int`, `short → ushort`). Widening from unsigned to a strictly larger signed type (e.g. `byte → short`, `ushort → int`) is permitted because no value is lost. This bullet governs **non-constant** expressions; an integer compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) converts by value under constant narrowing (below), which may cross signedness — `var b: byte := 50;` is exactly such a conversion.
- Between `decimal` and binary floats (`float`, `double`).
- Between an enum and its underlying integer.
- Between integers and `bool`.

**Constant narrowing.** An expression of integer type that is a **compile-time constant** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) implicitly converts to any integer type whose range contains its value: `var b: byte := 50;`, `Set(level: byte)` called as `Set(3)`, and enum constants of the underlying type ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) are all well-typed by this rule. The rule is **value-based, not type-based**: the source may be a compile-time constant of **any** integer type — not only `int` — and the target any integer type whose range contains the value, **across signedness** (`const N: long := 8; var b: byte := N;` is well-typed; a `uint`-typed constant `7` is admissible where `int` is expected); for non-constant expressions the conversion table and the never-implicit list above govern unchanged. A constant whose value does not fit the target's range is a **compile error** at the conversion site — never a silent truncation. The rule applies to constants only; a run-time `int` value still requires the explicit `byte(x)` narrowing of [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions). Constant narrowing applies at **every** position where this section's implicit conversions apply — there is no position carve-out: initializers, assignments, call arguments (`Set(3)`), returns, record positional arguments, collection-literal elements ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), and default arguments — and it participates in overload-resolution applicability ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)) and in the nullable lifting below.

**Nullable conversions.** For any type `T`, `T` implicitly converts to `T?`: for a reference type, the same reference viewed as nullable ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)); for a value type, the present-value wrapping ([§7.2](#sec-nullable-value-types)). Each implicit conversion of this section also **lifts** to the nullable forms: `S?` implicitly converts to `T?` whenever `S` implicitly converts to `T` — a present value converts by the underlying conversion, `null` converts to `null` (`int?` → `long?`); constant narrowing (above) participates for a present constant value. The two rules compose through at most one `?` on each side ([§7.10](#sec-generics-and-nullability): `?` is idempotent): `S` converts to `T?` via `S → T → T?`, so an `int` is admissible where a `long?` is expected.

<a id="sec-reference-conversions"></a>
**Reference conversions.** The
following conversions are implicit, and the term *implicit conversion*
throughout this document — including every citation of "the §5.1
conversions" — includes them:

- **identity**: every type converts to itself;
- **class to base class**, transitively, up to `Object`;
- **any type to `Object`**: reference types (classes including the heap
  arrays, interfaces, `string`, function types) directly; value types
  (primitives, records, enums, non-owning inline arrays, the unit type) by
  boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — move-only owning inline arrays excluded,
  since they cannot be boxed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing));
- **a type to an interface it implements or conforms to**: classes by
  declaration or inheritance ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration), including
  the compiler-generated `IDisposable`, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract));
  records and enums by declaration ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance),
  [§10.5](#sec-restrictions)), boxing; primitives by the compiler-provided
  conformances ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)), boxing;
- **interface to extended interface**, directly or transitively;
- **a type parameter to an interface or class its constraints guarantee
  conformance to** ([§14.2](#sec-constraints) — a type-bound constraint
  `where T: IFoo`/`where T: SomeClass`, directly or through a `where T: U`
  chain): inside the generic body a `T`-typed value converts to the bound;
  the conversion is realized at instantiation by the substituted type's own
  conversion of this section, boxing where the substitution is a value type;
- the **variance-induced conversions** of [§12.9](#sec-variance):
  `I<S…> → I<T…>` per the declared `in`/`out` markers, for reference-typed
  arguments only.

(Function-typed *values* additionally convert under the identity-preserving
variance rule of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability), and
method-reference *formation* may bridge any conversion of this section by
synthesizing an adapter, [§27.6](#sec-method-references) — both stated there.)

A reference conversion of a reference-typed value is representation-preserving
— the same reference viewed at a wider static type; the boxing rows allocate
the box but preserve the value ([§8.6](#sec-boxing) — subject to §8.6's
borrow-lifetime constraints for borrow-bearing records and reference-element
inline arrays). The **ownership state of the source expression carries
through unchanged**: upcasting an owned value yields an owned value of the
wider type (the usual transfer rules apply at the receiving position,
[§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)), and upcasting a borrow yields a borrow
with the same source — a reference conversion never transfers, discharges, or
creates a disposal obligation. The nullable lifting above composes: `Dog?`
converts to `Animal?` (a present reference by the underlying conversion,
`null` to `null`). Constant narrowing is unrelated to this subsection. For
overload resolution, reference conversions rank **co-equal** with the other
implicit conversions ([§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)): given
`M(a: Animal)` and `M(o: Object)`, the call `M(dog)` is ambiguous — upcast
explicitly. Bezel deliberately does not adopt C#'s better-conversion-target
refinement; one ranking rule ("exact beats converting") stays the whole
ranking story.

<a id="sec-explicit-conversions"></a>
### 5.2 Explicit conversions

Explicit conversion uses function-call syntax: the target type's name applied to the source value.

```bezel
var y: short := short(x);
var i: int := int(d);             // truncates toward zero
var c: char := char(n);           // n must be a valid code point
var f: double := double(m);       // decimal to double
```

Integer narrowing raises `OverflowException` if the value does not fit. Floating-point to integer truncates toward zero; `NaN`, `±Infinity`, and out-of-range values raise `OverflowException`. Integer to floating-point never overflows; precision may be lost.

**`bool` to integer.** An explicit conversion from `bool` to any integer type is admitted: `int(b)` yields `0` for `false` and `1` for `true` (total, never fails). The idiom turns a comparison into a number — `return int(r = null);`, branchless counting `sum := sum + int(x > 0);`. The directions are deliberately **asymmetric**: `bool(n)` remains an error in both the implicit and explicit forms ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) — a numeric-to-`bool` reading is partial and truthiness-shaped (which value is `true`? what of `2`?), exactly the ambiguity the no-truthiness rule ([§4.1](#sec-bool), rationale §17.1) exists to exclude; write the comparison (`n <> 0`) instead. A `bool` source likewise does not convert to `float`/`double`/`decimal` (no blessed numeric reading) or `char` (a code point, not a number).

A conversion between a signed and an unsigned integer type of the *same width* (`int` ↔ `uint`, `long` ↔ `ulong`, `short` ↔ `ushort`, `byte` ↔ `sbyte`) is likewise a checked narrowing: it raises `OverflowException` when the value is not representable in the destination type — a negative value cast to an unsigned type, or an unsigned value greater than the destination type's signed maximum. Such a cast is a *value* conversion, not a reinterpretation of bits: it preserves the numeric value or fails. To view the bit pattern of a same-width integer under the other signedness *without* a range check — reading a `uint` as the `int` with the identical representation — use [`BitConverter.Reinterpret<T>`](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-bitconverter), the standard library's bit-reinterpretation surface ([stdlib §2.12](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-bitconverter)).

Casting an integer to `char` requires the integer to fall in U+0000–U+10FFFF excluding the surrogate range; otherwise `OverflowException`.

**Floating-point, `decimal`, and `char` conversion semantics.** `double(m)` and `float(m)` for `decimal` `m` round to the nearest representable binary value and never fail (`float`'s and `double`'s finite ranges exceed `decimal`'s). `decimal(x)` for binary-float `x` yields the nearest representable `decimal` value; `NaN`, `±Infinity`, and magnitudes outside `decimal`'s range raise `OverflowException` (mirroring float-to-integer above — `decimal` has no non-finite values, [§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic)). `float(d)` for `double` `d` rounds to the nearest `float`; a magnitude beyond `float`'s finite range yields `±Infinity` and never raises — floating-point narrowing follows floating-point arithmetic's own overflow behavior ([§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic): overflow produces `±Infinity`), exactly as integer narrowing's `OverflowException` follows checked integer arithmetic ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)); `NaN` converts to `NaN`. The throw-vs-saturate split is therefore principled per target family, not an asymmetry. `I(c)` for `char` `c` and any integer type `I` converts the code-point value under the integer rules: the widening directions of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) always succeed, and narrower targets (`byte(c)`, `sbyte(c)`, `short(c)`) are checked narrowings raising `OverflowException` when the code point does not fit.

<a id="sec-nullable-casts"></a>
### 5.3 Nullable casts

```bezel
var y: long? := long?(x);             // nullable to nullable; null stays null
var m: int := int(n);                 // raises NullReferenceException if n is null
```

Casting a nullable to its non-nullable form requires the value to be non-null at runtime. The safer forms are `n!` (assert non-null then cast, [§7.8](#sec-null-forgiving)) and `n ?? default` (substitute a default).

**The general rule.** For a target type `T`, the nullable cast form `T?(x)` is admitted exactly when the corresponding non-nullable conversion `T(v)` is admitted from the non-nullable form of `x`'s type ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions), [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)). A `null` operand yields `null`; a present value `v` converts by `T(v)` under that conversion's own semantics, including its runtime checks (`OverflowException` on a non-fitting present value — for an enum target, [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)'s declared-constant check included — and so on). The non-nullable form `T(x)` applied to a nullable operand first requires the value to be present — `null` raises `NullReferenceException`, as above — and then converts identically.

<a id="sec-enum-casts"></a>
### 5.4 Enum casts

Enums require explicit casts to and from their underlying integer type:

```bezel
var n: int := int(p);                 // enum to int
var p: Priority := Priority(1);       // int to enum
```

<a id="sec-out-of-range-integer-to-enum-casts"></a>
An integer-to-enum cast `E(n)` is **checked against the declared constants**: it succeeds exactly when `n` equals the underlying value of some declared constant of `E`, and yields that value. When `n` is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) equal to no declared constant, the cast is a **compile error at the cast site** — the same posture as [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant-narrowing range error. When `n` is not a constant, a value equal to no declared constant raises `OverflowException` at runtime, the diagnostic naming the enum type and the value. In-range-vs-out-of-range is not a user-visible distinction: an `n` outside the underlying type's range is, a fortiori, equal to no declared constant, so the single rule subsumes the former range check — the same compile error for constants, the same `OverflowException` at runtime. **There is no value of an enum type that is not equal to a declared constant.** (Under duplicate constant values, [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values), the declared-value set is the set of distinct values: `E(1)` where `Legacy := 1, Current := 1` yields that one value.)

The checked cast is the assert-shaped tier — an undeclared value is a bug at its call sites. Boundary code for which an undeclared value is an expected input branches instead of catching: every enum carries the compiler-provided static member `E.FromUnderlyingOrNull(value: U): E?` ([§10.4](#sec-methods-properties-static-members)), which returns `null` where the cast would fault.

<a id="sec-non-int-underlying-types"></a>
#### Non-`int` underlying types

`int(p)` is the conventional spelling for "convert an enum value to its underlying integer," but the cast is only well-typed when the enum's underlying type is `int`. For an enum whose underlying type is `short`, `long`, or another integer type, the natural form names the underlying type — `short(p)`, `long(p)`, etc. The cast `int(p)` on a non-`int`-backed enum is treated as a two-step conversion: enum-to-underlying followed by integer-to-`int` widening (or narrowing, with overflow checks per [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)). For `byte`-backed `Priority`, `int(p)` is `int(byte(p))`, which always succeeds because `byte` widens to `int`. For `long`-backed `HttpStatus`, `int(s)` is `int(long(s))`, which raises `OverflowException` if the value exceeds `int.MaxValue` or is below `int.MinValue`. The general rule: name the underlying type for round-trip safety, and use `int(...)` only when the underlying type is `int` or fits in `int` without loss.

---

<a id="sec-arithmetic-and-overflow"></a>
## 6. Arithmetic and Overflow

<a id="sec-integer-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.1 Integer arithmetic

Operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, unary `-`, `++`, and `--` on integer types are checked for overflow. An operation whose mathematical result is not representable in the result type raises `OverflowException`.

```bezel
var a: int := 2_000_000_000;
var b: int := 2_000_000_000;
var c := a + b;                       // OverflowException
```

`++` and `--` are postfix-only and statement-only; they do not produce a value. See [§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators).

Division `/` between two integers truncates toward zero. `mod` follows the dividend's sign:

```bezel
var q := -7 / 3;                      // -2
var r := -7 mod 3;                    // -1
```

Division and `mod` raise `DivideByZeroException` when the right operand is zero.

`mod` is defined on integer types and on `decimal` (where it follows the same dividend-sign rule and raises `DivideByZeroException` when the divisor is zero). It is **not** defined on `float` or `double`; an expression of the form `x mod y` where either operand has a binary floating-point type is a compile error. The reason is that `mod` carries no floating-point semantics in this spec — the natural choice (IEEE 754 remainder, or C `fmod`) is a deliberate decision rather than a syntactic afterthought, and naming it explicitly avoids the ambiguity. The standard library exposes `Math.Fmod(x: double, y: double): double` for the C-compatible same-sign-as-dividend remainder, and `Math.IEEERemainder(x: double, y: double): double` for the IEEE 754 nearest-even form.

<a id="sec-mixed-type-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.2 Mixed-type arithmetic

When operands have different types, the smaller-range operand is implicitly promoted to the larger type using [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions). The result has the larger type. If no implicit conversion exists between the operand types (e.g. `double` and `decimal`), the operation is a compile error and an explicit cast is required.

<a id="sec-floating-point-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.3 Floating-point arithmetic

`float` and `double` arithmetic follows IEEE 754. Overflow produces `±Infinity`. Operations involving `NaN` propagate `NaN`. Division by zero produces `±Infinity` or `NaN`. No exception is raised.

Modulo on floating-point values is intentionally not provided as an operator. Use `Math.Fmod` (C-style same-sign-as-dividend) or `Math.IEEERemainder` (IEEE 754 nearest-even) instead; see [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic).

<a id="sec-decimal-arithmetic"></a>
### 6.4 Decimal arithmetic

`decimal` arithmetic raises `OverflowException` on overflow and `DivideByZeroException` on division by zero. There is no `Infinity` or `NaN` for `decimal`.

<a id="sec-bitwise-operations"></a>
### 6.5 Bitwise operations

Operators `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift), and unary `~` (complement) operate on the binary representation of integer values. They are not valid on `bool`, `char`, or floating-point types.

`~x` is the bitwise complement; for signed types, `~x = -(x + 1)`. The keyword `not` is boolean negation, valid only on `bool`. `not` is not user-overloadable; types wanting domain-specific inversion provide a named method (e.g. `.Negate()`) or overload `~` if a bitwise reading applies. `~` and `not` are not interchangeable.

A shift's result type is the type of its **left** operand. The right operand supplies only the shift count: it does **not** participate in the mixed-type promotion of [§6.2](#sec-mixed-type-arithmetic), so a narrower left operand is *not* widened to match a wider count (`byte << int` yields `byte`, not `int`). Left shift fills with zeros on the right. Right shift fills with the sign bit on signed types, zero on unsigned.

The shift count's **domain** is `0` through `width−1`, where width is the bit width of the **left (shifted) operand's type** — `0..7` for `byte`/`sbyte`, `0..15` for `short`/`ushort`, `0..31` for the 32-bit types (`int`/`uint`), `0..63` for the 64-bit types (`long`/`ulong`). A count outside the domain — negative, or ≥ width — is a fault: a **compile error** when the count is a compile-time constant ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)), and `OverflowException` at runtime otherwise. Within the domain, bits shifted beyond the left operand's width are discarded silently — that is the operation, exactly as `&` discards bits — and the result never faults. Code that wants the modular count deliberately writes it: `v << (k & 31)` (`& 63` for 64-bit left operands) — the mask is then in the source, visible and in-domain by construction. ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)'s mandatory-parenthesization rules do not cover shift-with-bitwise mixes, but `&` binds looser than `<<`, so the parentheses around `k & 31` are required by precedence — the spelling is unambiguous.) The constant-count diagnostic for a negative count notes the direction confusion: a negative count does not reverse the shift's direction — use the opposite operator, or mask deliberately with `& 31`.

Compound assignments: `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`. There is no `~=` (unary operators have no compound form).

<a id="sec-compound-assignments"></a>
### 6.6 Compound assignments

The compound assignment operators are `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`,
`|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, and `??=`. Unary operators have no compound forms
([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)).

**Desugaring.**
For every operator above except `??=`, the statement `x op= e` is equivalent
to `x := x op e` with the target evaluated **once**:

- every constituent of the left-hand side's lvalue chain (grammar A.6
  `LValue`) is evaluated exactly once, left to right: the base identifier or
  `this`, each mid-chain member hop (a property hop's getter is invoked once
  as part of locating the target), and every index expression in the chain;
- when the final segment is accessor-mediated (a property or an indexer), its
  getter and setter are each invoked exactly once — the getter produces the
  left operand, the setter stores the result;
- the order is: the LHS chain's constituent expressions, then the final
  segment's getter (where applicable), then `e`, then the operation, then the
  store.

[§17.6](#sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots)'s indexer desugaring is the
indexer instance of this rule. A.6's lvalue shape applies unchanged: a
method-call result cannot base the chain — extract it to a local first. The
store is an ordinary assignment: for an owned target,
[§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite applies, and an
assignment that may drop a live value is a throwable expression for
[§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s restoration analysis.

**Typing; the narrow-integer write-back.** Let T be the left-hand
side's type and R the type of `x op e` under the rules of this chapter
([§6.2](#sec-mixed-type-arithmetic) promotion, [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)
shifts and bitwise, [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions) overloads).
If R is T, or R implicitly converts to T ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)),
the result is stored directly. Otherwise, when **T is an integer type or
`char` and R is an integer type**, the result is converted back to T by the
corresponding [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions) **checked** narrowing:
`b += 10` on `b: byte` is `b := byte(b + 10)` — the addition runs in `int` per
§6.2, and a result outside `byte`'s range raises `OverflowException`
([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)'s checked posture; never a silent
truncation). For a `char` target the §5.2 code-point rules apply: `c += 1` is
`c := char(c + 1)`. In every other case the compound form is a **compile
error** naming the explicit remedy — notably a binary-float or `decimal`
result against a different LHS type (`b += 1.5`; `f += 2.5` where `f: float`
promotes to `double`): the §5.2 float narrowings round or truncate *silently*,
which is precisely the information loss [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s
admission line exists to exclude; write `f := float(f + 2.5);` when that loss
is intended. The write-back is scoped to the compound form only: plain
`b := b + 10` remains the §6.2/§5.1 compile error it has always been, so the
no-implicit-narrowing rule is undisturbed everywhere else. The shift forms
never need it: a shift's result already has the left operand's type
([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)). `x <<= k` and `x >>= k` inherit
[§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)'s count-domain rule through the desugaring: an
out-of-domain count is the same fault — compile error for a constant count,
`OverflowException` at runtime otherwise.

**`??=`** is not a read-modify-write: `x ??= e` assigns `e` only when `x`'s
current value is null, with the typing and ownership rules of
[§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=). The LHS chain is evaluated once as above,
the getter once; `e` is evaluated — and the setter invoked — only when the
assignment actually occurs.

**Events.** `+=`/`-=` whose left operand's static type is `EventSource<T>`,
`AsyncEventSource<T>`, or `SharedEventSource<T>` are the fixed subscription
desugaring of [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators), selected by that operand type
before this section applies; they are not compound assignments
([§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)).

**Operator overloads.** For an operand type overloading the underlying binary
operator, the desugaring applies with `x op e` resolved per
[§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions); the compound form is
well-typed exactly when the overload's result stores back under the typing
rule above (in practice: the result type implicitly converts to T). This
makes [§25.1](#sec-overloadable-operators)'s "desugar mechanically to
read-modify-write" precise.

```bezel
var b: byte := 250;
b += 4;                    // b := byte(b + 4) — 254, in range
b += 10;                   // byte(264) → OverflowException at runtime, never a wraparound
var checksum: byte := 0;
checksum ^= b;             // byte ^ byte : byte — R = T, no write-back involved
var n: int := 2;
var acc: byte := 40;
acc += n;                  // admitted: R = int; checked write-back at runtime (42)
n mod= 3;                  // n := n mod 3 — 2; a zero divisor raises DivideByZeroException (§6.1)
var s: short := 1;
s <<= 2;                   // R = short (§6.5) — 4, no write-back involved
var c: char := 'a';
c += 1;                    // c := char(c + 1) — 'b'; §5.2's code-point check applies
counts[category] += 1;     // §17.6's indexer instance: collection, index, getter, setter — once each
// var f: float := 1.0f;
// f += 2.5;               // compile error: R = double does not return to float implicitly —
//                         //   write f += 2.5f; (float promotion stays in-family) or
//                         //   f := float(f + 2.5); if the double-rounding is intended
```

---

<a id="sec-nullability-2"></a>
## 7. Nullability

<a id="sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types"></a>
### 7.1 Non-nullable and nullable types

A plain reference type is non-nullable; a `?` suffix produces its nullable form:

```bezel
var name: string := "Alice";        // non-nullable
var middle: string? := null;        // nullable
```

`string` and `string?` are distinct types. The compiler enforces the distinction at every assignment, parameter pass, and return.

A non-nullable reference type implicitly converts to its nullable form. The reverse requires a null check or `!`.

<a id="sec-nullable-value-types"></a>
### 7.2 Nullable value types

A value type wrapped in `?` is an optional: it either holds a value or `null`. `int?`, `Priority?`, and `DateTime?` are optional value types.

<a id="sec-assigning-null"></a>
### 7.3 Assigning null

Assigning `null` to a non-nullable target is a compile error.

<a id="sec-member-access-on-nullable-values"></a>
### 7.4 Member access on nullable values

Member access, method calls, and indexing on a nullable value are compile errors unless the compiler has narrowed it to non-null:

```bezel
var user: User? := GetUser();
if user <> null then
  Console.WriteLine(user.Name);     // narrowed to User here
end;
```

(A hole's *implicit `ToString` dispatch* on its operand inside an interpolated string is not a member access for this rule — [§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)'s null-rendering case defines it. Expressions *written inside* the hole remain governed by this section: `$"{user.Name}"` over `user: User?` is still a compile error.)

Narrowing also applies after early return, after `is not null`, inside the controlled block of a successful `is` test ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)), and — for an `out` recipient — in the region where a call's `bool` result is known to equal the callee's declared nullability postcondition ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)).

**How narrowing is established.** Narrowing is flow-sensitive: at each program point the compiler tracks, per local, whether its value is known non-null. The knowledge is established by:

- a null test — `x <> null` (narrowing the true branch), `x = null` (narrowing the *false* branch), `x is not null`, or a successful `is`/typed-pattern test ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as), [§19.3](#sec-patterns)) — in an `if`/`elif` condition (of the statement or of the [§20](#sec-the-if-expression) conditional atom, each condition narrowing its own branches), a `while` condition, a `when` guard, or a `(when …)` arm condition ([§19.1](#sec-forms), narrowing that arm's body);
- boolean composition of tests: in `A and B`, `B` (and the true branch) is checked under `A`'s true-facts; in `A or B`, `B` (and the false branch) sees `A`'s false-facts; `not` swaps the fact sets — the standard three-outcome flow analysis, so `x <> null and x.Length > 0` is well-typed. The `not`-swap applies to **null facts**; a *type-classification* fact is established only by the `is`/`is not` operators and typed patterns directly, never by `not`-composition — `not (x is T)` has the same truth value as `x is not T` but narrows neither branch ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators));
- an early exit: after `if x = null then return; end;` (or `throw`, `break`, `continue` in that branch), the surviving path is narrowed;
- assignment: after `x := expr;` where `expr`'s static type is non-nullable — or `expr` is itself narrowed non-null at that point — `x` is narrowed until invalidated; likewise after `x ??= expr;` with such an `expr` (on every path `x` then holds a non-null value, [§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=));
- a call to a method declaring a `when true`/`when false` nullability postcondition on an `out` recipient ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)): in any region where the call's `bool` result is statically known to equal the stated constant, the recipient is narrowed non-null, composing through boolean operators and early exits like any other fact.

**How narrowing is invalidated.** The narrowing of a variable is invalidated when, within the controlled block:

- the variable is reassigned from a nullable-typed expression; or
- the variable is passed as a `ref` **or `out`** argument (the callee may — for `out`, must ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — reassign it. The invalidation is deliberately **uniform over the parameter's declared nullability**: even a non-nullable `out T` parameter — whose mandatory assignment could soundly *re-establish* the fact — invalidates, one predictable rule rather than a nullability-dependent one; the sound non-nullable-`out` refinement is recorded as liftable, not implementation-optional — narrowing must not vary between conforming implementations); or
- the variable is **mutably captured** — assigned, or passed as `ref`/`out`, anywhere inside any lambda of the enclosing function body ([§27.5](#sec-closures)) — and the block performs *any* operation that can transfer control to user code: a method, constructor, accessor, or user-defined-operator call, an invocation of a function value, or an `await` (across which another continuation of the domain may run the closure, [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)). A mutably-captured local has exactly the unseen writer the field paragraph below names — "a closure invoked in between" — so after the first such operation the narrowing is gone; re-test, or copy to an uncaptured local (the same remedy as for fields). The rule is deliberately syntactic and conservative: any lambda in the body counts, whether or not it escapes, so the check needs no escape analysis. Straight-line check-then-use of a captured local (`if x <> null then x.M(); end;` — no call *between* the test and the use) remains accepted.

The compiler does not attempt deeper analysis of which methods could reassign which variables transitively; beyond the forms above, nothing invalidates a local's narrowing. A `const` local's narrowing ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), once established, is **never invalidated**: no invalidating form can apply to it — it cannot be reassigned, cannot be passed as `ref` or `out`, and cannot be mutably captured (assignment to a `const` is a compile error everywhere, lambda bodies included). A null test on a `const` local therefore narrows it for the remainder of its scope, across calls and `await`s; the field-copy idiom of this section is airtight when the copy is `const`.

<a id="sec-narrowing-applies-to-locals-only"></a>
#### Narrowing applies to locals — and `readonly` fields — only

The compiler narrows local variables and `readonly` fields; it never narrows mutable fields or properties. A field may be reassigned to `null` between a null check and a subsequent use by paths the compiler cannot see: a method call whose body (directly, or through another reference to the same object) writes the field, a closure invoked in between, re-entrant code reached from the checked expression itself, or — across an `await` — another continuation of the same domain interleaving at the suspension point ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)); foreign threads introduced through the FFI ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface), [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)) are the residual concurrent case. Narrowing a field would therefore manufacture TOCTOU (time-of-check / time-of-use) bugs the compiler cannot prevent.

The standard pattern is to copy a nullable field to a local before narrowing:

```bezel
var u := _user;
if u <> null then
  u.DoStuff();          // u is narrowed; safe regardless of _user changes
end;
```

Local-variable narrowing applies to the copy, which no other thread can observe. Accessing a nullable *mutable* field without first copying it to a local is a compile error when the access requires non-null.

**`readonly` fields narrow.** A nullable **`readonly`** field — instance or `static` — participates in flow narrowing, because the blanket refusal's premise (unseen writers) does not exist for it: outside its construction window ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)'s single-assignment rule) a `readonly` field has no writer on any path, through any alias, so no call, `await`, or closure can invalidate a fact about its value. The tracked shape is exactly **one field off an admitted root** — `this._f`, `TypeName._s`, or `local._f` where `local` is itself narrowing-tracked; a fact rides its root (reassigning `local` drops it), and **any non-final field segment makes a path non-trackable** (`a.b._f` establishes nothing — `a.b` is a mutable read). The rule does not apply inside the declaring type's constructors, field initializers, static constructor, or static field initializers (the assignment window); elsewhere it composes with construction's [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction) `this`-escape residual exactly as stated there: a during-construction narrowing test observes either the null watermark (establishing nothing) or the field's single assigned value, final by §22.8 — the residual is §22.7's, inherited, not enlarged. Mutable fields and properties are unchanged: copy to a local first (rationale [§6.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-field-narrowing-is-not-safe-across-threads)).

<a id="sec-null-conditional-access"></a>
### 7.5 Null-conditional access (`?.`)

`x?.M` returns null if `x` is null; otherwise it performs the access. The result type is always nullable:

```bezel
var name: string? := user?.Name;
var length: int? := user?.Name?.Length;
user?.Log("Accessed");
```

`?.` short-circuits: if any segment of a chain is null, the remainder is not evaluated.

<a id="sec-null-conditional-call-args"></a>
### 7.6 Null-conditional call (`?(args)`)

A function value of nullable function type may be invoked with `?(...)`:

```bezel
var handler: ((int) -> ())? := null;
handler?(42);                       // no-op when null
```

The result type is nullable (or `()` for procedure-typed values).

<a id="sec-null-coalescing-and-="></a>
### 7.7 Null-coalescing (`??` and `??=`)

`a ?? b` returns `a` if non-null, else `b`. **Typing:** for a left operand of type `T?`, the right operand must be implicitly convertible ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) to `T` or to `T?`; the result type is `T` when the right operand is non-nullable and `T?` when it is nullable — `user?.Name ?? "Anonymous"` is `string`, while `primary ?? fallback` over two `string?` values is `string?`; a right-associative chain stays nullable until a non-nullable operand terminates it (`a ?? b ?? ""` is `string`). When the operands are owned (or owned-nullable), `??` is a two-branch *expression* and its result ownership follows the same meet rule as an `if`/`else` join — see the producer table in [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows): `owned ?? owned` is owned (the chosen value is discharged once), and an owned arm mixed with a borrowed arm is rejected.

```bezel
var displayName: string := user?.Name ?? "Anonymous";
_cache ??= new Cache();             // assign only if currently null
```

<a id="sec-null-forgiving"></a>
### 7.8 Null-forgiving (`!`)

`x!` asserts non-nullness. If `x` is null at runtime, `NullReferenceException` is raised. The result is the non-nullable form of the expression. `!` is the only postfix `!` operator in the language; there is no prefix `!`.

<a id="sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields"></a>
### 7.9 Definite assignment for non-nullable fields

Every non-nullable field must be either:
- assigned a value in every constructor before the constructor returns, or
- given a field initializer at its declaration.

Definite-assignment analysis applies the same rule to non-nullable locals: a non-nullable local must be assigned before it is read.

The guarantee this rule exists to provide is operational: **no non-nullable field is ever observed unset**. For ordinary (hand-written) construction the constructor-scoped rule above delivers that guarantee together with the construction-time observation rules of [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction): code that can observe the object mid-construction — an instance call on `this`, an escape of `this`, a virtual dispatch — is admitted only where the observable fields are assigned, virtual dispatch from non-sealed constructor bodies is rejected, and the recorded residual routes (dispatch reached through helpers, escapes, or construction-time closure invocations, [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction)) are bounded by the null watermark and checked-mode `NullReferenceException` defined there. Synthesized deserialization is bound by the same rule with no exception: an owning-tree component and a plain borrowing back-edge are supplied as constructor arguments (bound before the constructor body runs), and a cycle-closing reference is a nullable `Weak<T>?` field — discharged by its null initializer at construction and wired afterward by ordinary mutation. No synthesized construction mode escapes the constructor-scoped rule; definite assignment holds for synthesized and hand-written construction alike (serialization synthesis, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis); rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization)).

<a id="sec-default-initialization"></a>
#### Default initialization

For fields of value type (primitives, records, enums, inline arrays, the unit type), the must-initialize rule is satisfied vacuously when the type has a well-defined default value: zero for numerics, `false` for `bool`, the all-default record for record types whose fields all have defaults, the all-zero/null inline array for inline-array types whose elements have defaults. A static or instance field of such a value type is implicitly initialized to that default. An explicit initializer is permitted and overrides the default. For value types whose default is not well-defined — records with non-nullable reference fields, inline arrays with non-nullable reference elements, owning inline arrays with non-nullable element type, enums with no declared zero-valued constant ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) — the field requires an explicit initializer per the same rules as non-nullable reference fields below.

For fields of nullable reference type (declared with `?`), the must-initialize rule is satisfied vacuously by `null`: nullable reference fields are implicitly initialized to `null`.

For fields of non-nullable reference type — class types (including `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`), interfaces, `string`, function types, declared without `?` — there is no default value, so the must-initialize rule is enforced strictly: the field requires either a field initializer or assignment in every constructor (for instance fields) or in the static constructor (for static fields). The compiler emits a definite-assignment error if neither path supplies a value.

The same split applies in the standard `var`-declaration case: a value-typed local whose type has a well-defined default can be declared without an initializer (gets the default), while one whose type's default is not well-defined (the carve-out above) must be assigned before it is read; a nullable local can be declared without an initializer (gets `null`); a non-nullable reference-typed local must be assigned before it is read.

<a id="sec-generics-and-nullability"></a>
### 7.10 Generics and nullability

Inside an unconstrained generic body, `T` is treated conservatively as possibly nullable. Storage of type `T` should be declared `T?`.

`where T: notnull` restricts T to non-nullable types. Inside the body, `T` is non-nullable.

`where T: class` restricts T to non-nullable reference types — classes (including `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`), interfaces, `string`, function types.

`where T: value` restricts T to non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices ([§35](#sec-choices)), primitives, inline arrays (all forms, including `[N owned]…` owning forms), and the unit type. A nullable value type (e.g. `int?`) does not satisfy the constraint ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)); inside the body, T is the non-nullable value type and `T?` is its nullable companion. Inside the body, operations that copy T (assignment, parameter passing by value, returning by value) are checked at instantiation: for move-only inline arrays ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), copy operations are replaced by moves, and any operation the generic body uses that requires copy semantics (e.g., reading T twice without an intervening assignment) is rejected at instantiation with a message naming the move-only type.

`where T: SomeClass` and `where T: IFoo` are *type-bound* constraints. They restrict T to non-nullable types conforming to the named type:
- `where T: SomeClass` admits SomeClass and its subclasses. Interfaces do not extend classes in Bezel, so this constraint admits class types only.
- `where T: IFoo` admits any non-nullable type that conforms to `IFoo`: classes that implement it (directly, by inheritance, or implicitly — `IDisposable`, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), records and enums that implement it, interfaces that extend it (directly or transitively), and primitives conforming through their standard-library declarations or the compiler-provided conformances of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members). See [§14.2](#sec-constraints) for the conformance rule and worked examples.

Inside the generic body, T is non-nullable under any type-bound constraint.

`T?` always means "the nullable form of T," regardless of constraint. Under `where T: notnull`, `T` is the non-nullable form and `T?` is the nullable companion.

**`?` is idempotent under substitution.** When an unconstrained `T` is instantiated with a nullable type `U?`, the substituted `T?` denotes `U?` itself — there is no two-level optional, consistent with the grammar (Appendix A: `Type ::= TypeNoNullable "?"?`, at most one `?`) and with [§8.6](#sec-boxing)'s single-wrapper boxing. Consequently an API whose result type is `T?` (e.g. the stdlib `FirstOrNull` family) cannot distinguish "no value" from "a present `null`" when instantiated at a nullable `T`; callers who need the distinction use the shape that carries it (`Count`/index checks, or the `Try` pattern). A field or local of **bare** type `T` under an unconstrained parameter follows [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s non-nullable-reference rules (must-initialize, no vacuous `null` default), since T may be instantiated non-nullable; *reads* remain conservatively possibly-null per this section.

<a id="sec-lifted-operators"></a>
### 7.11 Lifted operators

For a nullable value type `T?` whose underlying type `T` is a primitive on which a built-in operator ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types)) is defined, that operator **lifts** to the nullable form. Lifting is the natural completion of the null-safe equality already defined for `=`/`<>` ([§8.4](#sec-=-and)): the operators are defined on `T?` operands in terms of the underlying operator on `T`, with `null` handled uniformly. The rules differ by operator category.

**Arithmetic, bitwise, and shift operators.** The binary operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>` and the unary operators `+`, `-`, and `~` lift to yield `T?` (unary `+` per its [§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) identity semantics). A lifted binary operator produces `null` if *either* operand is `null`; a lifted unary operator produces `null` if its operand is `null`. A mixed expression in which one operand is `T?` and the other is the non-nullable `T` lifts as well — the non-nullable operand is treated as present (never `null`), and the result is `T?`. The runtime checks each operator already performs — `OverflowException` on integer overflow ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)), `DivideByZeroException` on integer or `decimal` division/`mod` by zero ([§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)) — apply only when both operands are present (non-null); when the lifted result is `null` by reason of a null operand, no underlying operation runs and no check fires. As stated above, an operator lifts only where it is defined on the underlying type `T`: the bitwise and shift operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `~`) therefore do **not** lift to `bool?` or `char?`, since they are not valid on `bool` or `char` ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)) — boolean combinations use `and`/`or`/`not`, which do not lift either (see *No three-valued logic* below).

**Relational operators.** The relational operators `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` lift to yield **`bool`** — *not* `bool?`. A lifted relational comparison yields `false` if *either* operand is `null`. This mirrors the rule that a `null` participant in an ordering comparison is not "less than" or "greater than" anything; the result is simply `false`. (Equality `=` and `<>` are unchanged — they are already null-safe per [§8.4](#sec-=-and), where `null = null` is `true` and `null = nonNull` is `false`.) Two boundary notes: lifted ordering deliberately breaks the usual `<=`-reflexivity-of-equality **on null** — `null = null` is `true` while `null <= null` is `false` — so code treating `a = b` as implying `a <= b` should narrow first (advisory — the comparison itself is legal and yields `false`). And the relational lifting is confined to nullable **value** types whose underlying type has an ordering: `bool?` operands do not lift ([§3.5](#sec-operators-on-primitive-types) defines no `bool` ordering), and nullable *reference* operands (`string?`) are outside this section entirely — ordering them is a compile error ([§4.6](#sec-string)).

**No three-valued logic.** Lifting does *not* introduce three-valued (`bool?`) logical operators. The boolean operators `and`, `or`, `not` ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) operate only on `bool`; there is no lifted `and`/`or`/`not` over `bool?`, and a `bool?` operand to a boolean operator is a compile error. Code that needs to combine `bool?` values handles the `null` case explicitly (e.g. with `??` ([§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)) or a narrowing check).

**User-defined operators.** Lifting applies to the built-in primitive operators only. Lifting of user-defined operators ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading)) declared on record or class types is **deferred**; a future revision may define how (or whether) a user-declared `operator +` on a value type lifts to its nullable form.

**Safety.** A lifted arithmetic/bitwise/shift result stays typed `T?`. It is therefore subject to the same narrowing discipline as any other nullable value: [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values) narrowing (or a null-coalescing/null-forgiving form) is still required before the result is used in a non-nullable position. Lifting never silently produces a non-nullable value from nullable operands; it only defines what the operators *mean* on nullable operands.

---

<a id="sec-the-object-class"></a>
## 8. The Object Class

<a id="sec-definition"></a>
### 8.1 Definition

```bezel
public class Object
  public method GetType(): Type;
  public virtual method Equals(other: Object?): bool;
  public virtual method GetHashCode(): int;
  public virtual method ToString(): string;
  public static method ReferenceEquals(a: Object?, b: Object?): bool;
end Object;
```

`Object` is a compiler intrinsic; method bodies are provided by the runtime. The declaration above defines the public surface. User code cannot redeclare or replace `Object`.

`Object` is the universal root. Every type derives from it: classes (including heap-array classes `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>`) directly through the inheritance chain, with `string`, interfaces, and function types reaching `Object` similarly via their reference-type heap representation; records, enums, primitives, inline arrays, and the unit type derive via boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) when used in `Object`-typed positions (subject to the inline-array boxing rules in [§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays)).

<a id="sec-gettype"></a>
### 8.2 `GetType`

`v.GetType()` returns the `Type` value for the runtime type of `v`. For a value-typed `v` the answer is always the static type — value types have no derivation, so runtime and static type coincide — and the call is answered from the static type with no observable boxing (move-only inline arrays, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), cannot be boxed ([§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays)) but may be asked their type — the receiver is borrowed, not copied). An implementation remains free to box internally where the type admits it; the result is identical either way.

`GetType` is non-virtual; runtime type identity is fixed at allocation and cannot be overridden.

`GetType` complements the `typeof(T)` expression ([§17.10](#sec-the-typeof-operator)), which produces the `Type` for a statically named type.

<a id="sec-equals-and-gethashcode"></a>
### 8.3 `Equals` and `GetHashCode`

`Equals` defines value-level equality. The compiler generates a default appropriate to each type kind:

| Type kind | Default `Equals` | Default `GetHashCode` |
|---|---|---|
| Class | Reference equality | Identity-based |
| Positional record | Field-by-field value equality (admissible component fields only, [§9.3](#sec-combined-form); otherwise no default and comparison is a compile error) | Hash of all positional fields |
| Body-only record | Auto-hashable ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)): property-by-property value equality; otherwise no default — `=`/`<>`/`.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` use is a compile error | Same |
| Enum | Underlying integer comparison | Hash of integer value |
| Primitive | Value comparison | Value-based |
| Inline array `[N]T`, `[N]T?` | Element-by-element value equality ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)) | Hash combining element hashes in slot order |
| Inline array `[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?` | Element-by-element equality via borrow ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) | Hash combining element hashes in slot order |

`GetHashCode` must satisfy: if `a.Equals(b)` then `a.GetHashCode() = b.GetHashCode()`. Hash collisions on non-equal values are permitted. The auto-generated `GetHashCode` for positional records combines per-field hashes in declaration order; the combining function **must be order-sensitive** (a commutative combiner such as plain XOR does not satisfy this): the hash of a sequence of component hashes must depend on their order, not only on their multiset, so `Pair(1, 2)` and `Pair(2, 1)` are not *systematically* hash-equal (incidental collisions remain permitted, as for any hash). The choice of combining algorithm is otherwise implementation-defined, subject to the hash-equality invariant and this order-sensitivity requirement.

A type that overrides `Equals` must also override `GetHashCode`. The compiler enforces this.

<a id="sec-identity-hash-assignment"></a>
**Identity hashes are assigned, not derived.** The identity-based default `GetHashCode` for classes is **assigned on first request**, not derived from the object's storage address: the runtime draws the value from a per-domain deterministic sequence (objects first hashed outside any domain draw from the startup/shutdown thread's sequence, [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)) and stores it with the object thereafter. Identity hash codes are therefore a function of the order in which objects' hashes are first requested — deterministic under [§30.13](#sec-determinism) — and never expose addresses. Programs must continue to treat identity hashes as opaque per-run values; only their stability within a run and their address-independence are promised.

<a id="sec-=-and"></a>
### 8.4 `=` and `<>`

`a = b` invokes `a.Equals(b)`, with a null-safe wrapper: `null = null` is `true`; `null = nonNull` and `nonNull = null` are `false`. `<>` is the negation.

For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`. Operator overloading of `=` and `<>` is not permitted on classes; classes customize equality by overriding `Equals`. Records and enums may overload `=` and `<>`.

`Object.ReferenceEquals(a, b)` compares object identity, ignoring any `Equals` override. It is an ordinary static method with `Object?` parameters, so value-typed arguments are **boxed before the comparison** and the result is the identity of the boxes ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)): a non-null value-typed argument produces a fresh box and compares unequal to every other argument — except boxed `()`, which an implementation may intern ([§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-the-unit-value)), making that comparison unspecified — while a **null** nullable-value argument boxes to the null reference ([§8.6](#sec-nullable-value-type-boxing)), so `ReferenceEquals(x, null)` is `true` for a null `int?` `x`. The compiler warns on any value-typed argument: the question being answered is box identity, which is almost never what the caller means.

<a id="sec-tostring"></a>
### 8.5 `ToString`

`ToString` is invoked implicitly inside string interpolation ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)) via virtual dispatch — for present values; a `null` value of a nullable-typed hole renders as the text `null` with no dispatch ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)). The compiler-generated default returns:

- For classes: the type's **qualified name** — the module-path-qualified rendering stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class) defines for `Type.FullName` (`"BankingApp.BankAccount"`; a generic instantiation renders per stdlib §2.13 rule 3, type arguments recursing). The default and `FullName` are one rendering contract, not two.
- For positional records: a representation of fields, e.g. `"Point(X: 10, Y: 20)"`.
- For body records that satisfy the auto-equality conditions ([§9.2](#sec-body-records) — only auto-properties, no manually-declared `Equals` or `GetHashCode`): a representation of auto-properties, formatted as `"TypeName(Prop1: value1, Prop2: value2)"`. Auto-`ToString` accompanies the auto-equality members, with one asymmetry: an `override ToString` replaces only the formatting — the record keeps auto-`Equals`/`GetHashCode`/`=` — while an `Equals`/`GetHashCode` override disqualifies the whole package ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)). This matches the analogous design in C# records and lets `Console.WriteLine(person)` produce useful output for auto-equality records without ceremony.
- For body records that do not satisfy auto-equality conditions, and for enums: the type's qualified name (the stdlib [§2.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-the-type-class) `FullName` rendering, as for classes). An enum may replace its default by declaring a plain `ToString(): string` member ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)); the replacement is used by every consumer, including interpolation and boxed dispatch.
- For inline arrays (all forms, including move-only `[N owned]…` arrays, whose receiver is borrowed for the call) and for the unit type: the type's name — `"[3]int"`-style for an inline array, `"()"` for unit (element-listing output is deliberately not synthesized — an inline array's elements may be class-typed borrows whose formatting is not the container's business).

The record heads' unqualified spelling is a deliberate asymmetry: positional-record and auto-equality formatting keeps the **unqualified** head (`"Point(X: 10, Y: 20)"`, [§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) — a record rendering already identifies itself by shape, while a bare class or enum default is *only* a name and therefore carries the module path.

The defaults above are generated for **every** type of the applicable kind, wherever declared — user modules and the standard library alike. The standard library's positional records (`Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `ArraySpan<T>`, `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`, …) carry the positional-record default like any other record (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans): the span records are purely user-level Bezel, standard language features throughout); `Range<T>` (a compiler-intrinsic body record, stdlib [§9.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ranget)) carries the auto-equality body-record default of the bullet above, rendering its auto-properties. Each component renders as its own `ToString` renders it (virtual dispatch — a class-typed component with no override renders its class default, the qualified name per the bullet above); a `null`-valued nullable component renders as the text `null` ([§18.5](#sec-interpolated-strings)'s rule). Rendering is a call-bounded borrow of the receiver and its components: the default's own execution neither retains, consumes, nor extends any borrow ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) is unaffected; a boxed receiver's call-bounded copy is [§8.6](#sec-boxing)'s rule, unchanged).

<a id="sec-boxing"></a>
### 8.6 Boxing

When a value type is used where `Object` (or an interface implemented by the value type) is expected, the value is **boxed**: a heap-allocated wrapper holds the value. Boxed values are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

<a id="sec-boxing-of-the-unit-value"></a>
#### Boxing of the unit value

The unit type `()` has exactly one value, so all boxings of `()` may share a single heap object. Implementations are permitted (but not required) to intern boxed `()` such that every boxing produces the same reference. Programs should not rely on boxed unit values being either reference-equal or reference-distinct; both interpretations are conforming. The only guarantee is the standard one: a boxed `()` value, when unboxed, yields `()`.

<a id="sec-nullable-value-type-boxing"></a>
#### Nullable value-type boxing

When a nullable value type `T?` is boxed:

- If the value is `null`, the result is a null `Object` reference.
- If the value is non-null, the result is a boxed `T` (the non-nullable form). The nullable wrapper is stripped during boxing.

Unboxing reverses the process: a null `Object` reference unboxes to `null` of the target nullable type; a non-null boxed `T` unboxes to a non-null `T?`.

<a id="sec-boxing-of-borrow-bearing-records"></a>
#### Boxing of borrow-bearing records

Boxing a borrow-bearing record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) is subject to the same borrow-lifetime constraints as any other operation on a borrow-bearing value. The boxed copy on the heap holds the same borrowed references as the source record; it does not extend their lifetimes. The compiler enforces: a boxed borrow-bearing record value may not be stored in a location that could outlive the source of any borrow the record contains. In practice, this means a borrow-bearing record may be boxed for a short-lived interface call (e.g. passing to a method accepting `Object`) provided the boxed value does not escape the borrow's source scope. Storing a boxed borrow-bearing record in a field, returning it from a method, or capturing it in a closure that escapes the source scope is rejected by the same rules as the unboxed form ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). The canonical sanctioned use is passing a span to a parameter of type `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>` (stdlib [§4.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ireadonlyspan)): the box is bounded by the call frame, the interface surface is escape-free by construction (no `GetEnumerator`, no `Slice`, no operation returning a borrow-retaining handle), and the source outlives the call in the common synchronous case. The contrasting *forbidden* case is the `IEnumerable<T>` enumerator path: `GetEnumerator()` returns a heap object that would hold the span's borrow across its own, unbounded lifetime, which the borrow tracker cannot bound — which is why spans do not implement `IEnumerable<T?>` ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)). The distinction is escaping (an enumerator/field/return/escaping-closure) versus call-bounded, not boxing per se. A borrow-bearing **choice** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) boxes under exactly these rules.

<a id="sec-boxing-of-inline-arrays"></a>
#### Boxing of inline arrays

Non-owning inline arrays (`[N]T` and `[N]T?`) are ordinary value types and box per the general rule. When the element type is a reference type, the boxed array carries borrows; the same borrow-lifetime constraints apply as for boxed borrow-bearing records (above).

Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed. Boxing a value type copies the value into a heap wrapper, but move-only types forbid copying ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). A program that needs the contents of an owning inline array to cross a boxed-value boundary must explicitly transfer ownership — typically by draining the inline array into a heap collection (`OwningArray<T>`), which is itself a class type and is passed by reference rather than boxed.

<a id="sec-dispose-is-not-on-object"></a>
### 8.7 `Dispose` is not on `Object`

`Dispose()` is class-only. The compiler generates `IDisposable` on every non-static class. Static classes, records, enums, choices, primitives, and inline arrays do not implement `IDisposable`.


---

<a id="sec-records"></a>
## 9. Records

A record is a value type. Records are stack-allocated or stored inline in their containing object. Records have value semantics: assignment copies the value.

<a id="sec-positional-records"></a>
### 9.1 Positional records

A record may declare positional fields in parentheses after its name:

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int);
record Person(Name: string, Age: int);
```

For each positional record, the compiler generates:

- A primary constructor whose parameters are the positional fields, in declaration order.
- Public read-only properties, one per positional field, with the same names.
- Value equality (`=`, `<>`) based on all positional fields (those marked `equality skip` excepted — [§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) — generated only when every participating positional field is of an admissible component type ([§9.3](#sec-combined-form)); a positional record with an inadmissible field declares fine, but comparing it is a compile error rather than silent reference equality.
- `GetHashCode` based on the same participating positional fields.
- `ToString` formatted as `"TypeName(Field1: value1, Field2: value2)"`.

Positional field names are PascalCase by convention; the compiler does not transform them.

A positional-only record ends with `;`:

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int);
```

<a id="sec-body-records"></a>
### 9.2 Body records

A body record declares members in a block. The body may contain methods, expression-bodied properties, additional constructors, and operator overloads:

```bezel
record Rectangle
  public readonly property Width: decimal;
  public readonly property Height: decimal;

  public constructor(width: decimal, height: decimal)
    Width := width;
    Height := height;
  end constructor;

  public method Area(): decimal => Width * Height;
end Rectangle;
```

<a id="sec-auto-generated-equality"></a>
#### Auto-generated equality

A body-only record receives auto-generated `=`, `<>`, `GetHashCode`, and `ToString` over its **auto-properties** (and only its auto-properties) when every **instance** member of the record **not marked `equality skip`** ([the clause below](#sec-equality-skip)) is one of:

- An auto-property whose type is an **admissible component type** (below) — or an auto-property marked `equality skip` regardless of its type (the clause removes it from the computation; [the `equality skip` clause](#sec-equality-skip) below).
- A method or expression-bodied (computed) property — these contribute no storage and do not participate in equality. What their bodies compute is irrelevant to eligibility — equality, hashing, and `ToString` are defined over storage only, so no behavior of a computed member can affect their correctness.
- An overload of a non-equality operator.
- A constructor — regardless of what its body does (see the eligibility note below).

**Static members are ignored**: `const` declarations, `static readonly` fields, and static methods and properties contribute no instance storage and neither qualify nor disqualify the record — a record may carry `Origin`-style constants and static factories without losing `=`. The same static-member exemption applies wherever this membership rule is reused ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).

**Admissible component types** (one recursive rule, applied per storage component):

- a primitive type, an enum, or `string`;
- another record that is itself auto-hashable (recursively, this same rule);
- `T?` where `T` is admissible — the comparison is the null-safe `=` of [§8.4](#sec-=-and)/[§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators);
- a non-owning inline array `[N]T` or `[N]T?` whose element type is admissible — the comparison is element-by-element per [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s inline-array rows;
- a **value-like choice** that is itself auto-hashable ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality) — recursively, this same list applied to every case's payload fields).

Such a record is said to be **auto-hashable** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)). The generated `=` compares each auto-property by its declared type's `=`; the generated `GetHashCode` combines per-property hashes; the generated `ToString` produces `"TypeName(Prop1: value1, Prop2: value2)"` over the auto-properties in declaration order (matching the positional-record form in [§8.5](#sec-tostring)). Computed (expression-bodied) properties are not part of the equality comparison or the ToString output even when they are visible on the public surface — equality and the auto-formatted representation are always over storage, never over derived values.

A body record is **not** auto-hashable — and `=` on it without an explicit overload is a compile error — when it contains:

- An explicit field declaration (storage that is not an auto-property) — **unless the field is marked `equality skip`** (the clause below), which removes it from the membership computation entirely: a skipped member cannot disqualify the record.
- An `override` of `Equals` or `GetHashCode`. Declaring either means the author has taken over equality, and the synthesized structural `=` would silently ignore the override; the record is therefore not auto-hashable, and `=`/`<>` (and the direct `.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` calls above) are a compile error unless the author also declares the `operator =`/`<>` overloads. (An `override` of `ToString` alone suppresses only the auto-`ToString`; auto-`Equals`/auto-`GetHashCode`/`=` remain — the author took over formatting, not equality.)

A validating or normalizing constructor is fully compatible with auto-equality. `with` bypasses constructors ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)); the synthesized `Deserialize` runs a matching declared constructor ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)).

Authors who want explicit equality on a record outside the auto-hashable set declare `=` and `<>` overloads in the body, along with `Equals(Object?)`, `Equals(T)`, and `GetHashCode` overrides as needed.

The compile error applies to the `=` and `<>` operators **and to direct calls of `.Equals(Object?)` and `.GetHashCode()`** on the record. Calling `someRecord.Equals(other)` or `someRecord.GetHashCode()` on a non-auto-hashable record without a user-defined override is a compile error pointing to the same fix as the `=` error: declare custom equality, or simplify the record to an auto-hashable form. The error covers `Equals(Object?)`, `Equals(T)` (when the record implements `IEquatable<T>`), and `GetHashCode`.

This rule is stricter than C#'s — C#'s `record` types always auto-generate equality, but C# *classes* fall back to reference equality on `.Equals(object?)` silently. Bezel records do not have C#'s "always auto-generate" guarantee (body records can opt out by including non-auto-property storage), and the silent reference-equality fallthrough on a value type would be a footgun: users expect content equality on records, and a body record's reference-equality `Equals` is virtually never the intended semantics. Forcing a compile error puts the choice in the user's hands.

The error is at the call site, not the declaration site; declaring a non-auto-hashable record is fine on its own. The error fires when user code attempts to invoke equality on it. Calls through `Object`-typed receivers (`var o: Object := someRecord; o.Equals(...)`) bypass the static-type check and reach the inherited `Object.Equals` at runtime, returning reference equality — the static-type-erasure escape hatch is unavoidable but is rare in practice.

A body-only record with zero auto-properties (and no other storage) is auto-hashable by the membership rule above. The generated `=` returns `true` for every pair of values; the generated `GetHashCode` returns a fixed implementation-defined constant; the generated `ToString` produces `"TypeName()"` — the type name followed by empty parens, the natural specialization of the property-listing format for zero properties. Such a record represents a singleton-by-value: every instance is equal to every other. The `with` expression on such a record is a compile error (no fields to replace), and `default(T)` produces the (single) value.

`with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) and `default` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) are independent of equality; they apply to any record that satisfies their own rules.

<a id="sec-equality-skip"></a>
