#### The `equality skip` clause

A storage component may carry the clause **`equality skip`** (`EqualityClause ::= "equality" "skip"`, Appendix [A.3](#sec-type-declarations)/[A.4](#sec-members); `equality` is a contextual keyword, Appendix [B.2](#sec-contextual-keywords) — exactly `serialized`'s row). The clause attaches to a positional field, an auto-property, an **explicit field declaration**, or a choice payload field ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)), mirroring `serialized skip`'s ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) grammar, placement, and discipline; only the `skip` form exists — rename and `optional` have no equality analogue, so the vocabulary is one word, closed.

A storage component marked `equality skip` is **removed from the auto-equality membership computation**: it does not participate in the generated `=`/`<>`, `Equals(T)`/`Equals(Object?)`, or `GetHashCode`, and it is exempt from the admissible-component-type requirement — a member whose type is inadmissible, including an explicit field declaration, does not disqualify the record when marked `equality skip`. Every other role of the member is untouched: an equality-skipped component is still storage, still a `with` target ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with) — the copy carries its value; a copied cache is at worst stale, the cache author's existing contract), still rendered by the generated `ToString` (one clause, one effect — renderings are not contracts), and still a serialized component when the type opts into [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) (the two packages' clauses are independent; [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s interaction rule). The membership computation is one computation with per-package clauses: wherever it is reused — [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s body-record eligibility, [§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s choice equality, [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s auto-hashable property — the reuse sees the clause of *its own* package applied to **participation** ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) applies `serialized skip`; this package applies `equality skip`), while the **eligibility gate** is one-directional: *[§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s* eligibility gate reads both packages' skips ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s gate sentence); the equality package's own gate ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s auto-hashable property) reads `equality skip` only, so gate and participation are the same set within a package — a `serialized skip` never rescues an equality-inadmissible component. One reach of the clause is worth naming where it meets [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties): the borrow-bearing property ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) is untouched by the skip, so an equality-skipped class-typed field leaves a borrow-bearing **record** auto-hashable — and hashable ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)'s hashable row), a reach previously available only through [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s five-member user-equality route — while a borrow-bearing **choice** stays non-hashable whatever its skips ([§35.7](#sec-choice-equality)'s value-like gate has no record analogue).

```bezel
record Interval
  public readonly property Lo: int;
  public readonly property Hi: int;
  private equality skip _cachedLen: int;    // excluded from =, Equals, GetHashCode —
                                            //   and the package survives the field
  public constructor(lo: int, hi: int)
    Lo := lo;
    Hi := hi;
    _cachedLen := hi - lo;
  end constructor;
end Interval;
// new Interval(1, 5) = new Interval(1, 5) is true whatever the cache states.
```

The worked consequences:

- **The rescue reaches the disqualifier list's first bullet only.** The *second* disqualifier — an `override` of `Equals`/`GetHashCode` — is untouched and unrescuable: the author who takes over equality has taken over all of it; `equality skip` composes with the *generated* members only. A record with both an equality-skipped member and an `Equals` override is simply not auto-hashable (the override governs) — and the skip clause on it is **not** an error: it is meaningful to a reader and future-proof against the override's removal. (Contrast [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s inert-annotation error, which fires when the *type* is outside synthesis entirely; here the type is a record and the package is merely suppressed.)
- **Hashing coherence cannot break ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)).** The generated `=` and the generated `GetHashCode` are computed over the *same* reduced member set: if `a = b`, every participating member compares equal, and the hash combines exactly those members' hashes in declaration order ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s order-sensitive combiner, unchanged) — so `a.GetHashCode() = b.GetHashCode()` holds by construction. No configuration exists in which a member is hashed but not compared, or compared but not hashed.
- **All members skipped.** A record whose every storage component is equality-skipped has an empty participating set and takes the zero-auto-property **equality and hashing** semantics above (`with` and `ToString` are unaffected — the storage is present): every pair of values equal, a fixed implementation-defined hash, `ToString` rendering the auto-properties, skipped or not. Defined, no diagnostic — the zero-property record draws none, and an all-skipped record is the same value semantically.
- **The recursive admissibility rule is unchanged in shape.** "Another record that is itself auto-hashable" evaluates the inner record *with its own skips applied* — the same reuse discipline, not a new rule: the property is [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)-derived, computed per type from its declaration, and the outer record consumes the inner's verdict. An inner record rescued by `equality skip` is admissible as a component exactly as any auto-hashable record is.
- **What the skip is not.** Not custom equality logic — skip only *excludes*; a record needing projection equality still declares the operators under [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule, the sanctioned route for logic. Not a mutability license — [§9.4](#sec-mutability)'s advice stands; a skipped *mutable* member is the expected use (a cache mutated behind `readonly` structure), but skipping does not make mutating *participating* members any safer. Not available to classes — classes have no auto-equality ([§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode): reference equality); nothing to skip.

The clause is admitted on storage components only. On a computed (expression-bodied) property, a method, a static member, an enum constant, or a choice *case* (the case is the discriminant — skipping it is incoherent), `equality skip` is a **compile error**, mirroring [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)'s inert-annotation rule: such members never participate in equality, and silently ignoring the clause would be the inert-looking-but-load-bearing annotation rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred) warns against. Adding or removing `equality skip` on a public type's member is a **breaking change** ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 3): it flips comparison results and hash values for clients, and can flip the auto-hashable/hashable derived properties; the artifact interface ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) carries the clause exactly as it carries `serialized` clauses.

<a id="sec-combined-form"></a>
### 9.3 Combined form

A record may have both positional fields and a body:

```bezel
record Vector2(X: double, Y: double)
  public method Length(): double => Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);

  public static method operator +(a: Vector2, b: Vector2): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(a.X + b.X, a.Y + b.Y);
end Vector2;
```

The auto-generated members are present and the body adds further members. Conflicts:

- The body may not declare a constructor with the same parameter list as the auto-generated primary constructor.
- The body may not declare a property with the same name as a positional field's auto-generated property.

**Eligibility of the combined form.** The [§9.2](#sec-body-records) membership and disqualifier rules apply to the combined form with the positional fields counted as storage components alongside the body's auto-properties: every storage component must be of an admissible component type, and a disqualifying body member (an `Equals`/`GetHashCode` override, or a member outside the §9.2 list) suppresses the auto-generated equality members — the declaration itself stays legal, and any *use* of `=`/`<>`/`.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` on the type gets §9.2's existing use-site error. The same use-site-error discipline applies to a **purely positional** record whose fields fall outside the admissible-component rule: it declares fine, but comparing it is a compile error rather than silent reference-shaped equality. A positional field may carry **`equality skip`** ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip); grammar A.3 `PositionalField`): the field is excluded from equality but present, constructed, and rendered, and — as everywhere — a skipped field's inadmissible type does not disqualify the record.

<a id="sec-mutability"></a>
### 9.4 Mutability

Properties auto-generated from positional fields are read-only. A record declared only with positional fields is immutable.

In the body form, properties may be declared with any mutability. Mutable records are permitted but are inadvisable: value-equality and hashing rely on the value being stable.

<a id="sec-non-destructive-update-with"></a>
### 9.5 Non-destructive update: `with`

A `with` expression produces a new record value with named fields replaced:

```bezel
var p1 := new Point(1, 2);
var p2 := p1 with(Y := 99);             // Point(1, 99)
var p3 := p2 with(X := 0, Y := 0);      // Point(0, 0)
```

Syntax: `recordExpr with(Name := value, ...)`. The parentheses are part of the suffix — the assignment list reads as a named-argument list ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) — and the suffix carries no `end`. A trailing comma after the last assignment is permitted. The source expression must be **record-typed**; `with` produces a copy with the named fields replaced — the original record value is unchanged. A `with` expression whose source is class-typed is a **compile error naming this rule** (the retired object-initializer reading, [§22.11](#sec-object-initializer-blocks)); the diagnostic names both remedies: named/optional constructor arguments ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), which run the constructor and respect its invariants, or binding the instance to a named local and assigning its members as statements. The discriminator is the source expression's **type kind**, never the presence of `new`: `new Point(1, 2) with(Y := 9)` has a record-typed source and is an ordinary record `with` applied to the freshly-constructed value; the same spelling on a class-typed `new` expression is rejected.

The named fields must be auto-generated positional-field properties (regardless of their read-only status), auto-properties declared in the record body, or public fields. A `with` target must be **accessible at the use site under the member's own declared accessibility** ([§13](#sec-visibility)): a `private` auto-property is a valid target only inside the declaring record. Because `with` copies storage directly and never invokes setters (below), **accessor-level** visibility is irrelevant — a `private set` does not restrict `with`, by the same logic that lets read-only positional-field properties, which have no setter at all, be targets. For body-only records, `with` targets any auto-property that has backing storage; expression-bodied (computed) properties are not valid targets. All other fields keep their values from the source record. The result has the same static type as the source. The `with` operation constructs the copy directly from the source's storage; it does not invoke setters, so read-only positional-field properties are valid targets even though they have no setter.

`with` copies field values directly; it does not invoke the record's constructor. A constructor that validates cross-field invariants (e.g. `Width > 0 and Height > 0`) is not re-run during `with`. If a record enforces invariants that may be violated by independent field replacement, the record should provide a named method for constrained updates rather than relying on `with`.

The `with` keyword has two uses across the language: record non-destructive update (this section) and cancellation in `await for ... with token` ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)). The two are syntactically distinguished by grammar position and shape: record `with(...)` is a parenthesized primary suffix following the source expression; `await for`'s `with` (no parenthesized assignment list — its content is a single `CancellationToken` expression) follows the iteration source and precedes `do`. In an `await for` header, `with` followed by `(` and `Identifier :=` is the record-update suffix binding to the source expression; any other `with` opens the cancellation clause.

<a id="sec-records-and-inheritance"></a>
### 9.6 Records and inheritance

A record cannot derive from another record or from a class (other than the implicit `Object` root). A record may implement any number of interfaces:

```bezel
record Point(X: int, Y: int): IComparable<Point>
  public method CompareTo(other: Point): int =>
    (when
      X <> other.X => (when
        X < other.X => -1,
        _ => 1),
      Y <> other.Y => (when
        Y < other.Y => -1,
        _ => 1),
      _ => 0);
end Point;
```

Records are implicitly sealed. A record may implement one or more interfaces; the interface names appear after a colon following the record name or positional fields.

<a id="sec-records-and-disposal"></a>
### 9.7 Records and disposal

Records cannot have destructors, `owned` fields, or implement `IDisposable`. Records also cannot have inline-array fields whose slots carry the `owned` marker (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`); such fields are move-only value types ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and records support only copy semantics. Reference-typed fields in records are always borrows; the record does not own what they point to. See [§28](#sec-resource-management).

A record type is a **borrow-bearing record** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — if it holds at least one *borrow-carrying* field of a non-runtime-managed type. A field is borrow-carrying when:

- Its type is a reference type (class or interface, nullable or not, including the `T?` forms).
- Its type is an inline array whose element type is a reference type (`[N]C`, `[N]C?` for class-or-interface C).
- Its type is another borrow-bearing record, or a borrow-bearing choice ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) (transitivity).

Reference-typed fields whose types are runtime-managed (`string`, function types, boxed value types) do not make the record borrow-bearing because runtime-managed values have unbounded lifetime by construction; the same is true of inline-array fields whose element type is a runtime-managed reference type. Borrow-bearing **choices** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) are subject to every rule of this section, with "record" read as "record or choice" throughout. Values of a borrow-bearing record are subject to the borrow lifetime rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). In particular:

- A borrow-bearing record value may not outlive the source of any borrow it contains. For inline-array-field borrows, this applies element-wise: every slot's source must outlive the record.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be **constructed from a temporary** bound to one of its borrow-carrying fields. A construction argument that is a temporary — a collection or array literal, or a fresh call result that is not bound to a named location — has a lifetime that ends at the construction expression, so the record would immediately outlive that borrow's source (a dangling borrow). For example, `new Bag([10, 20, 30])` where `record Bag(Items: Array<int>)` borrows the array literal is rejected; bind the source to a named local (`var xs := [10, 20, 30]; var b := new Bag(xs);`) whose scope outlives `b`, and pass that. The same no-temporary-source rejection applies to a fresh producer passed to a class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) — `new StreamReader(scoped new FileStream(...))` is rejected; bind the stream first).
- A borrow-bearing record value may not be stored in an **instance field of a class** (this specializes the umbrella rule into an explicit escape bullet, the same pattern as the closure bullet below). A class instance's lifetime is not bounded by any borrow source's scope, and a record-carried borrow — unlike a **direct** class-typed borrow field, whose every use is a member access through the reference and therefore hits the disposed-flag check ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s field-store rule, which is unchanged) — may be consumed through access paths with **no per-access disposed-flag check** (a span's buffer window is the canonical case). The checked-mode trust regime is therefore unavailable and the store is **rejected statically**. For a record whose every access *does* pass through a tracked reference (`CancellationToken`), the rejection is for **regime uniformity** — one rule for record-carried borrows, not a per-record judgment of access paths — rather than a missing backstop. Stores of the **null-source** form (every borrow component `null`) are admitted, mirroring the static-field exception below. The remedy is to store the *source* — an `owned` field of the underlying class (e.g. an `owned CancellationTokenSource` rather than a `CancellationToken`) or a direct class-typed borrow field — and re-derive the record view at the use site.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be stored in a static field of any type, *except* when every reference-typed field (and every reference-typed slot of every inline-array field) of the value is `null` (the **null-source** form). A static field of borrow-bearing record type may hold a value whose borrow-carrying components are all null; the type's accessors must handle this state explicitly. This exception exists to allow standard library "sentinel" values like `CancellationToken.None`, whose semantics are defined by the absence of a source rather than by holding one.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be returned from a method whose return-type rules cannot establish a sufficient lifetime for every borrow the record carries.
- A borrow-bearing record may not be captured by a closure that escapes its source's scope.
- A borrow-bearing record value may be **copied into a collection** only when every carried borrow's source provably outlives the collection's own binding scope: a store into a collection that is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or whose binding's scope strictly encloses a carried source's scope is rejected at the store site ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)'s copy slots carry this obligation). The check is the same structural scope comparison as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow rules; there is **no trust residual for record-carried borrows** (same reasoning as the instance-field bullet above). A collection of `CancellationToken`s whose source is declared before the collection remains expressible.

For typical short-lived uses — a record passed by value to a synchronous call frame, a `CancellationToken` ([§30.8](#sec-cancellation)) handed to an async call that completes before the source is disposed — these rules are automatic and require no annotation. (Asynchronous state-machine frames are the non-automatic case: borrow-bearing records are forbidden as `async` parameters and results, and constrained as locals across `await` — [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) — with `CancellationToken` as the single stdlib-certified exception, [§30.8](#sec-cancellation).)

As noted above, a record whose only reference-typed fields are of runtime-managed types (`string`, function types, boxed value types) is **not** a borrow-bearing record; runtime-managed values have unbounded lifetime by construction, so no borrow-lifetime rules apply.

<a id="sec-serialization-synthesis"></a>
### 9.8 Serialization synthesis

A record or enum that declares conformance to `ISerializable` and/or `IDeserializable` (standard library [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)) and satisfies the **synthesis-eligibility rule** below has the corresponding member bodies generated by the compiler. This is the same kind of opt-in-by-conformance, structural compile-time generation as auto-equality ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)); the eligibility rule, the recursive component check, and the compile-error discipline deliberately mirror it. Declaring the conformance is the opt-in; the synthesis is automatic when eligible and a compile error at the conformance declaration when not.

<a id="sec-synthesis-eligibility"></a>
#### Synthesis-eligibility

A type is **serialization-eligible** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — when it is a record or an enum and every serialized component is itself serializable:

- **Enums** are always serialization-eligible. The synthesized form writes the member *name* as a string (via `WriteString`) and reads it back by matching against the declared members; an encoded name matching no declared member raises `SerializationException` on read (on write no failing case exists — every enum value is a declared value, [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)). When several constants share one underlying value ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), the synthesized form writes the **first-declared** constant's name for that value and accepts every declared name on read (all denote the same value, so the round trip is stable). Writing the name rather than the underlying integer makes the encoded form stable against reordering or renumbering of members and self-describing in text formats; programs that need the integer form serialize `int(e)` (or the underlying-typed cast) explicitly through a hand-written `Serialize`.
- **Positional records** ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) are serialization-eligible when every positional field's type is serialization-eligible **and record-admissible** (the record clause below — heap collections and other class-typed components are class components only). The synthesized form is an object whose field names are the positional-field names in declaration order.
- **Body records** ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)) are serialization-eligible under exactly the auto-equality membership conditions of [§9.2](#sec-body-records) — the §9.2 member list and admissible-component rule are the single normative statement, applied here unchanged, evaluated with **both packages' skips applied** (the eligibility gate: a member marked `serialized skip` *or* `equality skip` ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) is structurally absent from the membership conditions for this check — see the interaction rule below) — *and* additionally every auto-property's type is serialization-eligible. The serialized components are the auto-properties in declaration order; computed (expression-bodied) properties are not serialized, exactly as they do not participate in equality or `ToString`. With the record clause below, positional and body records agree: a heap-collection component makes either form ineligible, with the same remedy.
- A component type is **serialization-eligible** when it is: a primitive (`bool`, the integer types, `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `char`); `string`; an enum; another serialization-eligible record; a value-like serialization-eligible choice ([the choice subsection](#sec-choice-serialization)); a serialization-eligible **synthesized class** (a class that declares `ISerializable`/`IDeserializable` and whose serialized components are each serialization-eligible, below); a `Shared<T>` or `Weak<T>` whose `T` is a serialization-eligible class; a nullable `T?` whose `T` is serialization-eligible (encoded as the value or `WriteNull`/`TryReadNull`); or a standard sequence collection (`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, etc., and inline arrays `[N]T`) whose element type is serialization-eligible (encoded with `BeginArray`/`EndArray`). A standard dictionary (`Dictionary<K, V>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`) is serialization-eligible when both `K` and `V` are serialization-eligible (encoded as an array of key/value pairs to admit non-string keys uniformly). Of these, the class-typed rows — synthesized classes, `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>`, and the heap collections (sequence and dictionary alike, which are class types, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds)) — are admissible in **class** components only; for records see the record clause below.

A type that declares `: ISerializable` or `: IDeserializable` but is **not** serialization-eligible is a **compile error at the conformance declaration**, naming the first offending member and the reason (mirroring the auto-equality non-membership error of [§9.2](#sec-body-records), but reported at the declaration rather than the use site, because the conformance declaration is the explicit opt-in and the obstruction should be reported where the promise is made). The error names the remedy: remove the conformance, make the offending component serializable, or hand-write `Serialize`/`Deserialize` (which suppresses synthesis — see below).

<a id="sec-tree-shaped-class-synthesis"></a>
##### Class serialization synthesis

A class opts into serialization synthesis by declaring `: ISerializable` and/or `: IDeserializable`; it needs no header shape clause, because the **serialized shape is read from the field types** — exactly as the owning-tree/back-edge partition has always been read from the `owned`/borrow annotations the language already requires. A field's type states its serialized role: an `owned` (or value-typed) field is an **owning edge**, written inline; a `Shared<T>` field is an **identity participant**, written once and referenced by identity at each alias; a `Weak<T>` field, and a plain borrowing field, are **back-references**. The graph a class serializes is a tree, a directed acyclic graph, or a cyclic graph as a consequence of those types — a class with no back-references serializes as a tree; one with borrowing or `Shared<T>` fields may alias; one with `Weak<T>` fields (or a `Shared<T>` that reaches an ancestor, the documented Shared-cycle leak, [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) may cycle — and the deserializer reconstructs whichever shape the field types and the wire identity tags describe, with no header assertion to declare or to police. (`sealed` is irrelevant to serialization: a sealed class follows the same eligibility rules and wire form as any other class.)

A class is serialization-eligible when every serialized component is itself serialization-eligible (recursively admitting other conforming classes, `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>` of an eligible class `T`, and owned collections of eligible elements).

A **record** cannot hold a class-typed component in its serialized set at all: a record's reference-typed fields are always borrows, and a borrow has no position in an owning spanning tree — there is no owner for an inline write to reconstruct against, and the synthesized `Deserialize` could not construct the record without binding a freshly-produced component to a borrowing field, which [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule rejects. The same holds for `Shared<T>`, `Weak<T>`, interface-typed, **and standard heap-collection** components (the heap collections are class types, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds), and the Deserialize argument above applies to them verbatim — a freshly-reconstructed `Array<T>` bound to a borrowing record field is exactly the shape §9.7 rejects, and no named-local workaround survives the record's return from `Deserialize`; the collection would have no owner). A record's serialized components must therefore be **record-admissible**: a primitive, `string`, an enum, another serialization-eligible record, **a value-like serialization-eligible choice ([the choice subsection below](#sec-choice-serialization) — matching [§9.2](#sec-body-records)'s admission of value-like choices as equality components)**, `T?` of a record-admissible `T`, or a non-owning inline array `[N]T`/`[N]T?` of record-admissible element type — value-shaped storage throughout. A record with a class-, interface-, `Shared<T>`-, `Weak<T>`-, or heap-collection-typed serialized component is not serialization-eligible — a compile error at the conformance declaration, naming the field. The remedy is an owning **class** envelope (a sealed class with an `owned` field serializes the same shape, above); `serialized skip` on the offending component where its type admits one (skip reconstructs with `default(T)`, a compile error for a non-nullable reference type, [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) — a non-nullable collection component must become nullable first, or use the envelope); or a hand-written `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. (A write-only admission — `ISerializable` without `IDeserializable` over collection components, which the read direction's argument does not reach — was considered and declined for uniformity: eligibility would become direction-dependent for exactly one component kind; recorded liftable.)

The serialized components of a class are its `owned` and value-typed fields and auto-properties, its `Shared<T>` and `Weak<T>` fields, and its plain **borrowing** reference fields, in declaration order. The `owned`/value edges form the **owning spanning tree**; a `Shared<T>` field is an **identity participant** (an owned share of a value reachable elsewhere by another handle); `Weak<T>` fields and plain borrowing fields are **back-edges** into the graph. This partition is read directly from the field types the language already requires — it is not inferred and not guessed.

**Synthesized `Serialize`.** The serializer assigns an identity tag the first time it reaches an object through an owning edge, and writes the object's components there. A `Shared<T>` field participates by identity: the tag is keyed on the **underlying value** the handle's `Get()` borrows (object-reference identity, [§8](#sec-the-object-class)) — so two independently `Clone()`d handles to one value collapse to one tag — written once at first occurrence and as a `$ref` at every later occurrence. A `Weak<T>` field and a plain borrowing field are never written inline; each is written as a `$ref` to the tag of the object it references (for a plain borrow the target is necessarily present in the owning tree, because a borrow's lifetime is bounded by an owner that outlives it; for a `Weak<T>` the target must be strongly reached elsewhere in the graph, enforced at read, below). No header assertion is made about aliasing or cycles: the field types fix which components alias and which are back-references, and the identity-tag mechanism records the actual sharing in the data.

**Synthesized `Deserialize`.** The synthesized factory reconstructs the owning spanning tree first, in **owner-before-borrower order**: each owned object is constructed by an ordinary call to its constructor. A `Shared<T>` component is reconstructed at its first (tagged) occurrence and registered in the tag→object table; each later `$ref` to that tag is bound by `Clone()`ing the registered handle (identity preserved, the shared count incremented). A plain borrowing field is supplied **as a constructor argument** resolved against the tag→object table — a directed acyclic graph admits an owner-before-borrower order, so the target precedes the borrower and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) is satisfied **unmodified**, with no observable intermediate state. A `Weak<T>` `$ref` is bound by `Downgrade()` from the reconstructed `Shared<T>` its tag resolves to; because a cycle-closing `Weak<T>` field is **nullable** (its target may be released), it is assigned after construction as ordinary mutation, so a cycle needs no two-phase window and [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) is again satisfied — the null initializer discharges it, the later wiring is ordinary assignment. The class return shape is [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)'s: `owned C` for a class that *holds* shared/weak components, and `owned Shared<C>` when the class *is* a shared node (the co-owned entry); the choice is locally decidable from the entry type.

**Constructor selection.** When the class declares more than one constructor, the synthesized `Deserialize` uses the *unique* constructor whose parameter list binds exactly the owning-tree components and plain borrowing fields, matched by name (order-insensitive and compared case-insensitively, so the conventional camelCase constructor parameter matches its PascalCase component; `serialized "<name>"` renames do not affect the parameter-name match, which uses the declared identifiers). `Shared<T>` aliases and nullable `Weak<T>?` back-edges are bound after construction (identity-table `Clone()`/`Downgrade()`), so they are not part of the constructor parameter match. If no constructor matches, or more than one does, the conformance declaration is a compile error naming the candidate constructors — the same compile-error discipline as the eligibility rule, reported where the opt-in is declared.

The synthesized deserializer preserves identity and enforces the one property the field types cannot decide:

- **Identity is preserved, never duplicated.** A `$ref` whose target has already been reconstructed binds to that object: a `Shared<T>` alias `Clone()`s the registered handle, a `Weak<T>` reference `Downgrade()`s it, and a plain borrow takes the resolved reference. The reference-unaware-serializer failure mode — distinct objects where the input shared one — cannot occur.
- **Weak-reachability is checked at read.** A `Weak<T>` `$ref` whose target is never strongly reached anywhere in the graph (no `Shared<T>` occurrence ever registered that tag) raises `SerializationException` — strong-reachability is a per-value property the field types cannot decide. A cheap static lint additionally flags, at the conformance declaration, a `Weak<T>` field in a class that serializes no `Shared<T>` of a matching `T`; the lint is a necessary-not-sufficient early check, not a replacement for the dynamic guarantee.

The serialized shape is **type-scoped** — read from the type's own field types, intrinsic to the type and identical for every caller, format, and call site — in contrast to the deserializer's *operation*-scoped unknown-field policy (stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)), a property of a particular read; the placement criterion is rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization).

A field typed as a base class holding a derived instance — **polymorphic dispatch** — is covered via the explicit `polymorphic` registry below; absent that registry, a base-class-typed component remains a synthesis-eligibility compile error for a type-driven serializable class (the synthesized `Deserialize` would have no way to choose the concrete type), and such components must be hand-written.

A serialized **cycle** closes through a `Weak<T>` back-edge on a `Shared<T>` spine, both ordinary owned handles, so the cyclic graph is constructed in ownership-valid Bezel and round-trips through the ownership checker. The wire form is the identity/`$ref` mechanism the owning-tree synthesis already establishes: the `Shared<T>` value carries an identity tag at its first occurrence, and the `Weak<T>` back-edge is written as a `$ref` to that tag. There is no two-phase construction and no self-contained-constructor restriction: a cycle-closing `Weak<T>?` field is nullable, so on deserialization it is bound after the spine is reconstructed by `Downgrade()`ing the `Shared<T>` its tag resolves to — ordinary post-construction mutation, with definite assignment ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)) discharged by the null initializer (rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization)).

<a id="sec-polymorphic-dispatch-synthesis"></a>
##### Polymorphic dispatch

A base class whose serialized components may, at run time, hold instances of registered derived classes declares a `polymorphic` registry as a member of its body:

```
public abstract class Shape: ISerializable, IDeserializable
  polymorphic ("circle": Circle, "square": Square);
  // ... other members ...
end Shape;
```

The registry is a closed, explicitly written map from a **wire discriminator string** to a **permitted concrete derived type**. There is no reflective discovery of subtypes: the only types the synthesized deserializer will ever construct for this hierarchy are those the registry names. This is the [§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection) explicit-registration-never-reflection principle applied directly — it is the reason a serialized type discriminator cannot be turned into an arbitrary-type construction primitive (the defect that made reflective `$type` binders a remote-code-execution vector elsewhere).

Each registry entry's discriminator must be a non-empty string literal, unique within the registry. Each named type must be assignable to the declaring class and must itself be type-driven serialization-eligible (declare `: ISerializable`/`: IDeserializable` with serialization-eligible components); a registered type that is not is a compile error at the registry. The registry is a member of a class that declares `: ISerializable`/`: IDeserializable` and has no dependence on any header clause — the registry governs which concrete type is chosen, and that type's own field types govern how its edges reconstruct. The declaring base class may be concrete (it registers a discriminator for itself like any other case) or abstract (it registers none for itself; an input discriminator naming the base is then a `SerializationException`).

**Synthesized `Serialize`.** When writing a component whose static type is a polymorphic base, the synthesized serializer writes the discriminator of the value's concrete run-time type as a distinguished leading field (the discriminator field name is `$type`, reserved within an object written for a polymorphic base; it precedes all component fields), followed by that concrete type's own synthesized form. A run-time type not present in the registry is a `SerializationException` at serialization — the closed set is enforced on both directions, never silently widened.

**Interaction with the identity/`$ref` mechanism.** When a polymorphic object is also a shared or cyclic reference target (the graph aliases or cycles through it), the discriminator and the identity tag coexist by a single rule: the object's **first** occurrence carries its identity tag and, because it is polymorphic, its `$type` discriminator, then its body; every **subsequent** occurrence is a pure `$ref` to that identity tag and carries **no** `$type` and no body. The concrete type is fixed at the first occurrence; a back-reference neither repeats nor may contradict it. On read, a `$ref` is resolved against the identity table (a `Shared<T>` alias by `Clone()`, a `Weak<T>` back-edge by `Downgrade()`) with no further dispatch — dispatch happened once, at the referent's first occurrence. This makes the wire form unambiguous for independent implementations regardless of how polymorphism, aliasing, and cycles combine.

**Synthesized `Deserialize`.** The discriminator is read **first**, before any component of the object, and consumed by dispatch — it is not bound as an ordinary component and is never subject to field-name customization, `serialized optional`, or the unknown-field policy (it is structural, not a data field). The deserializer looks the discriminator up in the registry, selects the concrete type's synthesized `Deserialize`, and delegates the remainder of the object to it (returning `owned Base`, the derived instance transferred as the base type, [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)). A discriminator string absent from the registry raises `SerializationException` — the closed-set assertion enforced dynamically, the same assert-and-enforce discipline as graph shape. Because the discriminator is consumed before component binding, it has no interaction with back-edge binding (whether the constructor-argument binding of a plain borrow or the `Clone()`/`Downgrade()` identity resolution of a `Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>` component): dispatch selects *which* concrete type's reconstruction path runs; that path is then exactly the type-driven reconstruction already specified for that concrete type.

The `polymorphic` registry is **type-scoped** for the same reason the serialized shape is: the permitted-subtype set is an intrinsic property of the base type's serialization contract — the hierarchy serializes against the same registry for every caller, format, and call site — the placement criterion of rationale [§5.22](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-driven-serialization). Polymorphic dispatch **composes uniformly with the type-driven model**: a registered type is reconstructed under whatever shape its own field types describe, including a cyclic shape closed by a `Weak<T>` back-edge. Dispatch selecting a concrete type does not interact with that type's identity or back-edge binding — the discriminator is consumed before any component or back-edge binding, so polymorphism is fully orthogonal to aliasing and cycles.

Classes that declare neither `ISerializable` nor `IDeserializable` remain outside synthesis entirely and participate only by hand-writing `Serialize` and a recognized static `Deserialize` ([§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary) of the standard library), exactly as before. Declaring the conformance is the only route into synthesis; the field types then fix the serialized shape — the owning-tree/identity/back-edge partition is read from the `owned`/`Shared<T>`/`Weak<T>`/borrow annotations, with no further assertion required.

<a id="sec-synthesized-serialize"></a>
#### Synthesized `Serialize`

For an eligible record, the synthesized `Serialize(s: ISerializer)` body is:

1. `s.BeginObject(n)` where `n` is the number of serialized components.
2. For each component in declaration order: `s.WriteFieldName("<name>")` followed by the component's encoding — `s.WriteInt`/`WriteString`/etc. for a primitive or `string`; the nested value's `Serialize(s)` for a serializable record; the enum-name string for an enum; `BeginArray`/per-element encoding/`EndArray` for a collection; `WriteNull` for a null nullable.
3. `s.EndObject()`.

For an eligible enum, the synthesized `Serialize` is `s.WriteString("<member-name>")` (no surrounding object) — no failing case exists ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)).

<a id="sec-synthesized-deserialize"></a>
#### Synthesized `Deserialize`

The synthesized recognized static factory has the value-type return shape of [§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary) — `Deserialize(d: IDeserializer): T` for a record or enum `T` (plain by-value; no `owned`, records and enums being value types). Its body:

1. `d.BeginObject()`; then repeatedly `d.ReadFieldName()` and dispatch on the name, reading each recognized component with the mirror operation (`d.ReadInt`, the nested type's `Deserialize`, etc.) into a local. When a read field name matches no declared component, the synthesized code calls `d.SkipValue()` ([§2.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-serialization-vocabulary)) — it does not itself decide whether an unknown field is an error. Whether reaching an unknown field is permitted is the *deserializer's* configured policy: a strict deserializer (the default) raises `SerializationException` from `ReadFieldName`/`SkipValue` on an unrecognized field; a deserializer configured to tolerate unknown fields skips the value and continues. Then `d.EndObject()`.
2. Construct the result. If the record declares one or more **explicit constructors**, the synthesized `Deserialize` calls the *unique* explicit constructor whose parameter list binds exactly the serialized components, matched by name — compared **case-insensitively**, so the conventional camelCase parameter matches its PascalCase component (`constructor(width: decimal, height: decimal)` binds `Width`/`Height`); `serialized "<name>"` renames do not affect the match, which uses declared identifiers. If explicit constructors exist but none matches, more than one matches, or the case-insensitive comparison leaves a parameter ambiguous between two components, the conformance declaration is a compile error naming the candidates — the same discipline as the class rule above, whose matching this rule shares. A record that declares **no** explicit constructor is constructed directly from the read components at the storage level — the same constructor-bypassing construction that `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)) and `default(T)` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) already perform; for a purely positional record this coincides with calling the auto-generated primary constructor in positional order. For an enum, read the name string and map it to the declared constant (under duplicate constant values, every declared name maps to its value — [§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)).

Field order in the input need not match declaration order — dispatch is by field name. A **missing** required component (one neither present nor `serialized optional`), a **duplicate** field name, a type mismatch, or a name not matching any enum constant raises `SerializationException` unconditionally — these are structural faults in the input regardless of policy. An **unknown** field (present in the input, matching no declared component) is the one case governed by *operation* policy rather than the synthesized code: it is an error by default and is skipped when the deserializer is configured to ignore unknown fields (stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)). This policy is deliberately a property of the deserialization operation, not an annotation on the type — the same type may be read strictly in one context and leniently in another, a decision that belongs to the caller with the input, not to the type's contract (rationale [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection)). The synthesized code is identical regardless of policy: it always skips an unrecognized field via the deserializer; strictness lives entirely in the deserializer. The construction is an ordinary constructor call at a static program point, so a record's field types, nullability, and definite-assignment rules are checked normally; this is the structural reason synthesis is sound where reflection was not ([§5.18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-type-identity-not-reflection)).

<a id="sec-field-name-customization"></a>
#### Field-name customization

By default the synthesized form uses each component's declared name as its serialized field name (and each enum member's declared name as its serialized value). A `serialized` clause on a positional field, an auto-property, or an enum constant customizes this. The clause vocabulary is closed (no user-defined forms, no parameters interpreted by external machinery, no runtime introspection — this is a compiler-recognized declaration modifier in the sense of [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)'s narrow-modifier escape hatch, deliberately *not* an attribute system). It expresses three independent effects — rename, exclude, tolerate — where rename and tolerate may combine and exclude is mutually exclusive with both:

- **`serialized "<name>"`** — the component is serialized and deserialized under `<name>` instead of its declared identifier. The string must be a non-empty literal and must be unique among the serialized names of the type's components (a collision is a compile error at the conformance declaration, mirroring the eligibility-error discipline). On an enum constant, the constant is encoded as `<name>` rather than its identifier.
- **`serialized optional`** — read/write tolerance for that component. On write, if the component is a nullable `T?` whose value is null, the field is omitted (rather than written as `WriteNull`); otherwise it is written normally. On read, a missing field yields `default(T)` instead of raising `SerializationException`; a present field is read normally. This is the per-field, *missing*-field tolerant-mode opt-in; it is orthogonal to the *unknown*-field policy, which is a property of the deserialization operation (the deserializer's configuration, stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)) rather than of the member or the type — the two leniencies compose freely. Not admitted on enum constants.
- **`serialized "<name>" optional`** — both of the above on the same component: renamed *and* tolerant. This is the common real-world case (an externally-named field that may be absent), so the grammar admits the combination directly rather than forcing a choice.
- **`serialized skip`** — the component is excluded from both directions entirely. The synthesized `Serialize` does not write it; the synthesized `Deserialize` does not read it and supplies the component's `default(T)` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) to the constructor. A `serialized skip` component whose type has no well-defined default is a compile error at the conformance declaration (the synthesized `Deserialize` would have no value to construct with). `skip` is mutually exclusive with a name or `optional` (excluding a field and renaming/tolerating it are contradictory; the grammar does not admit the combination). Not admitted on enum constants ([Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a) grammar note): an enum value is a single member, not an omittable field.

The clause attaches to the member it affects and is total: a component with no `serialized` clause is coded under its own name, always. There is no separate exhaustive key list to keep synchronized, so adding a component never silently drops it from serialization — the failure mode of an all-or-nothing customization list (rationale [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection)) does not arise. A `serialized` clause on a member of a type that declares no serialization conformance, or on a member of a type whose serialization is hand-written (synthesis suppressed — see below), is a compile error: the clause only has meaning as an input to synthesis, and silently ignoring it would be the kind of inert-looking-but-load-bearing annotation [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred) warns against.

`serialized skip` interacts with the eligibility rule by *removing* its component from consideration: a field that would otherwise make the type ineligible (a non-serializable component type) but is marked `serialized skip` does not disqualify the type, because it is no longer a serialized component. This is the supported way to make an otherwise-eligible record serializable when one field is of a non-serializable type and is not needed in the encoded form.

<a id="sec-choice-serialization"></a>
#### Choice serialization

A choice ([§35](#sec-choices)) opts in by declaring `: ISerializable` / `: IDeserializable`, exactly as records and enums do. A choice is **serialization-eligible** when it is value-like ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) and every payload field's type is serialization-eligible and record-admissible (value-shaped storage throughout; the borrow-bearing and owning classifications are never eligible — the same `Deserialize`-has-no-owner argument as for class-typed record fields). An ineligible conformance declaration is the compile error above, naming the first offending payload.

**Wire shape.** The synthesized `Serialize` writes an object whose distinguished leading field is the **case discriminator** `"$case"` — the case's declared name, or its `serialized "<name>"` rename — followed by the active case's payload fields by name, in declaration order, each encoded per its component rule; a payload-free case writes the object with only the discriminator. The `$case` field name joins the `$`-reserved set of stdlib [§2.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-concrete-serialization-formats)'s JSON mapping; a payload rename beginning with `$` is a compile error. The synthesized `Deserialize` reads the discriminator **first**, consumed by case dispatch before any component binding — it is structural, not a data field, and is never subject to `serialized optional` or the unknown-field policy, exactly the polymorphic-registry discipline above; an undeclared discriminator string raises `SerializationException`, as does an object that does not lead with the discriminator (dispatch must select the case before component binding can begin); the selected case's payloads then read under the standard missing/duplicate/unknown rules, and the value is constructed by the case's own construction form. The `serialized` clause on a **case** admits the rename form only (a case is not omittable — the enum-constant rule); on a **payload field** the full vocabulary applies (`skip` requiring a defaultable payload type). A choice all of whose cases are payload-free still writes the object form (uniformity; such a type should usually be an enum).

<a id="sec-suppression-and-interaction"></a>
#### Suppression and interaction

Hand-writing `Serialize` (respectively a recognized static `Deserialize`) **suppresses** synthesis of that direction, exactly as a manually declared `Equals`/`GetHashCode` suppresses auto-equality. The two directions are independent: a type may synthesize one and hand-write the other. Declaring `: ISerializable` without an eligible structure and without a hand-written `Serialize` is the compile error above; declaring it *with* a hand-written `Serialize` is always valid regardless of eligibility (the hand-written body is the contract).

Synthesis composes with auto-equality and `ToString`: a body record may be simultaneously auto-hashable and serialization-eligible; the feature sets are independent packages over the same auto-properties, each scoping the shared [§9.2](#sec-body-records) membership computation with its own clause. The `serialized` clause affects only serialization synthesis — it has no effect on auto-equality, `ToString`, `with`, or any other use of the member — and `equality skip` ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)) affects only auto-equality: **a clause never crosses packages' participation** (`equality skip` does not hide a member from the wire; `serialized skip` does not change what `=` compares). The one shared reading is the **eligibility gate**, and it runs in one direction only: where this section reuses §9.2's membership conditions to decide whether synthesis can run at all, a member skipped by *either* clause is not "a member outside the §9.2 list" for **this section's** eligibility check — which is what keeps a record with an equality-skipped explicit cache field serialization-eligible with no second clause (explicit fields were never serialized components, so the one clause suffices). The equality package's own gate reads `equality skip` alone ([§9.2](#sec-equality-skip)): a `serialized skip` never rescues an equality-inadmissible component. The `serialized` clause is a single closed grammar production ([Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a)); apart from it, `: ISerializable, IDeserializable` is ordinary interface-conformance syntax ([§11](#sec-classes-and-interfaces)) and the normative content is the eligibility rule, the generated-body semantics, and the customization semantics defined here. The wire shapes are normative so that independent implementations agree; the rationale for the specific choices (names not integers for enums, declaration order, key/value-pair dictionaries) and for the modifier-not-attribute design is in [§5.19](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-serialization-without-reflection).

---

<a id="sec-enums"></a>
## 10. Enums

An enum is a value type whose values are drawn from a fixed, named set of constants. Each value is backed by an integer at runtime. An enum is not implicitly convertible to or from its underlying integer type.

<a id="sec-basic-syntax"></a>
### 10.1 Basic syntax

```bezel
enum Priority
  Low, Medium, High;
end Priority;
```

This declares constants `Priority.Low`, `Priority.Medium`, `Priority.High` of type `Priority`. The default underlying values are 0, 1, 2 — assigned in declaration order from zero.

<a id="sec-explicit-values"></a>
### 10.2 Explicit values

```bezel
enum HttpStatus
  Ok := 200,
  Created := 201,
  NotFound := 404,
  ServerError := 500;
end HttpStatus;
```

Values must be compile-time constants ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) of the underlying type. Unspecified values continue from the previous explicit value, incrementing by 1.

**Duplicate constant values.** Two or more constants of one enum may share an underlying value, whether written explicitly (`Legacy := 1, Current := 1`) or produced by auto-increment continuation. Aliasing is legal and draws no diagnostic; but since an enum value *is* its underlying integer ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type)), same-valued constants denote **one value**: `Legacy = Current` is `true`, and no construct can distinguish them at run time. Three consequences follow from that identity: in a `case` over the enum, two arms — or two `|` alternatives — naming same-valued constants are a **compile error**, the later one being unreachable; exhaustiveness ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)) is over the set of distinct declared *values*, so an arm naming either alias covers both; and serialization synthesis ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)) writes the **first-declared** constant's name for a shared value and accepts every declared name on read.

<a id="sec-underlying-type"></a>
### 10.3 Underlying type

The default underlying type is `int`. A different integer type may be specified with a colon:

```bezel
enum HttpStatus: short
  Ok := 200,
  NotFound := 404;
end HttpStatus;
```

The underlying type must be one of `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort`, `int`, `uint`, `long`, `ulong`. All declared values must fit in the underlying type's range.

<a id="sec-methods-properties-static-members"></a>
### 10.4 Methods, properties, static members

An enum may declare instance methods, expression-bodied read-only properties, static methods, static read-only fields (including `static owned readonly`), `const` members, and operator overloads ([§25](#sec-operator-overloading); grammar A.3):

```bezel
enum Priority
  Low, Medium, High;

  public method IsUrgent(): bool => this = High;

  public property Name: string => (case this of
    Low => "Low",
    Medium => "Medium",
    High => "High");

  public static readonly All: Array<Priority> := [Low, Medium, High];

  public static method Parse(text: string): Priority?
    return (case text of
      "Low" => Low,
      "Medium" => Medium,
      "High" => High,
      _ => null);
  end Parse;
end Priority;
```

Inside an instance method, `this` refers to the current enum value.

The `Name` property's `case` lists only the declared constants, and that coverage is total: every value of `Priority` is a declared constant ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)), so the case expression is statically exhaustive over the whole value space and cannot raise `MatchFailureException` ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)). No defensive `_` arm is needed — or wanted: a `_` arm would silence the missing-arm diagnostic when a constant is added.

Static readonly fields on enums are initialized lazily on first use, following the same rules as class static fields ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)). Enum constants are compile-time values and are available before any static readonly initializer runs; a static readonly field initializer on an enum may freely reference the enum's declared constants.

Enum statics carry the full class-static surface rules. A `const` member (grammar A.4 `StaticConstDecl`) follows [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s class-level `const` rules: implicitly static, compile-time-constant initializer, primitive or `string` type. A static readonly field of class type may be marked `owned` — `public static owned readonly Cache: ConnectionPool := new ConnectionPool();` — enrolling it in [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit disposal; without `owned`, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s resource-bearing-static warning and its add-`owned` remedy apply on enums exactly as on classes. (Appendix A.4 `StaticReadonlyDecl` carries the `owned` slot.)

**The compiler-provided integer tier.** Every enum `E` with underlying type `U` ([§10.3](#sec-underlying-type)) carries one **compiler-provided** static member — no declaration is written, and no user declaration may override or overload it (it joins the type's surface the way [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s compiler-provided conformances join the primitives):

```bezel
public static method FromUnderlyingOrNull(value: U): E?;
```

`FromUnderlyingOrNull` returns the declared constant whose underlying value equals `value`, or `null` when there is none. It is **total** — it never raises. Under duplicate constant values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)) the result is the shared value (all aliases denote it). The parameter type is the underlying type `U` exactly: a wider integer in hand is narrowed explicitly first ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions), checked), keeping the two failure modes — out of `U`'s range vs. not a declared value — separately visible. The member is the branch-shaped tier beside the checked cast (stdlib §1's `*OrNull` tier): `E(n)` treats an undeclared value as a bug at the call site ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)); `E.FromUnderlyingOrNull(n)` lets boundary code state its policy in one line:

```bezel
// A parser validating a wire-read value (wire, trusted: int; ProtocolException
// stands for a user exception class):
var p := Priority.FromUnderlyingOrNull(wire)
         ?? throw new ProtocolException($"bad priority {wire}");    // reject
var p2 := Priority.FromUnderlyingOrNull(wire) ?? Priority.Low;      // tolerate with a default
var p3 := Priority(trusted);   // the checked cast is the assert: failure is a bug (§5.4)
```

<a id="sec-restrictions"></a>
### 10.5 Restrictions

An enum may not declare:

- Instance fields (the runtime representation is the underlying integer).
- Constructors.
- Block-form properties or properties with backing storage.
- Nested types.
- Indexers.
- Inheritance from another type.

Enum methods may not be declared `virtual`, `abstract`, `override`, or `sealed override`. Enums are implicitly sealed (no inheritance) and have no virtual-dispatch surface, so these modifiers carry no meaning on enum members and are rejected at compile time. Enum methods are always dispatched statically.

Static dispatch does not orphan the `Object`-virtual surface. An enum may declare, as plain (non-`override`) members, `Equals` taking the enum's own type (as [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s co-declaration rule already requires alongside an `=` overload), `GetHashCode(): int`, and `ToString(): string`. Each **replaces the compiler-generated default for every consumer**: direct calls, hash containers (`Set<E>` and `Dictionary<E, V>` reach the user's `Equals`/`GetHashCode`), string interpolation ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)), and virtual dispatch through a boxed reference ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) — the compiler populates the enum's box vtable with these members, a static wiring that is well-defined because enums are sealed. There is no override chain and no `base` access; the user member simply *is* the enum's implementation of that surface.

An enum may implement one or more interfaces. The interface names appear after the underlying type (if any) following a colon. The enum must provide matching public members for every interface member:

```bezel
enum Priority: IComparable<Priority>
  Low, Medium, High;

  public method CompareTo(other: Priority): int =>
    (when
      int(this) < int(other) => -1,
      int(this) > int(other) => 1,
      _ => 0);
end Priority;
```

When both an underlying type and interfaces are specified, the underlying type comes first: `enum Priority: int, IComparable<Priority>`.

<a id="sec-case-matching"></a>
### 10.6 Case matching

Inside a `case` whose scrutinee is an enum, the enum prefix may be omitted:

```bezel
case p of
  Low => Console.WriteLine("low"),
  Medium | High => Console.WriteLine("medium or high")
end;
```

---

<a id="sec-classes-and-interfaces"></a>
## 11. Classes and Interfaces

<a id="sec-class-declaration"></a>
### 11.1 Class declaration

A class is a reference type with optional inheritance, optional interfaces, and a member body:

```bezel
public class BankAccount: IBankAccount
  // members
end BankAccount;
```

A class may declare at most one base class and any number of interfaces. The base class, if any, is listed first, followed by interfaces, all comma-separated. There is no semicolon after the inheritance list.

If no base class is specified, the implicit base is `Object`.

<a id="sec-primary-constructors"></a>
#### Primary constructors

A class may declare parameters in parentheses after its name, analogous to a record's positional fields:

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal): IBankAccount
  private _name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;
end BankAccount;
```

The compiler generates a primary constructor whose parameter list matches the parenthesized declaration. The primary constructor's parameters are in scope throughout the class body — including field initializers, property initializers, the inheritance clause's base call, and the bodies of methods, properties, constructors, and destructors. Parameters referenced only in initializers do not generate backing fields; parameters referenced in method, property, constructor, or destructor bodies are captured into compiler-generated private fields. The capture is invisible at the source level — the parameter name resolves to the parameter in initializer positions and to the captured field in body positions, and the two reads observe the same value.

For each primary-constructor parameter, the compiler does **not** generate an auto-property (unlike records). The parameters are initialization-time values, optionally captured for body use; the class author decides which fields or properties to declare publicly. This keeps the class's public API explicit.

If the class has a base class that requires constructor arguments, the base's arguments appear in parentheses after the base class name in the inheritance list:

```bezel
public class SavingsAccount(name: string, balance: decimal, rate: decimal): BankAccount(name, balance)
  private _rate: decimal := rate;
end SavingsAccount;
```

This desugars to a primary constructor that chains to `base(name, balance)` before executing field initializers.

A class with a primary constructor may also declare additional constructors in its body using the `constructor` keyword; such constructors must chain to the primary constructor via `this(...)`:

```bezel
public class BankAccount(name: string, initialBalance: decimal)
  private _name: string := name;
  private _balance: decimal := initialBalance;

  public constructor(name: string)
    this(name, 0m);
  end constructor;
end BankAccount;
```

The primary constructor's visibility follows the class's visibility. The body may not redeclare a constructor with the same parameter list as the primary constructor.

Primary constructors interact with `owned` parameters: a primary-constructor parameter may be declared `owned`, and the same ownership-transfer rules as regular constructor parameters apply:

```bezel
public class ResourceHolder(owned resource: Stream)
  private owned _resource: Stream := resource;
end ResourceHolder;
```

An `owned` primary-constructor parameter referenced in a *body* position is captured as an `owned` field and disposed with the object; combining a body reference with an initializer that consumes the parameter is a compile error ([§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)).

<a id="sec-interface-declaration"></a>
### 11.2 Interface declaration

*(A class member implementing a `pure` interface member is declared `pure` — [§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch). Interface members may carry contract clauses, inherited by implementations and never restated; multi-root contracts combine per [§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance).)*

```bezel
interface IBankAccount
  method Deposit(amount: decimal);
  method Withdraw(amount: decimal);
  property Balance: decimal;
  readonly property AccountNumber: string;
  readonly property BalanceChanged: IEvent<BalanceChangedEvent>;
end IBankAccount;
```

Interface members are implicitly public, have no body, and end with `;`. A class implements an interface implicitly: by declaring matching public members.

A member **matches** an interface member when it is declared `public`, has the same name, the same arity, the same parameter modifiers (`ref`, `out`, `owned`, `scoped`), parameter types that are exactly equal under the interface's substitution, and a return type that is exactly equal under the interface's substitution. One narrow widening is permitted on parameter types:

1. **Nullability widening on parameters.** An implementation may declare a parameter as `T?` where the interface requires `T` (the implementation accepts more inputs than the interface promises to pass). The reverse — interface `T?`, implementation `T` — is rejected, because the implementation would refuse a `null` the interface promised to accept.
2. **No widening elsewhere.** Parameter types other than the nullability case must match exactly. Return types must match exactly (no covariance in this version). Parameter modifiers must match exactly: an interface declaring `out T` requires the implementation to declare `out T`, and the same applies to `ref`, `owned`, and `scoped`.

The asymmetry on nullability mirrors the standard contravariant-parameter / covariant-return reasoning: implementations may accept more than they were asked to. Bezel admits the parameter-nullability case because it is the common one (most concrete `Equals` implementations want to accept `null` cleanly), and because the type system can verify it without further machinery. The same allowance extends to `override` declarations ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)).

<a id="sec-owned-in-interface-signatures"></a>
#### `owned` in interface signatures

The "must match exactly" rule above applies to every position where `owned` may appear, compared — like the parameter and return types — **under the interface's substitution**: for a slot whose declared type is a bare type parameter of the interface, the marker is read from the substituted signature, so at a value or runtime-managed implementing type a declared `owned` marker is erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)) and the implementation is spelled without the marker (which the concrete type would reject). For concretely-typed slots, an implementing method's signature and the interface method's signature must agree on:

- **`owned` as a parameter modifier** (e.g. `M(owned t: T)`). Interface declaring `M(owned t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(owned t: T)`. Either both have `owned` or neither does.
- **`owned` on an `out` parameter** (e.g. `M(out owned t: T)`). Interface declaring `M(out owned t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(out owned t: T)`; interface declaring `M(out t: T)` requires implementation to declare `M(out t: T)`.
- **Use of an owning generic type** (e.g. `M(): OwningTask<T>`). Interface declaring `M(): OwningTask<T>` requires implementation to declare `M(): OwningTask<T>`; interface declaring `M(): Task<T>` requires implementation to declare `M(): Task<T>`. (Per [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument), `OwningTask<T>` and `Task<T>` are distinct named types with no implicit conversion; the same applies to `OwningArray<T>` vs `Array<T>` and the other owning/borrowing collection pairs.)
- **`owned` inside function-type parameters or return types** (e.g. `M(callback: (owned T) -> ())`). Same rule — exact match.

A mismatch in any position is a compile error at the implementing class. Two reasons for the strict rule:

1. **Loosening from `owned T` to `T` in a return type would leak ownership.** If the interface declares `Acquire(): OwningTask<Connection>` and the implementation declares `Acquire(): Task<Connection>`, callers calling through the interface receive `OwningTask<Connection>` per the static type and write `using var c := await source.Acquire();`. But the implementation produced a Pattern A task whose result is borrowed — the `using var` would dispose a borrow whose source is the task, which is also being disposed, leaving the disposal pattern incoherent.

2. **Tightening from `T` to `owned T` in a parameter would create undischarged ownership.** If the interface declares `Send(payload: T)` and the implementation declares `Send(owned payload: T)`, callers calling through the interface pass a borrow per the interface contract, but the implementation expects ownership transfer. The implementation would attempt to take ownership of a value the caller intended to retain, leaving the value's original owner with a dangling reference.

Bezel's stance is uniform: `owned` is part of the type-and-modifier signature, and signatures match exactly. There is no `owned`-direction variance.

**`scoped` in interface signatures.** The same exact-match rule
covers the `scoped` modifier, in both directions, for the same reason there is
no `owned`-direction variance: a `scoped`/unscoped mismatch changes the
*caller's* contract. An implementation adding `scoped` to a parameter the
interface declares plain would retain a callback — or store a class-typed
borrow — that callers through the interface admitted under a call-bounded,
non-retaining contract ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters),
[§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)): their captures were never checked against
a bound, and a class-typed argument was never marked or frozen — a
use-after-free shape. An implementation *dropping* the interface's `scoped`
is the safe direction semantically (the callee retains less than announced),
but it is rejected all the same: `scoped` is part of a function type's
identity ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)) and never distinguishes overloads
([§22.6](#sec-overloading)), so the matching rule that keeps signatures exact
elsewhere keeps it exact here — any variance would be a third, position-local
rule with no compensating capability. (This governs the **top-level**
parameter modifier; `scoped` *inside* a function-typed parameter's type was
always caught by the exact-type-equality clause above.)

An observable contract on an interface is an ordinary get-only property of type `IEvent<T>` (or `IAsyncEvent<T>`) — the interface face of the stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) event pattern, as `BalanceChanged` above (interface `event` members are retired with the member kind, [§24](#sec-events)). The implementing class satisfies it with the pattern's borrowing property; consumers reach only `Subscribe`.

An interface may extend other interfaces:

```bezel
interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

Multiple-interface inheritance is permitted. Diamond resolution: a single implementation in the implementing class satisfies all interface methods with the same signature. A read-write member satisfies a read-only interface member of the same name and type: if `IReadOnlyList<T>` declares `readonly property [i: int]: T` and `IList<T>` declares `property [i: int]: T`, a single read-write indexer in the implementing class satisfies both. `Add`, `Clear`, `Remove`, and the rest of the mutating surface in the example above are inherited from `ICollection<T>`. `Count` reaches `IList<T>` through two inheritance paths — through `IReadOnlyList<T>` via `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, and through `ICollection<T>` via `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` again — but both paths substitute to the same property declared on `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, so the implementing class satisfies both inherited declarations with a single property.

<a id="sec-member-body"></a>
### 11.3 Member body

A class body may contain fields, methods, properties, indexers, constructors, a destructor, operator overloads, nested types, and class-level constants.

Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly ([§13](#sec-visibility)). Interface members do not declare visibility (they are always public).

A type may not declare two members that are not distinguishable from each other. Two members **clash** when they have the same name and the type system cannot tell them apart: two fields, properties, or nested types with the same name; or two methods, constructors, or operator overloads with the same name that are not distinguishable as overloads ([§22.6](#sec-overloading)) — that is, that do not differ in number of parameters, parameter types, or the `ref`/`out` modifiers in a participating position (`owned` — ordinary or on `out` — and `scoped` never distinguish overloads, [§22.6](#sec-overloading)). A non-overloadable member — a field, property, or nested type — additionally clashes with **any** other member of the type that shares its name, regardless of kind: within a type a given name belongs either to exactly one non-overloadable member or to a single overload family of methods, constructors, or operators. A clash is a compile error at the second declaration, reported at the type, and names the conflicting members. Legal overloads — members of the same name that *are* distinguishable per [§22.6](#sec-overloading) — are unaffected; this rule rejects only the duplicates that overloading does not admit. The same rule applies to interface members within an interface declaration.

<a id="sec-block-endings"></a>
### 11.4 Block endings

A class ends with `end ClassName;`. Members may end with `end MemberName;` or `end;`; the named form is recommended. Control structures inside method bodies may end with plain `end;` or repeat their introducing keyword ([§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination)).

<a id="sec-modifier-order"></a>
### 11.5 Modifier order

When a member declaration carries multiple modifiers, they appear in this order:

```
visibility static (async | pure) (abstract | virtual | override | sealed override) (owned | scoped) readonly member-kind Name ...
```

`abstract`, `virtual`, `override`, and `sealed override` are mutually exclusive — at most one may appear. A non-virtual member carries none of them. `sealed override` seals a previously-virtual member against further overriding. `sealed` alone is a class-level modifier that prevents inheritance ([§12.4](#sec-sealing)); it does not appear on individual members.

`owned` ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)) — or, on function-typed fields, `scoped` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), which occupies the same slot and is mutually exclusive with it — appears between the virtual-modifier slot and `readonly`. It applies only to fields; methods, properties, and other members do not carry `owned`.
