The combination `static owned readonly` is the canonical form for a static field that owns a long-lived resource ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)).

The compiler rejects out-of-order modifiers.

<a id="sec-nested-types"></a>
### 11.6 Nested types

A class body may declare nested classes, records, enums, and interfaces. Nested types may be `public`, `internal`, `protected`, or `private`, and the visibility keyword is **required**: a nested type is a class member ([§11.3](#sec-member-body)), and [§13.3](#sec-class-members)'s explicit-visibility rule applies with no exception for nested types — omitting the keyword is a compile error, not a default. (The `Visibility?` in the reused type-declaration grammar productions serves [§13.2](#sec-top-level-types)'s default-`internal` rule for *top-level* declarations only; Appendix A.4 `NestedTypeDecl`.) A nested type's effective visibility is the more restrictive of its declared visibility and its enclosing class's visibility.

```bezel
public class Parser
  public record Token(Kind: TokenKind, Text: string, Line: int);

  public enum TokenKind
    Identifier, Number, Operator, EndOfFile;
  end TokenKind;
end Parser;
```

A nested type is referenced from outside as `Outer.Nested`. A nested class has access to all members (including `private`) of its enclosing class when it holds an instance of the enclosing class. The enclosing class similarly has full access to its nested types' members.

Nested types may themselves contain nested types. Nested types in records are permitted but uncommon.

A nested type is a *member* and lives in a type body; it is distinct from a **method-local** `record`/`enum` ([§21.10](#sec-local-type-declarations)), which is a body-scoped *statement* with no access surface. The visibility rules are deliberately opposite: a nested type **requires** the keyword (above), a local type **forbids** it — a member has an access surface to declare, a local does not. A local record's own body may itself contain §11.6 nested member types, which follow their own rules.

<a id="sec-static-classes"></a>
### 11.7 Static classes

A class declared `static` may contain only static members:

```bezel
public static class Utils
  public static method Max(a: int, b: int): int => (if a > b then a else b);
end Utils;
```

A static class may not be instantiated: `new` on a static class is a compile error. A static class may not have instance fields, instance methods, instance properties, indexers, constructors (other than a static constructor), or destructors. **Static `owned` fields are permitted:** `static owned readonly` fields and static owning-inline-array fields participate in [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit disposal exactly as on any other type — that mechanism is runtime-driven and independent of instance `Dispose()`. A static class may not be inherited from and does not implement interfaces.

Because a static class cannot be instantiated, it does not implement `IDisposable` — the compiler-generated `Dispose()` rule ([§8.7](#sec-dispose-is-not-on-object), [§28](#sec-resource-management)) applies only to non-static classes. The `abstract` and `static` modifiers are mutually exclusive, and `sealed` and `static` are mutually exclusive; combining either pair is a compile error. A class declared with the **`closed`** modifier is a **closed abstract class**: a class that cannot be instantiated directly and cannot be inherited from outside the declaring module. Classes derived from a `closed` base must be declared in the same module; the compiler rejects subclasses in other modules. A `closed` class may declare abstract members ([§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)) without carrying the `abstract` modifier — `closed` subsumes it — and combining `closed` with `abstract`, `sealed`, or `static` is a compile error. (Through v0.241 the semantics were spelled as the modifier pair `sealed abstract`; that spelling is rejected, the diagnostic naming `closed`.) The `closed` modifier is the recommended way to define a closed hierarchy for exhaustive `case` matching ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)):

```bezel
public closed class Shape
  public abstract method Area(): double;
end Shape;

public sealed class Circle(radius: double): Shape
  public readonly property Radius: double := radius;
  public override method Area(): double => Math.Pi * Radius * Radius;
end Circle;

public sealed class Square(side: double): Shape
  public readonly property Side: double := side;
  public override method Area(): double => Side * Side;
end Square;

public sealed class Triangle(baseLength: double, height: double): Shape
  public readonly property Base: double := baseLength;
  public readonly property Height: double := height;
  public override method Area(): double => 0.5 * Base * Height;
end Triangle;
```

Because `Shape` is `closed`, no class outside the declaring module may extend it. The compiler can therefore prove exhaustiveness of `case` matches over `Shape` without requiring a `_` arm, even across module boundaries.

<a id="sec-static-interface-members"></a>
### 11.8 Static interface members

An interface member may be declared `static`: a contract the conforming **type** — not an instance — must satisfy. Static interface members are **abstract-only** (no default bodies; the same diamond-avoidance posture as the declined default interface methods, rationale §17.4) and may be **methods** or **operators**; static constants and properties are deferred (spell a constant as a nullary method: `Zero()`).

```bezel
interface INumber<T> where T: INumber<T>
  static method Zero(): owned T;
  static operator +(a: T, b: T): owned T;
  static operator *(a: T, b: T): owned T;
end INumber;
```

**The recurrence constraint.** The self-referential form `where T: INumber<T>` is the ordinary generic-constraint machinery — no new syntax, no `Self` keyword (deliberately declined for v1: the recurrence is explicit and already expressible). A conforming type declares `class Meters: INumber<Meters>` and supplies the static members with exact signatures (the §11.2 matching rule, applied to statics) — exact against the **substituted** signature: at a value or runtime-managed conforming type a declared `owned` return or `out owned` slot is erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), so the witness is spelled without the marker (which would be a compile error on the concrete type); a class or interface conformer spells the marker exactly, and its witness bodies are checked under the ordinary transfer rules — a fresh value on every return path ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)).

**Dispatch through the type parameter.** In a generic body whose parameter `T` carries a static-interface constraint, `T.Member(...)` calls the conforming type's static member, and an operator applied to `T`-typed operands resolves through the constraint's static operators. Resolution happens **at instantiation** — a statement about *semantics*, not implementation strategy: the binding of `T.Member(...)`, and of constraint-sourced operators ([§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)), is fixed per concrete type argument, exactly as if each instantiation were compiled separately. An implementation may realize this by per-instantiation specialization or by shared code carrying a per-instantiation dispatch table — rationale §10's recorded strategy does both, specializing value-type substitutions and sharing reference-type ones — so long as the observable binding is the conforming type's member:

```bezel
public static method Sum<T>(items: Array<T>): owned T where T: INumber<T>
  var total := T.Zero();                          // owned at class/interface T; a plain value otherwise
  for var x in items do total := total + x; end;  // fresh result in; displaced total disposed (§28.7)
  return total;                                   // transfers; a by-value return at value T
end Sum;
```

At a class or interface substitution of `T`, `total` is an owned local: `T.Zero()` and each operator result transfer per stdlib §2.19's `owned` producer signatures, the loop's reassignment disposes the displaced previous total by drop-on-overwrite ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), and the `return` transfers to the caller. At value and runtime-managed substitutions the markers are erased and every step is a plain copy ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

**Static-member interfaces as ordinary types.** Declaring static members does not remove an interface from the ordinary type grammar: it remains usable as a variable, field, parameter, or return type, as a boxing target, and as an `is`/`is not`/`as` operand ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as)) — the tests behave as for any interface, since a runtime type conforms only by declaring the full member set, statics included, so there is no partial-conformance state to probe. Two consequences are normative. (1) Static interface members contribute **nothing to the instance surface**: through an interface-typed *value* only instance members are reachable, and calling a static member on the interface *name* (`INumber<int>.Zero()`) is a compile error — the interface declares no bodies to run. `T.Member(...)` dispatch requires a generic type **parameter** constrained by the interface: a value's static type names no single conforming type, so "static dispatch through a value" would be hidden dynamic dispatch, which Bezel declines. (2) An interface that declares static members may not mark its type parameters variant (`in`/`out`, [§12.9](#sec-variance)) — a compile error at the declaration: variance is defined by instance-reference assignability, the position rules have no recorded reading for static signatures, and invariance keeps the question closed until a use case arrives (recorded v1 bound, liftable).

**Primitive conformances (compiler-provided).** The primitive numeric tower (`byte`…`ulong`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`) conforms to the standard-library `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>`/`IParsable<T>` interfaces, and `char` to `ISteppable<char>`/`IParsable<char>` (stdlib §2.19), **without declaring them**: primitive operators are compiler intrinsics (§3.5), so the compiler bridges the intrinsic/declared split by treating each primitive as conforming with its intrinsic operations as the member bodies. User code observes no difference from a declared conformance. The bridge covers not only the intrinsic/declared operator split but also the `IParsable<T>.TryParse` **out-nullability** shape: the per-type witnesses declare `out result: T` (a concrete value type), while the interface declares `out owned value: T?` — the nullability required for user class conformers, for which `default(T)` is a compile error ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). A call through the constraint observes the declared slot under the class assumption, erased at value substitutions; a direct call observes `out result: T`. The stdlib §2.19 producer markers themselves (`owned` returns; the `out owned` slot) ask nothing extra of the bridge: at every primitive conformer they are erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)), so the intrinsic value operations witness the erased — unmarked — signatures directly.

**What this unblocks:** promoting the name-recognized `FromCollectionLiteral` (§15.4.1) to a real `ICollectionLiteralTarget<T>` and `IDeserializable`'s `Deserialize` (stdlib §2.14) to a true static interface method — both signatures were chosen for zero-source-change promotion; and replacing §16's compiler-intrinsic `Range<T>` element restriction with an `ISteppable<T>` constraint.

---

<a id="sec-inheritance-and-dispatch"></a>
## 12. Inheritance and Dispatch

<a id="sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default"></a>
### 12.1 Members are non-virtual by default

*(Purity at override boundaries: an `override` of a `pure` member restates `pure` — omission is a compile error; an override may add `pure` where the base is not (usable through the derived static type only); purity never narrows down a chain — [§22.15](#sec-pure-dispatch). Contract clauses at override boundaries: inherited verbatim, never restated; an override may add `ensures` and may not declare `requires` — [§22.16](#sec-contract-inheritance).)*

A method, property, or indexer is non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. To override a virtual member in a derived class, mark the matching member `override`. Visibility, return type, parameter types, and parameter modifiers must match the base member exactly, with one allowance: an override may declare a parameter as `T?` where the overridden member declares `T` — the same contravariant nullability widening [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration) grants interface implementations, admitted here for the same recorded reason (the override accepts more inputs than the virtual slot promises to pass; the reasoning applies verbatim). Widening is **monotone down the chain**: an override matches against the *nearest* overridden declaration, so once a parameter is `T?` a further override must keep it `T?` — narrowing back would let a `null` admitted through an intermediate static type reach a non-nullable parameter. The reverse direction (overridden `T?`, override `T`) is rejected, as in §11.2. Return types must still match exactly (no covariance in this version).

Parameter modifiers that must match: `ref`, `out`, `owned`, `scoped` (a `scoped`/unscoped mismatch changes the caller's capture/freeze contract in both directions, [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)). The `when true`/`when false` postcondition clause on an `out` parameter ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)) must match exactly as well — an override may neither add nor drop it. Return modifiers that must match: `owned`. A mismatch — for example, a base method declaring `Foo(owned x: T)` and the override declaring `Foo(x: T)` — is a compile error. The compiler does not infer or relax these modifiers across the override boundary, because they affect the method's contract rather than its implementation.

Fields, constructors, destructors, and static members may not be virtual.

<a id="sec-hiding-is-not-allowed"></a>
### 12.2 Hiding is not allowed

Declaring a member in a derived class with the same name as **any** inherited member **visible at the derived class's declaration site** is a compile error, unless the declaration is an `override` of a virtual member with a matching signature per [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) — exact, except for the parameter-nullability widening (`T` → `T?`) that §12.1 admits. This holds even when the signatures differ: a derived class cannot add an overload to an inherited method's name, and an inherited overload set does not extend across the inheritance boundary (Appendix C.1). To override a virtual base member, use `override`. To add a new member, choose a different name.

**The blocked-name set.** `public` and `protected` base members always block; an `internal` base member blocks exactly when it is visible at the derived declaration site ([§13.4](#sec-modules-and-internal) — the base class is in the same module); a `private` base member never blocks — two same-named `private` fields in base and derived are distinct members and legal, and a base class adding a `private` member is never a source-breaking change for subclasses that cannot see it — except that a derived class nested inside the base class ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)) sees the base's `private` members and is blocked by them. The rule's recorded motivation is shadowing a member the author *could see* (rationale [§8.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-member-hiding-is-forbidden)); an invisible member confuses no reader and no dispatch. When a base member was invisible at the derived declaration site, the derived declaration creates a **distinct member**: no override relationship and no shared overload family exist between the two. Name lookup — which already filters by visibility — *selects* a member by the receiver's static type ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)); the selected member then dispatches per its own §12.1 virtual-ness (an `internal virtual` base member keeps its own override chain). An access through the derived type's surface reaches the derived member; an access through a base-typed receiver reaches the base member — for every caller, including one that can see both. This residual is the deliberate scope of the no-shadow guarantee across module boundaries: a cross-module `internal` name collision is invisible at authoring time, and guarding against it would make a module's non-public member names a compatibility contract.

The rule is not limited to instance members. A static member's name is likewise unavailable for redeclaration in a derived class — static members cannot be virtual ([§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default)), so no `override` escape exists for them. Operator declarations are covered **per operator token**: a derived class may not declare an `operator <op>` overload when any base class declares an overload of the same token, whatever the parameter types. This is what keeps [§25.2](#sec-operator-overloading-restrictions)'s inherited-operator candidate set duplicate-free within a single inheritance chain — a chain contributes at most one declaring type per operator token, so derived-operand resolution never faces a base-vs-derived intra-chain ambiguity.

<a id="sec-base-member"></a>
### 12.3 `base.Member`

Inside a derived member, `base.Name(...)` calls the base class's implementation, bypassing virtual dispatch. `base` is legal only inside instance members of a derived class.

<a id="sec-sealing"></a>
### 12.4 Sealing

`sealed` on an override prevents further overriding. `sealed` on a class prevents inheritance from that class:

```bezel
public sealed override method Speak(): string => "Woof!";

public sealed class Bulldog: Dog
  // ...
end Bulldog;
```

`sealed` may not appear on a non-virtual, non-override member.

<a id="sec-abstract-classes-and-members"></a>
### 12.5 Abstract classes and members

`abstract` on a class permits abstract members and forbids direct instantiation. `abstract` on a member declares it without a body; every concrete subclass must override it.

```bezel
public abstract class Shape
  public abstract method Area(): decimal;
  public abstract property Name: string;

  public method Describe(): string => $"A {Name} with area {Area()}";
end Shape;
```

An abstract member ends with `;` and has no `end`. Abstract members are implicitly virtual; the `virtual` keyword is not written.

A class containing one or more abstract members must itself be `abstract` (or `closed`, [§11.7](#sec-static-classes)). An abstract class need not override every abstract member of its base.

`new` on an abstract or `closed` class is a compile error.

A call to an `abstract` (or any virtual-family) member on `this` from a constructor body is governed by [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction): rejected outside sealed, non-abstract classes.

<a id="sec-async-and-abstract"></a>
### 12.6 `async` and `abstract`

`async abstract` is a compile error. An abstract method whose implementations are expected to be asynchronous declares a `Task` or `Task<T>` return type without `async`:

```bezel
public abstract class DataSource
  public abstract method LoadAsync(): Task<string>;
  public abstract method SaveAsync(data: string): Task;
end DataSource;

public class FileSource: DataSource
  public async override method LoadAsync(): Task<string>
    return await File.ReadAllTextAsync(_path);
  end LoadAsync;

  public async override method SaveAsync(data: string): Task
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(_path, data);
  end SaveAsync;
end FileSource;
```

The same rule applies to interface members.

<a id="sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as"></a>
### 12.7 Type tests: `is`, `is not`, `as`

`is T` tests whether a value is an instance of `T` and produces `bool`. When the test succeeds and the tested expression is a simple variable, the variable is **flow-narrowed** to `T` within the controlled block:

```bezel
if animal is Dog then
  animal.Bark();        // animal narrowed to Dog
end;
```

Narrowing applies to the original variable. Reassignment within the controlled block invalidates the narrowing.

`is null` tests whether the value is null. `is not null` tests whether it is non-null and narrows to the non-nullable form.

`is not T` (for a non-null type T) does not narrow in the true branch (the value could be many non-T types). In the `else` branch, the value is known to be an instance of `T`, and the variable is narrowed to `T`.

In `else` branches: for `is null` and `is not null`, narrowing applies (the variable is known-null or non-null respectively); for `is T`, no narrowing in the else branch (the variable could be many non-T types); for `is not T`, the variable is narrowed to `T` in the else branch.

When two `is` tests are joined with `and`, both narrowings are in effect throughout the combined true branch.

`is` does not bind. There is no `is T name` syntax. To bind, use `as` (a recorded decline-with-reasons — rationale [§11.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-is-does-not-bind)):

```bezel
var dog: Dog? := animal as Dog;
if dog <> null then
  Console.WriteLine(dog.Name);
end;
```

`as` returns the value cast to the target type, or `null` if the cast fails. Its result is always nullable.

**Ownership.** Both `is` and `as` are **non-destructive on their operand**: the operation inspects the runtime type tag without moving from the operand. After `if x is T then ... end`, `x` retains whatever ownership state it had before the test; after `var r := x as T`, `x` still owns (or borrows) what it owned (or borrowed) before. The narrowing that `is` enables ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as) above) and the borrow that `as` produces ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)) do not transfer ownership; transferring ownership across a type test requires an explicit move from the original variable after narrowing.

<a id="sec-constructor-chaining"></a>
### 12.8 Constructor chaining

A derived class's constructor may chain to a base constructor:

```bezel
public constructor(name: string, balance: decimal, rate: decimal)
  base(name, balance);
  _rate := rate;
end constructor;
```

A `base(...)` call, if present, appears before the constructor body — it is syntactically distinct from the body's statements (see grammar A.4, `CtorChain`). If neither `base(...)` nor `this(...)` is written, the compiler inserts an implicit `base()` call (which requires the base class to have a parameterless constructor; otherwise the chain must be explicit).

`this(...)` chains to another constructor in the same class. At most one of `base(...)` or `this(...)` may appear, and only in the chaining position before the body.

A constructor in an abstract class is permitted; it runs only via `base(...)` from a concrete subclass.

<a id="sec-variance"></a>
### 12.9 Variance

Generic interface type parameters may be marked `out` (covariant) or `in` (contravariant):

```bezel
interface IEnumerable<out T>
  method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>;
end IEnumerable;

interface IComparer<in T>
  method Compare(a: T, b: T): int;
end IComparer;
```

`out` requires T to appear only in output positions (return types, read-only property types, `out` parameters). `in` requires T to appear only in input positions. The compiler enforces position constraints.

Position is composed across nested type constructors. A type parameter inside another generic type inherits position from that wrapper's variance: T inside `IEnumerator<T>` (where `IEnumerator` is `out T'`) has the same position the wrapper itself sits in. Function types are themselves variant (covariant in return, contravariant in parameter, see below), and the same composition rule applies. The practical consequence — relevant for event interfaces — is that T appearing inside the *parameter* of a function type that is itself the *parameter* of a method ends up in covariant position, because contravariant-of-contravariant is covariant. A concrete worked example: in `IEvent<out T>` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)), the method `Subscribe(scoped handler: (T) -> ())` places T inside `(T) -> ()` (contravariant in T) which is itself a parameter of `Subscribe` (an input, contravariant), giving T a covariant position overall — `out T` is sound.

Type parameters without `out` or `in` are invariant. Classes, records, and concrete generic types are always invariant — and the variance markers are **interface-only syntax**: `in`/`out` on a generic parameter of a class, record, method, or type alias ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)) is a **compile error** (makes the rejection explicit; the shared `GenericParam` grammar admits the marker everywhere and outside interface declarations it is rejected semantically, Appendix A.4). A marker the language cannot honor must not parse as decoration — `class Box<out T>` silently accepted-and-ignored would promise an assignability the type does not have. Additionally, an interface declaring **static members** may not mark its parameters variant ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)).

Variance applies only when the type argument is a reference type. `IEnumerable<int>` is a perfectly valid type and is used pervasively; what is rejected is the *variant assignment* of `IEnumerable<int>` to `IEnumerable<Object>`, which would require per-element boxing at every access. For value-typed T, the only legal assignment of `IEnumerable<T>` is to `IEnumerable<T>` itself or to `Object`. Reference-typed T admits the full covariant chain — `IEnumerable<Dog>` is assignable to `IEnumerable<Animal>` and to `IEnumerable<Object>` because the underlying references compose without conversion.

Function types are automatically variant — covariant in return type, contravariant in parameter types.

<a id="sec-variance-and-interface-inheritance"></a>
#### Variance and interface inheritance

A generic interface may extend a generic base whose variance is different from its own. The most common case in the standard library: `IList<T>` is invariant in T (it has mutating methods) and extends `IReadOnlyList<out T>` (which is covariant in T):

```bezel
public interface IReadOnlyCollection<out T>: IEnumerable<T>
  readonly property Count: int;
end IReadOnlyCollection;

public interface IReadOnlyList<out T>: IReadOnlyCollection<T>
  readonly property [i: int]: T;
end IReadOnlyList;

public interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

The extending interface instantiates the base's variant parameter with its own type parameter, holding the deriving interface's variance. The substitution is `IReadOnlyList<T>` where the bound T is whatever T the deriving interface has; if `IList<T>` has T invariant, then the inherited `IReadOnlyList<T>` is also invariant in T from `IList<T>`'s perspective. The base's covariance is *available* when accessed through the base type — `IReadOnlyList<Dog>` is assignable to `IReadOnlyList<Animal>` — but accessing the same instance through `IList<Dog>` does not admit the covariant assignment, because `IList<T>` is invariant.

This means an instance whose runtime type implements `IList<Dog>` is assignable to:
- `IList<Dog>` (exact match)
- `IReadOnlyList<Dog>`, `IReadOnlyList<Animal>`, `IReadOnlyList<Object>` (covariant chain via the read-only view)
- `IReadOnlyCollection<Dog>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<Animal>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<Object>` (covariant chain via the read-only-collection view)
- `ICollection<Dog>`, `IEnumerable<Dog>`, `IEnumerable<Animal>`, `IEnumerable<Object>` (other inherited interfaces, with their own variance)

It is *not* assignable to `IList<Animal>` — the variance of the base interface does not propagate through the deriving interface's signature.

The position-composition rules above continue to apply within each interface in isolation. The compiler enforces position constraints on each interface declaration independently: `IReadOnlyList<out T>` is checked with T in covariant position throughout its body; `IList<T>` is checked with T in any position throughout its body. The inheritance relation only fixes the type argument substituted into the base — it does not alter what positions T may legally appear in within the derived interface.

<a id="sec-inheritance-cycles"></a>
### 12.10 Inheritance cycles

An inheritance cycle is a compile error. A type may not, directly or transitively, list itself among its base types — neither as the base class of a class, nor as an extended interface of an interface. The relation followed is the union of base-class edges ([§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)) and extended-interface edges ([§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)); a cycle is any sequence of types where each lists the next as a base type and the sequence returns to its start. The simplest case is a type naming itself (`class C: C`); the general case is a chain (`class A: B`, `class B: C`, `class C: A`) and the mixed class/interface chains the relation admits. The compiler detects the cycle and reports an error naming the participating types; the cycle is never silently broken or otherwise tolerated.

---

<a id="sec-visibility"></a>
## 13. Visibility

<a id="sec-levels"></a>
### 13.1 Levels

Four levels:

| Level | Visible to |
|---|---|
| `public` | Anyone who can see the enclosing context |
| `internal` | Code in the same module |
| `protected` | The declaring class and all classes derived from it |
| `private` | The declaring class only |

`internal` and `protected` are incomparable: a derived class in a different module sees `protected` but not `internal`; an unrelated class in the same module sees `internal` but not `protected`.

<a id="sec-top-level-types"></a>
### 13.2 Top-level types

Top-level types may be `public` or `internal`. They may not be `protected` (no enclosing class) or `private` (no file-scope concept). The default is `internal`:

```bezel
public class BankAccount
  // ...
end BankAccount;

class Helper           // implicitly internal
  // ...
end Helper;
```

<a id="sec-class-members"></a>
### 13.3 Class members

Every class member must declare its visibility explicitly, with three exceptions:

- A `static constructor` carries no visibility keyword (the runtime is the only caller; see [§22.7](#sec-constructors)).
- A `polymorphic` registry declaration carries no visibility keyword (it is a compiler-consumed serialization map, not a callable member; see [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) and Appendix A.3).
- A `destructor` carries no visibility keyword. A destructor is an implementation hook called by the compiler-generated `Dispose()` method; it is not directly callable by user code. The customization point is `destructor`; the public surface is `Dispose()` (see [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)).

Outside these three cases, omitting the visibility keyword is a compile error. (The asymmetry with [§13.2](#sec-top-level-types)'s file-scope default is deliberate: file scope has one safe default — module-internal — while a member's four-way choice has none, so explicitness is demanded.)

Interface members do not declare visibility; they are implicitly public.

<a id="sec-modules-and-internal"></a>
### 13.4 Modules and `internal`

A module is the set of all source files declaring the same `module Name.Path;` **presented to the module's one compilation ([§2.8.1](#sec-module-identity-and-closure))**; `internal` access is closed by that compilation — no later source file joins a module by declaring its name, and within an SCC unit each member module's internals remain invisible to the other members. The dotted form is a single name; files in `Foo` get no special access to files in `Foo.Bar`.

A file declares exactly one module.

<a id="sec-no-combined-visibilities"></a>
### 13.5 No combined visibilities

Bezel does not provide combined forms (no `protected internal`, no `private protected`).

<a id="sec-accessor-visibility"></a>
### 13.6 Accessor visibility

A property or indexer's `get` or `set` may carry its own visibility, which must not be *less* restrictive than the property's overall visibility (equal visibility is permitted, though redundant; the useful form is a more restrictive accessor):

```bezel
public property Name: string
  get => _name;
  private set => _name := value;
end Name;
```

An accessor without explicit visibility inherits the property's overall visibility. An accessor visibility *less* restrictive than the property is a compile error.

The auto-property shorthand `public property Name: string private set;` is equivalent to the block form.

<a id="sec-visibility-and-inheritance"></a>
### 13.7 Visibility and inheritance

- An override must declare the same visibility as the base member.
- **Every type appearing in a member's signature must be at least as visible as the member.** The rule covers: field types, parameter types, return types, property types, indexer parameter and result types, and types named in `where` clauses on a public/protected member. The rule applies at every visibility level — a `public` member's signature types must be `public` (or more permissive); an `internal` member's signature types must be `internal` (or more); a `protected` member's must be at least `protected`; a `private` member is unconstrained (since `private` is the most restrictive level).
- A class's base class and implemented interfaces must be at least as visible as the class.

The signature-type-visibility rule applies to a member's *declared* signature. Generic-method type parameters whose substitution at the call site could narrow visibility are not constrained — the caller's substitution is the caller's choice, not the declarer's.

```bezel
public class Outer
  private class NestedPrivate
    // ...
  end NestedPrivate;
  
  // ERROR: _x is internal, but NestedPrivate is private — the field's
  //        type is not as visible as the field.
  internal _x: NestedPrivate;

  // OK: also private, matches NestedPrivate's visibility.
  private _y: NestedPrivate;
end Outer;
```

---

<a id="sec-generics"></a>
## 14. Generics

<a id="sec-generic-declarations"></a>
### 14.1 Generic declarations

Classes, interfaces, records, and methods may be generic:

```bezel
class MyArray<T>
  // ...
end MyArray;

interface IComparable<T>
  method CompareTo(other: T): int;
end IComparable;

record Pair<TFirst, TSecond>(First: TFirst, Second: TSecond);

static class Utils
  public static method Swap<T>(ref a: T, ref b: T)
    var temp := a;
    a := b;
    b := temp;
  end Swap;
end Utils;
```

Type parameters use angle brackets. Multiple parameters are comma-separated.

<a id="sec-constraints"></a>
### 14.2 Constraints

The `where` clause restricts the substitutions a type parameter accepts:

| Constraint | Accepts |
|---|---|
| *(none)* | Any type, nullable or not. T is treated conservatively as possibly nullable. |
| `where T: notnull` | Non-nullable types only (value or reference). A nullable type, value or reference, is excluded. |
| `where T: class` | Non-nullable reference types only — classes (including `Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, and other heap collection types), interfaces, `string`, function types. |
| `where T: value` | Non-nullable value types — records, enums, choices ([§35](#sec-choices)), primitives, inline arrays (all forms), the unit type. A nullable value type (e.g. `int?`) does **not** satisfy `value`. Generic body must use only move-compatible operations on T if T may be a move-only value — a move-only inline array or an owning-classified choice instantiation ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)). |
| `where T: SomeClass` | Non-nullable subtypes of `SomeClass` (the class itself and its descendants). Class types only; interfaces do not extend classes in Bezel. |
| `where T: IFoo` | Non-nullable types conforming to `IFoo`: classes implementing it, records and enums implementing it, interfaces extending it, and primitives conforming through their standard-library declarations or the compiler-provided conformances of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) (clause 5 below). See "Interface conformance" below. |
| `where T: U` (U a type parameter) | Non-nullable types assignable to the substitution for `U`. See "Type-parameter bounds" below. |
| `where T: new()` | Class types with a `public` parameterless constructor; value types (records, enums, primitives, inline arrays, the unit type) whose `default(T)` is well-defined ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)). |
| `where T: sendable` | Types whose **sendable** derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties), [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)) holds, decided by the §30.14 computation unchanged ("Derived-property constraints" below). Composes with the other forms (`where T: sendable, class` admits sendable class types). |
| `where T: hashable` | Types whose **hashable** derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) holds — consistent `Equals`/`GetHashCode`, usable as hash-container keys and elements — decided per instantiation by §3.6's computation. States in the signature what `Dictionary<K, V>`/`Set<T>` keys structurally require, so the diagnostic lands at the instantiation of the *user's* generic rather than deep inside the stdlib type. |

Constraints may be combined: `where T: class, IDisposable, new()` requires a non-nullable reference type that implements `IDisposable` and has a public parameterless constructor.

For `where T: new()`: a **class** substitution satisfies the constraint exactly when the class declares a parameterless constructor that is `public` — not merely accessible from some scope. Constraint satisfaction is a property of the type alone, checked wherever an instantiation occurs; keying it to accessibility would let the same substitution satisfy the constraint in one module and fail it in another. A **value-type** substitution — record (positional or body), enum, primitive, inline array, the unit type — satisfies the constraint exactly when `default(T)` is well-defined per [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator). Inside the generic body, `new T()` for a value substitution is equivalent to `default(T)`: for records this is the zero-valued record (admitting `record Point(X: int, Y: int)` while rejecting records with non-nullable reference fields); for enums it is the zero value — an enum with no declared zero-valued constant has no well-defined `default` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) and does not satisfy the constraint. For a class substitution, `new T()` produces an owned reference via the class's parameterless constructor under the standard ownership-discharge rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). Interface substitutions never satisfy `new()` — no constructor exists. **Choices never satisfy the value-type arm**: `default(C)` is undefined for every choice type ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator), [§35.10](#sec-choice-default-with)).

A type-bound constraint — naming a class or interface — implies non-null T. The reasoning is that nullable types `MyClass?` and `IFoo?` are distinct from their non-nullable forms ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)) and do not themselves implement the interfaces of their non-nullable counterparts: a `null` value satisfies no interface contract. Constraining on a class or interface name therefore admits only non-nullable substitutions, the same way `where T: class` does. Inside the generic body, T is non-nullable; `T?` is its nullable companion.

**`value` requires a non-nullable value type.** A nullable value type — `int?`, `Priority?`, `DateTime?`, and the nullable form of any record, enum, or inline array — does *not* satisfy `where T: value`. The `value` constraint admits only the non-nullable value type itself; `where T: value` then makes `T?` the nullable companion inside the body. The reasoning matches the type-bound case above: a nullable value type is a distinct type from its non-nullable form ([§7.1](#sec-non-nullable-and-nullable-types)), and its representation differs (it carries the additional `null` state). `where T: notnull` likewise excludes every nullable type — value or reference — for the same reason. To accept a nullable value type, write the constraint against the underlying value type and use `T?` in the body.

`T?` always denotes the nullable form of T. `default(T)` produces the zero/null value of T ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)).

Contradictory constraint combinations (e.g. `class, value`) are compile errors.

**Type-parameter bounds (`where T: U`).** A constraint whose bound is another type parameter — of the same declaration, or of the enclosing type — is grammatical and has subtype semantics: a substitution S for `T` satisfies `where T: U` exactly when S is non-nullable and is *assignable to* the substitution for `U` — identical to it, a subclass of a class substitution ([§12](#sec-inheritance-and-dispatch)), or a type conforming to an interface substitution (the conformance rule below). The check runs at instantiation, after both parameters are substituted. Inside the body, a `T`-typed value is usable in any `U`-typed position, and `T` conforms to every interface that `U`'s own constraints guarantee; an unconstrained `U` contributes only `Object`'s surface. Like every type-bound constraint, `where T: U` implies non-null `T` (`T?` is the nullable companion). A self-referential bound (`where T: T`) or a cycle among type-parameter bounds (`where T: U` together with `where U: T`) is a compile error at the declaration.

<a id="sec-derived-property-constraints"></a>
#### Derived-property constraints

A `where` clause may name a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) from the **admitted set** below. Satisfaction is decided per instantiation, after substitution, by the property's defining computation — the same evaluation §3.6 rule 2 already performs; the constraint adds no second definition of the property and can therefore never disagree with the property itself. Nothing is inferred and nothing propagates: a generic declaration that requires the property of a parameter writes the constraint; an unconstrained parameter never acquires it; a generic *type's own* properties remain computed from its structure at each instantiation (§3.6 rule 1 — the constraint is an admission filter on substitutions, never a declaration of the property). Inside the body, `T` counts as having the property wherever a rule of this specification demands it — the per-instantiation re-check for those interior uses is subsumed by the constraint, and one diagnostic (the constraint failure, at the instantiation site) replaces the interior one. Overrides and interface implementations inherit the constraint under the unchanged inheritance rule above. The admitted set grows only by recorded ruling — one property, one decision; there is no negated form and no user-extensible mechanism.

Admitted set of this revision: **`sendable`** ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)) and **`hashable`** (the §3.6 property of the same name).

A failed derived-property constraint is diagnosed at the instantiation site naming the constraint, the offending type argument, and the structural reason **as a component path** — §3.6 rule 4, sharpened: for `sendable`, the failing §30.14 rule and the field/element chain that violates it.

<a id="sec-interface-conformance"></a>
#### Interface conformance

For an interface I and a candidate type T, T **conforms to** I exactly when one of the following holds:

1. **T is a class** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause, that inherits from a class which conforms to I, or that conforms **implicitly** — every class conforms to `IDisposable` without listing it ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)). Implementation may be direct (the class declares the matching members), inherited (a base class declares them), or compiler-generated (the implicit `Dispose`).
2. **T is a record** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares matching members — auto-generated members count: the synthesized `Equals(T)` satisfies `IEquatable<T>` (stdlib §2.9's recorded convention — "Records implement this implicitly"). Records are sealed ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), so conformance is always direct, never inherited.
3. **T is an interface** that has I in its extension chain — either I is named directly in T's inheritance clause, or T extends an interface that itself conforms to I.
4. **T is an enum** that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares the matching public members ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)): `enum Priority: IComparable<Priority>` satisfies `where T: IComparable<T>` exactly as a record would — enum interface conformance exists precisely to make enums visible to interface-constrained generics (rationale §9.4).
5. **T is a primitive.** A primitive conforms to the interfaces its standard-library declaration lists: the keyword and PascalCase forms name one type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)), and stdlib §9 declares that type in record syntax, so `int` conforms to `IComparable<int>`/`IEquatable<int>` through the `Int32` declaration exactly as clause 2 reads for records. A primitive additionally carries the **compiler-provided conformances** of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members): the numeric tower conforms to the stdlib §2.19 `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>`/`IParsable<T>` interfaces, and `char` to `ISteppable<char>`/`IParsable<char>`, with no declaration listing them — the intrinsic operations serve as the member witnesses. (The primitive kind remains distinct from the record kind, [§3.1](#sec-type-kinds); this clause, not clause 2, is a primitive's conformance source.)
6. **T is a type parameter** whose constraints guarantee conformance to I ("Type-parameter bounds" above): a type-bound constraint naming I or an interface extending I, directly or through a `where T: U` chain.
7. **T is a choice** ([§35](#sec-choices)) that lists I (or any interface extending I) in its inheritance clause and declares the matching public members ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)) — the enum model. Choices are sealed, so conformance is always direct. For an owning-classified instantiation, conformance admits constraint satisfaction and generic dispatch but not the boxing *conversion* ([§35.8](#sec-choice-boxing)).

`where T: IFoo` admits exactly the substitutions for which T conforms to `IFoo` per the rule above. Inside the generic body, T's surface includes IFoo's members, regardless of which conformance category T belongs to; the body cannot tell whether T was satisfied by a class, a record, an enum, an interface, a primitive, or another type parameter, and does not need to.

<a id="sec-worked-example-where-t-idisposable"></a>
#### Worked example: `where T: IDisposable`

Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), and records cannot implement `IDisposable` ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)). Applying the conformance rule:

- Every non-nullable class type conforms (rule 1).
- No record type conforms (rule 2 fails because records cannot implement `IDisposable`).
- Interface types conform when they extend `IDisposable` (rule 3): `IAsyncDisposable`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, and any user-defined interface that lists `IDisposable` in its extension clause.

So `where T: IDisposable` admits the same *class* substitutions as `where T: class` (every class qualifies under both) but a strictly smaller set of *interface* substitutions (only `IDisposable`-extending interfaces, versus all interfaces under `where T: class`). The difference rarely matters in practice — programmers usually write `where T: IDisposable` when the body calls `Dispose()`, and that's exactly when admitting only `IDisposable`-conforming interfaces is what was wanted.

<a id="sec-worked-example-where-t-icomparableint"></a>
#### Worked example: `where T: IComparable<int>`

`IComparable<int>` is implemented by `int` itself — its standard-library declaration lists it (stdlib [§9.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-integer-types)), and `Int32` names the same type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)) — and by user-defined records and classes that implement it. Applying the conformance rule:

- `int` (rule 5): conforms — its standard-library declaration lists `IComparable<int>`. `Int32` names the same type ([§3.4](#sec-keyword-aliases-for-built-in-types)), not a separate conformer.
- Any user record listing `IComparable<int>` in its inheritance clause **and declaring the matching member** (rule 2 — `CompareTo` is not auto-generated; only the equality members are, [§9.2](#sec-body-records)): conforms. For example, `record Wrapper(value: int): IComparable<int>` with a declared `CompareTo(other: int): int`.
- Any user class implementing `IComparable<int>` (rule 1): conforms.
- An interface `IIntComparable: IComparable<int>` (rule 3): conforms.

`where T: IComparable<int>` therefore admits a mix of primitive, class, record, and interface substitutions — illustrating that interface constraints are not class-only, unlike the class-bound constraint `where T: SomeClass`.

<a id="sec-constraints-on-overrides"></a>
#### Constraints on overrides and interface implementations

An `override` of a generic method, and a method implementing a generic interface member, **inherits the overridden or implemented declaration's constraints**. Omitting the `where` clauses is the recommended spelling and means exactly the inherited set; the clauses may instead be restated in an equivalent form — the same constraint set per type parameter, compared **order-insensitively and after type-alias resolution** ([§27.8](#sec-type-aliases)): `where T: IFoo` and `where T: AliasOfIFoo` restate the same set — for readability. A **differing** clause — added, removed, narrowed, or widened relative to the inherited set — is a compile error naming the inherited constraints: dispatch flows through the base or interface signature, so its constraints are the only ones call sites are ever checked against — an *added* constraint on the override would go unenforced at every virtual call (unsound), and a *weakened* one would advertise admissions the dispatch surface never grants.

<a id="sec-generics-variance"></a>
### 14.3 Variance

See [§12.9](#sec-variance).

<a id="sec-owned-and-generic-type-arguments"></a>
<a id="sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument"></a>
<a id="sec-substitution-of-owned-bearing-type-arguments"></a>
<a id="sec-merged-declarations-and-form-dependent-members"></a>
<a id="sec-conditioning-method-existence-on-ts-modifier"></a>
### 14.4 `owned` and generic type arguments

**`owned` does not propagate through generic type arguments.** A generic argument's type is whatever class, value, or interface type is supplied; the `owned` modifier — which expresses an ownership-tracking obligation at a declaration position — does not attach to type arguments.

Specifically: the following are **not valid types**:

- `Array<owned T>`, `LinkedList<owned T>`, `Set<owned T>`, `Stack<owned T>`, `Queue<owned T>`, `Dictionary<owned K, V>`, `Dictionary<K, owned V>`, `Dictionary<owned K, owned V>` — replaced by named owning collection types (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)): `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>` (with `V: class`).
- `Task<owned T>` — replaced by `OwningTask<T>` (stdlib [§6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-threading)).
- `IEnumerable<owned T>`, `IEnumerator<owned T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<owned T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<owned T>` — replaced by `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`.
- `IList<owned T>`, `ICollection<owned T>` — replaced by `IOwningList<T>`, `IOwningCollection<T>`.

In every case, the replacement is a separate named class or interface declared in the standard library, with its own declaration, members, and inheritance.

This is a deliberate simplification. The owned and non-owned forms of these types have genuinely different semantics — an owning collection's `Add` takes ownership of the element; a borrowing collection's `Add` takes a borrow. The two forms are deliberately separate named types rather than one generic parameterized by an ownership modifier; the changelog's [v0.96→v0.97 entry](Bezel_Changelog.md#sec-v0-96-to-v0-97-changelog) records the decision and the alternatives.

The `owned` modifier itself remains. It appears in declaration positions: parameter declarations (`method Add(owned item: T)`), return type declarations (`method Acquire(): owned Connection`), field declarations (`private owned _resource: Connection`), local variables through `using var` (`using var c := Connect()`), and `out` parameter declarations (`out owned p: T`).

The admissible positions for `owned` are enumerated in [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear); types and positions that do not admit `owned` (record fields, inline-array element types, generic type arguments) reject the modifier at the position itself, not through any substitution rule.

<a id="sec-generic-constraints-and-class-types"></a>
#### Generic constraints and class types

Generic methods and types can constrain their parameters to class types via `where T: class` ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)). A class type C satisfies `where T: class`. A generic method with a `where T: class` constraint may be called with T = C; the call site supplies a value of type C (whether the value is owned or a borrow at that site is determined by the declaration position of the parameter the call argument flows into, not by T's identity; a call *result* whose declared return type is a bare type parameter is likewise classified by declaration shape — [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule — not by T's substitution).

Generic types that store class-typed values do not, by themselves, become "owning" by having a class type argument. `Array<MyClass>` stores borrows of `MyClass` — references whose ownership remains with whoever passed them in. To get an owning collection, the user reaches for `OwningArray<MyClass>` — a different class with different semantics.

**Class-only restriction on owning generics.** Most standard-library owning types (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningTask<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningCollection<T>`, `IOwningList<T>`) restrict their element type T to **class and interface types**. Value types are rejected at the instantiation site. The `where T: class` constraint in their declarations is a slight imprecision — per [§14.2](#sec-constraints) `where T: class` admits all non-nullable reference types (classes, interfaces, `string`, function types) — but the standard-library owning types are compiler-enforced to reject the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values). The reason: those types are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) and have no disposal obligation; owning them is degenerate. The error message at instantiation names the rejected type and points the reader to the relevant stdlib section.

`OwningBuffer<T>`, `Span<T>`, and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) are exceptions to this restriction. They admit T to be either class-typed (with ownership semantics as above) or value-typed (with plain value semantics — no per-slot ownership, no Dispose cascade, no `move` admission). They still reject the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values) and move-only value types (the owning inline arrays `[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)).

**Nullable class types and interfaces are admitted.** The owning-type instantiation rule checks the *underlying* type, not the nullable-wrapper. `OwningTask<Lock?>` (a Pattern B task whose result is `owned Lock | null`) is admitted because `Lock` is a class type; the nullability of the result is independent of the disposal obligation. The same applies to interface types: `OwningArray<IConnection>` is admitted because `IConnection` may be implemented by class types with real disposal obligations; iteration produces borrows of `IConnection`, and `Add(owned)` takes ownership of an `IConnection` reference whose runtime dispatch resolves to a real class's `Dispose()` at disposal time.

A user-defined generic type that needs to own its elements composes over `OwningArray<T>` (or another `Owned…` collection type):

```bezel
public class OwningCache<T> where T: class
  private owned _items: OwningArray<T>;

  public constructor() _items := new(); end;

  public method Add(owned item: T)
    _items.Add(move item);
  end Add;

  public method Drain(): owned IOwningEnumerable<T>
    return _items.Drain();
  end Drain;
end OwningCache;
```

This composition pattern works under the existing field-ownership and generic-type rules; no special mechanism is required. User-defined generic types with class-typed parameters that don't store anything owned (read-only views, transformations) just declare their members in the normal way.

<a id="sec-historical-references"></a>
#### Historical references

The changelog's [v0.77→v0.78](Bezel_Changelog.md#sec-v0-77-to-v0-78-changelog) through [v0.95→v0.96](Bezel_Changelog.md#sec-v0-95-to-v0-96-changelog) entries record the v0.78–v0.96 mechanisms by which `owned` was a generic-argument modifier, all removed in v0.97. This section's anchors (`sec-substitution-of-owned-bearing-type-arguments`, `sec-merged-declarations-and-form-dependent-members`, `sec-conditioning-method-existence-on-ts-modifier`) are preserved so that historical changelog links resolve.

<a id="sec-type-argument-inference"></a>
### 14.5 Type-argument inference for generic methods

A call to a generic method may omit the type-argument list; the compiler then
infers the method-level type arguments from the call.

**Scope.** Inference covers **method-level** type parameters only. Class-,
record-, and interface-level type arguments are never inferred from constructor
arguments: `new Pair(1, "x")` against `record Pair<TF, TS>(First: TF, Second: TS)`
is a compile error directing to explicit arguments (`new Pair<int, string>(1, "x")`)
or, where a target type exists, the `new()` shorthand ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)).
Extension-block-level parameters are inferred from the receiver first
([§26.5](#sec-resolution) step 2, this section's unification applied to the
extension head); the resulting substitution is in force while the method-level
parameters are inferred below.

**Explicit lists are all-or-nothing.** An explicit type-argument list
(`obj.Method<int>(args)`, [§22.12](#sec-static-members)/A.7) binds the declared
type parameters in declaration order and must supply exactly as many arguments
as the method declares type parameters. A shorter or a longer list is a compile
error; there are no partial lists. When a full explicit list is supplied, no
inference runs.

**Inputs and phases.** Inference runs after arity filtering and named-argument
binding ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) fix the
argument-to-parameter correspondence; omitted optional parameters contribute
nothing. It proceeds in three phases; every phase binds type parameters under
one **agreement rule** stated after them.

1. **Argument-driven unification.** Each argument whose type is
   self-determined — every non-function-typed argument, a function-typed
   *value*, and a lambda's **annotated** parameter types — is unified
   structurally against its parameter type (a bare `null` literal argument is
   not self-determined and contributes no binding):

   - a parameter type that is a bare type parameter `X` binds `X` to the
     argument's static type;
   - `X?` binds through the nullable wrapping: an argument of type `U?` binds
     `X` to `U`; a non-nullable argument of type `A` binds `X` to `A` (the
     present-value wrapping of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions));
   - a constructed parameter type `G<P1, …, Pn>` unifies component-wise and
     **invariantly** against an argument of the same generic type, or against
     the unique instantiation of `G` that the argument's type implements or
     extends (an `Array<int>` argument against `xs: IEnumerable<T>` binds
     `T` to `int`); an argument whose type reaches no instantiation of `G`
     makes the candidate inapplicable;
   - a function-typed parameter unifies component-wise; modifier slots
     (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`) must match exactly
     ([§27.1](#sec-function-types));
   - a `ref` or `out` parameter position unifies **exactly**: the parameter
     aliases the caller's location, so no conversion is admitted at the
     binding or later at the applicability check
     ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations));
   - a parameter type containing no type parameters contributes no bindings.

   Unification is over **static types, exactly**: no [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)
   conversion, no constant narrowing, and no variance step participates in
   *binding*. Conversions get their say afterward, argument by argument, at the
   [§22.6](#sec-overloading) applicability check against the substituted
   signature — which is why `var o: Object := Util.Id(5);` infers `T` as `int`
   from the argument and then converts the `int` result to `Object` as an
   ordinary assignment conversion.

2. **Function-typed arguments, left to right.** For each lambda-literal
   argument in argument order: the bindings established so far are substituted
   into its parameter's function type; if every parameter position of the
   lambda is then closed, the lambda's parameters take those types
   ([§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference) — a destructuring head acts as its
   annotation) and the body is typed ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)); the
   lambda's inferred return type then unifies against the function type's
   return position, binding type parameters still free. When the substituted
   return position contains **no** free type parameter, the lambda's inferred
   return type must equal it or implicitly convert to it
   ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)); otherwise the candidate is
   inapplicable — this is the general admission rule for lambda-literal
   arguments, stated with its ranking consequences in
   [§22.6](#sec-overloading). A later function-typed argument may use
   bindings an earlier one produced. A method-reference argument resolves
   against the substituted target per [§27.6](#sec-method-references); type
   parameters free in that target are bound by the winning candidate's
   signature under the exact-preferred ranking of
   [§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods). If a
   lambda's parameter positions are still open after this phase, inference
   fails: annotate the lambda's parameters or supply explicit type arguments.

3. **Target-typed completion.** A type parameter still unbound is bound from
   the call's **target type**, where the call site has one, by unifying the
   method's declared return type — current bindings applied — against the
   target; this unification may bind through the return type's base-class or
   implemented-interface positions (`Util.Empty<T>(): Array<T>` against a
   target `IEnumerable<int>` binds `T` to `int`) and through the nullable
   wrapping. The **target contexts** are: the initializer of a typed
   declaration (field or local), an assignment to a typed location, a `return`
   statement against a declared return type, a default parameter value, and an
   argument position whose parameter type is closed once the enclosing call's
   own phase-1 bindings are applied — [§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)'s
   `new()`-shorthand contexts, extended by typed assignments and determined
   argument positions. The target never overrides an argument-derived binding;
   it only completes. A type parameter that remains unbound — it appears in no
   self-determined argument position and no target context supplies it — is a
   compile error naming the parameter: supply explicit type arguments, or give
   the call a target (assign to a typed local, or return it from a method with
   a declared return type).

**Agreement.** All bindings a type parameter receives — across arguments,
lambda returns, and the target — must be the **same type**. Two different
bindings are an inference failure: a compile error naming the type parameter
and both types, remedied with explicit type arguments or an explicit cast.
The compiler computes no common supertype and no widened join —
`Util.Pick<T>(a: T, b: T)` called as `Pick(1, 2L)` or as `Pick(dog, animal)`
is an error, not `long` or `Animal` (the same declined-unification stance as
lambda return types, [§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions), and the `if`
expression's two-way rule, [§20](#sec-the-if-expression)). Constant
expressions contribute their static types (`Pick(b, 250)` for `b: byte` is an
error — `250` is an `int`); [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant
narrowing is a conversion-site rule and never participates in a join. With an
explicit list — `Pick<byte>(b, 250)` — the parameter type is `byte` and the
literal constant-narrows at the argument conversion site as usual.

**Constraints.** [§14.2](#sec-constraints) constraint satisfaction is checked
after inference completes, on the full substitution, exactly as for a written
type-argument list. Constraints do not act as inference sources in this
version (recorded as liftable).

**Interaction with overloading.** Inference is **per candidate** and precedes
applicability: each generic candidate infers against the call independently; a
candidate whose inference fails is inapplicable and drops out (the call then
resolves among the remaining candidates as usual). Surviving candidates enter
[§22.6](#sec-overloading) with their substituted signatures. A non-generic
candidate otherwise tied with a generic one wins ([§22.6](#sec-overloading) — the last comparison before ambiguity, after the defaulted-arity
tie-break).

**Failure diagnostics.** The two failure shapes carry distinct diagnostics,
both naming the type parameter: *unbindable* ("cannot infer the type argument
of `Empty`'s call from its arguments; it appears only in the return type, so a
target type is required — assign the result to a typed local or return it from
a method with a declared return type") and *conflicting* ("type parameter `T`
cannot be bound to both `int` and `long` — all arguments for a type parameter
must agree; write explicit type arguments"). Neither ever resolves by silent
choice.

```bezel
var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];

var doubled := xs.Select(lambda(x) => x * 2);      // block T = int from the receiver (§26.5);
                                             //   phase 2: lambda param x : int, body int ⇒ U = int
var byKey := xs.OrderBy(lambda(x) => x mod 3);     // TKey = int (phase 2); the §14.2 constraint
                                             //   check (IComparable<int>) runs after inference
var total := xs.Aggregate(0L, lambda(acc, x) => acc + x);
                                             // TAccum = long from the seed (phase 1);
                                             //   lambda checks as (long, int) -> long (phase 2)
var empty: Array<string> := Util.Empty();    // T = string from the target (phase 3)
var n := Util.CountOf(xs);                   // CountOf<T>(xs: IEnumerable<T>): int —
                                             //   Array<int> vs IEnumerable<T> ⇒ T = int (phase 1)
// var bad := Util.Pick(1, 2L);              // error: T bound to both int and long — agree, or
                                             //        Pick<long>(1, 2L)
// var loose := Util.Empty();                // error: T appears only in the return type —
                                             //        target or explicit argument required
```

<a id="sec-arrays"></a>
## 15. Arrays

Bezel provides two array kinds:

- **Inline arrays** `[N]T` — value-typed, fixed size set at compile time, stored inline in their enclosing context (stack frame, class storage, or record layout). No heap allocation, no `Dispose`.
- **Heap arrays** `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` — class types from the standard library, allocated with `new`, require disposal. May be used at fixed size (by not calling resize methods) or resizably (the natural use).

The two kinds serve different purposes. Inline arrays are a value-type storage primitive: they live in the place that holds them, copy by value (when copyable), and have no allocation cost. Heap arrays are the general-purpose container family: they grow and shrink, support iteration protocols, and carry the ownership obligations associated with their allocated storage.

<a id="sec-inline-arrays"></a>
<a id="sec-fixed-size-arrays"></a>
### 15.1 Inline arrays

The type `[N]T` is an inline array of N elements of type T. N is a compile-time integer constant; T is any type subject to the element-type rules below.

```bezel
var pixels: [16]byte;                    // 16 zero-initialized bytes
var matrix: [9]float;                    // 9 zero-initialized floats
var rgb:    [3]byte := [255, 128, 64];   // explicit initialization
```

**Size.** N must be a constant expression of integer type ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)): integer literals, `const` references, and arithmetic on these (e.g., `[BufferSize * 2]byte`) are the common forms. N must be greater than zero; `[0]T` is a compile error.

The size N is part of the type. `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types that do not interconvert.

**Element type.** The element type T may be:

- A value type (primitive or record): the array stores the values directly, inline.
- A class type (`C` or `C?`): the array stores references inline; the referenced objects live on the heap as usual.
- A runtime-managed reference type (`string`, function values): the array stores references inline; the underlying memory is managed by the runtime.

Inline arrays may not be elements of inline arrays in the form `[N][M]T` — multi-dimensional inline arrays are deferred to a future revision. The current spec admits only one-dimensional inline arrays.

**No nullable inline-array types.** Inline arrays themselves do not have a nullable form: `([3]int)?` is not admitted. The element type may be nullable (`[3]int?` is well-formed and denotes an inline array of nullable int), but the array as a whole always has a value. The grammar parses `[3]int?` greedily as "inline array of `int?`," not as "nullable inline array of `int`." The motivation: inline arrays are stored inline in their host, so a "null" inline array would have no natural representation (every slot would have to indicate "the whole array is absent"), and the use cases for a sentinel "no array yet" value are well-served by either a nullable wrapping record or a nullable class-typed reference to a heap array. Consequently an inline array is not an admissible `as` target ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)).

**Initialization.** When the element type T is *zero-initializable* — every value-typed T whose fields recursively zero-initialize, or any nullable type T? (an enum is zero-initializable only when it declares a zero-valued constant, [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)) — an inline array declaration without an explicit initializer is filled with zero or null values per slot:

```bezel
var counts: [10]int;             // 10 zeros
var maybe:  [5]Connection?;       // 5 nulls
var verts:  [3]Vertex;            // 3 zero-initialized Vertex records (if Vertex zero-initializes)
```

When the element type is a non-nullable class type or a record without default initialization, an explicit initializer is required at declaration. The initializer is a comma-separated list of N expressions in brackets:

```bezel
var rgb: [3]byte       := [255, 128, 64];
var pt:  [2]Point      := [new Point(0, 0), new Point(1, 1)];   // value-typed Point record
```

For non-nullable class-typed elements (`[N]C` without the `owned` slot marker), the elements stored in the array are *borrows* — the initializer expressions must be borrows of class instances already owned elsewhere, and those owners must outlive the inline array. To construct an inline array that *owns* its non-null class-typed slots, use the `[N owned]T` form ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)) with an initializer of owned expressions; ownership transfers from each expression into the array.

The list must contain exactly N elements; mismatch is a compile error.

<a id="sec-owning-inline-arrays"></a>
#### 15.1.1 Owning inline arrays

The form `[N owned]T` (or `[N owned]T?`) denotes an inline array whose slots own their (non-null) class-typed contents. T must be a class or interface type; value types and runtime-managed reference types are not admitted with the `owned` marker. When T is a generic type parameter, the class-or-interface restriction is checked at *instantiation* — a generic constraint `where T: class` admits broader types (including runtime-managed reference types) per [§14.2](#sec-constraints), so instantiating an inline array `[N owned]T?` with T = `string` or another non-class-or-interface type is a compile error at the instantiation site, paralleling the generic-class-fields rule of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).

```bezel
// Non-null owned slots; initializer required at declaration
var fixed: [3 owned]Connection := [
  Connect("primary"), Connect("secondary"), Connect("tertiary")
];

// Nullable owned slots; defaults to all null
var pool: [16 owned]Connection?;
```

An owning inline array is a *move-only* value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). Assignment transfers ownership rather than copying. Copying is forbidden, since copying would duplicate ownership of each slot's contents.

When an owning inline array's lifetime ends, the array's auto-dispose pass disposes each non-null slot. For locals, this happens at scope end via the standard owned-local discharge ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); for class fields, the enclosing class's destructor invokes the disposal.

The `move arr[i]` form is admitted on both `[N owned]T?` and `[N owned]T` slots ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). For nullable slots, the field-restoration rule is satisfied by assigning `null` to the slot. For non-nullable slots, restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T (e.g., a constructor call, another moved value, or a borrow promoted to ownership via a factory) — the same rule as for non-nullable `OwningArray<T>` slots ([§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt) of the standard library). Code that needs "leave the slot empty after take" requires the nullable form; non-nullable slots must always hold a value at every observable point.

<a id="sec-inline-array-members"></a>
<a id="sec-members-and-operations"></a>
#### 15.1.2 Members and operations

Every inline array `[N]T` (with any modifier combination) exposes:

- `arr.Length: int` — compile-time constant N.
- Indexer `arr[i]` for read and write. Bounds checking applies; a constant index proven in-range at compile time elides the check.
- `arr.ToArray(): owned Array<T>` — a fresh heap array of the N slots: value-typed slots copied; class-typed slots stored as borrows. For `[N owned]…` arrays the result borrows the slots — the inline array retains ownership, matching the iteration/equality borrow rule below.
- `arr.Contains(item: T): bool` — element-wise test using this section's structural equality. Through [§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)'s structural `Contains` lookup this makes `x in arr` well-formed with no grammar change.

Iteration over an inline array uses the standard `for var x in arr do … end` form. The compiler emits a direct indexed loop without involving the `IEnumerable<T>` protocol: inline arrays are not class types and do not implement interfaces. For value-typed T, each iteration variable `x` is a copy of the slot's value; for class-typed T, each `x` is a borrow of the slot's reference. For `[N owned]…` arrays, iteration produces borrows into the owned slots (the iteration variable is a borrow; the slot retains ownership); to consume slot contents, use explicit `move arr[i]` followed by restoration (assignment of `null` on `[N owned]T?` arrays, or assignment of a fresh owned T on `[N owned]T` arrays). Passing an inline array to a method expecting `IEnumerable<T>` is rejected: inline arrays declare no interface conformances (unlike records, which may implement interfaces), so the value does not satisfy the interface contract. Callers who need to forward the contents to an IEnumerable-taking method call `arr.ToArray()` (above) and pass the fresh heap array.

Two inline-array values of the same type are equal iff their elements are pairwise equal under the element type's equality. Inline arrays follow record-equality discipline: structural equality grounded in element equality, with no special cases. Owning inline arrays (`[N owned]…`) admit equality only via element borrow; the comparison reads each slot without taking ownership.

**Lifetime of inline arrays carrying borrows.** An inline array `[N]C` or `[N]C?` whose element type C is a reference type (class or interface) carries N (potentially null) borrows into its slots. When such an array is passed by value, returned from a method, stored as a field, or captured by a closure, the same borrow-lifetime rules apply that govern borrow-bearing records ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)): the array value may not outlive the source of any borrow in any of its slots. The compiler tracks this element-wise where possible; where it cannot prove safety, the program is rejected. Inline arrays of value-typed elements, runtime-managed reference-typed elements (`string`, function values), or that carry only owned slots (`[N owned]…`) are not borrow-bearing.

<a id="sec-inline-array-ffi"></a>
<a id="sec-ffi"></a>
#### 15.1.3 FFI

Inline arrays of FFI-pointee scalar elements (`[N]byte`, `[N]int`, `[N]float`, `[N]IntPtr`, `[N]Ptr<T>`, and similar — the element set of [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types): the integer types, `float`, `double`, and `bool`, plus the pointer-sized scalars) have C-equivalent storage layout: N elements packed contiguously, no header. Such arrays may appear as `extern` method **parameters** under [§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)'s by-address rule: the argument must be an assignable storage location, the call passes the address of that storage (C's array-to-pointer convention), and native reads and writes are visible to the caller after the call. `[N]T` is **not** admitted as an extern **return** type — C functions do not return arrays ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types)).

Inline arrays of class-typed, interface-typed, record-typed, or runtime-managed-reference-typed elements do not have C-equivalent layout and are not admitted in extern signatures (as fields of C-compatible records, [§32.13](#sec-c-compatible-records) restates the same scalar element set; inline arrays of C-compatible record elements are a recorded liftable bound, [§32.14](#sec-deferred-ffi-surface)). Owning inline arrays are not admitted. Multi-dimensional inline arrays remain deferred and not admitted at FFI boundaries.

<a id="sec-arrayt"></a>
