- A non-nullable reference type.
- A record any of whose declared fields is a non-nullable reference type. This check is recursive: if a record field is itself a record type, that inner record's fields are also checked.
- An inline array whose element type is a non-nullable reference type. `default([3]Connection)` (non-nullable Connection elements) is a compile error; the user must supply explicit initializers. Owning inline arrays `[N owned]T` (non-nullable owning) are likewise an error for the same reason.

In a generic body:

- For unconstrained `T`, `default(T)` is permitted but its result is treated as possibly null and cannot be assigned to a non-nullable T-typed location.
- Under `where T: notnull` with value-type substitutions, `default(T)` is non-null.
- Under `where T: value`, `default(T)` is always non-null.
- Under `where T: class` (or any type-bound constraint that implies non-null T per [§14.2](#sec-constraints)), `default(T)` is a compile error — the constraint guarantees T is non-nullable, and the null value `default(T)` would produce does not fit T's contract. To express the nullable counterpart, write `default(T?)`, which produces `null` of type `T?`.

A substitution whose `default` is not well-defined — an enum with no zero-valued constant included — is rejected at the instantiation site (the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 pattern).

<a id="sec-the-throw-expression"></a>
### 17.12 The `throw` expression

`throw` is an expression. Its operand is optional:

- `throw expr` raises the supplied exception — an owned instance of an `Exception`-derived class type (the operand rule is [§31.1](#sec-throwing)'s). Valid in any expression position.
- `throw` (no operand) re-raises the currently-handled exception with its stack trace preserved. Valid only as an expression appearing inside a catch arm body ([§31.2.4](#sec-bare-re-raise)).

Both forms have the bottom type — assignable to any expected type — because control transfers to the matching handler before any value is produced.

```bezel
public property [i: int]: double => (case i of
  0 => X,
  1 => Y,
  2 => Z,
  _ => throw new IndexOutOfRangeException());

var name := (if user <> null then user.Name
             else throw new InvalidOperationException("user is null"));

var config := LoadConfig() ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("no config");

try
  DoWork();
catch
  var ex: TransientException => Retry(ex),
  var ex: Exception => throw          // bare throw: re-raises the current exception
end;
```

The statement form `throw;` (with the trailing semicolon, [§21.8](#sec-throw)) continues to work and is equivalent to the bare expression form followed by a semicolon. The two forms are interchangeable inside a catch arm body; the expression form is shorter and is preferred when the re-raise is the entire body of an arm.

Bare `throw` outside a catch arm body is a compile error, with the same diagnostic as the statement form `throw;` outside a catch context.

<a id="sec-the-discard-_"></a>
### 17.13 The discard `_`

The bare token `_` is **reserved** ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), Appendix [B.1](#sec-reserved-keywords)): it is never an identifier — never declarable, never readable as a name. It is a *discard* — a sink that consumes or ignores a value without binding it. Every position in which `_` can appear is one of the sanctioned forms of this section — a discard or wildcard, an ignore, or the anonymous owning binding — or a compile error whose diagnostic names the sanctioned forms (the rejected positions are listed below). A discard is valid exactly where receiving-and-ignoring a value is coherent, and an error everywhere else. Identifiers merely *containing* underscores (`_camelCase`, `_f`) are ordinary identifiers and unaffected by this section.

**Pattern position.** Inside a `case` arm or destructuring pattern, `_` matches any value without binding. (The `when` construct's `_` catch-all arm, [§19.1](#sec-forms), is the same wildcard reading.)

```bezel
case shape of
  Circle(_) => "circle",
  Rectangle(_, _) => "rectangle",
  _ => "other"
end;
```

**Out-argument position.** As a positional argument with the `out` modifier, `_` discards the out-parameter result.

```bezel
if dict.TryGetValue(key, out _) then    // we only care that it was present
  // ...
end;
```

`out _` does not introduce a variable; the receiving slot is internal to the compiler and is not observable. The argument is type-inferred from the parameter's declared type. A type annotation on `out _` is not permitted (`out _: int` is a syntax error), mirroring the rule for `out var name` ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)) — **a bare ignore takes its type from context, never an annotation**, one rule uniform across every ignore form of this section (`out _`, lambda-parameter `_`, `for var _`). The discard composes with `out` only: **`ref _` is a compile error** — a `ref` argument reads its operand, which a discard cannot supply; pass a named location ([§22.3](#sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations)). (An `out` parameter is pure output, so "receive and ignore" is coherent.) `out var _` is likewise a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)).

**Discard statement.** The form `_ := expression;` evaluates `expression` and discards its value. The discard statement is syntactically distinct from assignment: `_` is not an lvalue, and the form is recognized lexically by the leading `_` token.

The discard statement's legality depends on the static type of `expression`:

- **Value types, `string`, primitives, and other runtime-managed types:** discard is always permitted. No disposal is required, so the discard is purely cosmetic — it suppresses the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) *unused result* warning.

  ```bezel
  _ := ComputeChecksum();                // returns int; cosmetic discard
  _ := someStringBuilder.ToString();     // returns string; runtime-managed
  ```

  Inline arrays without owned slots (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) are ordinary value types and follow this rule.

- **Move-only values:** `_ := expression;` where `expression` produces a move-only value (an owning inline array `[N owned]T?`/`[N owned]T`, or an owning-classified choice — [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) is **permitted** and disposes the value at the end of the discard statement — the discard is an *unbound owned temporary* ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), reclaimed once the statement completes. Its owned slots — for a choice, the active case's owned payloads — are disposed in the usual order. (This is the explicit "dispose this owned result now" form, parallel to the non-trivial-dispose class case below.)

- **Trivial-dispose class types ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)):** discard is permitted. The value is freed at the end of the discard statement — the same unbound-owned-temporary timing as the non-trivial case below ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — and the free runs no user code (the class has none to run, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). The discard therefore remains purely cosmetic in the sense that it changes nothing: an undiscarded trivial-dispose result is freed at the same boundary, with no warning either way (the ceremony exemption).

  ```bezel
  _ := new Random();                     // Random is trivial-dispose
  _ := new StringBuilder();              // trivial-dispose
  _ := items.ToArray();                  // trivial-dispose (§28.9): freed at end of statement; no user code runs
  ```

- **Non-trivial-dispose class types:** discard is **permitted** and disposes the value at the end of the discard statement. The discard is an *unbound owned temporary* ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): `_ := expression;` evaluates `expression`, runs its `Dispose()` once the statement completes, and reclaims it. This is the explicit "I want this owned result disposed now" form — useful when an `owned`-returning method's result is not needed (`_ := OpenLog();` — for an illustrative `OpenLog(): owned FileStream` — closes the fresh stream at end of statement, rather than holding it to scope end as `using var _ := …` would).

  ```bezel
  _ := new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);   // OK: opened, then disposed at end of statement
  ```

  The difference from `using var _ := expression;` is **disposal timing**, not legality: `_ := …` disposes at end of *statement*; `using var _ := …` disposes at end of *scope*. Both work for any class type. (Auto-drop, [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement), makes the obligation always satisfiable; the discard names the immediate-disposal point.)

- **Interface-typed expressions:** discard is **permitted** and disposes the value at the end of the discard statement, calling `Dispose()` on the *runtime* type (disposal is virtual). Because the discard disposes rather than abandons, there is no cross-module hazard: an interface reference may bind any conforming implementation, and a future implementation in another module may add a non-trivial destructor, but whatever the runtime type, `_ := expr;` disposes it correctly. `using var _ := expr;` remains available when end-of-*scope* (rather than end-of-statement) disposal is wanted.

- **`Task` and `Task<T>`:** discard is a compile error (Tasks have a destructor that handles continuation cleanup and exception propagation). Use `Task.FireAndForget(expression)` for supervised fire-and-forget, or `using var _ := expression;` to dispose at scope end. The error message names `Task.FireAndForget` specifically.

```bezel
_ := DoTelemetryAsync();                 // ERROR: Task is non-trivial-dispose
Task.FireAndForget(DoTelemetryAsync());  // OK — supervised

using var _ := new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);     // OK — disposed at scope end
```

**Discard of a named owned binding.** `_ := x;` where `x` is a named owned binding — an owned local or an `owned` parameter — is an **announced consume**: the value is disposed at the end of the discard statement, and `x` is thereafter treated exactly as explicitly disposed ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) — the scope-end pass skips it; a later read falls under the use-after-dispose regime of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), and a join with a still-owned path yields maybe-consumed). No transfer marker is required and `_ := move x;` is not a form: the discard sink is itself the source-visible announcement — the same no-marker logic as `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and `owned` returns. For the same reason the consume-site freeze does not apply ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)'s recorded announced-kill boundary — the disposed flag is the runtime backstop). The type-keyed legality list above is unchanged: a named `Task`/`Task<T>` binding still may not be discarded. By contrast, a discard whose operand is in **borrow state** — `_ := b;` on a borrowed local or parameter, `_ := obj.Field;`, a discarded borrow-returning call result — disposes nothing: the discard is purely cosmetic (it silences the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) unused-result warning where one would fire), and the value's owner keeps the obligation.

The discard form acknowledges a deliberately-unused value *and* discharges its disposal obligation: for an owned class or move-only value, `_ := …` disposes it at end of statement. The disposal contract remains universal — a class instance with a non-trivial `Dispose()` reaches an owned location, becomes the operand of `using var`, is explicitly disposed, is discarded with `_ := …`, or is auto-dropped at scope end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) — but no path leaks. The only discards that remain errors are `Task`/`Task<T>` (use `Task.FireAndForget`, since disposing a task abandons a running operation — a semantic, not a leak, concern).

**Ignore forms.** Two binding positions admit `_` as a **true ignore** — accepted, binding nothing: a **lambda parameter** ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)) — the ignored slot still contributes to the function type, and because nothing is named several ignores may coexist (`lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal) — and a **`for` loop variable** ([§21.4](#sec-the-for-statement)) — `for var _ in xs do … end;` iterates for effects with the element unbound, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s semantics unchanged (in an owning iteration the unbound element is disposed per iteration exactly as a bound-but-unused one is). No parameter modifier and no type annotation composes with a bare ignore.

**Rejected positions.** Everything else is a compile error whose diagnostic names the sanctioned forms: `var _ := e;` and `const _ := e;` (`_` is a discard, not a declarable name — the diagnostic names both remedies, `_ := e;` for end-of-statement release or `using var _ := e;` for the anonymous scope-end hold; [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)); `out var _` and `ref _` (above); every declaration named `_` — a method or constructor parameter (parameter names are call-site-addressable API surface, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments), carried by the artifact interface, [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface) — choose a name), a field, property, method, type, module, enum constant, choice case, loop label ([§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue)), or alias; the binding spellings of `_` — a pattern binding (`case x of var _ =>`, [§19.3](#sec-patterns)) and a catch-arm binding (`catch var _: E =>`, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)), where the bare wildcard already means match-without-binding (write `_`, or the bindingless `catch E =>`), and a binding-atom clause (`(var _ := E; body)`, [§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)), whose remedy is naming the binding or restructuring the expression — the statement remedies above are not spellable inside the atom; and a bare `_` in expression position (`_` is not a value — nothing binds it, so no such read can resolve).

<a id="sec-recap-of-the-difference-between-discard-and-using-var-_"></a>
<a id="sec-the-anonymous-owning-binding"></a>
#### The anonymous owning binding `using var _`

`using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := …;` in async contexts, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) is the **one `_` form that owns storage**: it binds the value to an unnamed scope-bound local — scope-end disposal, non-reassignability, and every other [§28.10](#sec-using-var) rule of a named `using var`, the borrow-pin case included — and binds **no name**: `_` is not in scope after the declaration, and nothing can read the value. The ordinary `using var` ascription is retained (`using var _: Stream := …;`): the no-annotation rule governs the bare ignores of this section, not this binding. It is the scope-end counterpart of the discard statement; the choice between the two is one of **disposal timing**, not legality:

```bezel
_ := expression;            // value evaluated; if owned, disposed at END OF
                            //   STATEMENT (an unbound owned temporary). For a
                            //   value/runtime-managed type, dropped — the
                            //   discard only silences the unused-result
                            //   warning; a trivial-dispose class value is
                            //   freed at end of statement, no user code
                            //   running (§28.9). (Task/Task<T> excepted:
                            //   use Task.FireAndForget.)

using var _ := expression;  // value bound to an unnamed local that is
                            //   disposed at END OF SCOPE; works for any
                            //   class type.
```

Use `_ := …` to dispose an owned result you do not need *now*; use `using var _ := …` when the value must outlive the statement but you do not want to name it.

<a id="sec-constant-expressions"></a>
### 17.14 Constant expressions

Several rules key on an expression being a **compile-time constant**: `const`
initializers (class-level, [§22.12](#sec-static-members); local, grammar A.6),
enum member values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), constant narrowing
([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), inline-array sizes ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)),
and static duplicate-key detection in dictionary literals
([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)). This section defines the term; grammar
A.8's `ConstExpr` (and A.5's `ConstIntExpr`) refer here.

A **constant expression** is built from exactly these forms:

- a literal, excluding interpolated strings: integer, floating-point, and
  character literals, string literals, `true`, `false`, `null` (A.8);
- a reference to a `const` member — class-level, local, or the
  compiler-provided constants of the primitive wrapper types
  (`int.MaxValue`, stdlib §1) — or to an enum constant;
- `nameof(…)` ([§17.9](#sec-the-nameof-operator));
- the unary operators `-`, `+`, `~`, and `not` applied to a constant operand;
- the binary arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`), bitwise and shift (`&`,
  `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`), comparison (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `=`, `<>`), and
  boolean (`and`, `or`) operators applied to constant operands of primitive
  or `string` type — including `+` as constant `string` concatenation, which
  folds;
- the `if` expression `(if c then a else b)` ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)) whose
  condition and both branches are constant expressions;
- a parenthesized constant expression.

Nothing else is constant. In particular: explicit conversions (`byte(x)` —
constant narrowing at the use site covers the useful direction; casts in
constants are recorded as liftable), `default(T)` (declined-liftable: for
primitives it folds trivially, but the sublanguage is literal-rooted and
`0`/`false`/`0.0` already spell those values), `typeof` (a `Type` is a
runtime object), `new`, collection literals, interpolated strings, and calls
of any kind (including operator overloads — the operators above are the
built-in primitive/string operators only) are not constant expressions.

**Evaluation.** A constant expression is evaluated at compile time under the
*same semantics* the expression has at run time — [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)
checked integer arithmetic, [§6.3](#sec-floating-point-arithmetic) IEEE 754
(overflow to `±Infinity` and `NaN` propagation are *values*, not faults),
[§6.4](#sec-decimal-arithmetic) decimal, [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)
bitwise and shift semantics, [§20](#sec-the-if-expression)'s and the boolean
operators' short-circuiting (an operand that would not be evaluated at run
time is not evaluated at compile time and contributes no fault). An evaluation
**fault** — integer or `decimal` overflow, division or `mod` by zero, a shift
count outside the [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations) domain — is a
**compile error at the constant expression**, never a deferred runtime fault:
`const B := 2147483647 + 1;`, `const D := 5 / 0;`, and `const F := 1 << 64;`
are rejected where they are written, the same posture as
[§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s constant-narrowing range error.

**Type restriction on `const`.** The two conditions — a constant-expression
initializer *and* a declared or inferred type that is a primitive value type or
`string` — define the **compile-time classification** of a `const` declaration
([§22.12](#sec-static-members)) and remain mandatory for class-level and
`static const` declarations. A *local* `const` failing either condition is a
**runtime const** ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)) rather than an
error; a reference to a local `const` is a constant expression only when the
declaration is compile-time-classified.

`case`-pattern constants are the narrower syntactic form `Constant` of
grammar A.8 — a possibly-negated literal, an enum constant, or a named
`const` reference — not the full sublanguage; [§19.3](#sec-patterns) is
unchanged.

```bezel
const H := int.MaxValue / 2;              // 1073741823 : int
const Flags: long := (1 << 10) | (1 << 3); // folds under §6.5 semantics (parens for clarity;
                                           //   shift-with-bitwise is not a §17.2 mandatory mix)
const Greeting := "Hello, " + "world";    // constant string concatenation
const Who := nameof(Greeting);            // "Greeting"
const Cap := (if Flags > 0 then 64 else 32);     // constant conditional
// const B := 2147483647 + 1;             // compile error: constant evaluation overflows (§6.1)
// const F := 1 << 64;                    // compile error: shift count outside 0..31, the int
//                                        //   left operand's domain (§6.5)
// const S := $"v{H}";                    // compile error: interpolated strings are not constant
```

<a id="sec-the-binding-atom"></a>
### 17.15 The binding atom

The binding atom names a subexpression within expression position (grammar A.7 `BindExpr`, the PrimaryAtom family):

```
(var name := initializer; body)
(var a := E1; var b := E2; body)
```

The parentheses are part of the form: in atom-start position, `(` followed by the reserved `var` — which begins no other expression — commits the reading at the second token, exactly as the `(if …)`, `(case …)`, and `(when …)` atoms commit ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)); in call- and index-argument position the atom supplies its own pair. Each **clause** — `var x := E;` or `var x: T := E;` — introduces one binding and is terminated by `;` (no expression contains a top-level `;`, so the clause's extent is unambiguous); at least one clause is required; clauses chain; the **body** is one full expression, and the atom's value, type, and ownership classification are the body's. The atom takes no precedence-table entry ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)): it is self-delimited and composes in any operand position, exactly as the other paren atoms do.

```bezel
var area := (var w := bounds.Width(); w * w);
var label := (var n := items.Count; (if n = 1 then "one item" else $"{n} items"));
```

**It is binding, not assignment-in-expression.** Each binding is initialized exactly once, at its clause, by ordinary evaluation in textual order — clauses first, body last, every clause on every evaluation. Like a runtime `const` ([§21.1](#sec-runtime-const-locals)), a binding is **not an assignable location**: assignment, compound assignment, `++`/`--`, and binding to a `ref` or `out` parameter are compile errors naming this rule (assignment forms are statements and cannot be spelled *inside* the atom at all; the location rule additionally covers a `do`-bodied lambda within the atom that captures the binding). A lambda may capture a binding by read, under the ordinary capture rules ([§27](#sec-lambdas-and-function-types)).

**Scope and typing.** A binding is in scope from the end of its own clause: the subsequent clauses' initializers and the body see it; its own initializer does not; nothing outside the atom ever does. A binding whose name is already in scope — a local, a parameter, or an earlier binding of the same atom — follows the same duplicate-declaration rule as a [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) local in a nested scope. Each clause types exactly as the [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations) declaration statement it is spelled as: the type is ascribed (with typed-context widening, [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) or inferred from the initializer; a bare `null` initializer requires a nullable ascription (`var x: T? := null;` — the binding is then permanently null, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s dead-null warning applying, since no later assignment exists). The atom is **not** a constant expression ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s inductive set is unchanged; admission of all-constant atoms is recorded liftable). In statement position the atom is an ordinary expression statement — [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)'s discard regime applies to the body's value — but at statement level the declaration statements it abbreviates are the idiomatic spelling.

**Ownership rides the kernel** ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); the atom adds no new ownership rules. A clause is a *binding form*: a borrow initializer makes its binding a borrow carrying the initializer's source set ([K2](#sec-kernel-k2)); a marked transfer `var y := move x;` is [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s binding transfer, consuming the outer binding on the atom's straight-line evaluation; an owned production makes its binding a **named unbound owned temporary whose boundary is the atom itself** ([K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8), this revision): if still undischarged when the atom completes, it is disposed there — after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order, exception edges discharging by the unwinding pass ([K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)) — with no must-use warning (a temporary's disposal is the language's job, not an unclaimed obligation). Within the atom such a binding is an ordinary named owned binding: [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s consuming positions (an `owned` argument, an explicit `Dispose()`) discharge it and the atom-boundary disposal then does not run. A borrow whose source is an atom binding may not escape the atom — in the body's value or any other holder — per [K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8): rejected, never lifetime-extended; bind at statement level (`using var`, [§28.10](#sec-using-var)) when the value must outlive the expression. The body is **not** among [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked-transfer positions in this revision (no `move x` body; an atom cannot transfer its own binding out as its result; recorded liftable with the other A.7 positional bounds).

**In contract clauses** ([§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses)) the atom is admitted — it is the form's motivating position: clauses are expression-only and pure, so without the atom a clause using a subresult twice would have to recompute it. Clause initializers and the body are checked under the clause rules expression-wise ([§22.16](#sec-clause-typing)); owned productions cannot arise there (the pure fragment's records-only allocation, [§22.15](#sec-pure-body-rules)), so clause atoms never carry disposals.

<a id="sec-literals-and-strings"></a>
## 18. Literals and Strings

<a id="sec-numeric-literals"></a>
### 18.1 Numeric literals

Integer literals:
```bezel
42                  // int
0xFF                // hex
0b10101010          // binary
1_234_567           // digit separators allowed except at start/end
42L                 // long
42U                 // uint
42UL                // ulong
```

Floating-point and decimal literals:
```bezel
3.14                // double
3.14f               // float
-1.23e-4            // scientific notation, double
1.23456789m         // decimal
1.23e2m             // scientific notation, decimal
```

Suffixes are case-insensitive: `L`/`l`, `U`/`u`, `F`/`f`, `M`/`m`. The compiler does not silently promote integer literals: in an untyped context `3_000_000_000` is a compile error without an `L` suffix. (In a context with an explicitly declared integer target the literal is admitted at the declared type when it fits — the typed-context widening of [§4.2](#sec-integer-types).)

<a id="sec-boolean-and-null-literals"></a>
### 18.2 Boolean and null literals

`true`, `false`, `null`.

<a id="sec-character-literals"></a>
### 18.3 Character literals

```bezel
'a'         '\n'      '\t'      '\r'      '\\'      '\''
'\u0041'              // 4 hex digits, BMP
'\U0001F600'          // 8 hex digits, full code point range
'\x41'                // 1–4 hex digits
```

Escape sequences resolving to U+D800–U+DFFF are compile errors.

<a id="sec-string-literals"></a>
### 18.4 String literals

```bezel
"Hello, Bezel!"
"Line 1\nLine 2"      // escapes processed
```

<a id="sec-interpolated-strings"></a>
### 18.5 Interpolated strings

A `$` prefix introduces interpolation. Any expression may appear inside `{}`:

```bezel
var greeting := $"Hello, {name}!";
var msg := $"({point.X}, {point.Y}) - area = {point.Area()}";
```

An interpolation may include alignment and a format specifier:

```
{expression}
{expression,alignment}
{expression:format}
{expression,alignment:format}
```

- Alignment is a signed integer; positive right-aligns in a field of that width, negative left-aligns. Wider results overflow the field.
- Format is a type-specific string passed to the value's formatter — see the dispatch rule below.

```bezel
$"{amount:F2}"           // "1234.50"
$"{ratio:P1}"            // "85.0%"
$"{value:X}"             // "FF"
$"{date:yyyy-MM-dd}"
$"|{name,20}|"           // right-aligned in 20-character field
$"{amount,12:F2}"
```

**Format dispatch.** A hole *without* a format spec formats via the value's ordinary `ToString()` ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)). A hole *with* a format spec dispatches to `ToString(format: string)`: the primitive and temporal types provide it intrinsically (the specifier vocabulary and its invariant-culture semantics are normative in stdlib [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)); a **user** type opts in by implementing the auto-imported interface `IFormattable` (stdlib [§2.18](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-iformattable)). A format spec on an operand whose type is neither intrinsically formattable nor `IFormattable` is a **compile error** naming this rule. An unrecognized specifier at runtime raises `FormatException` (the defined-fault rule, stdlib §2.18).

**Nullable holes.** A hole expression may have
a nullable type; no narrowing is required. When the value is `null` at render
time, the hole renders as the four-character text `null`, and no `ToString()`
or `ToString(format)` dispatch occurs — [§8.5](#sec-tostring)'s implicit
invocation is defined for present values. A format spec on a nullable-typed
hole is checked at compile time against the **non-nullable form** of the
operand's type under the dispatch rule above (the type-formattability check;
specifier recognition remains the runtime rule above), and the spec is simply
not invoked when the value is null. The alignment applies to the rendered
text `null` exactly as to any other rendered text (it participates in field
padding). The hole is not a [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values)
member access: the dispatch is performed by the language with a defined null
case, the same posture as the null-safe `=`/`<>` of [§8.4](#sec-=-and) — and
unlike [§4.6](#sec-string)'s ordering rule, where a null participant has no
defensible result, rendering one does: making it *visible*. Rendering `null`
rather than the empty string keeps absent values diagnosable in output.

```bezel
var name: string? := null;
Console.WriteLine($"user={name}");     // prints: user=null
var x: double? := null;
Console.WriteLine($"[{x,8:F2}]");      // prints: [    null] — the type-formattability check
                                       //   applies to double; F2 is not invoked on null;
                                       //   the alignment pads the text
x := 3.0;
Console.WriteLine($"[{x,8:F2}]");      // prints: [    3.00] — present value: ordinary dispatch
```

**Hole delimitation (normative).** Inside `{…}` the lexer tracks nesting of `(` `)` `[` `]` `{` `}` and skips nested string/char literals (recognized by their own opening quote and parsed as complete literals; they do not terminate the outer string). The alignment `,` and the format-spec `:` are recognized only at the **top nesting level** of the hole; the first top-level `,` begins the alignment, the first top-level `:` begins the format spec. Consequently `{d[k]:F2}` needs no parenthesization tricks (`[…]` nests its colon) and `{(if c then a else b),8}` aligns the conditional. The tracked pairs are exactly `()`, `[]`, `{}` — balanced `<…>` is **deliberately not tracked**: the generic-arguments reading of `<` is a parser-level commitment ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s balanced-scan-plus-continuation rule), and this boundary rule stays implementable without a parser; a lexer-level `<`-balance test would also re-cut legal holes like `{x < y,8}`, a comparison with an alignment. A **multi-argument** generic-arguments list at the hole's top level is therefore cut at its comma — `{Cache<int, string>.Default}` is a compile error at the mis-cut fragment — and the remedy is the same parenthesization as for the conditional above: `{(Cache<int, string>.Default)}`. Single-argument forms (`{Cache<string>.Default}`) contain no top-level `,` and need nothing. The format spec runs from its `:` to the hole's closing `}`; braces do not appear inside a format spec (a `{` there is a compile error).

**Literal braces.** In interpolated strings (`$"…"` and `$@"…"`), a doubled brace denotes a literal brace: `{{` produces `{`, `}}` produces `}`. An unescaped `}` that does not close a hole is a compile error; write `}}` for a literal closing brace. Non-interpolated strings are unaffected (braces are ordinary characters there).

<a id="sec-verbatim-strings"></a>
### 18.6 Verbatim strings

A `@` prefix suppresses escape processing. Verbatim strings may span multiple lines; line breaks become part of the string value.

```bezel
var path := @"C:\Users\Bezel\Program.bzl";
var sql := @"SELECT name, age
FROM users
WHERE active = 1";
```

Inside a verbatim string, `""` produces a single `"`.

<a id="sec-interpolated-verbatim-strings"></a>
### 18.7 Interpolated verbatim strings

`$@` combines both:

```bezel
var documentPath := $@"C:\Users\{user}\Documents\report.pdf";
```

<a id="sec-escape-sequences-non-verbatim"></a>
### 18.8 Escape sequences (non-verbatim)

| Escape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\n` | Newline (LF) |
| `\r` | Carriage return |
| `\t` | Horizontal tab |
| `\\` | Backslash |
| `\"` | Double quote |
| `\'` | Single quote |
| `\0` | Null character |
| `\a` | Alert (bell) |
| `\b` | Backspace |
| `\f` | Form feed |
| `\v` | Vertical tab |
| `\uXXXX` | Unicode scalar value, BMP only |
| `\UXXXXXXXX` | Unicode scalar value, full range |
| `\xH..H` | Hex escape, 1–4 digits, BMP only |

The `\x` escape greedily consumes the maximum number of valid hexadecimal digits, up to 4. In the string `"\x41BC"`, the escape is `\x41BC` (U+41BC), not `\x41` followed by `BC`. To produce the two-digit escape `\x41` followed by the literal characters `BC`, use concatenation (`"\x41" + "BC"`) or the `\u` form (`"\u0041BC"`).

Surrogate escapes (U+D800–U+DFFF) are compile errors.

---

<a id="sec-the-case-construct"></a>
## 19. The `case` and `when` Constructs

`case` is multi-way pattern matching against a scrutinee. Its sibling `when` is multi-way **condition** dispatch with no scrutinee — each arm is a boolean test, and the first true arm wins. Both are single constructs that produce a value; in statement position, the value is discarded per the [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions) rules (applied per arm — see below). **Expression-position type:** the construct's type is the left-fold of its arm-body types under the [§20](#sec-the-if-expression) common-type rule (`throw` arms are bottom-typed and impose no constraint). Only the selected arm's body is evaluated. They share the same arm bodies ([§19.2](#sec-arms)) and appear in either position, with the closer keyed to the position: in expression position each is a parenthesized, self-delimited **atom** — `(case … of …)` / `(when …)`, expression-bodied arms only — and in statement position each is an `end`-terminated **statement** (`case … of … end case?;` / `when … end when?;`, grammar A.6 `CaseStmt`/`WhenStmt`) whose arms may also be single statements or `do … end` blocks.

<a id="sec-forms"></a>
### 19.1 Forms

**`case` (scrutinee form)** — `case expression of` followed by arms. The scrutinee is evaluated once and matched against each pattern in order. `case` **always** takes a scrutinee; a `case` written with no scrutinee expression is a syntax error — use `when` for condition dispatch.

**The `of` delimiter.** The keyword `of` terminates the scrutinee and introduces the arms — the Pascal-heritage spelling (`case x of`). Because the boundary is explicit, the scrutinee is a **full Expression** with no precedence restriction and no parenthesization rule: `case x - 1 of`, `case flags & mask of`, and `case lo..hi of` are all direct. A first pattern may begin with any pattern token — a negative range bound in particular — with no possibility of the scrutinee absorbing it:

```bezel
case delta of
  -10..-6 => "strongly down",
  ..<0    => "down",
  0       => "flat",
  _       => "up"
end;
```

A missing `of` is a syntax error at the first arm token; the diagnostic names the delimiter ("expected `of` after the case scrutinee").

```bezel
var grade := (case score of
  90..100 => "A",
  80..89 => "B",
  70..<80 => "C",
  _ => "F");
```

**`when` (condition dispatch)** — `when` followed by arms whose patterns are full boolean expressions. The arms are evaluated in textual order; the first whose expression is `true` is selected. This subsumes the `if`/`elif` chain. `when` takes no scrutinee.

```bezel
var grade := (when
  score >= 90 => "A",
  score >= 80 => "B",
  score >= 70 => "C",
  _ => "F");
```

`when` exists in both expression position (above) and statement position:

```bezel
when
  score >= 90 => Console.WriteLine("A"),
  score >= 70 => Console.WriteLine("C"),
  _          => Console.WriteLine("F")
end;
```

A `when` arm's expression must have type `bool` ([§4.1](#sec-bool)). The `_` catch-all is permitted as the last arm and behaves as an always-true condition. Because `when` has no scrutinee, it is never statically exhaustive: in expression position, supply a `_` arm or the compiler warns that an unmatched dispatch raises `MatchFailureException` ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)).

<a id="sec-arms"></a>
### 19.2 Arms

Each arm has the form `pattern => body`. An arm body has three possible shapes:

- **An expression** (any Bezel expression — literal, method call, another `case`, etc.). This is the only form valid in expression-position `case` (where the whole `case` produces a value).
- **A single statement** (e.g. `=> _x := y;`, `=> return;`, `=> throw new ArgumentException("nope");`). Valid in *statement-position* `case` only. The statement's terminating `;` ends the arm body, and the arm separator `,` follows. This is the convenient form for the common one-line arm body that is a statement rather than an expression.
- **A `do … end` block** of statements. Has type `()` and produces no value, so it is valid in statement-position `case` only. Use this when the arm body needs multiple statements.

In an expression-position `case` or `when`, an arm result may be the **marked transfer** `move x` ([§28.3](#sec-producers), K3.4): the named binding is consumed on the path where that arm is selected, and is per-path consumed after the construct ([K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)). An arm result marking the *scrutinee's own binding* is always rejected by the consume-site freeze — the scrutinee borrow is live through the selected arm's completion ([K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8), [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)); transfer after the construct instead.

Multi-statement logic in *expression-position* arms is extracted into a helper method or local lambda — both produce values, and the extraction makes the arm's intent visible at its declaration site:

```bezel
var description := (case score of
  > 90 => "excellent",
  > 70 => "good",
  > 50 => "passing",
  _    => Classify(score));          // helper for the multi-step case

private static method Classify(score: int): string
  Log("low score: " + score.ToString());
  return (if score < 0 then "invalid" else "failing");
end Classify;
```

Calls to a helper are zero-overhead in the common case (the compiler is permitted to inline them) and keep the arm body to a single expression. The extraction also gives the per-arm logic a name a reader can use, and localizes any side effects the arm performs — both of which are valuable independent of the syntactic question. Rationale [§5.13](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-no-block-expressions) discusses why Bezel does not provide a value-returning `do ... end` form.

`return` inside an arm exits the enclosing callable, not the arm. `case` cannot be exited "early" via `return`; restructure into helper methods.

Arms are comma-separated. A trailing comma after the last arm is optional. In expression position, the ownership of the `case`/`when` result follows the arm-meet rule of [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table — identical to `??` and the `if` expression ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)).

<a id="sec-patterns"></a>
### 19.3 Patterns

**Constants:** `1`, `42`, `-7`, `"hello"`, `Priority.High`. A leading `-` on a numeric literal is part of the constant pattern (grammar A.8).

**Alternatives:** `2 | 3 | 4 | 5` matches any of these. The alternative separator is `|` (grammar: `AltPattern`); the comma means exactly one thing in pattern context — the separator of arms and of positional slots — so no `=>` lookahead is needed to tell them apart. In `1 | 2 => "low", 3 => "high"`, the first arm matches 1 or 2; the second arm matches 3.

In an alternative list, every member must be **binding-free**: a constant (a literal, an enum constant, or a named `const`), a **payload-free choice case name** ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) — nullary, binding-free, and countable toward exhaustiveness like an enum constant), a **range pattern**, or a **relational pattern** — ranges and relationals admitted; like constants they bind nothing and contribute pure membership tests, so `1..5 | 10 => …` and `< 0 | > 100 => …` are single arms. A member that resolves to a *type* is a compile error in a `case` pattern — grouped type tests are written as separate arms; types alter exhaustiveness and binding analysis, which is exactly what the recorded constants-only reasoning targeted (rationale §3.8). Range and relational alternative members do not contribute to static exhaustiveness proofs ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) counts declared constants, not extents), and an alternative list binds nothing regardless of member kind. (`catch` arms, whose members are exclusively types, use the same `|` spelling for their multi-type alternatives — [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally).)

Because the alternative separator `|` is distinct from the slot separator `,`, alternatives are available **per slot** inside a positional destructuring pattern: `TwoColor(Color.Red | Color.Blue, var x)` is a two-slot pattern whose first position matches either color. Alternative members are binding-free per the rule above, so a binding (`var c`) cannot appear inside an alternative list (constants, ranges, and relationals can).

**No collision with bitwise-or (normative note).** `|` is the bitwise-or operator in expressions, but the expression positions embedded in patterns — a relational pattern's operand and a range pattern's bounds — parse at the Shift level or tighter, *below* `|`, so a `|` at pattern level is always the alternative separator. A scrutinee-level `|` belongs to the scrutinee expression (delimited by `of`, [§19.1](#sec-forms)); the [§17.2](#sec-mandatory-parenthesization) mandatory-parenthesization discipline covers any residual mixed reading.

**Inclusive and exclusive ranges:** `90..100`, `0..<60`. Open-ended forms allowed: `..<0` (less than 0), `31..` (at least 31).

**Relational:** `> 70`, `< 50`, `<= 100`, `>= 0`. Compares the scrutinee against the right-hand operand.

**Type patterns without binding:** `string`, `int`, `Dog`. Subtypes match: a `Dog` value matches an `Animal` pattern. Subtype matching is a property of *reference-typed* scrutinees. Over an **unboxed value-typed scrutinee** (a primitive, record, enum, or inline array), a type pattern is a **static** test — the value's runtime and static type coincide ([§8.2](#sec-gettype)) — so over a non-nullable value scrutinee a type pattern naming its exact type always matches (over a *nullable* value scrutinee `T?`, the `T` pattern remains the null-rejecting refutable test of [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)), and a pattern naming any *reference* type (a class, an interface — including one the value type implements — `string`, or `Object`) is a compile error: the pattern could never discriminate at runtime, and matching it would require an implicit boxing conversion, which pattern position never performs ([§8.6](#sec-boxing) boxing is a conversion at value-use sites; a pattern naming any *other* type is likewise rejected under this section's pattern/scrutinee compatibility rules). To test a value against an interface it implements, box explicitly via an `Object`-ascribed binding and match the boxed scrutinee: `var o: Object := p;` then `case o of var q: IShape => …`. The same applies to type patterns with binding (`var q: IShape`).

**Type patterns with binding:** `var n: int`, `var d: Dog`. The bound name is in scope in that arm's `when` guard and body (matching the `catch`-arm rule, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).

**Type parameters as pattern types:** in a generic body, a type parameter may be used as a pattern type — `var x: T` and bare `T` test against the **substituted** type argument, per instantiation, the same rule as catch arms ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)); all type-pattern rules then apply to the substituted type, including the null rule ([§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)).

**Record destructuring:** `Point(x, y)`, `MyRecord(a, b, c)`. The type name followed by parenthesized bindings matches the type and binds positional fields by position. The number of bindings must match the record's positional-field count. Individual positions may be discarded with `_`: `Point(_, y)`. Destructuring patterns compose with `when` guards and with subtype matching.

Destructuring applies to records and choice cases ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)) — the positional binding is over a record's positional fields ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) or a choice case's payload fields. Classes do not have a positional-destructuring surface, even when they declare a primary constructor ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)): primary-constructor parameters are not auto-promoted to public properties, and the positional shape is not part of the class's pattern-match surface. To match a class hierarchy, use a type-test pattern (`Dog`, `var d: Dog`) and access fields through the bound name. The [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) exhaustive-match example over a `closed` class hierarchy uses this form.

Inside a positional destructuring pattern, a naked identifier is interpreted as a binding for that position — `Point(x, y)` binds `x` and `y` (it does not type-test the positions against types named `x` and `y`). The naked-identifier form is the common shorthand; the explicit `Point(var x, var y)` is also accepted and means the same thing. The naked-identifier form is *not* available outside positional destructuring: at the top level of a pattern, an identifier alone is parsed as a type test, so a binding requires the explicit `var` form (`var x` or `var x: T`). Nested patterns inside a destructuring (e.g. `Outer(Inner(x))`) follow the same rule recursively.

**Named destructuring:** `Rect(Width = var w, Height = var h)`, `Header(Version = 1, Body = var b)`. A destructuring pattern's parenthesized slot list may be written **by name** instead of by position: each named slot is `Identifier "=" Pattern` (grammar A.7 `NamedSlot`), where the `Identifier` names a member of the pattern's type and the pattern after `=` interrogates that member. A slot list is **either** positional **or** named, never mixed in one pattern (v1); mixing (`Rect(3, Height = var h)`) is a compile error naming the rule. At least one slot is required, as for the positional form.

The `=` is the interrogation reading of [§8.4](#sec-=-and), not an assignment: a call site *constructs* by name with `:=` (`new Rect(Width := 3)`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), while a pattern *asks* whether a member holds a value (`Rect(Width = 3)` — "is `Width` 3?"), which is exactly what `=` means. No new token is introduced and no collision arises: `=` is not a pattern relational operator (grammar A.7 admits only `<` `>` `<=` `>=`, and a bare constant already means equals), and the expression positions embedded in a slot pattern — relational operands and range bounds — parse at the Shift level or tighter ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)), below equality, so no pattern-interior expression can absorb a slot's `=`.

A named slot's `Identifier` resolves against the pattern's type, by kind:

- **Record** — a positional field's auto-generated property ([§9.1](#sec-positional-records)) or a body auto-property ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)). Computed (expression-bodied) record properties are not named-slot targets in v1 — the storage-only set, the same targets `with` takes ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)).
- **Choice case** — a payload field name of the case the pattern's head names ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§35.5](#sec-case-patterns), with the [§19.8](#sec-inside-enum-scrutinees)/[§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) prefix-omission rule); the head names the case, not the choice type.
- **Class** — a **public readable instance property**, stored or computed, declared or inherited ([§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers)). Positional destructuring deliberately gives classes no pattern surface (above); the named form is the by-name match surface a class's public readable properties are, and reading one transfers nothing.

An unknown name, a duplicate name in one slot list, a write-only property ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)), an indexer ([§23.4](#sec-indexers)), a static member, or — on a class — a field or method rather than a property, is a compile error at the pattern, each naming its rule. Enums and primitives have no named-destructure form (they have no slot surface). An interface-typed pattern head is not admitted in v1. Resolution honours ordinary member visibility ([§13](#sec-visibility)); v1 fixes the class set to *public* readable properties.

Matching `T(N1 = p1, …, Nk = pk)` proceeds like the positional form: the **type test comes first** (subtype matching for a class hierarchy, the case-tag test for a choice case; a named pattern therefore never matches `null`, [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null), and no slot is read on a failed type test), then the named members are read in **textual order**, short-circuiting on the first refuted slot. Each read is the ordinary member read — a record field copy/borrow, a choice payload read, or a **class property getter invocation** — and a getter *runs* during matching: [§19.4](#sec-guards)'s first-match arm order makes the getter-evaluation order deterministic and observable, and a getter that throws propagates out of the `case` construct from the arm being tried (`pure` and contract-bearing getters keep their [§22.15](#sec-pure-members)/[§22.16](#sec-contract-clauses) semantics; matching adds no purity requirement). Each slot's right-hand side is a **full pattern** (grammar A.7 `AltPattern`): a binding (`var w`), `_`, a constant, `null`, a range, a relational, a per-slot `|` alternative among binding-free members (§19.3, unchanged), a type test, or a nested destructuring — named or positional — recursively. A **constant slot is the equality test** `scrutinee.N = c` under the slot's declared type's `=` ([§8.4](#sec-=-and), null-safe, lifted per [§7.11](#sec-lifted-operators) for a nullable slot); a constant slot whose declared type does not bear `=` (e.g. a non-auto-hashable record, [§9.2](#sec-body-records)) is a compile error at the pattern — the same use-site discipline as writing the comparison out.

A naked identifier on a named slot's right-hand side is **not** a binding. Directly after `=` — the interrogation operator — it resolves as at the top level of a pattern: a constant reference or a type test by name resolution, so `Rect(Width = w)` is an equality test when `w` names a `const`. The positional naked-binding shorthand (above) is scoped to positional slots, where there is no `=` to misread; a binding in a named slot is spelled `var w`.

**Named-slot bindings and ownership.** [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s pattern-binding ownership rule applies verbatim to every named slot: the binding is a **borrow**, non-destructive on the scrutinee — for a class property, a borrow whose source is the scrutinee ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) producers, the instance-getter row); for a value-typed record/choice payload, a copy; for `string`/runtime-managed, a shared reference. A named slot never transfers: a getter may not return a fresh owned value ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), so no slot read can mint an obligation, and in an **owning match** ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)) named slots do **not** transfer — an owned payload matched by a named slot is borrowed during the arm and disposed at construct completion by the standard [§35.5](#sec-owning-match-traces) machinery, exactly as a discarded slot. A program that wants an owned payload transferred writes the positional destructure.

**Var patterns:** `var t`. Matches any value, binds it. Almost always combined with a `when` guard.

**Discard `_`:** Matches any value, binds nothing. When used as a top-level pattern (a catch-all arm), it must be the last arm (see [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); inside destructuring patterns (`Point(_, y)`), `_` may appear in any position with no last-arm restriction.

**Pattern binding and ownership.** A pattern binding (`var d: Dog`, the naked identifier `x` in `Point(x, y)`, or the unconstrained `var t`) is **non-destructive on the scrutinee**: the scrutinee retains whatever ownership state it had, and the bound name is a borrow whose source is the scrutinee's source. This matches the `as` operator's behavior ([§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)). When the scrutinee is an owned local of class type and the user wants to transfer ownership through a pattern match, the user moves from the original scrutinee variable after the case construct selects an arm — the case construct itself never moves from the scrutinee. For value-type scrutinees, the binding is a copy by the standard value-type rules; for runtime-managed scrutinees (`string`, function values), the binding is a shared reference. For a scrutinee of **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning inline array; for an owning *choice* scrutinee, the borrowing/owning match split of [§35.5](#sec-choice-matching) governs), the binding is a **borrow** of the value: a copy is forbidden and the case construct never moves from the scrutinee, so the borrow form is the only consistent option — the same reasoning as closure capture of a move-only local ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). Slot reads through the binding are admitted; `move s[i]` through the binding is rejected (the binding does not own the array). The narrowing produced by the case arm is purely informational about the type tag; it does not change the ownership state of the scrutinee.

<a id="sec-guards"></a>
### 19.4 Guards

A `when` clause adds a runtime guard:

```bezel
case temperature of
  var t when t > 30 => Console.WriteLine($"Hot: {t}"),
  var t when t < 0 => Console.WriteLine($"Freezing: {t}"),
  var t => Console.WriteLine($"Mild: {t}")
end;
```

Arms are evaluated in textual order. The first arm whose pattern matches *and* whose guard is true is selected.

The guard keyword `when` (after a pattern, within an arm) is distinct from the `when` *construct* keyword ([§19.1](#sec-forms), at the start of an expression or statement); position disambiguates the two, so no parsing conflict arises.

<a id="sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null"></a>
### 19.5 Type-pattern matching never matches `null`

A bare type pattern `T` matches only non-null values. A typed binding pattern `var n: T` also matches only non-null values — the type annotation makes it a type-constrained binding, not an unconditional binding. `null` is matched only by the explicit `null` pattern, by untyped `var x` patterns (which bind any value including null), or by `_`.

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness"></a>
### 19.6 Exhaustiveness

If `_` appears, it must be the last arm; placing it earlier is a compile error.

A `case` with no `_` arm is permitted. In statement position, an unmatched value falls through with no action — except for a statement-`case` that [§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement) grants totality, whose no-match edge is statically dead and is lowered as a defined trap rather than a fall-through. In expression position, an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException` at runtime; the compiler warns when it cannot prove exhaustiveness statically.

A `when` construct is governed by the same no-match rule, but having no scrutinee it is never statically exhaustive: the static-proof cases below all reason about a scrutinee's type. A `when` with no `_` arm in expression position therefore always draws the non-exhaustiveness warning; supply a `_` arm to make the dispatch total.

The compiler proves exhaustiveness statically in the following cases:

- **Any scrutinee — irrefutable arm:** some arm is irrefutable — an unguarded `_`, or an unguarded untyped `var x` pattern (which binds any value, including `null`, [§19.5](#sec-type-pattern-matching-never-matches-null)).
- **Enum scrutinee:** every declared constant has a matching pattern — a constant pattern ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) naming it directly or as a member of a `|` alternative list, a `var` binding, or `_`. Coverage is by **value**: under duplicate constant values ([§10.2](#sec-explicit-values)), an arm naming either alias covers both. Because every producer of an enum value yields a declared value ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts), [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis), [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), a statically exhaustive enum `case` cannot raise `MatchFailureException`.
- **Choice scrutinee:** every declared case is covered by an unguarded arm — a payload-free case by a constant-style pattern naming it, directly or as a member of a `|` alternative list; a payload-carrying case by a positional destructuring pattern for it whose every slot is **irrefutable** (a binding or `_`). Guarded arms contribute nothing (the rule), and an arm whose slot patterns are refutable (a constant, range, relational, alternative, or nested destructuring slot) covers only part of its case's value space and likewise contributes nothing; coverage is counted per case name, one level deep ([§35.6](#sec-choice-exhaustiveness)). When every case is covered, no `_` arm is required — including across module boundaries: the case set is closed by the declaration, so the cross-module rule below applies with "leaf type" read as "declared case", and adding a case to a published choice is a source-breaking change for consumers exactly as adding a sealed leaf is. Generic choice scrutinees need no per-instantiation analysis: coverage is by case name, not by type.
- **Bool scrutinee:** both `true` and `false` are covered.
- **Sealed class hierarchy scrutinee:** when the scrutinee's static type is a `closed` class, or an `abstract` class whose only direct subclasses are themselves `sealed` or recursively form a closed set, and every leaf type in the closed hierarchy is matched by a type pattern (with or without binding), no `_` arm is required. A **leaf type** is every **concrete** (neither `abstract` nor `closed`) class in the closed set — including a concrete class that itself has subclasses: its exact-runtime-class instances exist, so the childless-only reading would claim a proof while such a value matches no arm. Abstract and `closed` members of the set have no instances ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes), [§12.5](#sec-abstract-classes-and-members)) and need no arm. A leaf is **covered** when some unguarded type pattern it is assignable to matches it — subtype matching, [§19.3](#sec-patterns) — so an arm for a concrete intermediate also covers its concrete descendants; to discriminate, place the descendant's arm first ([§19.4](#sec-guards) first-match order). This is the runtime test's static image (for non-generic hierarchies; see the *Generic hierarchies* subsection): every non-null value's runtime class is some concrete member of the closed set, so covering each concrete member covers every value. The leaves may be matched in any order; the analysis is purely on type coverage. When the root or any leaf is generic, leaf coverage is **not attempted** and the match is completable only by an irrefutable arm (the *Generic hierarchies* subsection below). Class leaves are matched by type-test patterns (`var c: Circle => ...`); positional destructuring ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) applies to record leaves, not to class leaves. A `closed` class ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)) provides the strongest guarantee: no subclass outside the declaring module can exist, so exhaustiveness holds across module boundaries.
- **Nullable scrutinee:** under the rules above plus an explicit `null` pattern.

An arm carrying a `when` guard contributes **nothing** to static exhaustiveness (the compiler does not evaluate guards): the analysis considers only unguarded patterns. A match whose every arm is guarded is therefore never statically exhaustive — in expression position it draws the warning and raises `MatchFailureException` if every guard declines at run time.

**Named-destructure arms.** An unguarded arm whose pattern is a named destructuring `T(N1 = p1, …, Nk = pk)` ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)) contributes to static exhaustiveness **exactly where an unguarded arm covering `T` by the rules above would** — a type pattern for a sealed-hierarchy leaf, or, for a choice case, where the all-slots-irrefutable positional destructure would (the choice bullet above) — **if and only if every named slot is irrefutable** (a binding or `_`). Any refutable slot (a constant, `null`, range, relational, alternative list, type test, or nested destructuring) makes the arm contribute nothing, exactly as a refutable positional slot does: coverage is counted per type or case name, one level deep, with **no per-property value-space analysis** in v1 (`Rect(Width = 1..100)` arms never sum to coverage of `Rect`, whatever the property's type). Consequently a sealed hierarchy is matched exhaustively with no `_` arm by named-destructure arms whose slots are all irrefutable, exactly as by bare type patterns.

```bezel
public closed class Shape ... end Shape;
public sealed class Circle: Shape ... end Circle;
public sealed class Square: Shape ... end Square;
public sealed class Triangle: Shape ... end Triangle;

var area := (case shape of
  var c: Circle => Math.Pi * c.Radius * c.Radius,
  var s: Square => s.Side * s.Side,
  var t: Triangle => 0.5 * t.Base * t.Height);                       // exhaustive: every leaf covered, no _ needed
```

When the hierarchy is open (the base is neither `closed` nor an abstract class whose transitive subclass set is closed per the rule above), exhaustiveness cannot be proven statically and the warning is emitted unless the user supplies `_`.

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness-generic-leaves"></a>
#### Generic hierarchies: leaf coverage is not attempted

When the closed hierarchy's root or any leaf is generic, leaf coverage is **not attempted**: type patterns name single instantiations, and the compiler attempts no leaf-inhabitation analysis against the scrutinee type, so no arrangement of type-pattern arms is a static proof — including the sub-case in which every leaf is non-generic and all are named, whose proof the retired v0.196–v0.244 *determination rule* did discharge (per-leaf root-instantiation matching, solution filtering by constraint satisfaction, and the exempt/determined/undetermined classification — retired at v0.245; see the changelog entry and rationale [§8.2](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-class-hierarchy-exhaustiveness-in-case)). Such a `case` is completable only by an **irrefutable arm** — an unguarded `_` or an unguarded untyped `var` — and draws the non-exhaustiveness warning without one; the warning names the generic hierarchy and prescribes the `_` arm and, for value-shaped sums, a `choice` ([§35](#sec-choices)), whose exhaustiveness is counted by case name ([§35.6](#sec-choice-exhaustiveness)) and needs no `_`. This applies across module boundaries exactly as within one: the analysis is not attempted at any scrutinee type. (If evidence for `_`-free generic-leaf matching ever arrives, the recorded reopening shape is the **existential pattern** — a type pattern matching a generic leaf at *any* instantiation, with its attendant binding-surface questions — which would make such coverage expressible with no per-leaf computation; it is a language extension needing its own RFC, not a reading of this rule. Rationale §8.2 carries the record.)

<a id="sec-exhaustiveness-across-module-boundaries"></a>
#### Exhaustiveness across module boundaries

Exhaustiveness is established at compile time against the visible set of leaf types. When a `case` matches over a sealed hierarchy declared in another module, the closed set is computed from that module's source as it appeared at compile time. If a downstream version of the declaring module adds a new sealed leaf, existing exhaustive matches in dependent modules become non-exhaustive — recompiling against the new version will emit the missing-arm warning, and at runtime an unmatched value raises `MatchFailureException`.

The recommended discipline is treating any addition of a leaf type to a sealed hierarchy as a source-breaking change for consumers. Alternatively, a producer who anticipates extension points can leave the base class non-sealed; consumers will then be required to supply a `_` arm, which handles future leaves automatically.

<a id="sec-termination"></a>
### 19.7 Termination

The closer is keyed to the position. In expression position the construct is a parenthesized atom — it opens with `(case` (or `(when`) and its closing parenthesis is the terminator; there is no `end`. In statement position it is an `end`-terminated statement, with the statement's `;` following the `end`:

```bezel
var grade := (case score of
  90..100 => "A",
  _ => "F");             // the atom's ')' closes the case; ';' ends the declaration

case month of
  1 => Console.WriteLine("Jan"),
  _ => Console.WriteLine("Other")
end;                    // statement position: 'end' closes the case; ';' the statement
```

The atom is self-delimited and composes inside any expression position, including inside string interpolations and as another arm's body. In call- and index-argument position its parentheses are its own — the argument list's do not substitute: `f((case x of 1 => a, 2 => b), y)`.

<a id="sec-inside-enum-scrutinees"></a>
### 19.8 Inside enum scrutinees

When the scrutinee has an enum type, the enum prefix may be omitted in patterns. See [§10.6](#sec-case-matching) for details and examples. The same omission applies within a `case` over a choice scrutinee ([§35.5](#sec-choice-matching)): a case name resolves to a case pattern, never a type test.

---

<a id="sec-the-if-expression"></a>
## 20. The `if` Expression

The `if` expression selects between values, condition-first, as a parenthesized, self-delimiting atom (grammar A.7 `IfExpr`, the PrimaryAtom family):

```
(if condition then trueValue else falseValue)
(if c1 then v1 elif c2 then v2 else fallback)
```

The parentheses are part of the form: in atom-start position, `(` followed by the reserved `if` — which begins no other expression — commits the reading at the second token, and the matching `)` closes the atom; there is no `end`. In call- and index-argument position the leading `(` is the argument list's own, so the atom supplies its pair — `f((if c then a else b))`. The reserved `then`, `elif`, and `else` separate the segments; the `else` branch is mandatory (an expression produces a value on every path); and each condition and branch is a **full expression** with no precedence restriction — in particular, a `throw` branch is admitted in *any* branch position.

Both branches must have a common type. **The common type:** the common type of branch types A and B is whichever of the two the other implicitly converts into — identical types trivially; [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) widening (including constant narrowing); non-nullable `T` into `T?`; a subtype into its base class or implemented interface (a [§5.1](#sec-reference-conversions) reference conversion). If neither converts into the other, the expression is a compile error directing to an explicit conversion or upcast — there is **no** sibling-class least-upper-bound search (deliberately unlike the nearest-common-base rule of [§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns), which applies only to multi-type catch bindings). A `throw` branch is bottom-typed ([§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)) and imposes no constraint. A bare `null` branch likewise imposes no constraint of its own: it target-types to the **nullable form** of the other branches' common type — `(if c then s else null)` with `s: string` has type `string?`; its ownership is [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s null-arm absorption; an all-`null` arm set has no type and is a compile error. There is **no branch-level target-typing** beyond the bare-`null` rule: a branch whose form requires a target type from context — a collection literal ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)), the `new()` shorthand ([§17.7](#sec-the-new-operator)), a bare case construction ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)) — is a compile error inside an `if` expression even when the whole expression occupies a target-typed position; write the statement form, or construct each arm through a typed expression. (Recorded decline, liftable — #3042.) Conditions are evaluated in textual order; the first `true` condition selects its branch, the `else` branch is selected when none holds, and only the selected branch is evaluated. When the branches are class-typed, the expression's **ownership** is the arm-meet of [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table: owned arms meet to owned, borrowed arms to borrowed with unioned source constraints, mixed arms are rejected; an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding written as a branch is a borrow arm, and the **marked** branch `move x` — `x` a local binding or `owned` parameter — transfers, consuming on the path where its branch is selected and leaving the binding per-path consumed after the construct ([§28.3](#sec-producers), [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)): `var best := (if fresh.Score() > cached.Score() then move fresh else move cached);`.

```bezel
var max := (if a > b then a else b);
var status := (if age >= 18 then "adult" else "minor");
```

Multi-way selection chains with `elif`, in the statement form's word order:

```bezel
var grade := (if score >= 90 then "A"
              elif score >= 80 then "B"
              elif score >= 70 then "C"
              else "F");
```

For many-way selection over one scrutinee, `case` is preferred ([§19](#sec-the-case-construct)).

The atom takes no precedence-table entry ([§17.1](#sec-precedence)): it is self-delimited and composes in any operand position without further parenthesization, exactly as the `case` and `when` atoms do.

---

<a id="sec-statements"></a>
## 21. Statements

Every statement terminates with `;`. Control structures terminate with `end;`.

<a id="sec-variable-declarations"></a>
### 21.1 Variable declarations

```bezel
var balance: decimal;                 // explicit type, no initializer
var count: int := 0;                  // explicit type with initializer
var greeting := "Hello";              // type inferred
const Pi: double := 3.14159;          // const with explicit type
const MaxUsers := 1000;               // const with inferred type
```

A non-nullable local must be assigned before it is read ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)).

A local cannot be named `_`: the bare underscore is the reserved discard token ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). `var _ := e;` is a compile error whose diagnostic names both sanctioned spellings — `_ := e;` to evaluate and release the value at end of statement, or `using var _ := e;` to hold it anonymously until scope end ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), [§28.10](#sec-using-var)); `const _ := e;` is likewise rejected (a never-readable constant is useless by construction).

<a id="sec-runtime-const-locals"></a>
#### Runtime `const` locals

A local `const` declaration admits any initializer expression. The declaration is classified by the initializer's *form* and the declaration's type:

- **Compile-time constant** — the initializer is a constant expression by [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)'s inductive definition *and* the declared or inferred type is a primitive value type or `string`. Semantics unchanged: the name denotes a compile-time value, admissible in `case` patterns (A.8 `Constant`), in other constant expressions, in inline-array sizes, and in constant narrowing. An evaluation fault in a form-constant initializer remains a **compile error at the declaration** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) — a faulting constant expression is never reclassified as a runtime const.
- **Runtime const** — every other admissible initializer. The declaration is a **single-assignment local binding**: initialized exactly once, at its declaration, by ordinary runtime evaluation. A reference to it is *not* a constant expression; a use in any compile-time position above is a compile error naming the declaration and its first non-constant subexpression.

A `const` local of either classification is not an assignable location: assignment, compound assignment, `++`/`--`, and binding to a `ref` or `out` parameter are compile errors naming the declaration. A lambda may capture a `const` local by read; the mutable-capture forms are excluded by the same rule. The initializer is mandatory (grammar A.6) — there is no declare-then-assign form. Class-level `const` (including `static const`, [§22.12](#sec-static-members)) is unchanged: member-level runtime single-assignment is `readonly`/`static readonly`.

**Ownership.** The initializer of a runtime `const` must not be an **owned production** ([§28.3](#sec-producers)): the binding never takes a disposal obligation and never holds an affine (consumable) value. Admitted: value-typed expressions (records included — a borrow-bearing record value carries [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s ordinary source obligations), `string` and other runtime-managed values, `null` (the binding is then permanently null; [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s dead-null warning applies), and **borrows** — the binding is then a borrow carrying the initializer's source-liveness constraints, exactly as a plain unmarked `var` alias: the consume-site freeze ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)) sees it as any other live local borrow, and its constraint on the source ends at its last use (it does **not** scope-pin the source; pinning remains [§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s job). Rejected, with a diagnostic naming this rule and the `using var` remedy: a fresh `new`, an `owned`-returning call, a `Task`-family call, a deferred-activation producer (a lazy query, `Drain()`, `ReceiveAll()` — affine values, [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)), a `move` (the marked transfer `const y := move x;` included — not a form), and a move-only value ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). *(`const` bindings never change state — not by assignment, not by consumption, not by disposal; an owned, never-reassigned, scope-disposed local already exists: `using var`.)* In a generic body, an initializer whose ownership depends on the substitution is enforced per instantiation category ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2), with the diagnostic naming the instantiation; a body needing uniform admissibility across kinds writes `using var`.

```bezel
const n := items.Count + 1;          // runtime const: int
const name := user.Name;             // runtime const: string (runtime-managed)
const conn := pool.Primary;          // runtime const: a borrow, source pool

const cfg := LoadConfig();           // error: an owned production; bind owned
                                     //   values with `using var` (§28.10)
```

<a id="sec-the-if-statement"></a>
### 21.2 The `if` statement

```bezel
if amount > 0 then
  Balance := Balance + amount;
end;

if score >= 90 then
  grade := "A";
elif score >= 80 then
  grade := "B";
elif score >= 70 then
  grade := "C";
else
  grade := "F";
end;
```

The condition must be `bool`.

<a id="sec-the-while-statement"></a>
### 21.3 The `while` statement

A `while` statement may carry a loop label (`scan: while … do … end scan;`) — [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue).

```bezel
while i < 10 do
  Console.WriteLine(i);
  i := i + 1;
end;
```

<a id="sec-the-for-statement"></a>
### 21.4 The `for` statement

A `for` (or `await for`) statement may carry a loop label — [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue).

`for` iterates any iterable source. This includes values whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>` ([§29](#sec-iteration-2)), inline arrays `[N]T` (which do not implement `IEnumerable<T>` but support direct indexed iteration through a compiler intrinsic, [§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)), and `Range<T>` values (which the compiler may optimize into counted loops):

```bezel
for var i in 1..10 do Console.WriteLine(i); end;
for var i in 0..<n step 2 do Process(i); end;
for var t in transactions do Process(t); end;

for var entry in dict do
  Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Key} -> {entry.Value}");
end;
```

`for` always declares its loop variable with `var`. An optional type annotation must match or be implicitly convertible from the source's element type:

```bezel
for var x: int in source do ... end;
```

The loop variable may be the ignore `_` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): `for var _ in source do … end;` iterates for the body's effects with the element unbound — nothing is named, and the body cannot read the element. A type ascription on the ignore is rejected (`for var _: T in …` — a bare ignore takes its type from context, never an annotation, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). The iteration protocol's borrow/ownership semantics ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) are unchanged by the spelling; in an owning iteration ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s owning path) the unbound element is disposed at each iteration's end exactly as a bound-but-unused iteration variable would be.

The loop variable is freshly bound on each iteration: a lambda captured inside the body sees the value of that specific iteration. Because the binding is fresh each iteration, assigning to the loop variable inside the body affects only that iteration — it does not alter how many iterations run, nor the next iteration's value, even when the source is a `Range<T>` the compiler has optimized into a counted loop.

If the source is empty, the body does not execute.

For async iteration, see `await for` ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)).

<a id="sec-break-and-continue"></a>
### 21.5 `break` and `continue`

`break` exits a loop; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and advances to the next. The unlabeled forms target the immediately enclosing loop. Neither is legal outside a loop; doing so is a compile error.

**Loop labels.** A `while`, `for`, or `await for` statement may be prefixed with a *loop label* — an identifier followed by `:` ([§21.3](#sec-the-while-statement), [§21.4](#sec-the-for-statement), grammar A.6). Only loop statements take a loop label.
