The label names the loop: a labeled loop is a *named construct* in the sense of [§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination), so its `end` may repeat the loop label (`end scan;`); because the construct now has a name, the introducing-keyword closer (`end for;`, `end while;`) applies only to unlabeled loops, and bare `end;` remains valid everywhere.

```bezel
scan: for var row in rows do
  for var cell in row do
    if cell.Bad then break scan; end;
  end;
end scan;
```

**Labeled forms.** `break name;` exits the enclosing loop labeled `name`; `continue name;` skips the rest of that loop's current iteration and advances it. `name` must be the loop label of a **lexically enclosing** loop statement in the **same callable body**; anything else is a compile error naming the labels in scope. The labeled forms are legal exactly where the unlabeled forms are — the label changes which loop is targeted, never where the statement may appear.

After `break name;`, execution continues at the first statement after the labeled loop. `continue name;` transfers control to the labeled loop's *advance point*: for `while`, the condition; for `for` and `await for`, the iteration-advance of the [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) desugaring — the next `MoveNext()`/`MoveNextAsync()` call on the enumerator paths, and the index/step increment (which then falls into the bound check) on the direct-indexed and counted forms. A `continue`, labeled or not, never re-runs the source expression or the enumerator acquisition, and never skips an advance.

On the way to its target, the jump exits every intervening scope — inner loop bodies, `do … end` blocks, `try` bodies — and each performs its ordinary exit obligations ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§28.10](#sec-using-var), [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)): `using var`/`await using var` disposals and pending `finally` blocks run in reverse order of establishment, and the jump is a body-exit edge of every loop body it exits, so each such body's iteration variable is subject to its own [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rule at the jump site. The labeled forms add or alter no disposal rule.

**Label scope, namespace, and duplicates.** A loop label is in scope throughout its loop statement and lives in a namespace of its own: it is never resolved against — and never collides with — variables, parameters, types, or members, and it is not an expression (a local `scan` and a label `scan` may coexist; `nameof` does not accept a label). A loop label that repeats a label already in scope at its declaration — the label of an enclosing labeled loop in the same callable body — is a compile error at the inner label: labels do not shadow. Loops that do not enclose one another may reuse a label freely; their labels are never simultaneously in scope. `_` is not a valid loop label: a label is a declaration, and `_` cannot be declared ([§1.3](#sec-identifiers), [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).

**Callable boundary.** The enclosing-loop search — for the labeled and unlabeled forms alike — is confined to the callable ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)'s list: method, constructor, destructor, lambda, property accessor, indexer accessor) whose body contains the statement. A `break` or `continue` inside a lambda cannot target a loop of the defining method, labeled or not; a compile error. A loop label is correspondingly visible only within its own callable body: a loop inside a lambda may reuse an enclosing method's label without conflict, since the outer label is not in scope there.

Neither may exit a `finally` block: inside a `finally`, a `break` or `continue` — labeled or unlabeled — whose target loop lies **outside** the `finally` is a compile error — the same rule as `return` in a `finally` ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement), [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)). When the `finally` runs during exception propagation, such a jump would abandon the in-flight exception silently. Loops wholly inside the `finally`, and jumps among them, are unaffected.

<a id="sec-do-end-blocks"></a>
### 21.6 `do ... end` blocks

A `do ... end` block groups statements as a single statement and limits the lifetime of locals. Two purposes:

1. **Scoping.** Locals declared in a block are visible only until the matching `end`. `using var` resources ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) are disposed when the block ends.
2. **Multi-statement bodies.** Anywhere a single statement is expected, `do ... end` containing several statements stands in.

```bezel
public method ProcessLargeFile(filename: string)
  var result := 0;

  do
    using var fs := new FileStream(filename, FileMode.Open);
    var data := fs.ReadAll();
    result := ProcessData(data);
  end;
  // fs has been disposed here

  Console.WriteLine($"Result = {result}");
end ProcessLargeFile;
```

When a `do ... end` block ends:
1. `using var` declarations within the block are disposed in reverse declaration order.
2. Local variables declared within the block go out of scope.

Loops use `do` as part of their syntax; `for ... do ... end` and `while ... do ... end` are not separate `do ... end` blocks.

<a id="sec-the-return-statement"></a>
### 21.7 The `return` statement

```bezel
return;                   // exit with no value
return expression;        // exit with a value
```

`return` exits the nearest enclosing **callable** — method, constructor, destructor, lambda, property accessor, or indexer accessor. It is unaffected by `do ... end`, loops, `case` arms, and `try`/`catch`/`finally`.

Form rules:

- A method or accessor with a return type must `return expression;` on every exit path.
- A method or accessor with no return type uses `return;` to exit early; falling off the end is implicit.
- Constructors and destructors use `return;` to exit early. `return expression;` is a compile error.
- Lambdas follow the same rule as methods.

The top-level operand of `return expression;` in a body with a declared return type is a **declared-result position**: when the declared type (for an `async` body, the declared `Task<T>`'s result type, [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) is — nullability stripped — a choice with a case of the written name, a bare case construction target-types against it ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)).

**Statement-`case` totality.** A statement-position `case` ([§19.7](#sec-termination)) counts as exiting on every path — so a callable may end with it, with no trailing `return` — when both hold: **(i)** [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) proves the match statically exhaustive by a **closed-value-space** proof: the irrefutable-arm bullet — an unguarded `_` or an unguarded untyped `var` binding, one proof in both spellings ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)), which closes the match over **any** scrutinee kind; the choice bullet ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration) closes the case set by declaration); the bool bullet (no conversion manufactures a third value, [§4.1](#sec-bool)); the sealed-hierarchy bullet ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes) closes the concrete-class set for a `closed` root, and the same bullet's plain-`abstract` closed-set condition closes it under [§2.8](#sec-module-identity)'s compilation-closure view — *leaf* as defined in §19.6); the **enum** constants-coverage bullet ([§5.4](#sec-enum-casts) closes the value space to the declared values: every producer of an enum value yields a declared value — checked casts, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) deserialization, [§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)'s zero-constant requirement — so the no-match fall-through of a statically exhaustive enum `case` statement is unreachable, [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)'s restored guarantee); or any of these under the nullable bullet with its explicit `null` arm; and **(ii)** every arm's body itself exits on every path (`return`, `throw`, or a nested total construct). Guarded arms must satisfy (ii) like any other arm but contribute nothing to (i) (the [§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness) rule). For a `case` granted totality under this rule, the no-match edge is statically dead; an implementation lowers it as a defined trap (raising `MatchFailureException` or aborting) rather than fall-through, so that the grant's soundness never rests on the exhaustiveness computation alone (as-if: the trap is unreachable in a conforming implementation). No other exhaustiveness proof feeds condition (i): a warning-only proof over an *open* value space (an open hierarchy, a `when` construct) grants nothing.

**Compound statements carry no special grant.** A callable may equally end with an `if`/`elif`/`else`, a `try`/`catch`/`finally`, or any other compound statement: a compound statement satisfies the every-exit-path rule by **ordinary reachability over its completion edges** — it counts as exiting on every path exactly when no path through it completes normally (an `if` chain exits when it has an `else` and every branch exits; a `try` exits when its `finally` block exits on every path — which only a `throw` or a non-terminating path can realize, `return` being rejected in a `finally` (below) — or when the `try` body and every `catch` arm do). The statement-`case` rule above is the sole grant keyed to an exhaustiveness proof.

`return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error.

`return` inside a lambda exits the lambda, not the method that defined it.

<a id="sec-throw"></a>
### 21.8 `throw`

`throw new SomeException(...)` raises an exception. `throw;` (inside a catch arm's body) re-raises the current exception as a statement. The expression form `throw` (without the trailing semicolon, [§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)) is equivalent and may appear anywhere an expression is expected within a catch arm body. See [§31](#sec-exception-handling).

<a id="sec-statement-form-of-expressions"></a>
### 21.9 Statement form of expressions

A method call, an `await` expression, or any other expression whose result is `()` may appear as a statement on its own line, terminated with `;`. A `case`/`when` in statement position also stands alone as a statement; its value handling is **per arm**: an *expression*-bodied arm whose value is non-`()` gets this section's discard warning — and the non-trivial-dispose / interface / `Task` hard error — applied at that arm; statement-bodied and `do … end` arms have type `()` and are exempt.

An expression statement whose result is a non-`()` type is permitted but the compiler emits a warning: the result is silently discarded, which may indicate a bug (a return value the programmer forgot to use). **One exemption: the fluent-receiver discard.** A discarded **method-call** result draws no warning when it is a [§28.3](#sec-producers) **borrow** whose source set lies within the statement's receiver chain **and** whose static type equals the receiver's static type — the `return this` fluent shape (`sb.Append(x);`, stdlib §3.1, chained calls included): the caller still holds the receiver, so nothing computed is lost. Both conditions are load-bearing: dropping the type test would silence same-source *queries* (`FirstOrNull()`-class results are receiver-sourced too), and the exemption deliberately covers method calls only, not accessor reads. A fluent method whose declared return is a *base* of the receiver's type stays warned — conservative by design; `_ := …` remains available ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). Owned results and every other borrow keep this section's regime unchanged. To suppress the warning, use the discard form `_ := expression;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — but only when the result type allows it. For non-trivial-dispose class types, for **interface types** — an interface's conformance set is open, so its implementations' trivial-dispose status cannot be proven across modules and an interface-typed result is treated as **possibly-non-trivial-dispose**, the same unknowability reasoning that makes interface-typed discards dispose the runtime type ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — and for `Task`, the warning is replaced by a hard error directing the caller to the discard `_ := expression;` (immediate disposal, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_) — for an interface, disposal of the runtime type; not available for `Task`), `using var _ := expression;` (scope-end disposal), an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` as appropriate.

Method calls returning `()` and `await` expressions on `Task` (no result) are the common cases; no warning is emitted for these.

<a id="sec-local-type-declarations"></a>
### 21.10 Local type declarations

A `record` or `enum` may be declared as a **statement**, scoped to the enclosing body like a local variable (grammar A.6 `LocalTypeDecl ::= RecordDecl | EnumDecl`). The local type is an **ordinary nominal record or enum** — every §9 (records) and §10 (enums) rule applies unchanged; the sole relaxation is *where the declaration may appear*. The form lets a shape used once — a projection's result record, a small closed constant set scoped to one algorithm — live next to its single use instead of at module or class level.

```bezel
public static method Render(users: Array<User>): string
  record NameAge(Name: string, Age: int);   // local: visible only to end Render
  var rows := users.Select(lambda(u) => new NameAge(u.Name, u.Age)).ToArray();
  var sb := new StringBuilder();
  for var row in rows do
    sb.AppendLine($"{row.Name}: {row.Age}");
  end;
  return sb.ToString();
end Render;
```

**Grammar and admissible positions.** `record` and `enum` are reserved ([§1.4](#sec-keywords), Appendix B.1) and begin no other statement, so the statement reading commits at the first token and no existing program changes meaning. Two slots of the reused Appendix A.3 productions are restricted semantically: the `Visibility?` slot **must be empty** — a local type has no access surface (there is no "outside" holding a reference), so a visibility keyword is a compile error naming the rule; this deliberately contrasts with [§11.6](#sec-nested-types) nested types, where the keyword is *required* because a member has an access surface to declare. The `GenericParams?` slot **must be empty** (v1) — a local type declares no type parameters of its own. `LocalTypeDecl` is admitted wherever a `Statement` is: method, constructor, destructor, and accessor bodies, lambda `do`-bodies, `do … end` blocks, loop bodies, and statement-position arm bodies. "Method-local" reads throughout as *body-local*.

**Scope and name discipline.** A local type's name is in scope from its declaration statement to the end of the **innermost enclosing statement block** — exactly a local variable's scope ([§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations), [§21.6](#sec-do-end-blocks)). The declaration must precede first use; local types are therefore order-significant, and a local type's field types may name only types already in scope (module-visible types, the enclosing class's nested types, and *earlier* local types) — no forward references, hence no mutually recursive local types. Within its scope the name is an ordinary type reference in **body positions**: local-variable ascriptions, `new`, generic arguments (`Array<NameAge>`), `typeof`/`nameof`/`default`, casts and type patterns, and lambda-parameter ascriptions. The name may **not** appear in any **member signature** — parameter, return, field/property/indexer, generic-constraint, or base/interface positions — which is a compile error naming that rule (*"a method-local type may not appear in a member signature"*); the name is simply not in scope at any signature, but the rule is stated so the diagnostic is the named one. The declared name may **not shadow** any type name visible at the declaration point (a local `NameAge` silently shadowing a module-level `NameAge` is a trap, not a convenience — the collision is an error), nor collide with another declaration in the same body's declaration space (another local type or a local variable, the [§11.3](#sec-member-body)-style clash discipline applied to the body). Two *different* methods may each declare `record Row(…)`: the names never meet, and the types are distinct.

**Restrictions (v1).** A local type may not **reference an enclosing generic parameter** (an enclosing method's or class's `T`) — a compile error naming the rule; such a type would be implicitly generic, making its identity, [§9.2](#sec-body-records) equality synthesis, [§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) serialization synthesis, and boxed conformances per-instantiation, a genuine design space disproportionate to the concrete-field motivating case, and a `forbid → allow` widening is compatible where the reverse would break. A welcome consequence of the restriction: a local type's identity is **instantiation-independent** — one nominal type per declaration even inside a generic body, so a public generic's carried body ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) carries it as ordinary body content with no per-instantiation identity questions. `choice` may **not** be declared locally (its payload-derived three-way classification, announced-owning-match obligations, and coverage machinery are a heavier admission deserving its own study — recorded liftable with evidence); `class` and `interface` may not (a class carries ownership, destructors, and the §28 disposal machinery — body-scoped kernel surface for no recorded need; an interface is a contract for an outside a local has none of).

**Semantics — an ordinary nominal type.** Identity is **per-declaration**: two same-shaped local records in different methods are distinct types (nominal, deliberately — no structural unification, which is exactly the anonymous-types discipline the language declines). Auto-equality ([§9.2](#sec-body-records)), `with` ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)), auto-`ToString` ([§8.5](#sec-tostring)), serialization synthesis ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis) — eligibility by field types, conformance declared as usual), interface implementation ([§9.6](#sec-records-and-inheritance)), and the derived type properties ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) — auto-hashable, borrow-bearing per [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal), sendable per [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types), serialization-eligible) are all computed by their existing rules from the declaration. A local `enum` is a §10 enum wholesale: constants, explicit values, underlying types, methods, interface conformances, and `case` matching with prefix omission ([§10.6](#sec-case-matching)) and enum-scrutinee exhaustiveness ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)) inside the scope. Static members are admitted as on any record/enum (a local type's `static readonly` state is program-lived under [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order), like any other static).

**Boxing and escape — the one subtle rule, stated exactly as far as [§8.6](#sec-boxing) already goes.** A **non-borrow-bearing** local record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) — no borrow-carrying fields; `string`/runtime-managed fields do not count) that implements an interface may be **returned boxed through that interface**: the type identity escapes *unnameably*, the precedent being a `private` nested type ([§11.6](#sec-nested-types)) escaping through a public interface today, and such a box is genuinely self-contained — records carry no disposal ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal): records cannot implement `IDisposable`) and a non-borrow-bearing record holds no references whose sources it could outlive. A **borrow-bearing** local record boxes under [§8.6](#sec-boxing) *Boxing of borrow-bearing records* **unchanged**: a short-lived, call-bounded box is admitted, and storing such a box in a field, returning it from a method, or capturing it in a closure that escapes the source scope stays rejected by the same [§8.6](#sec-boxing)/[§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) rules as the unboxed form. The locality of the declaration adds **no new admission**: the case an unqualified admission would wrongly bless — `record View(Cell: Widget)` declared over a `using var` widget and returned boxed through an interface, the widget disposed at the method's end and the box left dangling — is exactly what §8.6's existing rejection stops, fully engaged for local records.

---

<a id="sec-methods-and-constructors"></a>
## 22. Methods and Constructors

<a id="sec-method-declarations"></a>
### 22.1 Method declarations

```bezel
public method Add(a: int, b: int): int
  return a + b;
end Add;

public method PrintGreeting(name: string)
  Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {name}!");
end PrintGreeting;
```

A method has a return type after `:`, or no `:` clause for a procedure (return type `()`).

<a id="sec-expression-bodied-methods"></a>
### 22.2 Expression-bodied methods

When the body is a single expression, `=> expression` replaces the block. A method with **no declared return type** may also use a single *assignment* as its arrow body: `public method SetTotal(v: int) => _total := v;` — the same shape the accessor form `set => _x := value;` has always had; the asymmetry between the two identical declaration contexts was the one indefensible gap in the arrow-body family (the remaining per-context differences are recorded with reasons in the rationale). On a method with a declared return type the assignment form is an error (an assignment produces no value):

```bezel
public method Area(): decimal => Width * Height;
public method Max(a: int, b: int): int => (if a > b then a else b);
```

An expression body under a declared return type is a **declared-result position** ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)): a bare choice-case construction in it target-types against the declared type, exactly as a `return` operand does ([§21.7](#sec-the-return-statement)).

<a id="sec-parameter-modifiers"></a>
### 22.3 Parameter modifiers

- `ref` — pass by reference. The caller writes `ref` at the call site. The variable must be initialized before the call.
- `out` — output parameter. The caller writes `out`. The variable need not be initialized before the call. The callee must assign every `out` parameter on every **normal-completion (return) path** (a path that exits by `throw` carries no assignment obligation); failing to do so is a compile error. `out` is **copy-out-on-normal-return**: within the callee the parameter denotes a callee-local slot, freely readable after assignment; on normal return the slot's value is copied to the caller's recipient; on an exception exit the recipient is untouched — an inline `out var` recipient stays unassigned ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)) and a pre-existing recipient keeps its prior value. An implementation may pass a hidden reference, but a partial write must never be observable on the exception edge. For `out owned`, the callee-local slot is an owned slot: a value assigned to it before a later `throw` is discharged by the callee's ordinary exception-path discharge ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), its disposal established at the assignment ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) — ownership reaches the caller only on normal return, so the value has exactly one owner at every instant (Appendix [C.3](#sec-appendix-c)).
- `owned` — ownership transfer. See [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer). **Call-site marker:** when the argument is a **named owned binding** — an owned local or an `owned` parameter, which the call leaves moved-from — the caller writes the transfer marker at the call site: `M(move x)` (an identifier-operand `move` expression, [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) — the marker is part of the argument expression, not an argument modifier). A **fresh producer** — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, an operator result, or a `move obj._field` — stays unmarked: no live binding is invalidated, so there is nothing to announce. Omitting the marker on a named owned binding is a compile error naming the fix ("this call consumes `x`; write `M(move x)`"); writing it on a borrow, a fresh producer, or a non-`owned` parameter position is likewise an error (at a non-`owned` position the diagnostic names the borrow default — an owned expression may not feed a borrow slot). This is the visibility rule the other destructive modes already follow (`ref`/`out` at call sites), spelled with the same verb as the field take-out (`move x.f`, rationale §5.10).
- `out owned` — output parameter that produces an owned value. The callee assigns an owned value through the parameter; the caller receives ownership and must discharge it (typically with `out using var` at the call site, [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)). The combination `out owned` is the only modifier compound; the others are mutually exclusive.
- `scoped` — storage-bounded retention ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). On a *function-typed* parameter: the callee may store the callback, bounded by the storing object's lifetime; the caller's captures are checked against that bound. On a **class- or interface-typed** parameter: the callee may store the *borrow* in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object; the caller's argument is checked against the same bound and **frozen** until the bound's scope exits, upgrading [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s residual-trust back-reference to a static guarantee. **Call-site marker:** a class- or interface-typed `scoped` argument is written `M(scoped x)` — the same announce-at-the-site discipline as the `move` marker above, though `scoped` remains an *argument modifier*: it marks a lending mode, not an action, and the asymmetry is deliberate; a fresh producer is rejected ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule — bind it first). Function-typed arguments (lambda literals, method references) carry no call-site marker — their admission is capture-based. A function-typed parameter *without* `scoped` is **call-bounded**: the callee may invoke the callback during the call but may not retain it past the call ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). *(the transfer marker likewise appears in local binding and assignment positions — `var y := move x;`, `y := move x;` — [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows).)*

<a id="sec-ref-and-out-argument-locations"></a>
#### `ref` and `out` argument locations

A `ref` or `out` argument must be an **assignable storage location** — the
[§17.6](#sec-the-increment-and-decrement-operators) lvalue categories: a mutable
local variable, a writable field, an indexer slot, or a property with an
accessible setter — subject to: no `using var` binding ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s
pin); no `readonly` field outside its assignable context ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers));
and two recorded v1 bounds (liftable): no location of **owned state** — an owned
local or `owned` parameter, an `owned` field, an owning-collection or
owning-inline-array slot — because a `ref` write is an assignment through an
alias, invisible to the drop-on-overwrite and consume-site-freeze machinery
that [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)/[§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)
key on syntactically visible stores (remedies: pass a borrow, use `owned`
parameters/returns, or `move`); and no mutable static **field or
auto-property** admitted by [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2, whose store
semantics are defined for direct assignment only. A **block-form**
(accessor-bodied) static property is not such a static: it is an admitted
property target, taken through the copy-in / copy-out bracket below like any
other property with an accessible setter. A `ref` argument must additionally be definitely
assigned before the call. For plain `out`, the same categories apply, plus the
inline declarations `out var x` and the discard `out _` ([§22.6](#sec-overloading));
for `out owned`, the accepted forms remain exactly the inline
`out using var x` / `out owned var x` of [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations).

**Exact referent type.** The argument's static type must be **exactly** the
parameter's referent type. Because the parameter aliases the caller's location,
no [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) implicit conversion is admitted — not even
a widening one that an ordinary by-value argument would take at the
[§22.6](#sec-overloading) applicability check ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)'s
exact-unification bullet is this rule's inference-time instance).

**`ref` local and field targets alias; accessor targets bracket.** A `ref` argument
naming a mutable local or writable field is a true alias: callee writes are
visible through the caller's location immediately (the `Swap(ref a, ref b)`
semantics [§14.1](#sec-generic-declarations) presupposes). An **indexer slot or
property** target is instead **copy-in / copy-out** under
[§17.6](#sec-increment-decrement-on-indexer-slots)'s evaluate-once discipline:
the receiver and every index expression are evaluated exactly once, in
[§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s call-site textual
order; for `ref`, the getter is called once to produce the callee's slot value
(for `out` no getter call occurs); on **normal return** the setter is called
once with the slot's final value. Write-backs for multiple accessor-mediated
arguments run in argument textual order — `Swap(ref a[i], ref a[i])` is
defined, the textually later write-back winning — and on an exception exit no
write-back occurs, composing with the copy-out rule above. Accessor-mediated
arguments are never aliases of each other or of anything else during the call.

<a id="sec-inline-out-declarations"></a>
### 22.4 Inline `out` declarations

```bezel
var success := parser.TryParse("42", out var num);
```

`out var name` declares a new variable inline. Its type is inferred from the method's `out` parameter declaration; an explicit type annotation is not permitted in the inline form. `out var _` is a compile error — it would declare nothing; write `out _`, which already means exactly this ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).

The variable's scope is the enclosing block, from the call onward. It is in scope in both branches of any surrounding `if` and after the call.

**Scope is not definite assignment.** The scope rule above says only where the name may appear; whether a read is *legal* follows the ordinary definite-assignment rules for locals ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields), [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations)), applied path-sensitively: an inline `out` variable counts as **assigned only on control-flow paths where the introducing call was actually evaluated**. Under short-circuit operators and conditional expressions the distinction is live. After `if flag and parser.TryParse(s, out var n) then ... end;`, the variable is definitely assigned *inside* the `then` branch — control reaches it only if the call ran (and returned `true`) — but not after the `if`, where a path exists on which `flag` was `false` and the call never executed. The analysis is required to honor the standard short-circuit facts (`A and Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when the whole expression is `true`; `A or Call(out var x)` assigns `x` when it is `false`), so the idiomatic guarded read stays accepted. On a path where the call may not have run, a read of a **non-nullable-reference-typed** out variable is a compile error, exactly as for any other unassigned non-nullable local; value-typed and nullable out variables follow [§7.9](#sec-default-initialization)'s default-initialization rules (the default value or `null` is what such a path observes). An `out using var` disposal obligation likewise attaches only on paths where the call executed **and completed normally**: under [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s copy-out rule a call that threw assigned nothing to the recipient — the assigned-but-unreturned value, if any, was discharged callee-side — so the throw edge carries neither the assignment fact nor the obligation.

For disposal-aware inline declarations, use `out using var`:

```bezel
factory.TryCreate(config, out using var conn);
// conn disposed at end of enclosing block
```

When a method parameter is declared `out owned`, the callee produces an owned value through the output parameter, and the caller's call-site syntax must reflect this. The accepted forms at the call site of an `out owned` parameter are `out using var x` (a scope-bound owned local) and `out owned var x` (an owned local with the standard owned-local discharge rules applying); both produce an owned location for the callee to write through. Plain `out var x` is **not** accepted at the call site of an `out owned` parameter — the resulting value's ownership would have nowhere to go. The full call-site / parameter-modifier compatibility rules are given in [§22.6](#sec-overloading).

<a id="sec-out-nullability-postcondition"></a>
#### Nullability postcondition on `out` parameters

*(this clause **is** a proven-tier contract clause — normatively, `out p: T? when true` on a `bool`-returning method carries `static ensures(not result or p <> null)`, discharged by this section's flow analysis; [§22.16](#sec-when-clause-unification). The `when` spelling remains the surface form; nothing here changes.)*

A `bool`-returning method may declare, on an `out` (or `out owned`) parameter of nullable type, the clause **`when true`** (or **`when false`**) after the parameter's type:

```bezel
public method TryGetCached(name: string, out conn: Connection? when true): bool;
```

The clause is a **compiler-checked postcondition**: on every path of the declaring body that returns the stated constant, the value assigned to the parameter must be provably non-null at the return ([§7](#sec-nullability-2)'s narrowing rules apply inside the callee); a violating path is a compile error in the declaring body. Paths returning the other constant carry no obligation (they typically assign `null`).

At the call site, the compiler narrows the `out` recipient exactly as if the caller had performed an explicit null test: in any region where the call's `bool` result is statically known to equal the stated constant — the controlled branch of `if TryX(…, out var c) then`, an `and`-conjunct, an early-exit guard — the recipient is treated as non-null, so [§22.6](#sec-practical-pattern)'s `c!` becomes plain `c`. The narrowing is invalidated by the standard rules of [§7.4](#sec-member-access-on-nullable-values). The clause is admitted **only** on `out`/`out owned` parameters of nullable type in `bool`-returning methods; anywhere else it is a compile error. It is part of the method's contract like the other parameter modifiers — an override must repeat it ([§12](#sec-inheritance-and-dispatch)'s modifier-match rule) — and it does not create a distinct overload.

This is the declared, checked form of the Try convention's flow narrowing ([§22.6](#sec-practical-pattern), stdlib §1). The design is a *declared, checked* contract, not a structural inference over every `bool`-plus-nullable-out method: an undeclared method keeps requiring the explicit `!`, so no signature silently gains a postcondition its body was never checked against. (Bezel deliberately has no attribute system; this is a compiler-recognized declaration clause in the sense of rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)'s narrow-modifier escape hatch, like `serialized`.)

<a id="sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments"></a>
### 22.5 Optional parameters and named arguments

```bezel
public method Log(message: string, level: string := "INFO", timestamp: bool := true)
  // ...
end Log;

Log("System started", timestamp := false);
Log(level := "ERROR", message := "Failed");
```

Named arguments may appear in any order after positional arguments. **The named form is for plain-value arguments only:** a `ref`/`out` argument, and an argument whose root is the transfer marker (`move x`, [§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)), is passed positionally — `M(out var result := n)` has no reading and does not parse (Appendix A.4 Argument), and `M(item := move x)` is a compile error naming this rule, exactly as its v0.245 spelling was.

**Defaults and modifiers.** A default value is permitted only on parameters with **no modifier or `owned`** (an `owned` default is the owned-allocation form this section already blesses, e.g. a factory-call default); a default-value expression that **produces an owned value of non-trivial-dispose class type** ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) is admitted only when the parameter itself is declared `owned` — the parameter then receives ownership per [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)/[§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) and the callee discharges it — and is a **compile error on a plain (borrowing) parameter**, naming the undischargeable fresh instance (a trivial-dispose producer, e.g. a `new StringBuilder()` default, stays admissible on either form: on a plain parameter the materialized default is a compiler-introduced unbound owned temporary of the **calling statement** — owned by the call's full expression, freed at its [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — and the plain parameter borrows it call-bounded); `ref` and `out` parameters can never carry defaults — both require a caller-side location, which an omitted argument cannot supply. Every parameter after the first defaulted parameter must itself have a default.

**Evaluation order.** A call's **supplied** argument expressions are evaluated in **call-site textual order** — left to right as written, for positional and named arguments alike; naming an argument changes which parameter it binds to, never when it runs (`M(b := Next(), a := Next())` evaluates the `b` expression first). **Defaults for omitted parameters** are evaluated after all supplied arguments, in **parameter-list declaration order**; a default-value expression that reads an earlier parameter (below) observes that parameter's value for this call, whether supplied or itself just defaulted. The order is observable through side-effecting arguments and non-constant defaults (`DateTime.Now`, factory calls) and is normative; it matches C#'s treatment of supplied arguments.

<a id="sec-evaluation-timing"></a>
#### Evaluation timing

A default-value expression is evaluated **at each call site** where the default is used — not at the method's declaration site. The expression is re-evaluated every time a caller omits the parameter; the syntax `level: string := "INFO"` does not bind a single shared `"INFO"` instance to the parameter once and reuse it across calls.

This rule lets default-value expressions be non-constant:

```bezel
public method OpenAsync(path: string, timeout: TimeSpan := TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))
public method LogAt(message: string, at: DateTime := DateTime.Now)
public method NewBuffer(size: int := 4096, fill: byte := 0)
```

`TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)` and `DateTime.Now` evaluate per call. The first two examples produce a fresh value each time the default is taken; the third uses an integer literal whose evaluation is observably the same per call. There is no Python-style "default value is constructed once at definition and shared across calls" footgun: each call that omits a parameter materializes the default expression's value fresh, per call — the materialized value belongs to the **caller's side** of the call (the calling statement's full expression, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), never to the callee's activation frame.

For default values whose expression has owned-allocation semantics (constructing a new class instance, returning an `owned` from a factory), the per-call evaluation produces a fresh owned instance per call. When the parameter is declared `owned` — which *Defaults and modifiers* above requires whenever the produced class is non-trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes)) — the parameter receives ownership through the standard parameter-passing rules ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers), [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)) and the callee discharges it. A trivial-dispose producer admitted on a **plain** parameter is owned on the **caller's side**: the materialized default is a compiler-introduced unbound owned temporary of the call's full expression, freed at that expression's [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), with the plain parameter a call-bounded borrow of it — so the admission is derived from the ordinary temporary rules, not from an exemption, and a callee that stores its plain parameter carries exactly the recorded residual of any unbound owned temporary passed as a plain argument ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries), [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)), no new trust category. (Recorded as liftable, not adopted: nothing in this derivation is specific to trivial-dispose — a fresh plain-parameter default of any class type is equally call-boundable; that widening of the non-trivial rejection above is recorded for a future revision.) In every case the default-value expression must be type-valid in the parameter's position — the most natural pattern remains a factory method returning `owned T` bound to an `owned` parameter.

<a id="sec-permitted-default-value-expressions"></a>
#### Permitted default-value expressions

A default-value expression must be type-compatible with the parameter's declared type and must be free of side-effects on captured locals (the expression is a function-of-call-site, not a function-of-the-frame-containing-the-call). Specifically, a default-value expression may:

- be a literal, constant, or `default(T)`;
- call static methods, including factory methods that return owned instances;
- read other static state (with the usual static-initialization rules);
- read other parameters appearing **earlier** in the same parameter list (e.g. `M(a: int, b: int := a + 1)` is permitted; later-parameter forward references are not).

A default-value expression may not:

- reference instance state (`this`, instance fields, instance properties) — the default belongs to the method's signature, not to a particular receiver's frame;
- reference local variables (the call site's frame is not in scope);
- contain `await` (defaults are not async expressions; an async default would suspend an in-progress call before the body started, which has no clear semantics).

<a id="sec-comparison-with-c#"></a>
#### Comparison with C#

C# requires default-value expressions to be compile-time constants (`int x = 42` is fine; `DateTime t = DateTime.Now` is a compile error). Bezel's call-site evaluation is strictly more expressive: anywhere C#'s rule allows a default, Bezel does too, and additional cases (factory calls, `Now`-style defaults) become available without resorting to `null`-then-coalesce patterns.

The C# choice was driven by ABI stability: the default value is encoded into the method's metadata at the *call site* (the compiler inlines the constant into each caller), so changing the default in the callee doesn't update existing callers without recompilation. Bezel does not make this metadata-encoding promise — defaults are part of the called method's signature, evaluated by the callee or by code generated at the call site against the callee's signature, depending on implementation. Recompilation against a new version of a library may pick up a changed default; this is expected and matches the rest of Bezel's source-compatibility model.

The evaluation-site freedom is mechanical only, never semantic: a default participates in the call per *Evaluation timing* above, and any owned value it produces is received and discharged by the `owned` parameter it initializes ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments) *Defaults and modifiers*) — so no observable disposal-point divergence between callee-evaluated and call-site-generated implementations exists.

<a id="sec-overloading"></a>
### 22.6 Overloading

Methods and constructors may be overloaded by parameter list. Overload resolution considers number, types, and the `ref`/`out` modifiers — overloads differing in any of these are distinguishable. `owned` — in any position, including on an `out` parameter — and `scoped` never distinguish overloads (below).

**Generic candidates.** A generic method enters overload resolution
only after per-candidate type-argument inference ([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference)):
inference runs independently for each generic candidate, and a candidate whose
inference fails is **inapplicable** — the call resolves among the remaining
candidates without error from the failed one. Surviving candidates enter the
ranking below with their substituted signatures. When a non-generic candidate
and a generic candidate are both applicable, and neither the ranking below nor
the defaulted-arity tie-break separates them, the **non-generic candidate is
selected** — the specific declaration is the author's stated intent for that
argument shape. The non-generic preference is the **last** comparison before
ambiguity; in particular the defaulted-arity tie-break applies first:
`M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` on the call `M(5)` resolve to the
*generic* candidate — it fills no default — preserving that tie-break's
compatibility reasoning (adding an optional-parameter overload never re-routes
existing calls), while `Show(x: int)` and `Show<T>(x: T)` on `Show(5)` resolve
to the non-generic. Two generic candidates remain subject to the ordinary
ambiguity rule.

<a id="sec-owned-and-overload-resolution"></a>
#### `owned` and overload resolution

`owned` on an **ordinary parameter** (without `out`) does *not* participate in overload resolution. Two overloads that differ only by `owned` on a parameter — e.g. `M(t: T)` and `M(owned t: T)` — are a compile error. The reason is that ordinary `owned` describes a contract about the argument's lifetime rather than its type; the call-site syntax (`M(value)`) does not visibly distinguish the two forms, so permitting them as overloads would force the caller to know the resolution outcome to write a correct ownership transfer. APIs that need both ownership-transferring and borrowing forms must use distinct method names — `Append` versus `AppendOwned`, or the `FromResult` / `FromOwnedResult` pattern. *(note: the call-site marker `M(move x)` (§22.3) makes the two forms visibly distinct for named-binding arguments, satisfying this paragraph's own carve-out criterion — but the overload ban deliberately **stands** for now; lifting it drags stdlib renames and resolution rules with it and is recorded as a follow-on, not adopted here.)*

`scoped` does not participate in overload resolution either: two overloads differing only in `scoped` on a parameter — `M(cb: () -> ())` and `M(scoped cb: () -> ())` — are a compile error, for the same reason. A function-typed argument carries no call-site marker at all (admission is capture-based, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), so the caller could not select between the pair; a class- or interface-typed argument's `M(scoped x)` marker ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) announces the freeze to the reader but is deliberately not a resolution signal — the language has no resolution-by-call-site-form rule (below) rather than adding a second. (`scoped` remains part of *function-type* identity, [§27.1](#sec-function-types): `(scoped () -> ()) -> ()` and `(() -> ()) -> ()` are distinct types. This rule is about selecting between same-name methods, not about type identity.)

`owned` on an **`out` parameter** is no different: **two methods differing only in the `owned` qualifier on an `out` parameter are a compile error**, exactly like the ordinary-parameter pair above. A binding-form distinction is rejected because it would carry no weight and real cost: the standard library never declares the same-name pair — the borrow/take split is expressed with distinct names everywhere (`TryGetValue` vs `TryPopValue`, `TryPeek` vs `TryPop`) — while the rule would require a dedicated `out _` ambiguity remedy and make `out` the only position where resolution consults how the caller *binds* a result rather than what the caller *passes*. APIs expose borrowing and owning forms under distinct method names, the same remedy as for ordinary `owned`.

The call-site form must still **match** the declaration ([§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations)): `out var x` produces a borrow location and is accepted only against a plain `out` parameter; `out using var x` (and the inline `out owned var x`) produce an owned location and are accepted only against `out owned`. A caller cannot write `out using var` against a plain `out` parameter (the result would have no owned source), nor plain `out var` against an `out owned` parameter (the resulting value's ownership would have nowhere to go). These are compatibility checks against the *resolved* signature, not resolution signals. (An explicit type annotation on the inline `out` declaration is not permitted — the type is inferred from the callee's parameter, [§22.4](#sec-inline-out-declarations). Overloads that differ in the out parameter's *type* remain legal; when the inline form's inference is ambiguous between them, disambiguate by pre-declaring a typed local and passing plain `out x`.)

**`out _`.** The discard form applies to both parameter kinds: against `out T` the received value is simply dropped ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); against `out owned T` the discarded value is an unbound owned temporary disposed at the end of the full statement ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)). No ambiguity rule for `out _` against an out/out-owned pair is needed — the pair itself is not declarable.

The stance is now uniform: **neither `owned` (in any position, including on `out`) nor `scoped` ever participates in overload resolution** — only arity, parameter types, and the `ref`/`out` modifiers distinguish overloads. `ref` parameters do not admit `owned` (a `ref` location is borrowed by definition); `in` parameters do not exist as a separate modifier in Bezel.

<a id="sec-practical-pattern"></a>
#### Practical pattern

The common use is a pair of "try" methods exposing borrow and take forms under **distinct names** — the convention the standard library uses everywhere (`TryGetValue` vs `TryPopValue` on `OwningDictionary`, `TryPeek` vs `TryPop` on `OwningStack`):

```bezel
public class ConnectionPool  // declaration sketch; method bodies elided
  // Borrow a cached connection; the pool retains ownership.
  public method TryGetCached(name: string, out conn: Connection? when true): bool;

  // Take a cached connection out of the pool; the caller assumes ownership.
  public method TryTakeCached(name: string, out owned conn: Connection? when true): bool;
end ConnectionPool;

// Caller A: borrows a cached connection (pool retains it)
if pool.TryGetCached("primary", out var c) then
  UseConnection(c);     // narrowed non-null by the `when true` postcondition (§22.4)
end;

// Caller B: takes ownership of a cached connection (pool no longer holds it)
if pool.TryTakeCached("primary", out using var c) then
  UseConnection(c);     // owned, narrowed non-null; disposed at scope end
end;
```

Each name has one signature, and each call site's binding form matches its callee's declaration (the same-name pair differing only in `out` vs `out owned` is a compile error).

The implementation of the take-form (`TryTakeCached`) uses [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s `move` expression on the pool's internal owned-element collection to transfer ownership from pool to caller. A typical body using a `OwningDictionary<string, Connection>` for the pool storage has the shape:

```bezel
private owned _cache: OwningDictionary<string, Connection>;

public method TryTakeCached(name: string, out owned conn: Connection? when true): bool
  if not _cache.ContainsKey(name) then
    conn := null;
    return false;
  end;
  conn := _cache.PopValue(name);    // takes ownership, removes from dictionary
  return true;
end TryTakeCached;
```

The out parameter is typed `Connection?` (nullable) so that the false-return path can write `null` — `default(Connection)` is a compile error for a non-nullable reference type ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator)), and the type system requires every `out` parameter to be assigned on every return path ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) — throw paths carry no obligation, which is what lets a Try body open throwable resources before assigning). Callers consume with `out using var`; the `when true` clause narrows the recipient after the bool guard:

```bezel
if pool.TryTakeCached("primary", out using var c) then
  // c is owned Connection? — narrowed non-null here by the `when true` postcondition
  UseConnection(c);
end;
```

The `when true` clause on the declaration is the documentation point: the API contract — "true return implies `conn` is non-null" — is stated in the signature, checked in the callee's body, and consumed by the caller's flow analysis ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) — landing the flow-narrowing revision earlier versions deferred). Against a `Try` method *without* the clause, the explicit `!` remains required after the bool guard.

The `PopValue` method on `OwningDictionary<K, V>` ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements), std lib [§4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)) removes the entry and returns ownership of the value. After the call, the pool no longer holds the connection; the `out owned` parameter `conn` carries the obligation to the caller.

For pool implementations that prefer index-based storage, `OwningArray<Connection>.PopAt(i)` provides the analogous take-and-remove operation. For the simplest case of a single-slot cache, an `owned Connection?` field with `move _slot!` followed by `_slot := null` (per [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)'s nullable-field detach pattern) is also valid — the choice between dictionary, array, and single-field forms is about how the pool indexes its connections, not about how ownership flows out.

<a id="sec-implicit-conversion-ranking"></a>
#### Implicit conversions and tie-breaking

The rules above (number, type, `ref`/`out`, and the `owned`-on-`out` carve-out) determine which overloads are **applicable** to a call. When more than one overload remains applicable because an argument matches several candidates through different implicit conversions ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), the compiler selects among them by the following precedence. This tie-breaking is applied only after arity and named-argument binding ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) have already filtered the set to the applicable candidates.

For a single argument position, one candidate is **better** than another when the better candidate requires *no* implicit conversion (the argument's static type matches the parameter type exactly) and the other requires an implicit conversion. An exact match is the only relation that distinguishes one applicable candidate from another at an argument position; two candidates that both require an implicit conversion at the same position are **equally ranked** there, regardless of which conversion each uses. Bezel does not rank one built-in implicit conversion above another: §5.1 admits a conversion only when no programmer-visible information is lost (or, for the wide-integer-to-float cases, when an explicit cast would be unjustified noise), so all admitted implicit conversions are treated as co-equal for resolution purposes. This includes the reference conversions of [§5.1](#sec-reference-conversions): `M(a: Animal)` versus `M(o: Object)` on a `Dog` argument is ambiguous — neither candidate is exact — and the caller upcasts explicitly.

**Lambda-literal arguments.** A lambda literal has no static type of
its own; applicability and ranking at that argument position are decided by
its **inferred return type**. The lambda's parameters take the candidate's
(substituted) parameter types ([§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference)) and the
body is typed ([§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)); the candidate is
**applicable** at the position when the lambda's inferred return type equals
the candidate's return slot, implicitly converts to it
([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)), or binds it
([§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2 — a return slot containing a
free type parameter); for a procedure slot (`-> ()`),
[§27.3](#sec-lambda-expressions)'s value/procedure classification decides
instead. The candidate is **exact** at the position when the inferred return
type equals the return slot after type-argument substitution, and *converting*
otherwise — which is how `xs.Sum(lambda(x) => x * 2)` over an `Array<int>` selects
the `(T) -> int` overload of the stdlib `Sum` family: the `int`-returning
candidate is exact and the others convert. When no candidate is exact, the
co-equal rule above applies unchanged: `bytes.Sum(lambda(x) => x)` over an
`Array<byte>` is ambiguous — every candidate converts the `byte` body
result — remedied by widening in the body (`lambda(x) => int(x)`).

A candidate is **unambiguously better** than another when it is better-or-equal on every argument position and strictly better (an exact match where the other converts) on at least one. The call resolves to a candidate that is unambiguously better than every other applicable candidate.

**Defaulted-arity tie-break.** When the applicable candidates differ in whether defaults must be filled for omitted optional parameters ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)), one further comparison applies before declaring ambiguity: a candidate applicable **without filling any default** is preferred over a candidate that fills one or more, provided the no-defaults candidate is better-or-equal at every supplied-argument position under the ranking above. `M(5)` against `M(n: int)` and `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` resolves to `M(int)` — without this rule the call would be permanently ambiguous, and the explicit-cast remedy below cannot express "the fewer-parameter candidate". The tie-break distinguishes only all-arguments-supplied from some-defaults-filled; two candidates that both fill defaults remain subject to the ambiguity rule (the compiler declines to guess which omission the caller meant). This is C#'s rule, adopted with C#'s reasoning: adding an optional parameter to an overload set must not break existing calls that were exact against the shorter signature. The tie-break also separates generic from non-generic candidates, and does so **before** the non-generic-over-generic preference (the generic-candidates paragraph above): `M(5)` against `M(n: int, m: int := 0)` and `M<T>(x: T)` resolves to the generic — the candidate that fills no default — so this rule's compatibility reasoning holds for generic overload sets too.

If no candidate is unambiguously better — because each of two candidates is exact on a different argument, or because the remaining candidates all rely on implicit conversions that this rule treats as equally ranked — the call is **ambiguous** and is a compile error. The compiler reports the error and cites the candidate overloads; it never silently selects one. The caller resolves the ambiguity by adding an explicit cast ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)) to an argument so that exactly one candidate becomes an exact match (or so that all but one candidate become inapplicable).

If no candidate is applicable at all — every candidate would require a conversion that §5.1 does not admit as implicit — the call is a compile error with no candidates cited, because no overload was reachable.

This mirrors the resolution of overloaded method references ([§27.6](#sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods)), where the absence of a unique winner is likewise a compile error citing the candidates, and it follows the same "explicit over implicit" stance that motivates Bezel's omission of user-defined conversion operators ([§25.4](#sec-no-user-defined-conversion-operators)): when two overloads serve a call equally well, the compiler declines to guess and requires the call site to be explicit.

**Example 1 — exact match preferred over a conversion.**

```bezel
public class Logger
  public method Log(level: int);
  public method Log(level: long);
end Logger;

var lg := new Logger();
var n: int := 10;

lg.Log(n);            // n is int: exact match — calls Log(int), not the int→long widening
lg.Log(42);           // 42 is an int literal: exact match — calls Log(int)
lg.Log(42L);          // 42L is a long literal: exact match — calls Log(long)
```

**Example 2 — two equally-ranked conversions: ambiguous.**

```bezel
public class Converter
  public method Convert(n: long): string => "long";
  public method Convert(n: float): string => "float";
end Converter;

var cvt := new Converter();
var a: int := 10;

cvt.Convert(a);
// a is int. Neither candidate is an exact match.
//   Convert(long):  int→long  is implicit (§5.1).
//   Convert(float): int→float is implicit (§5.1).
// Both conversions are admitted by §5.1 and are equally ranked: neither
// candidate is better at the single argument position.
// Ambiguous call — compile error citing both candidates.
// Disambiguate with an explicit cast so exactly one is exact:
//   cvt.Convert(long(a));     // selects Convert(long)
//   cvt.Convert(float(a));    // selects Convert(float)
```

**Example 3 — exact on one argument, conversion on the other: unambiguously better.**

```bezel
public class Pair
  public method Apply(x: int, y: long): string => "int,long";
  public method Apply(x: int, y: int): string  => "int,int";
end Pair;

var p := new Pair();
var a: int := 5;
var b: int := 9;

p.Apply(a, b);
// arg x (int): exact in both — tie.
// arg y (int): exact in Apply(int,int); requires int→long in Apply(int,long).
// Apply(int,int) is better-or-equal on x and strictly better on y ⇒ unambiguously better.
// Resolves to Apply(int, int).
```

**Example 4 — each candidate exact on a different argument: ambiguous.**

```bezel
public class Calculator
  public method Compute(a: int, b: long): string => "int,long";
  public method Compute(a: long, b: int): string => "long,int";
end Calculator;

var calc := new Calculator();
var x: int := 5;
var y: int := 10;

calc.Compute(x, y);
// arg a (int): exact in Compute(int,long); int→long conversion in Compute(long,int).
// arg b (int): int→long conversion in Compute(int,long); exact in Compute(long,int).
// Each candidate is strictly better on a different argument; neither dominates.
// Ambiguous call — compile error citing both candidates.
// Disambiguate:
//   calc.Compute(x, long(y));    // makes Compute(int,long) exact on both ⇒ selects it
//   calc.Compute(long(x), y);    // makes Compute(long,int) exact on both ⇒ selects it
```

**Example 5 — no reachable candidate: error with no candidates cited.**

```bezel
public class Transformer
  public method Transform(x: int);
  public method Transform(x: decimal);
end Transformer;

var t := new Transformer();
var n: float := 2.5f;

t.Transform(n);
// float→int is not implicit (§5.1: float's only implicit target is double).
// float→decimal is not implicit (§5.1: decimal and binary floats never mix implicitly).
// No candidate is applicable ⇒ compile error, no candidates cited (none reachable).
// The caller must convert explicitly, e.g. t.Transform(int(n)) or t.Transform(decimal(n)).
```

**Example 6 — applicability filtering removes a candidate, leaving one winner.**

```bezel
public class Handler
  public method Process(n: sbyte): string => "sbyte";
  public method Process(n: ushort): string => "ushort";
end Handler;

var h := new Handler();
var val: byte := 50;

h.Process(val);
// byte→sbyte is NOT implicit (§5.1: signed/unsigned same-or-narrower width never implicit).
//   ⇒ Process(sbyte) is not applicable.
// byte→ushort IS implicit (§5.1, byte row).
//   ⇒ Process(ushort) is the only applicable candidate.
// Resolves to Process(ushort). No ambiguity — only one candidate survived applicability.
```

The rule applies identically to constructor overload sets ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)): a `new T(...)` call is resolved among `T`'s constructors by the same exact-match-then-ambiguity precedence.

<a id="sec-constructors"></a>
### 22.7 Constructors

```bezel
public constructor(name: string, balance: decimal)
  _name := name;
  _balance := balance;
end constructor;
```

Constructors return no value. Multiple constructors are permitted; chaining uses `this(...)` or `base(...)` in the chaining position before the body ([§12.8](#sec-constructor-chaining)). When a class has a primary constructor ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), an additional restriction applies: only the primary may chain to `base(...)`; convenience constructors must chain via `this(...)`.

A static constructor runs once before the type's first use. It carries no access modifier (the runtime is the only caller) and no parameters:

```bezel
class Utils
  static constructor()
    // ...
  end constructor;
end Utils;
```

A static constructor body may use `try`/`catch`. An exception caught inside the body does not transition the type to the failed state — the constructor completes normally and static initialization is considered successful. The failed state is entered only when an exception escapes the static initializer entirely. If the static initializer (the static field initializers, the static constructor body, or both) throws an *uncaught* exception, the type is left in a permanently failed state:

- Every subsequent access to a static member of the type — field read, field write, method call, property read or write, indexer — raises `TypeInitializationException` whose `InnerException` is the original exception (for the [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) cycle backstop, the cached instance is the runtime-synthesized one and `InnerException` is `null`).
- The state is not recoverable: re-running static initialization is not attempted.
- Static fields whose initializers had not yet run remain at their default values, but those defaults are not observable: every access raises. For non-nullable reference fields, where no default value exists ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)), this rule is satisfied vacuously — every access to the type raises before any field read could occur, so the absence of a value is never observed. The compiler's definite-assignment analysis is not violated, because the failed-state machinery intercepts every access before any read of the field.
- Static fields whose initializers completed successfully before the failing initializer have their values; if any such field is `owned`, its value will be disposed at program exit per [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order). The runtime makes no guarantee about ordering of disposal across types when one of the types is in a failed state.

The `TypeInitializationException` is constructed at the moment the exception escapes the initializer, and **the access that triggered initialization observes it too**: the original exception never propagates raw out of static initialization; it is observable only as `InnerException`. The instance constructed on first failure is the one cached and rethrown; the triggering access and every subsequent access see the same cached `TypeInitializationException` instance. (When the escaping exception is itself the `TypeInitializationException` synthesized by [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s cycle backstop, that instance is cached directly — no double wrapping.)

The rules above resolve into two scenarios:

| Scenario | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Static initializer (field initializer or static constructor body) throws an exception that escapes the initializer. | Type enters permanently failed state. Every subsequent access raises `TypeInitializationException` whose `InnerException` is the original (`null` for the [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) cycle-backstop instance, which has no original). Owned static fields whose initializers had already completed are disposed at program exit. |
| Static initializer encounters an exception but catches it via `try`/`catch` inside the body. | Type initializes normally. The caught exception did not escape; subsequent member access proceeds without raising. Remaining initializers and the constructor body run as usual. |

<a id="sec-observing-this-during-construction"></a>
#### Observing `this` during construction

During construction, the object is built base-first ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)): when a class C's
constructor body runs, C's own field initializers have run (step 2) but a
*derived* class's have not — and C's body itself assigns C's remaining fields as
it executes. Three rules keep [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)'s
guarantee true while `this` is under construction:

1. **The observation gate.** In a constructor body, a **synchronous observation
   of `this`** — an instance method, block-form accessor, or indexer invocation
   with receiver `this` (explicit or implicit); `this` as an argument; `this`
   stored anywhere; `this` as an `is`/`is not`/`as` operand or `case` scrutinee —
   is admitted only at points where **every field of the declaring class that
   [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields) requires to be
   explicitly initialized** is definitely assigned on every reaching path.
   Direct field assignments and reads, and **auto-property** assignments and
   reads (compiler-known storage, [§23.1](#sec-auto-properties) — each is the
   backing field's assignment or read, and the assignment counts toward the
   gate), are not observations — they keep their existing definite-assignment
   rules ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression), constructors paragraph). Fields
   with initializers count as assigned at body entry. In the **chaining
   position** (`base(...)`/`this(...)` arguments, a primary constructor's
   inheritance-clause base call) no field of the declaring class is yet
   assigned, so any observation of `this` there is a compile error. A
   constructor chaining via `this(...)` enters its body with every such field
   assigned (the chained-to constructor's own [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)
   obligation), so the gate is satisfied at entry.
2. **No virtual dispatch from constructor bodies of non-sealed classes.** A
   call from a constructor body to a `virtual`, `override`, or `abstract`
   member with receiver `this` — any dispatching call not through `base.` — is
   a compile error unless the declaring class is `sealed` and not `abstract`.
   During construction the runtime type may be a derived class whose field
   initializers have not yet run; dispatch would enter derived code over unset
   fields (the template-method-in-constructor footgun). In a sealed,
   non-abstract class the dispatch target is statically bounded and the call is
   admitted under rule 1's gate; `base.M()` is non-dispatching and likewise
   needs only rule 1.
3. **Closures observe at invocation, not at capture.** Capturing `this` in a
   lambda or method reference is not a synchronous observation and is not gated
   by rule 1 — whether the capture is legal is [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s
   question, unchanged (form 3's owned-field subscription — stdlib
   [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) — stays the
   standard observer pattern). An admitted `this`-capturing closure
   that is nevertheless *invoked before construction completes* — possible only
   if the constructor itself, directly or transitively, causes the invocation
   (instance event sources are domain-serial, stdlib §6.5) — is a construction-time
   observation under the residual below.

**The recorded residual.** These checks reject every unsafe observation they
can see and are **not a completeness guarantee** (the same bound as
[§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s cycle approximation): a virtual
call or derived-type downcast inside a non-virtual helper called after the
gate, external code reached by an admitted `this`-escape that dispatches back,
or a during-construction closure invocation can still enter a derived class's
code before its initializers ran. The runtime bound is defined: before
construction begins, every reference-typed field of the allocation is
initialized to `null` and every defaultable value-typed field to its
[§7.9](#sec-default-initialization) default (normative); a read of a
non-nullable reference field still at that null watermark raises
`NullReferenceException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) in **checked
disposal mode** ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) and, unchecked, observes the
watermark `null` with undefined behavior on any use requiring non-null — the
same checked/unchecked split as use-after-dispose.

<a id="sec-field-initializers"></a>
### 22.8 Field initializers

A field declared in a class or record may include an initializer:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private _balance: decimal := 0m;
  private owned _transactions: Array<Transaction> := new Array<Transaction>();
  private _createdAt: DateTime := DateTime.Now;
end BankAccount;
```

A field declared `readonly` may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor body; assignment anywhere else is a compile error. `readonly` on a field is analogous to `readonly` on an auto-property ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)).

Field initializers run as part of construction in textual declaration order. The full sequence for a constructor:

0. Primary-constructor parameters ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) that are referenced in body positions (method, property, constructor, or destructor bodies) are captured into their compiler-generated private fields; parameters referenced only in initializer positions are not captured ([§11.1](#sec-class-declaration)). This step is omitted for classes without a primary constructor.
1. The base or chained constructor call (`base(...)`, `this(...)`, or implicit `base()`). For a `this(...)` chain, the chained-to constructor runs to completion (its own steps of this sequence) before control returns here.
2. Field initializers, in declaration order — executed **only** by a constructor whose step 1 is `base(...)` or the implicit `base()` (see below).
3. The constructor body.

**Field initializers run exactly once per instance construction.** They execute as step 2 of the constructor whose chaining position holds `base(...)` or the implicit `base()` — the constructor at the end of any `this(...)` chain. A constructor that chains via `this(...)` **skips steps 0 and 2**: its effective sequence is the chained `this(...)` call, then its own body. (Step 0 is vacuous for such a constructor anyway: only non-primary constructors may chain via `this(...)` ([§22.7](#sec-constructors), [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), and primary-parameter capture happens inside the chained-to primary.) Read without this rule, step 1's run-to-completion parenthetical plus an unconditional step 2 would run every field initializer twice under `this(...)` chaining — repeating allocations and initializer side effects, assigning `readonly` fields twice, and, for `owned` fields, disposing and recreating each initializer's value under [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s drop-on-overwrite. The once-only rule matches C# and the reference implementation.

Primary-constructor parameter capture occurs first so that the `base(...)`/`this(...)` argument expressions (step 1), field initializers (step 2), and the body (step 3) may reference the captured parameters by name. Step 0 is observable only through ordering: the captured fields are initialized before any user-written code runs.

Field initializers may reference: constants, literals, static members of any class, `new` expressions, lambdas that capture only the above, primary-constructor parameters ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)), and `typeof` expressions.

Field initializers may **not** reference: `this`, instance members, `base`, virtual methods, or any expression that would observe `this` indirectly.

The base-call-before-field-initializers ordering matches primary-constructor inheritance ([§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)) and C#, Java, and C++, and it keeps exception safety simple: when a derived field initializer throws, the base subobject is fully constructed and can be cleanly disposed by the runtime ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)).

<a id="sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety"></a>
### 22.9 Owned fields and exception safety

When construction throws, the compiler unwinds the partially-constructed instance in **reverse declaration order** within the derived class (the [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) pass — for primary-constructor capture fields, ordered after declared fields per [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability), this disposes captures first), then the base subobject ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers)):

- An exception during the **base or chained constructor call** (step 1) leaves no derived state to clean up **beyond step 0's owned primary-constructor capture fields ([§22.8](#sec-field-initializers), [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)), which are already populated and are disposed in reverse declaration order before the exception propagates** — the base ctor's own exception-safety logic disposes whatever it had constructed of the base subobject. The exception propagates to the derived ctor's caller; the derived instance is never observable.
- An exception during a **field initializer** (step 2) triggers disposal of any earlier derived owned fields whose initializers completed, in reverse declaration order, followed by the base subobject's `Dispose()` (which the runtime invokes because the base ctor completed successfully). The exception then propagates.
- An exception in the **constructor body** (step 3) triggers disposal of every owned field assigned during initialization (step 2) and the base subobject. Owned fields assigned imperatively in the body are also disposed if assigned successfully before the throwing statement.
- An exception in a **`this(...)`-chaining constructor** follows the same shape one level up (completing the [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) once-only rule). A throw during the chained call itself is the first case above, with one precision for the `this(...)` reading: the chained-to constructor's unwinding has by then disposed everything its steps initialized — *including derived fields*, since field initializers ran as its step 2 — so there is nothing further to dispose. If the chaining constructor's **body** throws, the chained-to construction completed and the instance is at that point fully initialized: the runtime disposes it through the normal generated-`Dispose()` path ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)) before the exception propagates.

Owned primary-constructor **capture fields**, populated at step 0, participate in every case above as owned fields whose initialization completed first: they are disposed in the same reverse-declaration-order pass (captures before declared fields, [§22.10](#sec-capture-rule-and-layout-stability)), and the capture **moves** the parameter, so no [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) parameter-level discharge ever also claims the value. An `owned` primary parameter that was *not* captured (referenced only in initializer positions) still holds its value on any construction throw before its consuming initializer ran — a step-1 throw, or a step-2 throw from an earlier initializer — and is discharged as an ordinary `owned` parameter by the exception-path discharge; once its consuming initializer has run, the owning field's disposal covers it. One owner at every instant, on every edge (Appendix [C.3](#sec-appendix-c)).
