**`ContractViolationException`** joins the built-in hierarchy ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)), deriving directly from `Exception` — clause evaluation is a language operation, like the indexer's `IndexOutOfRangeException`. It is catchable; its `Message` carries the clause kind, the member, and the clause's source text. Programs must not use it for control flow — it reports a bug (a caller bug for `requires`, an implementation bug for `ensures`/`invariant`), not an outcome.

**`requires` violations are always-on**: an unproven `requires` clause is compiled as a runtime check in every build mode; it is never elided. (A proven clause is discharged statically and compiles to nothing — elision-by-proof is the only elision. An implementation may additionally elide the check at a particular call site it can statically discharge — unobservable by purity — but the clause's recorded tier stays checked.) This is the always-on posture of the `throw new ArgumentException(…)` prologue the clause replaces; the remedy for hot paths is the proven ratchet, not a knob.

**`ensures` and `invariant` run under checked-contracts mode** — a per-build choice between two conformance modes, independent of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s disposal-checking mode: in **unchecked (release) mode** — the default — unproven `ensures` and `invariant` clauses are not evaluated; in **checked-contracts mode** they are evaluated at this section's points, a `false` clause raising `ContractViolationException`. The two modes give identical observable behavior for every program whose checked clauses never evaluate `false` and never fault: clauses are pure, so non-evaluation is unobservable by construction — the deliberate contrast with §28.2, whose release relaxation is undefined behavior. `requires` clauses are outside the mode entirely.

<a id="sec-contract-tiers"></a>
#### The tier system: proven / checked / assumed

Every contract clause occupies exactly one **tier**, determined statically per clause: **proven** — discharged statically at the clause's discharge site, never evaluated at runtime, zero cost in every mode (prover soundness is a conformance obligation); **checked** — compiled to a runtime evaluation at this section's points, under the mode rules above; **assumed** — stated and carried, neither proven nor evaluated (unpopulated in this revision; reserved for contract clauses on `extern` declarations, to be designed jointly with the extern-purity question).

**Discharge sites differ by clause kind.** An `ensures` or `invariant` clause is discharged at the **declaring body**: the prover shows every normal-completion path establishes it — `static ensures`/`static invariant` makes an unprovable body a compile error at the declaration ([§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s existing rule). A `requires` clause is the body's assumption; its discharge site is **every call site**: the caller's compiler substitutes the actual arguments into the clause and discharges the instance — `static requires` makes an undischargeable call a compile error at that call, and the callee compiles no runtime check because every admitted call carries a proof. A **`static requires` clause may mention only state its call sites can see** (the member's parameters, and members visible to every caller); a `static requires` over non-public state is a compile error at the declaration. Checked `requires` clauses are unrestricted.

**The current prover floor** — exactly two things inhabit the proven tier: a clause whose expression (after call-site substitution, for `requires`) is a **constant expression** ([§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions)) folding to `true` (folding to `false` is a compile error at the clause — a statically violated contract; a faulting constant folding is a compile error per §17.14's own rule); and the `when true`/`when false` postconditions of [§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition) — which this section defines as `static ensures` clauses, proven by the existing [§7](#sec-nullability-2) nullability flow analysis over the declaring body. Essentially every authored clause is therefore **checked**: the runtime tier stands alone, and the prover grows under a fixed meaning. The **Contract proving** conformance feature (Appendix [D.2](#sec-extended-features)) fixes the extended prover fragment now, so the `static` qualifier's meaning never drifts: linear integer arithmetic over parameters, fields, `result`, and `old` captures (under [§6.1](#sec-integer-arithmetic)'s checked semantics); null tests composed with §7's flow narrowing; and case analysis over enums, closed hierarchies ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)), and choice cases ([§35](#sec-choices)). Everything outside the fragment stays checked; `static` on an out-of-fragment clause is an error, never a silent downgrade to a runtime check.

<a id="sec-contract-inheritance"></a>
#### Inheritance, interfaces, and dispatch

Contracts are **slot-bound**: a clause declared on a virtual or abstract member, or on an interface member, is part of that slot's contract and binds every override and implementation.

1. **Clauses are inherited verbatim, never restated.** An override or implementing member does not repeat the base or interface clauses; its invocations are checked against them wherever the member is reached, directly or by dispatch.
2. **An override or implementation may add `ensures` clauses**, conjoined with the inherited ones at its return edges — strengthening the postcondition, always sound for callers. A caller through the base static type cannot name the added guarantee; every execution honors it.
3. **An override or implementation may not declare `requires` clauses.** Strengthening a precondition breaks every caller dispatching through the base contract, and no weakening syntax exists in this revision: the override's effective precondition is the inherited one, verbatim.
4. **Multiple contract roots combine soundly.** A member reachable through several contract-bearing declarations has: effective `requires` = the **disjunction over roots** of each root's clause conjunction (a caller reached the member through *some* static type and established that root's precondition); effective `ensures` = the **conjunction of all roots'** clauses plus the member's own additions. Roots evaluate in inheritance-declaration order, clauses in declaration order within a root; `requires` evaluation short-circuits at the first satisfied root; if none is satisfied the violation names every root's failed clause set.
5. **Monotone down the chain**: an override inherits from its nearest overridden declaration transitively; `ensures` additions accumulate and nothing is dropped mid-chain.
6. **Clause context is the declaring type**: an inherited clause evaluates as declaring-type code (it may read the base's `private` fields), and `result` in an inherited `ensures` binds to the actual invocation's returned value (type-identical by §12.1's exact-return-match rule).
7. **Abstract members carry clauses** — the intended home: the slot's contract written where the slot is declared, every concrete subclass bound.

Clauses never distinguish overloads and are not part of [§22.6](#sec-overloading) resolution; two members differing only in clauses are the same signature and clash.

<a id="sec-class-invariants"></a>
#### Class invariants

An **invariant member** (`invariant(E);`) declares a predicate over the instance's state, checked under this section's clause rules in the context of the declaring class (its `private` fields readable; `old` and `result` rejected). The **class invariant** of C is the conjunction of every invariant member of C and of every base class, evaluated base-first, declaration order within each class. The invariant is an *observable-boundary* property: it must hold whenever the instance is observable from outside itself, and it may be freely false while the instance is operating on itself.

**The instrumentation set** — the invariant is evaluated at exactly these points, in checked-contracts mode:

- **Construction exit**: the normal completion of the **most-derived constructor** of a construction, of any visibility, after its body and its `ensures` clauses. A base constructor completing as part of a derived construction is *not* an instrumentation point (the [§22.8](#sec-field-initializers) sequence is interior — derived initializers have not run), nor is a `this(...)`-chained-to constructor completing mid-chain. Every fresh instance satisfies its full dynamic class invariant before it is observable; a violation raises `ContractViolationException` and the partially-constructed instance unwinds under [§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)'s ordinary machinery.
- **Entry and normal exit** of every `public` instance **method**. Order at entry: `requires` clauses, then the invariant; at exit: `ensures` clauses, then the invariant.
- **Entry and normal exit** of every `public` **setter** — block-form, auto-property, indexer, `set(owned)` alike. (Auto-property assignments inside constructors are backing-field stores, not accessor invocations, so construction does not double-check.)
- **Getters are exempt**, with the residual recorded: a mutating block-form getter escapes invariant checking; the recommended getter is a [§22.15](#sec-pure-members) pure one, which cannot mutate.
- **Never instrumented:** non-public methods and setters, static members, destructors, and `Dispose` (disposal legitimately tears the state down); throw exits check nothing.

**The visibility boundary and the `this`-reentrancy exemption.** Public-only is the boundary: non-public calls are the implementation's interior, where an algorithm may pass through broken intermediate states (`internal` is interior — module-mates are co-implementors, not clients). A call whose receiver is `this` — explicit or implicit — from inside any instance member of the class or a subclass enters the member's **unchecked face**: no invariant evaluation at that call's entry or exit. Every instrumented public member compiles to a checked face (entry checks → unchecked face → exit checks) and an unchecked face (the body); call sites with syntactic receiver `this` bind to the unchecked face — statically decidable, including for virtual dispatch (a `this`-receiver dispatching call reaches the dynamic target's unchecked face). Calls on *other* instances of the same class check normally. Invariant evaluation itself runs as interior code, so a clause may call a `pure` public method of the same instance without recursion. **Dispatch checks the dynamic class's invariant**: an external call through a base-typed reference evaluates the full dynamic class invariant — base and derived conjunction — at the dynamic target's checked face.

Construction composes with [§22.7](#sec-observing-this-during-construction) exactly: at the most-derived constructor's normal completion every §7.9-required field of every class in the chain is definitely assigned, so evaluating the invariant is admitted by the observation gate by construction. The recorded residual is inherited, not enlarged: a during-construction `this`-escape re-entering a public method from outside the instance hits a checked face over fields still at the null watermark, faulting per §22.7's stated bound. Invariant evaluation is a boundary-time read of instance state in the calling domain — no new cross-domain access arises, and no rule of [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)/[§30.14](#sec-sendable-types) changes.

**Out of scope in this revision**, each recorded: record invariants (constructor-exit plus a `with`-update instrumentation point — a later design); interface-declared invariants (need interface carriage to transport); static-class and static-state invariants (an `invariant` in a static class is a compile error — no instance boundary exists); `static invariant` parses from day one and is useful when the prover fragment lands.

<a id="sec-contract-scope"></a>
#### Scope

In scope: instance, static, and extension methods (the receiver is a borrow, [§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions), readable in clauses); constructors; abstract methods; interface methods and static interface members; record and enum methods (`old` over receiver fields captures by the value rules; the *invariant* member is class-only); generic members (clauses type-check once at the declaration under constraints — constraint-typed receivers offer no pure members in this revision, so clauses over bare-`T` values are near-inexpressible, recorded honestly); `Main`.

**Async methods: `requires` only.** A `requires` on an `async` method evaluates in the **synchronous prefix** — after argument binding, before any body statement and therefore before the first suspension ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) — so a violation surfaces synchronously at the call expression, on the caller's own stack, not through the task. `ensures` on an `async` method is rejected in this revision (the settlement-time design — evaluation in the completing frame before delivery, faulting the task, `old` captures living in the state-machine frame — is recorded in proposal 0043 §10.1 and staged for its own verification pass). Clauses on **iterator methods** are rejected (calling one executes none of its body, so no coherent evaluation point exists; eager `requires`-at-call is the recorded revisit). No clauses on **accessors**, **operators**, or **lambdas** in this revision (each recorded liftable; a lambda's contract belongs to its function type — the same abstracted-position bucket as function-type purity). No clauses on **`extern` declarations** (the assumed tier's intended client, designed jointly with extern purity), **destructors**, or **static constructors**.

<a id="sec-when-clause-unification"></a>
#### The `when`-clause identity

[§22.4](#sec-out-nullability-postcondition)'s nullability postcondition **is** a proven-tier contract clause. Normatively, for a `bool`-returning method, `method M(…, out p: T? when true, …): bool` is `method M(…, out p: T?, …): bool` carrying the clause `static ensures(not result or p <> null)` (and `when false` correspondingly `static ensures(result or p <> null)`). Everything §22.4 mandates falls out of this section's rules: the declaring-body obligation is the §7 flow prover discharging a `static ensures` at its discharge site; the evaluation point is this section's; the call-site narrowing is caller-side **consumption of a proven ensures** — the first shipped instance of the consumption pattern the prover fragment generalizes. The `when true`/`when false` spelling remains the surface form — no source changes anywhere; writing the desugared `static ensures` form directly is equally legal and is the same declaration. One rule is deliberately retained rather than generalized: [§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) requires an override to repeat the `when` clause exactly — the zero-migration reading; a postcondition is never weakened under either reading.

<a id="sec-properties-and-indexers"></a>
## 23. Properties and Indexers

A property is a member that looks like a field on access. An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by a parameter list in square brackets.

<a id="sec-auto-properties"></a>
### 23.1 Auto-properties

```bezel
public property Name: string;                         // read-write
public property Id: int private set;                  // read-write with private setter
public readonly property AccountNumber: string;       // read-only
public readonly property Pi: double := 3.141592653589793;  // read-only with initializer
```

The compiler generates the backing field. A `readonly` auto-property may be assigned only in a field initializer or in a constructor.

<a id="sec-expression-bodied-read-only-properties"></a>
### 23.2 Expression-bodied read-only properties

**`readonly` has one meaning: it is written exactly where shape cannot express read-onlyness** — auto-properties ([§23.1](#sec-auto-properties)) and interface properties, whose accessor sets are declared, not shaped. On every body-bearing form — an expression-bodied property or indexer, a get-only block form, and the expression-bodied properties of choices, enums, and extensions — read-onlyness is already expressed by the shape, and writing `readonly` there is a compile error (the grammar's `readonly?` slots on those productions are over-admissions, rejected semantically per the shared-production policy); on a block form declaring a setter it is contradictory and likewise an error.

```bezel
public property Area: decimal => Width * Height;
public property IsEmpty: bool => _count = 0;
public property FullName: string => $"{FirstName} {LastName}";
```

An expression-bodied property's (or indexer's) body is checked against the declared type and is a **declared-result position** for choice-case constructions ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)); a **getter's** expression body under the property's declared type ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties)) is the same position (a setter's body is checked against no result type and is not).

<a id="sec-block-form-properties"></a>
### 23.3 Block-form properties

```bezel
public property Balance: decimal
  get => _balance;
  set => do
    if value < 0m then throw new ArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative"); end;
    _balance := value;
  end;
end Balance;
```

The implicit setter parameter is `value`. Each accessor uses `=> expression` or `=> do ... end`. A read-only property in block form omits `set`; a write-only property omits `get`.

Accessor visibility ([§13.6](#sec-accessor-visibility)) may make a getter or setter more restrictive than the property as a whole.

**Explicit setter parameter modifier.** The setter's implicit `value` parameter has no modifier by default and takes a borrow of the property's declared type. For owning collections (like `OwningArray<T>`'s indexer setter) the setter needs to take ownership of the new value (and dispose the previous slot value). Write an explicit `set(owned)` parameter spec to declare an owned-taking setter:

```bezel
public class OwningArray<T> where T: class
  public property [i: int]: T
    get;                     // implicit value: T, borrow-returning
    set(owned);              // explicit owned: takes owned T;
                             //   disposes previous slot value
  end;
end OwningArray;
```

The spelling `set(owned)` keeps the implicit name `value`; the spelling `set(owned x)` renames the parameter to `x`. The parameter's type is always the property's declared type, so it is not repeated. The form is admitted on block-form properties and indexers; abstract/interface accessor bodies (`;`-terminated) carry the spec the same way (`set(owned);`). The standard-library owning collection types (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`) use this form for their indexer setters; the owning-collection interfaces (`IOwningList<T>`) declare it on their abstract indexer setters. Assignment through a `set(owned)` property or indexer is an announced owned-consuming position: a named owned binding on the right-hand side is consumed with no call-site transfer marker — and writing one is an error naming the announcement ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)).

<a id="sec-indexers"></a>
### 23.4 Indexers

An indexer is a property whose name is replaced by `[parameters]`:

```bezel
public property [i: int]: string => _items[i];        // expression-bodied

public property [row: int, col: int]: double => _grid[row * _width + col];

public property [key: string]: int
  get => _values[key];
  set => do
    if value < 0 then throw new ArgumentException("must be non-negative"); end;
    _values[key] := value;
  end;
end;
```

A block-form indexer's `end` clause has no name to reference; it is plain `end;`.

Inside a member of a class with its own indexer, `this[i]` is required (the brackets need a left-hand side).

Indexers may be declared in interfaces with the body-less form (write `readonly` before `property` to expose only a getter):

```bezel
interface IList<T>: IReadOnlyList<T>, ICollection<T>
  property [i: int]: T;
end IList;
```

Indexers may be overloaded by parameter type list. They participate in `virtual`/`override`/`sealed`/`abstract` like methods.

Records may declare read-only indexers. Body-form records with mutable properties may declare read-write indexers; positional-only records may not.

<a id="sec-properties-and-indexers-restrictions"></a>
### 23.5 Restrictions

- Enums may not declare indexers.
- Static indexers are not supported.
- `ref` and `out` parameters are not allowed in indexer parameter lists.
- Index arguments are **positional-only**. The named-argument form (`Identifier :=`, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) is not admitted at an index position — a compile error naming this rule. Indexer parameters may not declare default values, so [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s optional-parameter and named-binding machinery is never reached from an index position; an indexer's parameter names are declaration-internal, not caller-bindable API surface (consistent with [§23.4](#sec-indexers)'s overloading by parameter *type* list).
- Assigning to a member of a value-typed indexer result is a compile error: `g[0].X := 5` would modify a discarded copy. Read, modify, write back through the setter.
- Properties and indexers whose declared type is a move-only value type (an owning inline array, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) are not admitted. A getter would need to either copy the move-only value (forbidden by move-only semantics) or move it out of the backing storage (which would leave the storage in moved-from state, conflicting with the property abstraction). Programs that need to expose an owning inline-array field interactively use a regular public field (with the inline array's `owned` slot marker conveying the ownership) or, for transfer-out semantics, an explicit method that returns the owned value.

<a id="sec-events-on-interfaces"></a>
## 24. Events (retired member kind)

Retired. The `event` member kind no longer exists: an event is the two-declaration library pattern documented normatively in stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource) — a `private owned readonly` source field and a public borrowing property of the interface face — with identical subscriber-side call sites and semantics (rationale §13.6). The `+=`/`-=` subscription desugaring remains language-defined at [§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators); shared (cross-domain) publication points use the `ISharedEvent<T>`/`SharedEventSource<T>` pair under [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 5. The word `event` remains reserved (Appendix B.3): an `event` declaration is a reserved-word error, and the migration spelling is stdlib §6.5's pattern. The section anchors are retained for citation stability; the prior definition and the decision record are in the [changelog](Bezel_Changelog.md).

<a id="sec-operator-overloading"></a>
## 25. Operator Overloading

Records, enums, and classes may overload operators. Operators are declared as `public static` methods using the `operator` keyword — **`public` is required**: an operator invoked through `a + b` syntax has no call-site spelling that could name a restricted member, so any other visibility is a compile error (Appendix A.4's OperatorDecl admits only `public static`).

<a id="sec-overloadable-operators"></a>
### 25.1 Overloadable operators

- Unary: `+`, `-`, `~`, `++`, `--`
- Binary: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `mod`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`
- Comparison: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `=`, `<>`

`not` is **not** user-overloadable. It is the boolean-negation operator and applies only to `bool` ([§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)); types wanting a domain-specific inversion provide a named method (`.Negate()`, `.Inverted()`) or overload `~` if a bitwise reading applies. This is the one place where Bezel explicitly excludes a unary operator from the overload set in favor of a named method, so that the boolean reading of `not` is preserved at every call site.

The following operators are also not overloadable, for various reasons:

- The null-forgiving `!`, the null-coalescing `??`, and the type-test operators `is`, `is not`, `as` — these have null-aware or type-system semantics fixed by the language; user types do not customize them.
- Range operators `..` and `..<` — these construct values of the language-built-in `Range<T>` type ([§16](#sec-range-expressions)); user types do not customize them.
- The `in` operator — customization is via the structural `Contains` lookup ([§17.5](#sec-the-in-operator)).
- Assignment and compound-assignment operators (`:=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `mod=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `??=`) — Bezel has no compound-operator overload mechanism; the compound forms desugar mechanically to read-modify-write using the underlying binary operator's overload, with the evaluation counts and result typing of [§6.6](#sec-compound-assignments).
- The `+=` and `-=` event-subscription forms ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) — a fixed, language-defined desugaring available only on `EventSource<T>`, `AsyncEventSource<T>`, and `SharedEventSource<T>`; they are not operator overloads and are not part of the user-overloadable surface.
- The short-circuit boolean operators `and` and `or` — like `not`, they are fixed on `bool`; their short-circuit evaluation cannot be expressed by a user method's eager parameters, so they are not overloadable. Element access `[ ]` is customized through indexers ([§23.4](#sec-indexers)), not through operator overloads.

<a id="sec-operator-overloading-restrictions"></a>
### 25.2 Restrictions and resolution

**Declaring-type operand.** At least one parameter of an operator overload must be the declaring type; a binary overload may pair the declaring type with any other type in either position (as `DateTime.operator +(t: TimeSpan, d: DateTime)` does). An operator whose parameters never mention the declaring type would be unreachable by the resolution rule below.

**Resolution.** For `a <op> b` on non-primitive operands, the candidate set is the union of the `operator <op>` overloads declared on the **static types of both operands, including declarations inherited from their base classes** (a derived-typed operand reaches its base's operators, as in C#: no user-facing upcast exists that could reach them otherwise, and [§12.2](#sec-hiding-is-not-allowed)'s no-hiding rule — which covers operator declarations per token, stated explicitly there — prevents a derived class from redeclaring an operator token its base declares, so one chain contributes no duplicate candidates). A derived-typed operand satisfies a base-typed parameter by the ordinary argument rules. Parameters match operands **in order** — there is no automatic commutation (`4 - v` is not matched against `operator -(v: V, n: int)`). If distinct applicable overloads are found on both operand types, the expression is a compile error citing the candidates (mirroring [§22.6](#sec-overloading)'s the-compiler-declines-to-guess stance). A unary operator consults the operand's type and its base classes, likewise.

**Type-parameter operands (connecting this section to [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)).** A generic type parameter declares no operators of its own; for an operand whose static type is a type parameter `T`, the candidate set is drawn from the **static-interface constraints** on `T` ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)): the `static operator` members those interfaces declare, matched in order as above and bound at instantiation to the conforming type's own declarations. The complete-group rule below does double duty here: because every concrete type that declares one of `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` must declare all four, a constraint interface that declares any one of them (the stdlib `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>` declare `<` alone) entitles the generic body to **all four** — each use still resolves at instantiation to the conforming type's *own* declaration of that operator, never by synthesizing `a > b` from `b < a`. The same holds for the `=`/`<>` pair. Primitive substitutions satisfy the entitlement through their intrinsic operator set ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s compiler-provided conformances, §3.5).

- `=` and `<>` may **not** be overloaded on classes or on inline arrays. For classes, `=` always invokes `Equals`. For inline arrays, the language-defined structural equality of [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode) is the only `=` available; inline arrays cannot be extended ([§26.2](#sec-what-can-be-extended)), so the overload mechanism does not reach them. Records and enums may overload `=` and `<>`.
- Comparison operators must be overloaded as a complete group: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` together; `=` and `<>` together.
- `++` and `--` are postfix-only and statement-only. There is no separate prefix overload; the single overload is used in the one permitted position.
- **Operator parameters admit no parameter modifiers.** `ref`, `out`, `owned`, and `scoped` on an operator's parameter list are rejected semantically — the grammar admits them through the shared `Param` production, the same over-admit-and-reject pattern as [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)'s primary constructors. Operands are received as plain borrows (or value copies) under their type kinds; the return slot's optional `owned` (grammar A.4) is the sole ownership annotation on operators. Operator operand positions therefore never consume a named owned binding — the transfer marker is not admitted in operator-operand position (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)), and under this rule none is needed. (The keyword-announced operand consumes — `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)), a Pattern B `await x`, an owning-iterator `yield return x` — are separate, non-operator positions, enumerated in [§28.3](#sec-producers).)

When a record overloads `=` and `<>`, the overloaded operators are invoked for `a = b` and `a <> b` directly — they do not delegate to `Equals`. The auto-generated or user-supplied `Equals(Object?)` and `Equals(T)` methods continue to exist; they are reachable via `.Equals(...)` call syntax and are what collections and pattern matching use.

**Co-declaration rule (compiler-enforced).** A record or enum that overloads `=`/`<>` with **both operands of the declaring type** must also declare `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode` — on a record, `override GetHashCode`; on an enum, a plain `GetHashCode(): int`, since enum members never carry `override` ([§10.5](#sec-restrictions)) — the same discipline, and the same diagnostic style, as [§8.3](#sec-equals-and-gethashcode)'s Equals→GetHashCode pairing. The three surfaces (`=`, `Equals`, hashing) can otherwise silently diverge exactly where it hurts: `a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct. The rule does not force delegation (operator overloads admit heterogeneous operand types, so "the operator is the body of Equals" is ill-defined in general); it forces the author to *state* all three, so a divergence is a visible choice rather than an accident. Heterogeneous-operand overloads (`T = U`) carry no such obligation. (The compiler-intrinsic `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` operator declarations in stdlib §10 predate and are exempt from the rule.)

<a id="sec-examples"></a>
### 25.3 Examples

```bezel
record Vector2(X: double, Y: double)
  public static method operator +(left: Vector2, right: Vector2): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(left.X + right.X, left.Y + right.Y);

  public static method operator *(v: Vector2, scalar: double): Vector2 =>
    new Vector2(v.X * scalar, v.Y * scalar);
end Vector2;

record Counter(Value: int)
  public static method operator ++(c: Counter): Counter =>
    new Counter(c.Value + 1);
end Counter;
```

Bitwise complement is overloadable for types with a natural bit-pattern or set-complement reading:

```bezel
record BitMask(Bits: ulong)
  public static method operator ~(m: BitMask): BitMask =>
    new BitMask(~m.Bits);
end BitMask;
```

For domain-specific inversion that does not match a bitwise reading, define a named method instead:

```bezel
record TriBool(Value: int)
  public method Negate(): TriBool => (case Value of
    0 => new TriBool(1),
    1 => new TriBool(0),
    _ => this);
end TriBool;
```

The named method form makes the inversion explicit at the call site (`t.Negate()` rather than `not t`), which is preferable when the operation departs from the boolean reading of `not` ([§14.4](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-not-is-not-user-overloadable) of the design rationale).

When an operator overload is block-bodied (statements followed by `end`, rather than the expression form `=> ...`), the optional name in the closing `end` is written as `end operator OpToken;` — e.g. `end operator ~;` or `end operator +;`. The named-end form is recommended for non-trivial operator bodies.

<a id="sec-no-user-defined-conversion-operators"></a>
### 25.4 No user-defined conversion operators

User-defined types — records and classes — cannot declare implicit or explicit conversion operators. There is no syntactic form for declaring "convert from S to T" on a user type; the explicit-cast expression `T(value)` ([§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions)) and the implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) apply only to the built-in conversions enumerated in [§5](#sec-type-conversions) and to the compiler-intrinsic conversions on `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` ([§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr)).

To express a conversion between user types, define a named factory or instance method:

```bezel
// Construction-style conversion: factory method on the destination type.
record Money(Amount: decimal, Currency: string)
  public static method FromDecimal(amount: decimal, currency: string): Money =>
    new Money(amount, currency);
end Money;

// Projection-style conversion: instance method on the source type.
record User(Id: int, Name: string, Email: string);

record UserDto(Id: int, Name: string, Email: string)
  public method ToUser(): User => new User(Id, Name, Email);
end UserDto;
```

The named-method form is preferred over conversion operators for several reasons:

- The conversion is visible at the call site (`UserDto.ToUser()` rather than `(User)dto`); a reader sees what is happening without needing to look up declarations.
- The conversion's name can communicate intent (`FromDecimal`, `FromInt`, `ToReadOnly`) where a cast cannot.
- Overload resolution does not have to consider user-defined conversions; the conversion is a regular method call subject to ordinary resolution rules.
- The pattern composes with the rest of the language (extension methods, fluent chaining) without requiring any conversion-specific extensions.

C# supports both `implicit` and `explicit` user-defined conversion operators. Bezel deliberately omits both. The implicit form is widely considered a misfeature in retrospect even within the C# community — it makes overload resolution opaque and lets unintended conversions slip into expressions silently. The explicit form is less harmful but offers no advantage over a named method with the same compile-time check. Bezel's stance — visible conversions everywhere, with the compiler enforcing the visibility — is consistent with [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)'s rule that implicit conversions exist only when no programmer-visible information is lost, and with [§6.2](#sec-mixed-type-arithmetic)'s prohibition on implicit `decimal`/binary-float mixing.

The compiler-intrinsic conversions on `IntPtr` and `UIntPtr` ([§32.7](#sec-pointers-and-intptr)) — explicit casts to and from `long` and `ulong` — are not user-defined and are not covered by this rule. They exist because `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` are intrinsic FFI-boundary types whose explicit-cast forms are part of the compiler's pointer-handling surface, not a user-overridable mechanism.

---

<a id="sec-extension-blocks"></a>
## 26. Extension Blocks

An extension block adds methods and computed read-only properties to a type without modifying the type's source.

<a id="sec-extension-blocks-declaration"></a>
### 26.1 Declaration

*(Extension methods and expression-bodied extension properties may be declared `pure` — [§22.15](#sec-pure-members); the receiver borrow composes with the read rules.)*

```bezel
extension string
  public property IsBlank: bool => this.Length = 0 or this.Trim().Length = 0;
  public method Words(): owned Array<string> => this.Split(' ');
end;
```

An extension block is declared at module level. It may be `public` or `internal` (default `internal`). The block ends with `end;` or `end extension;` ([§1.6](#sec-statements-and-termination)).

Inside the block, methods and computed properties are written as if they were instance members. `this` refers to the receiver.

<a id="sec-what-can-be-extended"></a>
### 26.2 What can be extended

- Classes (including `Object`).
- Interfaces.
- Records.
- Enums.
- Built-in primitive types.

What cannot be extended:

- Type parameters (`extension T` is meaningless).
- Nullable types directly (`extension int?`). Extend the non-nullable form; callers handle nullability at the call site with `?.` ([§7.5](#sec-null-conditional-access)).
- Function types.
- Choices. The extendable list above is closed against the choice kind — no [§14.2](#sec-constraints) constraint names the value-like classification bound a payload-generic extension surface would need, and the value-payload combinator surface of stdlib `Result<T, E>` is **compiler-provided** ([§35.2](#sec-choice-members)), not an extension block.
- Inline-array types (`extension [N]T`). Inline arrays are value-typed but their identity is per-size — `[3]int` and `[4]int` are distinct types — so an extension declaration would have to fix N, making the form rarely useful. Operations that should work across multiple inline-array sizes are typically written as static methods that take a specific inline-array type per overload, or that take a heap-array view (`Array<T>`) that the caller constructs from the inline array's contents.

<a id="sec-extension-blocks-restrictions"></a>
### 26.3 Restrictions

- Only methods and computed read-only properties. An extension property is **expression-bodied only** (`property Name: Type => expr;`) — the block-accessor form is not admitted; multi-statement logic goes in a method.
- No fields, auto-properties, constructors, destructors, or `owned` fields.
- No operator overloads.
- No indexers.
- No `static` members: a `static` modifier inside an extension block is a compile error. An extension block adds receiver-directed members only; statics resolve against the extended type's own declarations ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)), and admitting extension statics would need its own resolution, merging, and ambiguity story for no recorded need. Write a static method on a static class instead.
- No `virtual`, `override`, `abstract`, or `sealed` — extensions are statically dispatched.
- Extension members must be declared `public` or `internal`; `protected` and `private` are compile errors — an extension block has no declaring class and no inheritance, so [§13.1](#sec-levels)'s definitions for those levels do not apply. The member's effective visibility is the more restrictive of the block's reach and the member's own declaration (mirroring [§11.6](#sec-nested-types)'s nested-type rule).
- Extension members see only the extended type's public API. From the same module, `internal` members are also visible.

<a id="sec-generic-extensions"></a>
### 26.4 Generic extensions

**Type-parameter binding.** In the extended type's argument positions, each **bare single-segment non-nullable identifier** introduces a fresh block-level type parameter — *always*, shadowing any same-named type in scope (the compiler warns on such shadowing). This is the only implicit type-parameter binding in the language, so the rule is stated exactly: multiple parameters are permitted (`extension Dictionary<K, V>`); a **concrete** instantiation is written with keyword/primitive types, qualified names, or generic instantiations (`extension IEnumerable<int>`, `extension IEnumerable<Array<byte>>`), none of which are bare single-segment identifiers. The alternative — resolving the identifier against scope and only binding when unresolved — is declined: it would let an unrelated type declaration elsewhere silently re-mean an extension block (action at a distance). The binding rule applies at **any nesting depth** of the extended type's argument positions: `extension IEnumerable<Array<T>>` binds `T`, and `extension Dictionary<K, Array<V>>` binds `K` and `V`. A **nullable-marked** identifier in an argument position (`extension Array<T?>`) binds nothing and is a compile error naming this rule — only the bare non-nullable identifier introduces a parameter. Nothing is lost by the rejection: a bare `T` already unifies with nullable arguments (`extension Array<T>` applies to `Array<int?>` with `T = int?`); the only capability a `T?` head would add — constraining a block to *only* nullable instantiations — is deferred until a need is recorded.

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: IComparable<T>
  public method Sort(): owned Array<T>
    var items := this.ToArray();
    // ...
    return items;
  end Sort;
end;
```

The block-level type parameter is in scope throughout the block. Methods may introduce their own type parameters:

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T>
  public method Map<U>(transform: (T) -> U): owned Array<U>
    var result := new Array<U>();
    for var item in this do
      result.Add(transform(item));
    end;
    return result;
  end Map;
end;
```

A `where` clause on the block constrains which instantiations of the extended type the extension applies to.

<a id="sec-resolution"></a>
### 26.5 Resolution

When the compiler encounters `x.Foo(args)`:

1. **Instance members win — by name.** If `x`'s declared type (or any base type) *declares* any instance member named `Foo` — of any arity, applicability, or accessibility — instance resolution is committed and extension blocks are **never consulted** for that name on that receiver. If the committed instance lookup then fails (no applicable overload, [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)/[§22.6](#sec-overloading), or the member is inaccessible, [§13.1](#sec-levels)), the call is a compile error citing the instance member(s); it does not fall back to an extension (the diagnostic should note a same-named extension where one exists). Blocking by *name* rather than by applicability or accessibility keeps resolution predictable: whether a call reaches an instance member or an extension never depends on argument types or the caller's access level, so changing an overload's signature or a member's visibility cannot silently re-route a call across the instance/extension boundary.
2. **Extension members.** If the receiver's type declares no instance member of that name, the compiler searches the current module and all imported modules for extension blocks on `x`'s type, base types, or implemented interfaces, considering only extension members visible at the call site ([§26.3](#sec-extension-blocks-restrictions)'s effective-visibility rule). When an extension block is declared on a generic type (e.g. `extension IEnumerable<T>`), the block-level type parameter is inferred from the receiver's type: if `x` has type `Array<int>` and `Array<int>` implements `IEnumerable<int>`, then `T` is inferred as `int`. The receiver-driven inference is the unification of [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) applied to the extension head: the receiver's static type is unified against the declared head, exactly and structurally, binding the block-level parameters.
3. **Most specific type wins.** Extensions on the most specific type are preferred per the subtype ordering below.
4. **Ambiguity.** If two equally-specific extensions match, the call is a compile error. Because extension blocks are nameless, the diagnostic must identify each candidate by what it *has*: its **defining module**, its **declared head including any `where` clause**, and its **declaration site**. The remedies are the mechanisms that exist: remove or narrow a conflicting import; hoist the intended behavior into a helper static method (taking the receiver as a parameter) on a static class and call that; or, when the colliding blocks are under the author's control, give the members **distinct names** — the posture [§22.6](#sec-overloading) records for same-name declarations that cannot be soundly auto-ranked (the specialized member takes a distinct name, or the blocks merge into one member that dispatches internally). No call-site syntax qualifies an extension's defining type, because extension blocks are nameless and extensions have no static-invocation form; a first-class extension-disambiguation spelling is deferred, not designed here (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)).

Adding a real method to a type silently takes priority over an extension with the same name — by design.

Extensions are resolved on the **compile-time** type of the receiver, not the runtime type. Polymorphism requires `virtual`, not extensions.

<a id="sec-specificity-ordering"></a>
#### 26.5.1 Specificity ordering

For receiver type R, specificity ranks the **applicable** candidates: extension members of the called name that match the call's arity and argument types, from blocks whose head matches R (step 2 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution)), with block-level `where` clauses satisfied by the arguments inferred from the receiver. A `where` clause is an *applicability* filter, never a ranking signal.

An extension on E1 is **more specific** than one on E2 when E1 is a subtype of E2 and E2 is not a subtype of E1. The subtype test is evaluated on the **receiver-substituted heads**: each candidate's declared extension head has its block-level type parameters replaced by the arguments inferred from the receiver (step 2 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution)) before the test runs. Derived class beats base class; class beats interface implemented by that class; derived interface beats extended interface. So for a receiver of type `Array<int>`: `extension Array<T>` (substituted head `Array<int>`) is more specific than `extension IEnumerable<T>` (substituted head `IEnumerable<int>`), because `Array<int>` is a subtype of `IEnumerable<int>`.

If neither candidate's substituted head is a proper subtype of the other's, the candidates are equally specific and rule 4 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution) produces an ambiguity error. In particular, candidates with **identical substituted heads** never auto-rank: neither a more-concrete-looking declared head (`extension IEnumerable<int>` and `extension IEnumerable<T>` are indistinguishable after substitution for an `Array<int>` receiver) nor a stronger `where` clause on the same head makes one candidate more specific than the other. Auto-ranked specialization is declined, with a recorded re-addition condition (rationale [§17.10](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-auto-ranked-extension-specificity)).

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: value
  // where T: value — the for-based body returns the iteration variable, which
  // at a class or interface substitution would be an enumerator-sourced borrow
  // that may not escape the loop (§28.3, §29.2, v0.235); at value substitutions
  // the return copies the value and the admission is vacuous.
  public method First(): T
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

extension Array<T>
  public method First(): T
    if this.Count = 0 then throw new InvalidOperationException("empty array"); end;
    return this[0];
  end First;
end;

var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];
var f := xs.First();     // selects the Array<T> member — substituted head Array<int>
                         // is a subtype of substituted head IEnumerable<int>
```

By contrast, two candidates whose substituted heads are identical are equally specific. If both of the following blocks are visible at the call site, the call is a compile error:

```bezel
extension IEnumerable<T> where T: value
  public method First(): T
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

extension IEnumerable<int>
  public method First(): int
    // a hand-specialized int form
    for var item in this do return item; end;
    throw new InvalidOperationException("empty sequence");
  end First;
end;

var xs: Array<int> := [1, 2, 3];
var f := xs.First();     // ERROR: ambiguous — both substituted heads are IEnumerable<int>
```

The diagnostic names both candidates (rule 4 of [§26.5](#sec-resolution)); the remedies are rule 4's: narrow an import, hoist into a static-class helper, or — when both blocks are under the author's control — give the members distinct names.

<a id="sec-multiple-blocks-for-the-same-type"></a>
### 26.6 Multiple blocks for the same type

Multiple `extension` blocks targeting the same type may appear across files in the same module. The compiler merges them. Duplicate signatures are a compile error.

<a id="sec-ownership-in-extensions"></a>
### 26.7 Ownership in extensions

The receiver is always a borrow; extensions cannot store `this`, return it as `owned`, or dispose it. Other parameters may be `owned`, following normal method rules. Extensions may return `owned` values.

---

<a id="sec-lambdas-and-function-types"></a>
## 27. Lambdas and Function Types

Functions are first-class values: stored, passed, returned, held in fields.

<a id="sec-function-types"></a>
### 27.1 Function types

A function type is written `(params) -> returnType`:

```bezel
var add: (int, int) -> int;
var isPositive: (int) -> bool;
var log: (string) -> ();              // procedure
var noop: () -> ();
var now: () -> DateTime;
```

The parallel with method declarations:

| Method | Function type |
|---|---|
| `method Foo(x: int): bool` | `(int) -> bool` |
| `method Foo(x: int)` | `(int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(): int` | `() -> int` |
| `method Foo()` | `() -> ()` |
| `method Foo(owned t: T)` | `(owned T) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(ref n: int)` | `(ref int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(out r: int)` | `(out int) -> ()` |
| `method Foo(out owned r: T)` | `(out owned T) -> ()` |

A method without a return type has function type returning `()`.

Function types may include the parameter modifiers `owned`, `ref`, `out`, `scoped`, and the combination `out owned`. The modifier is part of the type — `(T) -> ()` and `(owned T) -> ()` are distinct function types, and the same applies to the other modifier forms. Function-type compatibility requires modifiers to match exactly; there is no implicit conversion between modified and unmodified parameter slots. The available modifier combinations match those of method declarations ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) and grammar A.4). A `scoped` parameter position is likewise part of a function signature's identity, like `ref`/`out` ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)): `(scoped () -> Task) -> ()` and `(() -> Task) -> ()` are distinct types with no conversion between them.

Function types may include parameter names. Names are documentation only; they do not affect type identity:

```bezel
var handler: (itemId: int, quantity: int, priority: int) -> bool;
```

`(int, int, int) -> bool` and the named form are the same type. Calls are positional.

<a id="sec-function-type-assignability"></a>
#### 27.1.1 Function-type assignability

A function-typed **value** may be used where a different function type is expected under one narrow variance rule; everything else requires an exact match:

- **Parameter slots** of class or interface type are **contravariant**: the target's parameter type must implicitly *reference*-convert to the value's ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions), reference conversions only) — a `(Animal) -> ()` value is usable where `(Dog) -> ()` is expected.
- The **return slot**, when of class or interface type, is **covariant**: the value's return type must implicitly reference-convert to the target's — a `() -> Dog` value is usable as `() -> Animal`.
- **Value-typed, record-typed, and primitive slots are invariant.** No numeric widening, boxing, or other representation-changing conversion applies to a slot of an already-constructed function value: there is no adapter object to perform it.
- **Modifier slots** (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`out owned`/`scoped`) must match **exactly** ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)); per-slot nullability follows the standard [§7](#sec-nullability-2) rules.
- **`Task`-family return slots are announcement-bearing:** a function-typed value whose return slot (nullability stripped) is a `Task`-family type is usable only where the target's return slot is also a `Task`-family type — covariance applies *within* the family (`() -> Task<int>` is usable as `() -> Task`) and never across its boundary (`() -> Task<int>` is not usable as `() -> Object`). The unmarked `Task`-family return is container-ownership-transferring ([§28.3](#sec-producers)) — the same announcement-by-declared-type logic as an `owned` return — so it takes the modifier slots' exact-match discipline rather than the concrete-class covariance rule: retyping it to a non-family slot would erase the calls-mint announcement, and an invocation through the retyped face would classify the minted frame as a borrow — a leak. The same boundary governs **method-reference formation** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)): formation over a callee whose declared return type is `Task`-family may bridge only to a `Task`-family target slot (and a property reference over a `Task`-family-typed property is rejected outright — [§27.6](#sec-method-references)).

Assignability under this rule preserves **identity**: the value is the same function object viewed at a compatible function type (like interface variance, [§12.9](#sec-variance)), so function-value equality ([§27.7.1](#sec-equality-of-function-values)) is unaffected by the retyping. This *value*-assignability rule is distinct from **method-reference formation** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)): forming a reference from a *named method* against a target type may bridge any [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) implicit conversion, because the compiler synthesizes the adapter at the formation site; once formed, the value obeys the narrower rule above. This subsection is the single normative statement of these criteria; [§27.6](#sec-method-references) defers to it.

<a id="sec-lambda-parameter-modifiers"></a>
#### Lambda parameter modifiers

Lambda parameters may carry the same modifiers when the target function type expects them:

```bezel
var attach: (owned EventHandler) -> () := lambda(owned h) => _handlers.Add(h);
```

When the target type is known from context, the lambda's parameter modifiers may be omitted in source — the compiler infers them from the target. When inferring is not possible (a `var` introduction with no target context), the modifier must be written explicitly to produce a function value of the modified type.

<a id="sec-nullable-function-types"></a>
### 27.2 Nullable function types

```bezel
var callback: ((int) -> bool)?;       // nullable function returning bool
var nullableReturn: (int) -> bool?;   // non-null function returning a nullable bool
```

The parentheses around the function type are required before `?`. Without them, the `?` would attach to the return type.

<a id="sec-lambda-expressions"></a>
### 27.3 Lambda expressions

A lambda expression is **keyword-led** (grammar A.7 `LambdaExpr`): the reserved word `lambda` — preceded by `async` for the asynchronous form ([§30.6](#sec-async-lambdas)) — then a parenthesized parameter list (the empty pair for zero parameters; there is no paren-free form), an optional **return-type ascription**, `=>`, and the body. The keyword commits the parse at its first token — `lambda` begins no other expression or statement — the same committed-reading property the paren atoms have ([§17.1](#sec-precedence) note); in particular, a parenthesized construct followed by `=>` (a `when`-guard arm, a grouped expression) can never be read as a lambda prefix.

Expression body:
```bezel
var twice := lambda(x: int) => x * 2;
var greet := lambda(name: string) => $"Hello, {name}!";
```

Block body:
```bezel
var processItem := lambda(item: Item) => do
  var normalized := Normalize(item);
  var enriched := Enrich(normalized);
  return enriched;
end;
```

Inside a value-returning block-bodied lambda, `return` is required on every exit path.

**Ignored parameters.** A parameter slot may be the ignore `_` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): it is accepted, binds nothing, and contributes its slot to the lambda's function type as normal — under a target type `(T, U) -> U`, `lambda(_, x) => x` ignores its first argument. Because nothing is named, several ignores may coexist: `lambda(_, _) => 0` is legal. No parameter modifier and no type annotation compose with the bare ignore — `FuncParamMods` with `_` is rejected (a `ref` parameter reads and writes through its operand, which an ignore cannot supply, and a `scoped` parameter that binds nothing stores nothing), and a typed ignore slot is spelled by the target type, exactly the [§27.4](#sec-parameter-type-inference) inference story. The destructure-slot `_` ([§27.4](#sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring)) is the same nothing-is-bound reading per slot.

**Which block-bodied lambdas return a value.** A block-bodied lambda is a **procedure lambda** — its type is `(…) -> ()` — exactly when no path through its body executes a value-carrying `return e;`: its exits are bare `return;` and falling off the end. A body where one path returns a value and another exits without one is a compile error, the same totality rule as for methods. A target type, when present, is checked against this classification — a procedure-bodied lambda does not convert to a value-returning function type, nor the reverse.

**The return-type ascription.** Between the parameter list and `=>`, a lambda may ascribe its return type: `lambda(x: int): long => x * 2`. The ascription is **optional everywhere inference succeeds** — it is never a new obligation — and when present it behaves exactly as a method's declared return type: each `return e;` (and an expression body) is checked against it under [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions), including implicit widening (`return dog;` under `: Animal`); the typed-context literal widening of [§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions) applies to it (`lambda(): long => 3_000_000_000`); and a declared nullable return is the target that admits `null`-producing arms ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)). A unit ascription (`: ()`) declares a procedure lambda. When both a target type and an ascription are present, they must agree under [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s return rule — the ascription never bridges a conversion the value itself could not. An ascribed lambda's `return` operands and expression body are **declared-result positions** for choice-case constructions ([§35.3](#sec-choice-construction)) — the ascription is a written declared result type, exactly as a method's.

**Return-type inference without a target.** In a context with no target type, a value-returning block-bodied lambda's return type is inferred only when **every** `return e;` expression in the body has the *same* type; otherwise the lambda is a compile error asking for a target type, a return-type ascription (this section), or an ascribed variable type. The compiler does not unify divergent return types to a common supertype — an inference that silently computed `Animal` from `return dog;` and `return cat;` would make the lambda's type sensitive to distant hierarchy edits; the programmer states the intended type instead (the explicit-over-implicit stance of [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking)). The ascription is the on-site spelling of that statement:

```bezel
var classify := lambda(score: int): string? => do
  if score < 0 then return null; end;
  if score >= 90 then return "A"; end;
  return "pass";
end;
```

Expression-bodied lambdas need no inference rule: the body expression's type is the return type, and a body of type `()` makes a procedure lambda.

For procedure lambdas, the body may also be a single expression whose result is discarded:
```bezel
var log := lambda(msg: string) => Console.WriteLine(msg);
```

<a id="sec-parameter-type-inference"></a>
### 27.4 Parameter type inference

When the lambda's target type is known from context, parameter type annotations may be omitted:

```bezel
var doubled := numbers.Select(lambda(x) => x * 2);
var positives := numbers.Where(lambda(x) => x > 0);
```

In top-level contexts with no target type (`var f := lambda(x) => x * 2;`), parameter types must be specified.

<a id="sec-lambda-parameter-destructuring"></a>
#### Lambda-parameter record destructuring

A lambda parameter may be a positional record **destructuring** in place of an identifier:

```bezel
var labels := entries.Select(lambda(Entry(k, v)) => $"{k}: {v}");
var positives := points.Where(lambda(Point(x, _)) => x > 0);
```

The form reuses [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s positional-destructuring spelling with parameter-position restrictions. A destructuring parameter is a **binding form, not a test**, so only irrefutable elements are admitted:

- The head must name a **positional record type**, and it must be *exactly* the parameter's type: when a target type supplies the parameter type, a head naming any other type is a compile error (no subtype test, nothing to fail at runtime); when no target type is available, the head *is* the annotation — `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => …` alone types the parameter as `Entry`.
- Each slot is a naked identifier binding, a discard `_`, or a nested destructuring meeting the same rules; the slot count must equal the record's positional-field count. Constants, ranges, relationals, type tests, `var`-form bindings, and alternatives are compile errors in parameter position — they are refutable, and a parameter list is not a `case`.
- The destructuring parameter admits no modifiers (`ref`, `scoped`) and no separate type annotation — the head carries the type.

Semantics are by desugaring: `lambda(Entry(k, v)) => body` behaves exactly as `lambda(p: Entry) => do var k := p.«first field»; var v := p.«second field»; …body… end` — each binding is an ordinary read of the corresponding positional field at body entry, with the standard ownership meaning ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)): a copy for value-typed fields, a **borrow** of the argument's field for class-typed fields, a shared reference for runtime-managed fields. Nothing is consumed: the record argument is untouched, the bindings own nothing, and the lambda's function type is unchanged by the spelling (`(Entry) -> R`).

<a id="sec-closures"></a>
### 27.5 Closures

A lambda may reference variables from its enclosing scope. Captured variables are heap-allocated in a closure object. Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa. (For a captured **owned** binding the sharing is read-only in the ownership sense: the lambda may not assign to it, transfer from it, or dispose it — [§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings).)

```bezel
public method MakeCounter(): () -> int
  var count := 0;
  return lambda() => do
    count := count + 1;
    return count;
  end;
end MakeCounter;
```

For `for` loop variables, each iteration produces a fresh binding. A lambda captured inside the body sees that iteration's value.

<a id="sec-method-references"></a>
### 27.6 Method references

When a lambda's body is just a call to an existing method, the method reference may be used directly:

```bezel
var parsed := strings.Select(int.Parse);
var lengths := names.Select(string.Length);       // property reference
var sorted := numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs);          // static method
var greetings := names.Select(greeter.Greet);    // bound instance method
```

Method references work for static methods, instance methods (the instance is captured at formation — by reference for class-typed receivers, **by copy** for value-shaped (record) receivers, which is what denies record receivers identity in [§27.7.1](#sec-equality-of-function-values)), properties, and extension methods. A property reference produces the getter; its type is `(Receiver) -> PropertyType` for instance properties and `() -> PropertyType` for static properties. Whether the property also has a setter is irrelevant; setter references are not supported. The reference's signature must be compatible with the target function type: its parameter and return types unify with the target's under the standard implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)) — the same criterion applied to an overloaded reference (below) — while modifier slots (`owned`/`ref`/`out`/`scoped`) must match exactly. (Formation may bridge representation-changing conversions by synthesizing an adapter at the reference site; assignability between two already-formed function-typed *values* is the narrower variance rule of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability). Return-slot bridging respects the `Task`-family boundary of [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability).)

A property reference over a property whose declared type (nullability stripped) is a **`Task`-family type** is rejected at the formation site: the reference's function type would carry a `Task`-family return slot, whose invocation the rule classifies as an owned mint ([§28.3](#sec-producers), *Task-family calls produce owned frames*), while the underlying getter lends its storage ([§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet)'s source-owns-task rule) — formation would pair two owners over one stored task. Read the property directly and consume the task through [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s admitted borrow positions, or wrap a genuine task *producer* (a method reference over a `Task`-returning method remains the ordinary, admissible spelling). The same mint/lend boundary governs return-slot bridging at formation generally ([§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s family rule).

A method reference over a **static** callee whose declared return type (nullability stripped) is one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interfaces or a lazy query — the iterator convention's frame-minting factories ([§28.3](#sec-producers) *Iterator and iterable returns*: "callers must discharge the ownership obligation") — may be formed only against a target slot whose return (nullability stripped) is also such an interface, or left at the callee's own type: bridging it to any other return slot (`() -> Object`, a concrete class or interface type) is rejected at the formation site — the retyped face would erase the frame-mint announcement, and an invocation through it would classify under the producers row as a borrow: a leaked caller-owned frame. References over *instance* iterable-returning callees are outside this fence (their calls lend under axiom A2's recorded keying — receiver-sourced — and are soundly borrow-classified through any slot). Iterable-to-iterable bridging and the iterable-typed slot's own invocation classification remain an open question; the routes this fence cannot see (a *formed* value retyped through a typed intermediate; a bare-parameter slot at an iterable substitution) are that issue's recorded seam ([§28.3](#sec-producers) row parenthetical; [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s narrowed residual).

For an extension method, the reference uses the extended type's name as qualifier; the resulting function has the receiver as its first parameter:

```bezel
import System.Collections.Linq;
var counter: (IEnumerable<int>) -> int := IEnumerable<int>.Count;
```

Indexers cannot be used as method references; the parameter list makes the natural function type ambiguous.

<a id="sec-method-references-to-overloaded-methods"></a>
#### Method references to overloaded methods

When the named method (or property) is overloaded, the reference is resolved using the **target function type** at the use site. The compiler selects the overload whose parameter types and return type unify with the target's parameter and return types under the standard implicit-conversion rules ([§5.1](#sec-implicit-conversions)):

```bezel
var sortedByAbs := numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs);     // double or int? Resolved
                                                  //   from numbers.ElementType
                                                  //   and OrderBy's target type.
```

If `numbers` has type `Array<int>`, `OrderBy<TKey>` expects a `(int) -> TKey`; the reference `Math.Abs` resolves to the `Math.Abs(int): int` overload. If `numbers` is `Array<double>`, the same reference resolves to `Math.Abs(double): double`.

**Selection among several unifying candidates: exact-preferred.** More
than one overload may unify with the target — against `(int) -> TKey`,
`Math.Abs(long): long` also unifies, the target's `int` parameter converting
to `long`. Among unifying candidates, one whose parameter types — and return
type, where the target's return position is closed — match the target's
**exactly** is preferred; candidates that unify only through conversion are
co-equal (the [§22.6](#sec-implicit-conversion-ranking) posture applied to the
reference's signature), so absent an exact candidate the reference is
ambiguous and the compiler reports the candidates. This is the
**exact-preferred ranking** that [§14.5](#sec-type-argument-inference) phase 2
cites: `numbers.OrderBy(Math.Abs)` over `Array<int>` selects `Abs(int): int` —
exact at the closed parameter position, binding `TKey := int` — and the
converting overloads lose to it.

When no target type is available (e.g., `var f := Math.Abs;` with no annotation), the reference is ambiguous and the compiler reports an error pointing to the candidate overloads. The user disambiguates by adding a type annotation: `var f: (int) -> int := Math.Abs;`.

When a name `T.M` could resolve to either a *static* member of `T` or an *instance method reference* of `T` (a method requiring a receiver), the static member wins. The instance form has no separate syntax in this version — if both interpretations apply and the programmer wants the instance form, the disambiguation is to use a lambda: `lambda(t: T) => t.M(...)`. This case is rare in practice; it arises only when `T` declares an instance method named `M` and a static member also named `M`, which is unusual style.

<a id="sec-calling-function-values"></a>
### 27.7 Calling function values

```bezel
var sum := add(2, 3);

var maybeHandler: ((int) -> ())? := null;
maybeHandler?(42);                      // null-conditional call; no-op when null
```

The null-conditional call result is nullable.

<a id="sec-equality-of-function-values"></a>
#### 27.7.1 Equality of function values

Function-typed values compare with `=` and `<>` by the following rule (normative):

- A **lambda** (closure) value equals only itself — reference equality on the closure instance. Two separately-constructed lambdas with identical source text are *not* equal, even if they capture the same variables.
- A **method reference** equals another method reference **iff** both denote the **same method** and, for instance references, are bound to the **same receiver** — receiver sameness being reference identity for class-typed receivers. A static (or extension-method) reference to `M` equals every other reference to `M`. Repeated evaluations of `obj.Method` on the same class-typed `obj` are therefore **guaranteed equal**: equality is defined on the (method, receiver) pair, so whether the implementation caches or re-allocates the underlying function object is unobservable.
- A method reference whose receiver is **value-shaped** (a record — [§27.6](#sec-method-references) captures the instance by copy) has no receiver identity: two separate evaluations compare **unequal** (each holds a distinct copy); only the same function object equals itself — and since every store-once spelling (a function-typed local or field passed to `+=`) is rejected at the scoped `Add` position by [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s admission bound 3, deterministic `-=` unsubscription for record receivers is not expressible in v1 (recorded below); use `Subscribe` and the owned `Subscription` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)). *(Alternative declined: defining receiver sameness by the record's own `Equals` would drag user equality dispatch into function-value comparison and make `-=` matching sensitive to value mutation between subscribe and unsubscribe; recorded in the changelog entry.)*
- A lambda never equals a method reference, and property references follow the method-reference rule (the getter is the method).

The practical consequence: function values should still not be used as dictionary keys or set elements, but event unsubscription is deterministic for named methods: `EventSource<T>.Remove` — and the `-=` desugaring ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)) — matches handlers by the function-value equality above, so `+=`/`-=` with a named method reference on a class-typed receiver reliably unsubscribes (same method, same receiver). `+=`/`-=` with separately-constructed lambdas does not match (each lambda is a fresh closure object).

The reliable pattern for `+=` followed by later `-=` is a **named method reference**: same method + same class-typed receiver compare equal (the rule above), so re-evaluated references match — and a method reference is one of the verified argument forms that [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s v1 admission bound 3 admits at the scoped `Add` position. (The `+=`/`-=` forms require a source-typed operand ([§17.2](#sec-notes-on-operators)), which under the stdlib §6.5 event pattern is the publisher's private field; the examples below are publisher-side code, where `_clicked += OnButtonClicked` is [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s form-4 self-capture admission (chain root `this`). A method reference passed at *another* publisher instance's `+=` additionally faces the form-4 declared-before test.)

```bezel
_clicked += OnButtonClicked;
// later:
_clicked -= OnButtonClicked;   // same method, same receiver: matches and unsubscribes
```

For a **lambda** handler, deterministic unsubscription goes through `Subscribe` and the owned `Subscription` (stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)). A lambda equals only itself, and the store-once spelling that would preserve the single closure instance — a function-typed field or local passed to `+=` — is **not admissible** at the subscription site: `Add` is a `scoped` (storing) position, and [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s admission bound 3 rejects function-typed locals and field reads as unverifiable argument forms (the verified forms are lambda literals and method references). The anti-pattern below therefore also silently fails to unsubscribe — each lambda is a fresh closure object:

```bezel
_clicked += lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y);
// later:
_clicked -= lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y);   // a different lambda, no match
```

```bezel
// The lambda form with deterministic teardown — and the form that also works
// anywhere, since Subscribe is on the IEvent<T> face:
using var sub := button.Clicked.Subscribe(lambda(e) => UpdateStatus(e.X, e.Y));
// disposing sub severs the registration (stdlib §6.5)
```

For named methods bound to **record** (value-shaped) receivers, deterministic `-=` unsubscription is **not expressible in v1** (recorded): the equality rule requires the very same function object, and every store-once spelling — a function-typed local or field — is rejected at the `Add` site by [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) bound 3. The remedy is `Subscribe` plus the owned `Subscription`, which needs no equality match at all. (Bound 3 is marked *liftable*; a future revision admitting provably-single-assignment private fields at scoped call sites would make the store-once form expressible again.)

<a id="sec-type-aliases"></a>
### 27.8 Type aliases

A `type` declaration introduces an alias for any existing type, binding with `:=` like every other binding in the language:

```bezel
type UserId := int;
type ConnectionPool := Dictionary<string, Array<Connection>>;

/// <summary>Handles an HTTP response.</summary>
/// <param name="status">The HTTP status code.</param>
/// <returns>True if handled successfully.</returns>
type ResponseHandler := (status: int, body: string, elapsed: TimeSpan) -> bool;
```

A type alias is a pure synonym — it does not create a new type. `UserId` and `int` are interchangeable.

For genuinely distinct types (`UserId` and `OrderId` should not be interchangeable despite both being `int`), use a single-field record:

```bezel
record UserId(Value: int);
record OrderId(Value: int);
```

Type aliases may be declared at module level. A module-level alias is always **module-internal**: `TypeAliasDecl` admits no visibility keyword (Appendix [A.2](#sec-source-file)), the alias is never among the public names an `import` makes visible ([§2.2](#sec-imports)), and it is not part of the public surface the module's interface describes ([§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)) — an importing module that wants the same shorthand declares its own alias (aliases are free; they create no type). Exportable aliases are deferred (rationale [§18](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-things-deferred)).

<a id="sec-generic-type-aliases"></a>
#### Generic type aliases

A type alias may declare type parameters:

```bezel
type Handler<T> := (T, string?) -> bool;
type Lookup<K, V> := Dictionary<K, Array<V>>;
type Predicate<T> := (T) -> bool;
type Reducer<T, TAccum> := (TAccum, T) -> TAccum;
```

Each instantiation of the alias is interchangeable with the corresponding instantiation of the aliased type. `Lookup<string, int>` and `Dictionary<string, Array<int>>` are the same type.

Generic aliases may carry constraints, written exactly as on generic methods:

```bezel
type Sorted<T> := IOrderedEnumerable<T> where T: IComparable<T>;
```

The constraint applies to the alias's parameter; uses of the alias must satisfy it.

A generic alias may not reference itself (no recursive aliases) and must resolve to a concrete type after substitution. Aliases of aliases are permitted:

```bezel
type IntPredicate := Predicate<int>;       // Predicate<int>, which is (int) -> bool
```

Type aliases — generic or not — see through to the aliased type for identity, equality, method dispatch, and overload resolution. They are a naming convenience, not a separate type kind.

---

<a id="sec-resource-management"></a>
## 28. Resource Management

Bezel has no garbage collector. Class instances are heap-allocated by `new` and must be disposed exactly once. Records, enums, and primitives need no disposal — their memory is reclaimed when their containing scope exits.

A small set of types are **runtime-managed** and exempt from manual disposal: `string`, boxed value types, and lambda closures ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
