For **trivial-dispose** class instances ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — classes whose disposal provably runs no user code and releases only memory: no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no fields of owning-inline-array type ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)), and a trivial-dispose base; this is a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — the exemption is one of **ceremony, not lifetime**. Ownership of every trivial-dispose instance is tracked exactly as for any other class: the instance has exactly one statically-known owner at every point (the [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) classification it carries), and the compiler inserts a **free** — logical disposal followed by reclamation, running no user code ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) — at that owner's release point. What the classification waives is the ceremony: no `using var` is needed, no must-use warning fires, and the discard `_ := …` does no cleanup work ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) K1.6). **No runtime lifetime mechanism exists for user-defined classes at all** — no reference counts, no regions, no heap scanning, no pauses: the runtime-managed tier above is exactly `string`, boxed values, and function values, and every class the user can write — trivial-dispose or not — is freed by compiler-inserted code at a statically-known point. The no-garbage-collector claim is therefore unconditional for class instances. The universal contract — every class instance reaches an owned location, becomes the operand of `using var`, is explicitly disposed, is discarded with `_ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), or is auto-dropped at scope end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) — is satisfied for trivial-dispose instances by the compiler's inserted free, without forcing programmers to write `using var _ := new MarkerObject();` for objects whose disposal does nothing.

The discard form `_ := expr;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) disposes the value at the end of the discard statement for any class or interface type (an unbound owned temporary, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries); for a trivial-dispose operand the disposal is the compiler's free — same timing, no user code); it is rejected at compile time only for `Task` and `Task<T>`, whose disposal would abandon a running operation. For supervised fire-and-forget on tasks, use `Task.FireAndForget` ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)).

<a id="sec-summary-of-disposal-obligations-by-type-kind"></a>
#### Summary of disposal obligations by type kind

| Type kind | Disposal required? | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Classes | Yes — exactly once | `using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), `owned` fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), explicit `.Dispose()`, discard `_ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), or auto-drop at scope end ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) |
| Interface-typed locations | Yes — treated as class | `using var` or `owned` field; discard via `_ := …` is **permitted** — it disposes via runtime dispatch at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), so a future non-trivial implementation poses no cross-module hazard |
| Records | No | Stack-allocated or inline; no heap block to release |
| Enums | No | Value type; no heap block |
| Primitives | No | Value type; no heap block |
| `string` | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Boxed value types | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Function values | No — runtime-managed | `Dispose()` is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Inline arrays `[N]T` (without `owned` slots) | No | Value type; stored inline in enclosing context; no separate allocation to dispose ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) |
| Inline arrays `[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T` (with `owned` slots) | No, indirectly | Move-only value type; the array's host (class field, local) discharges by disposing each (non-null) slot ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) |
| `Array<T>` and other borrowing collections | No — trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) | The instance is compiler-freed at its owner's release point; the backing storage is part of the instance's single allocation, released by that one free (a layout fact, not a lifetime mechanism); `Dispose()` runs no user code. Elements are borrows and are never disposed — nor disposable through the collection (owning-family collections own and cascade, [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)) |
| `OwningArray<T>` and other owning collections | Yes — class types | Dispose cascades through owned elements ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)) |

<a id="sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear"></a>
### 28.1 Where the `owned` modifier can appear

The `owned` modifier appears in specific declaration positions. It is **admissible** in the following positions:

- **Method parameter declarations.** `method M(owned p: T)` — the parameter takes ownership of the value at the call site; the method body is responsible for discharging it before returning.
- **Return type declarations.** `method Acquire(): owned Connection` — the return value is an owned reference; the caller assumes responsibility for its disposal.
- **Field declarations on classes.** `private owned _resource: Connection` — the field stores an owned reference; the containing class's destructor disposes it.
- **Local variables via `using var`.** `using var c := Connect()` — the local is owned and is disposed at scope exit.
- **`out` parameter declarations.** `out owned p: T` — the parameter is an out-position that produces an owned reference for the caller to take.
- **Function-type parameter slots.** `(owned T) -> ()` — the parameter slot of a function type may carry `owned`. The modifier is part of the function type's identity (see [§27.1](#sec-function-types)); `(T) -> ()` and `(owned T) -> ()` are distinct types.
- **Function-type return slots.** `() -> owned Connection` — the return slot of a function type may carry `owned`. The same identity rule applies.
- **Lambda parameters.** `lambda(owned x) => ...` or `lambda(owned x: T) => ...` — a lambda's parameter list carries the same modifiers as the target function type expects.
- **Choice payload fields.** `Fetched(owned response: Response)` — the payload slot takes ownership at construction and the active case's owned payloads are disposed with the value ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration), [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)); admissibility and the bare-type-parameter erasure follow the type requirement below.
- **Inline-array slot marker.** `[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?` — the `owned` keyword placed between the size and the closing bracket marks the inline array's slots as owned (see [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). The array becomes a move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). This is the type-level position for owning inline arrays; an owning-inline-array field on a class does **not** additionally carry the `owned` field modifier (the slot marker already conveys the obligation).

The modifier is **not admissible** in the following positions:

- **Record fields.** Records cannot have owned fields per [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).
- **Inline-array element types.** Writing `[N](owned T)` is not a well-formed syntax — `owned` on inline arrays appears in the slot-marker position `[N owned]T`, not on the element type. To hold owned elements in a resizable collection, use `OwningArray<T>`.
- **Generic type arguments.** This version does not admit `owned` on generic type arguments ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument)). Use named owning collection types (stdlib [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)) or `OwningTask<T>` (stdlib [§6](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-threading)) when the use case requires an owning generic.

Function-type parameters and return types *do* admit `owned` — `(owned T) -> ()` is the function-type form of `method M(owned t: T)`, and is a distinct type from `(T) -> ()` per [§27.1](#sec-function-types). The modifier is part of the function type's identity.

**Type requirement (bare-type-parameter arm revised).** In the method-parameter, return-type, `out`-parameter, lambda-parameter, choice-payload ([§35.1](#sec-choice-declaration)), and function-type parameter/return slot positions above, `owned` requires the declared type — nullability stripped — to be a **class type, an interface type, or a bare type parameter**; for a **move-only value type** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) the modifier is admitted-but-redundant (the type's own move semantics already transfer the obligation). On any other type — a primitive, `string`, a function type, an ordinary record, an enum, a non-owning inline array, or the unit type — `owned` is a **compile error**: such values carry no disposal obligation to transfer ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), the same reasoning as [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s field restriction and [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s rejection of `OwningTask<T>` at non-class T. For a **bare type parameter** the marker's meaning is fixed **per instantiation** (superseding the instantiation-site rejection — the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 pattern, the same pre-substitution-keying/per-instantiation-enforcement split as [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule): the generic body type-checks under the class-or-interface assumption; at a **class or interface** substitution the marker has its ordinary transfer meaning; at a **move-only value** substitution it is admitted-but-redundant, as for the concrete type; and at every **other value or runtime-managed** substitution it is **erased by the substitution** — the substituted signature is the unmarked one: no obligation exists to transfer ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), parameters and returns pass by value, an `out owned` slot delivers a plain value, marker-keyed call-site and binding forms written under the class assumption remain admissible with no-op effect ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)'s uniform admissibility), the marker does not survive into a substituted function type's identity (`(owned T) -> ()` at `T = int` *is* `(int) -> ()`, [§27.1](#sec-function-types)), and every rule keyed on the marker — [§11.2](#sec-interface-declaration)/[§12.1](#sec-members-are-non-virtual-by-default) signature matching, [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s call-site marker — reads the erased substituted form. Erasure changes substituted signatures, never classification keys: a declared `owned T` return remains outside [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s bare-type-parameter rule at every instantiation. Rejecting these instantiations instead made the `owned` spelling unusable for any fresh-producing generic whose domain admits value substitutions: precisely the signatures the static-return rule directs at the spelling ([§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)) and the static-interface producer members of stdlib §2.19. Two rejections remain. A declaration whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions outright (`where T: value`) rejects the marker **at the declaration** — it could never be more than redundant, the concrete-type reasoning above applied at the only point it is decidable. And [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s generic **field** rule is deliberately unchanged — an `owned` field at an inadmissible substitution stays an instantiation-site error, because a field marker commits the containing type's shape (destructor synthesis, the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) derived properties) in a way a call-boundary marker does not; the asymmetry is recorded, liftable if a mixed-domain owning-slot case arrives. Authors who intend the marker to be meaningful at every instantiation still constrain the domain (`where T: IDisposable` excludes the runtime-managed reference types at the declaration, [§14.2](#sec-constraints)).

The rules for how `owned` interacts with method bodies, control flow, and disposal are in the subsections that follow.

<a id="sec-the-idisposable-contract"></a>
### 28.2 The `IDisposable` contract

Every class implicitly implements `IDisposable` via a compiler-generated `Dispose()`:

```bezel
interface IDisposable
  method Dispose();
end IDisposable;
```

`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops. The compiler-generated `Dispose()` is thread-safe with respect to idempotency: concurrent calls from multiple threads will execute the disposal logic exactly once; all other concurrent callers observe the no-op path. (Within a single execution domain concurrent calls cannot arise — [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model) — and they cannot arise across domains either, since domains share no mutable state ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)); the thread-safety guarantee matters where disposal is reachable from foreign threads through the FFI.) This machinery — the idempotent, flag-setting disposal together with the checked-disposal mode below — is the runtime backstop the ownership kernel records as [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-kernel)).

<a id="sec-checked-disposal"></a>
#### Use after disposal; checked disposal mode

Use of an instance after its first `Dispose()` is a program error. How the error manifests depends on the *disposal-checking mode*, a per-build choice between two conformance modes:

- **Unchecked (release) mode** — use of a disposed instance is undefined behavior. This is the default.
- **Checked mode** — any instance member access on a logically-disposed instance — an instance method call (including interface and virtual dispatch), a property or indexer accessor invocation, or a field access through the reference — raises `DisposedAccessException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)). A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes.

The two modes give identical observable behavior for every program that never uses a disposed instance. A program that would raise `DisposedAccessException` in checked mode has undefined behavior in unchecked mode: unchecked mode is the release-build relaxation of the checked semantics, not a different language.

Checked mode is implementable with state the language already requires: idempotent disposal implies a per-instance disposed flag, and the split between logical disposal and physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) gives the implementation latitude to defer reclaiming a disposed instance's memory in checked mode (quarantine, delayed free) so that the flag remains readable after disposal. The check itself is a flag test on member entry; implementations are expected to omit it entirely in unchecked builds, so unchecked builds pay no cost for the mode's existence.

**The compiler-inserted free participates in this machinery.** The free the compiler inserts for a **trivial-dispose** instance at its owner's release point ([§28](#sec-resource-management)'s preamble, [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) is **logical disposal followed by reclamation**: it sets the per-instance disposed flag and runs no user code (the class has none to run). Riding the flag is what makes checked mode's backstop uniform across the language: a member access through a surviving borrow of a freed trivial-dispose instance — a store-rule residual, a retained fresh `Add` argument ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals), [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)) — raises `DisposedAccessException` deterministically, exactly as for a non-trivial class; no class in the language dangles without this backstop. The costs are stated and checked-mode-only: trivial-dispose instances carry the per-instance flag word, member access through a borrow is a live flag test in checked mode, and [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s logical/physical split may quarantine their physical reclamation; unchecked builds pay nothing, per this section's existing posture.

The compiler additionally **must** emit a compile-time warning when a local variable is used (read, borrowed from, or consumed) after an explicit `Dispose()` call — or a discard of the binding ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — on the same variable that dominates the use site on every path: the straight-line subset of use-after-dispose (derives: [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) + [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)). A *conditional* kill is treated more strictly: at a join of an explicitly-disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is **maybe-consumed** and a later use is a compile error ([§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)).

`Dispose()` is not on `Object`; it is class-only. Records, enums, primitives, and inline arrays do not implement `IDisposable`.

User code does not implement `Dispose()` directly. The customization points are:

- A `destructor` for cleanup logic.
- `owned` fields for fields that should be disposed with the containing object.

**Scoped-callback backstop.** In checked disposal mode, invoking a callback stored under a `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) after its bounding object's disposal has completed — a violation of the callee's quiescence obligation — faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`, exactly like any other member access through a logically-disposed instance.

<a id="sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows"></a>
### 28.3 Local variables, ownership, and borrows

Bezel tracks two kinds of class-typed reference at compile time:

- **Owned** — the holder is responsible for disposing the referenced object exactly once.
- **Borrowed** — the holder is not responsible for disposal; the reference is valid only for as long as some other holder (the *source*) keeps the object alive.

The `owned` keyword ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields), [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)) marks fields, parameters, and return types as owned. Local variables are not annotated; their ownership state is inferred from how they are introduced.

<a id="sec-ownership-kernel"></a>
#### The ownership kernel (K1–K9)

Every rule of this chapter and of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) is one of: a kernel principle below, a derivation from them, or a recorded axiom (register at the end of this subsection; reasons in the rationale). Derivation and axiom tags — *derives: K…* / *axiom A…* — mark the classification at each rule as the chapter's subsections are brought under the kernel. A future revision that adds an ownership rule states which kind it is.

<a id="sec-kernel-k1"></a>
**K1 — Value classification.** At every program point, every expression and binding of class or interface type (K1.6 exempts the runtime-managed remainder) has exactly one ownership classification — the two reference kinds of this section's opening, completed by the transfer and analysis states:

1. **owned** — the holder carries the disposal obligation: dispose exactly once, on every path.
2. **borrowed** — no obligation; validity is bounded by the borrow's source set (K2).
3. **moved-from** — the obligation has transferred out; the binding or slot is unreadable until reassigned, and discharge machinery skips it ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)).
4. **maybe-consumed** — the K7 join of owned with moved-from or explicitly-disposed; unreadable; scope-end disposal is per-path.

   Three auxiliary bookkeeping states complete the analysis: **uninitialized** (declared, unassigned — unreadable, [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)); **polymorphic-null** (`var x: T? := null;` before the first non-null assignment — adopts the state of that assignment; a null arm or RHS is compatible with either target, having no value to own); and **explicitly-disposed** (the binding after a disposing announced kill, K4.2 — scope-end machinery skips it, and a straight-line read falls under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning regime rather than the moved-from error).

5. **Atoms.** Fresh productions are owned: `new`, reference-typed collection literals, `owned`-returning calls, `move` results, owned operator results. Reads of storage lend: a field, property, indexer, or slot read is a borrow whose source is the storage's holder. Reads of named bindings lend unless the position consumes (K3): an unmarked read of an owned binding is a borrow of the binding. Calls lend by default: an instance method's plain (non-`owned`) class-typed return is a borrow whose source is the receiver — sound jointly with the callee-side admission rules (K2.4); a static callee's plain class- or interface-typed return is admissible only where the declared type announces the classification, and is otherwise rejected at the declaration (the static-return rule, *Factory methods* below). (The *Producers* table below is the worked enumeration.)
6. **The runtime-managed exemption; the trivial-dispose ceremony exemption.** Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation; `owned` markers over them are inadmissible or erased per instantiation ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)). Trivial-dispose class instances ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) carry the classification **and the free obligation**, but the obligation's *user-visible* content is empty and its discharge is never demanded *of the program*: any undischarged trivial-dispose value is freed silently by the compiler at its owner's release point — no warning (the ceremony exemption), no user code (the class has none to run; the free sets the disposed flag, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). The exemption is ceremony-only: the borrow half of the machinery — source sets, escape checks, the freeze — is demanded over trivial-sourced references everywhere, and every rule of this chapter reads them by its letter.
7. **One holder.** An obligation has exactly one holder at a time; every transfer moves it, never copies it. Copy-semantics holders (record fields) therefore cannot hold obligations ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)).

<a id="sec-kernel-k2"></a>
**K2 — The source algebra.** Every borrow carries a **source set**. A source is one of:

- a **named location**: a local binding, a parameter, `this`, a field path rooted at a live object, or static storage — the one distinguished *always-live* source (process-lived, disposed only at exit, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order));
- a **frame** (K6): a task, iterator/enumerator frame, or lazy query value, itself an ordinarily-classified value;
- a **full-expression temporary**: an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), live exactly to its K8 boundary.

The taxonomy defines what a source *is* and how it bounds a borrow; which source kinds a particular operand position accepts — [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s awaited-task positions are the worked case — remains that construct's own enumeration.

1. **Weakest source bounds.** A borrow is valid only where *every* source in its set is live; equivalently, it is bounded by its weakest source.
2. **Union under composition.** Joins, `??` and arm meets, transitive re-borrows, and frame carriage combine borrows by taking the union of their source sets.
3. **Escape must be bounded.** A borrow may not reach a holder — a binding of wider scope, a field, a collection, a frame, a return — whose lifetime the checker cannot bound by the borrow's source set. Where scopes are statically comparable (locals, temporaries, loop back edges), violation is rejected. Where they are not, an admission is made only under K4's posture: a structural, decidable check at the site plus a recorded residual obligation with a named backstop ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)).
4. **Signature-level re-establishment.** A callee's declared signature announces its result's source set as a function of the call's receiver and arguments — the bare-type-parameter source set, the deferred-activation frame's carried sources — and every caller re-establishes the set against its own actuals. A borrow whose source no caller could re-establish (a scope-bound local, a temporary, an unannounced parameter source) may not be returned.

<a id="sec-kernel-k3"></a>
**K3 — Discharge and consumption.** The obligation on an owned value is discharged at exactly one of the **owned-consuming positions**, enumerated here once:

1. store into an `owned` field or owning-collection slot, including through a `set(owned)` accessor ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties));
2. `return` under an `owned` return type, or — non-`async` bodies — under an unmarked `Task`-family return type;
3. an `owned` argument under the call-site marker ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers));
4. a marked binding or assignment transfer — `var y := move x;`, `y := move x;`, `using var y := move x;` (the anonymous adoption `using var _ := move x;` included, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — the marked owning-match scrutinee `case move x of …` ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)) — and the **marked arm transfer**: `move x` as an if-expression branch or an expression-`case`/`when` arm result ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression), [§19.2](#sec-arms)), consuming on the path where its arm is selected;
5. the operand of a Pattern B `await` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal));
6. the owned parameter-or-plain-local source of a Pattern A chaining `return await` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal));
7. the operand of `yield return` in an owning iterator ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership));
8. the operand of `throw` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand));
9. the announced-consume discard `_ := x;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_));
10. an explicit `Dispose()` (or `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`) on an owned receiver — the receiver-classification rules, including the declaring-type field admission, are [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s;
11. reassignment of an owned location — a K3 consume of the *displaced* value, disposed after the RHS is evaluated (drop-on-overwrite, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields));
12. for move-only values ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), any store into an owning location.

   The twelve positions fall into three families: **stores into announced owned destinations** (1–4, 12); **ownership-taking kills and transfers** (5–10) — of which 5, 8, 9, and 10 are exactly [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)'s announced kills, that clause being the one definition site of the announced-kill set and of each kill's disposal moment; and **displacement** (11).

   Three principles govern the enumeration:

13. **Announcement.** A consume is spelled by the transfer marker (`move x`) except where the target or keyword already announces it — a declared `owned` slot or return, a `set(owned)` accessor, an unmarked `Task`-family return, an owning iterator's declared interface, `throw`, `await` of an `OwningTask<T>`, the discard. An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**: `var b := a;` is always a borrow for class-typed `a`. (Move-only *value* types move on unmarked assignment and plain parameter passing, per [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s own scope note; K3.12.) Fresh producers need no marker anywhere (no live binding is invalidated).
14. **Affinity.** An owned value that reaches its scope's end undischarged and not moved-from is disposed there implicitly; the implicit drop of a plain-`var` local or undischarged `owned` parameter carries the must-use warning (a lint over a sound program).
15. **Edge parity.** The exception edge performs the same implicit disposal as the normal edge, on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack; the only difference is the lint. Unbound temporaries join the same stack at their production.

<a id="sec-kernel-k4"></a>
**K4 — Kills, announcement, and the backstop posture.** A **kill** ends a value's life under its current holder: a *disposing* kill runs `Dispose()` and sets the per-instance disposed flag; a *transferring* kill leaves the value alive under a new holder, setting nothing. The posture, in three clauses:

1. **The backstop.** Disposal is idempotent and flag-setting; in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) any later use through any alias faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`, and unchecked mode is the same language with the check elided. This is the runtime backstop every trust admission names.
2. **Announced kills.** A kill that is both **keyword-visible at the kill site** and **flag-backstopped** is permitted while borrows of the value live: the announcement is the reader's notice and the flag is the safety net. The closed set, with each kill's disposal moment:
   - explicit `Dispose()` (and the `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()` spellings) — disposes at the call;
   - the discard `_ := x;` — disposes at the end of the discard statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_));
   - `throw x` — the exception machinery disposes after the matching catch arm completes (or at program termination if uncaught) ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand));
   - Pattern B `await x` on an owned `OwningTask<T>` binding — the await's implicit task disposal, on all outgoing edges including fault/cancel ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)).

   The post-kill state splits by kill kind: after a *disposing* announced kill (`Dispose()`, the discard) the binding is **explicitly-disposed** — straight-line use afterward is a mandatory warning under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s regime; after `throw x` or a Pattern B `await`, the operand binding is **moved-from** — a later read is an error until reassigned. A *conditional* kill of either kind joins to maybe-consumed (K7) and later use is an error.
3. **Recorded trust, or nothing.** Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped — the domain clause: a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set — the rule must either reject statically or carry an **individually recorded trust clause**. The recorded clauses (field-held, collection-held, and frame-held borrows versus domain transfer; [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) are the model's honest limit, and no new admission may be made without recording its clause or its backstop.

<a id="sec-kernel-k5"></a>
**K5 — The freeze.** Consuming an owned **binding** (a local or `owned` parameter; K3 positions) while a live local borrow of its current value exists is a compile error — **unless the consume is a K4 announced kill** (*unfrozen ⟺ announced ∧ flag-backstopped*) **or the Pattern A chaining case of clause 4, the one recorded structural override**. Placements:

1. moves, marked transfers, owned-slot stores, owned returns — the unmarked `Task`-family return of a non-`async` body included ([K3.2](#sec-kernel-k3)) — and owning-iterator `yield return` are frozen — transferring kills, alive under a new holder, no flag ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership));
2. drop-on-overwrite of a binding is frozen although it disposes — the reassignment is not keyword-visible as a kill of the *old* value ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields));
3. the [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) announced kills are unfrozen — each is announced at the site and flag-backstopped, so the criterion admits it; the closed set and its members are stated once, at K4.2;
4. a Pattern A chaining `return await x` is unfrozen — not by the criterion (it is a transferring kill: alive under a new holder, no flag) but by **vacuity**, the recorded override: its new holder (the outer task) cannot dispose the chained task before the body, `finally` blocks included, completes — no body borrow can outlive the kill ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal));
5. the freeze is **body-local by construction**: liveness is the backward dataflow over one body, borrows are traced through `using var` pins, live closures, and borrow-bearing record locals ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), and this is why a closure may not consume its captured owned bindings (K2 + decidability);
6. **fields and collection slots are not frozen**: slot aliases are not body-local, and a slot kill disposes — the K4 backstop is real there; the slot kill *by move* is instead governed by K4.3's domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze), [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership));
7. a [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) storage admission **strengthens** the freeze over the admitted captures to cover announced kills as well — stated with its reason at [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters), under axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)'s forms.

<a id="sec-kernel-k6"></a>
**K6 — Frames are values.** A deferred activation — a task (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`), an iterator or async-iterator frame (enumerable or enumerator, borrowing or owning), a lazy query — is a **value** with an ordinary K1 classification that additionally **carries a source set** (K2): the constructing call's receiver, its plain reference-typed arguments, and the capture-set contributions of its plain function-typed arguments, transitively.

1. **The bound.** Carried sources must outlive the frame's bound: **settlement** for a task ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)); **completion or disposal** for an iterator frame ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation), [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)); the **single consumption point** for a lazy query, which is thereby affine ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)).
2. **Announcement by declared type.** Frame-carrying classification is keyed on the callee's declared, pre-substitution return type — a `Task`-family type, a [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interface, a lazy query — and every caller re-establishes the carried set against its own actuals (K2.4). This is what admits returning a composed frame, and what rejects a returned frame carrying a scope-bound local, `using var`, or temporary.
3. **Containers: calls mint, storage lends — for tasks.** A call whose declared return type is `Task`-family produces a fresh **owned** frame at every call site; a read of task **storage** (property, field, slot) lends a borrow of the storage; callee-side, the unmarked `Task`-family return type transfers the container like an `owned` return. The keying to the task family alone is axiom A2.
4. **Frames versus the freeze.** Frame-held borrows live in the frame, not in any local borrow binding, so K5 cannot see them; their outlives-obligation is the K4.3-recorded settlement clause ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)), discharged trivially by awaiting before any source's scope exits and structurally by `TaskScope`. The abandonment idioms carry the residual explicitly.
5. **Interaction with K8.** A frame sourced by an unbound temporary must itself be consumed to its bound within the same full expression; a frame that escapes the expression is rejected — the reject-not-extend posture.

<a id="sec-kernel-k7"></a>
**K7 — The join rule.** At every control-flow join — statement merges, `??`, `if` expressions, expression-position `case`/`when` arms, loop back edges — a variable's or expression's state is the lattice meet, owned ⊑ borrowed:

1. owned ⊓ owned = **owned**, obligation carried forward (for expression arms: exactly one arm's value exists at runtime, so exactly one obligation);
2. borrowed ⊓ borrowed = **borrowed**, carrying the union of the arms' source sets (K2.2);
3. owned ⊓ borrowed = **rejected** — no single state is correct, and demoting owned would silently drop an obligation; the program equalizes the arms first;
4. owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path;
5. `null`-literal and bottom-typed (`throw`) arms absorb to the other arm's state.

The direction is deliberate: rejection at 3 rather than demotion is what makes the meet leak-free (rationale [§5.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-lattice-direction-at-control-flow-joins)).

<a id="sec-kernel-k8"></a>
**K8 — The full-expression boundary.** A **full expression** is a maximal expression — not a subexpression of any larger expression — at the enumerated positions (initializers, assignment RHSs, expression statements, each *evaluation* of a condition or guard, `for` sources, `return`/`throw`/`yield return` operands, `case` scrutinees).

1. Unbound owned temporaries are disposed at their full expression's end, after their uses; on the exception edge, during unwinding in reverse production order.
2. Conditions and guards are per-evaluation boundaries: temporaries never accumulate across iterations.
3. A `case` scrutinee's boundary is the whole construct — pattern bindings are borrows of the scrutinee, and the temporary survives arm selection, guard evaluation, and the selected arm's completion — in statement position exactly as in expression position.
4. A temporary is an admissible borrow source only within its boundary; a borrow or frame that would escape it is **rejected, never lifetime-extended** — the language has no general lifetime-extension mechanism ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal); rationale [§5.24](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-full-expression-boundary)).
5. A binding atom ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) is the boundary for its own bindings: a binding whose initializer is an owned production is a **named unbound owned temporary** whose boundary is the atom — disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged, after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order; clause 4 applies to the atom boundary verbatim.

<a id="sec-kernel-k9"></a>
**K9 — Fields are object state, not scope state.** A field's obligation belongs to the object: it is discharged by the destructor cascade (owned fields, reverse declaration order) or by drop-on-overwrite, never by any scope's end, and no scope-end machinery ever touches it. Consequences:

1. every plain read of an owned field lends (K1.5); the only owned read is `move x.f` — and `move coll[i]` for owning slots — which puts the slot in moved-from state ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression));
2. **the restoration rule**: every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot: the object must never escape the method with a hole a destructor could observe ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression));
3. a destructor body is exempt from restoration (teardown: no future read exists), and a constructor's `move` is governed by definite assignment before first assignment ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields));
4. static owned fields admit no `move`: the restoration obligation is scoped to a single method, and static state is observable across method boundaries, so no per-method window can cover it ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression), [§22.12](#sec-static-members));
5. drop-on-overwrite (K3.11) is RHS-first, so a throwing RHS leaves the slot untouched and still-owned — restoration idioms (`_resource := fresh;` onto a moved-from slot) are non-throwable ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)).

The build-before-take discipline and the throwable-expression classification are derivations under K9, stated in [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression); the per-slot conservative tracking for non-constant indices is stated in [§28.11](#sec-move-on-a-collection-slot).

<a id="sec-axiom-register"></a>
#### The axiom register (A1–A14)

Twelve axioms (and two tombstones). Each is a rule the kernel cannot derive — a recorded design decision — and each is the extension point a future ruling in its area must name; a tombstone row records a retired axiom and points at the retiring revision's changelog entry. Ordering is by home section; one-line reasons here, full recorded reasons in rationale [§5.26](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-ownership-kernel). Axiom ids are stable: new axioms append; a deleted axiom leaves a tombstone row pointing at the deleting revision's changelog entry.

| # | Axiom | Home | Recorded reason (one line) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | *Retired.* The prior axiom and its decision record are in the [changelog](Bezel_Changelog.md). | — | — |
| A2 | Calls-mint is keyed to the `Task` family only; iterable calls classify under the ordinary call rules (the K1.5 receiver-borrow default; static iterable returns are the iterator convention's announced carve) | [§28.3](#sec-producers); rationale §12.10 | Uniform calls-mint is unsound for iterables — the stored-collection-view idiom (`Items(): IEnumerable<Item>` returning `_items`) is legitimate and common; the instance fresh-frame face announces with `owned` instead, and the owning heads take no unmarked instance spelling at all ([§28.3](#sec-iterable-instance-returns); the owning-head rejection preserved). |
| A3 | The two-container async design: `Task<T>` (class T) = shared borrows, `OwningTask<T>` = single owned transfer | [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal); rationale §12.1–§12.2 | A surface design choice (fan-out vs. acquisition); the kernel checks both, forces neither. |
| A4 | Accessor read faces are lend-only: property and indexer *types* carry no `owned`, and a getter may not return a fresh owned value; `set(owned)` is the announced write face (K3.1) | [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention), [§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers) | Signature predictability: every accessor read classifies as a borrow with no marker position available; factories are methods. |
| A5 | `using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out | [§28.10](#sec-using-var); rationale §5.23 | Declared-intent form; scope-pinning is its entire meaning (kept strict deliberately at the affine transition). |
| A6 | `Task`/`Task<T>` may not be discarded; `Task.FireAndForget` is the routed spelling | [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_); rationale §5.23 | Semantic, not memory: abandoning a running operation is a decision, not a disposal. |
| A7 | The transfer marker is not admitted in `??`-operand or operator-operand position: identifier-operand `move` there is rejected, and a named owned binding written bare is a borrow arm. (The arm half — if-expression branches, expression-`case`/`when` arm results — is a K3.4 derivation; the `??` lift stays gated on the null-evaluated-transfer ruling, sequenced after the v0.246 marker unification so that rule, if ever adopted, lands in the unified spelling.) | [§28.3](#sec-producers), [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) | Recorded liftable bound, narrowed — and purely semantic: the marker has parsed in these positions since v0.209 (MarkedTransfer was a PrimaryAtom, pinned by `marked_transfer_positions_2080.bzl`), so the axiom's content is the recorded rejection, not a spelling gap — the v0.246 rewording corrects the row's earlier loose wording, not a v0.246 consequence; the `??` half awaits the null-evaluated-transfer ruling, the operator half a use case. No-silent-consume (K3.13) stays uniform: the unmarked read is a borrow arm. |
| A8 | *Retired.* The prior axiom and its decision record are in the [changelog](Bezel_Changelog.md). | — | — |
| A9 | The two collection families: borrowing by default, owning as separately named types | [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership); rationale §5.3 | The recorded resolution; the declined merged-generic form is rationale §5.3/§5.11's record. |
| A10 | Stdlib certification grants: `CancellationToken`'s source-outlives-settlement certification; the legacy completion-source admission | [§30.1](#sec-async-methods), [§30.8](#sec-cancellation), [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet) | A named allowlist of trust granted to specific stdlib types — by construction not derivable; each entry normatively stated at its type. |
| A11 | The [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) bounding-object resolution forms (1–5) and the ratified v1 admission bounds | [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) | Decidability engineering: the chosen static story for "capture source outlives bounding object"; several bounds marked liftable. |
| A12 | Pattern A chaining's disposal-timing dispensation for a `using var` source (deferral to the outer task's teardown) | [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) kind 2 | A recorded timing carve against A5's pin — not a move (the slot lives in the frame); exactly-once is preserved transitively. |
| A13 | Move-only inline-array whole-value reassignment does not dispose displaced slots (warning-backed) | [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) | Recorded debt: interacts with the open inline-array-disposal design; the one carve-out on the exactly-once claim. |

<a id="sec-ownership-state-of-locals"></a>
#### Ownership state of locals

A local's ownership state is one of [K1](#sec-kernel-k1)'s classifications, inferred from the form that introduces the local (the state names and their meanings — including the auxiliary **uninitialized**, **polymorphic-null**, and **explicitly-disposed** states — are K1's):

- `using var x := expr;` where `expr` is an owned producer or a marked transfer (`using var x := move y;`) is **owned**, additionally subject to scope-based disposal at the end of the enclosing block. When `expr` is a borrow — including an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding — `x` is instead a **borrow-pin** with no disposal obligation ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)).
- `var x := expr;` takes the ownership state of `expr` (see *Producers* below); plain `var` does not change the state. A read of a *named owned binding* on the right-hand side is a **borrow** unless it carries the explicit transfer marker — `var y := move x;` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers); see *Move semantics for owned locals* below).
- `var x: T;` without an initializer is **uninitialized** and may not be read until assigned.

Reassignment to an existing `var x` is state-matched (derives: [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)): an **owned-state** LHS requires an owned RHS — a fresh producer, or a named owned binding under the explicit transfer marker (`x := move y;`) — and disposes the displaced value per drop-on-overwrite ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), subject to the consume-site freeze below; a **borrowed-state** LHS requires a borrow (or `null`) RHS. A LHS in the **polymorphic null state** (`var x: T? := null;` before its first non-null assignment — the null-literal producers row) adopts the state of its first non-null RHS: owned from a fresh producer *or a marked transfer*, borrowed from an unmarked binding read or any other borrow. Assigning a borrow to an owned-state LHS, or an owned value to a borrowed-state LHS, is rejected — the mismatch would silently drop or double-hold a disposal obligation.

At every control-flow join the compiler applies [K7](#sec-kernel-k7)'s meet to each variable's tracked state: same-state branches merge — owned ⊓ owned carries the obligation forward, borrowed ⊓ borrowed carries the **union of the branches' source sets** (K7.2: merging a parameter-sourced borrow with a receiver-sourced borrow is therefore fine; rejection arises only at a later use or escape that violates a carried constraint) — a mixed owned/borrowed merge is **rejected** (K7.3), and a join of owned with **moved-from** or explicitly-disposed yields **maybe-consumed** (K7.4): the variable may not be read, borrowed from, or consumed after the join, and may not flow around a loop back edge into any use; scope-end auto-drop applies per-path (the same per-slot tracking [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) uses). The analysis is keyed on the definite-assignment machinery of [§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields); diagnostics should point at the offending use, not the declaration.

To compile a mixed merge, the program must equalize the branches before the merge. The two standard patterns, as worked examples:

```bezel
// Pattern 1: equalize to borrowed — both branches bind x to a source
// that outlives the merge.
var x: Stream;                       // x will be a borrow at the merge
if condition then
  using var scratch := new Stream(); // owned: used and discharged in-branch
  scratch.WarmUp();
  primary.Reset(scratch);            // scratch's work is done here
  x := primary.Stream;               // x borrows primary (outlives the if)
else
  x := otherSource.Stream;           // x borrows otherSource (outlives the if)
end;
// At the merge, x is borrowed on both branches, and both sources
// (primary, otherSource) outlive the merge point. The using var
// scratch was discharged at its own scope end; x never borrowed it.

// Pattern 2: produce an owned value on both branches.
var x: Stream;
if condition then
  x := new Stream();
else
  x := otherSource.CloneStream();   // returns owned Stream
end;
// At the merge, x is owned on both branches.
// x reaches an owned slot, is disposed, or auto-drops at scope end (§28.3).
```

Where one branch is a **named owned binding**, the marked arm transfer ([K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)) writes the same equalization as one expression: `var x := (if useFresh then new Stream() else move cached);` — both arms owned, `cached` consumed only on the selected path and per-path consumed after the construct ([K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)).

Equalizing to borrowed (Pattern 1) does not merely require both branches to *be* borrows — it requires each branch's borrow source to outlive the merge point ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)). Binding `x` in one branch to a borrow of a `using var` that is discharged at that branch's end does **not** equalize the merge: it produces a borrow whose source is already gone by the time `x` is read after the `if`, and the borrow-lifetime rule rejects it exactly as it rejects any other use of a borrow past its source's scope. The `using var` in such a branch must complete its own work and be discharged *within* the branch; `x` must take its post-merge value from a source that lives past the `if` (as `primary` and `otherSource` do above).

<a id="sec-producers"></a>
#### Producers

The ownership state of an expression is determined by the expression form — the worked enumeration under [K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1); rule-carrying rows carry their derivation tags:

| Expression | Ownership |
|---|---|
| `null` literal; `default(T?)` and any other `default` form producing `null` ([§17.11](#sec-the-default-operator) — the bridge is §17.11's value rule, deliberately not [§17.14](#sec-constant-expressions) constancy, which `default` does not have) | Context-typed. The literal — and a null-producing `default` expression, which this row covers identically — is admissible in any position whose declared type is nullable. For ownership: `null` has no value to own, so it is **compatible with either an owned target or a borrowed target**. Assigning `null` to an owned location leaves that location in the owned-currently-null state (disposal of null is a no-op). Assigning `null` to a borrowed location is the borrowed-currently-null value with no source. For a local declared `var x: T? := null;` — or initialized from a null-producing `default` form — the local's ownership state is determined by the *next* non-null assignment to `x`: assigning an owned value makes `x` owned thereafter; assigning a borrowed value makes `x` borrowed. Before that next assignment, `x` is in a polymorphic null state that supports either subsequent transition. Locals that remain at null for their entire lifetime are statically dead-storable; the compiler may emit a warning but the program is well-formed. |
| `new T(...)` | Owned |
| Collection literal (`[1, 2, 3]`) targeting a reference type (`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`, `Set<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, etc.) | Owned |
| Collection literal (`[1, 2, 3]`) targeting an inline-array type (`[N]T`, including `[N owned]T?`) | Not applicable — produces a value. For move-only `[N owned]…` targets, the value is move-only ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). |
| Method call returning `owned T` | Owned. For a **bare-type-parameter** `owned` return at a value or runtime-managed instantiation the marker is erased by the substitution ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)) and the result is a plain value — the value-typed call row below governs. |
| Method call returning `T` (no `owned`) | Borrowed — instance method: source is the receiver; extension method: source is the receiver parameter ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions)). A **static** callee never reaches this row: a static method's non-`owned` class- or interface-typed return type is admissible only where the declared type itself announces the classification — a `Task`-family type (owned; the exception below), a [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interface (a caller-owned frame; the iterator convention), or a bare type parameter with a non-empty potential source set (a borrow; the second exception below) — and any other such static signature is rejected at its declaration (see *Factory methods and sourceless returns* below). **Exception (derives: [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6) — the family keying is axiom A2):** a call whose declared return type is a `Task`-family type (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`) is **Owned**, with no warning — instance, static, or otherwise (see *Task-family calls produce owned frames* below). Property, field, and indexer reads of `Task`-family type are not calls and remain borrows of their storage. (A property *reference* over a `Task`-family-typed property is rejected at formation, [§27.6](#sec-method-references) — the lend face may not inhabit a mint-announcing slot.) **Second exception (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)):** a call whose declared return type is a **bare type parameter** — or whose callee implements or overrides a generic declaration whose declared return type is one — is never this row's case: at class or interface instantiations it is a **borrow** of the call's receiver and its T-reaching plain arguments, falling back to the factory rule only when that potential source set is structurally empty (see *Bare-type-parameter returns* below). |
| Field access `obj.f` where `f` is `owned` | Borrowed (source: `obj`) |
| `move obj.f` where `f` is `owned` | Owned. Field is left in moved-from state and must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)). |
| Field access `obj.f` where `f` is not `owned` | Borrowed (source: `obj`) |
| Indexer access `coll[i]` | Borrowed (qualified by family, reconciling [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)). Owning-family collection: source is `coll`, and the borrow is additionally valid only until the slot is mutated (an indexer-set, `Remove*`, or `Clear` disposes the referent — a mid-scope value kill not statically tracked per slot; checked-mode backstop, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), stdlib §4.5). Borrowing-family collection: the true source is the element's original owner ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy) — the collection is a transit point); the compiler cannot identify that owner structurally and enforces the collection binding as the proxy bound, the owner-outlives-use residual being the same trust regime as field-held borrows. |
| Range slice `arr[r]` on `Array<T>` ([§15.6](#sec-slicing)) | Owned — a fresh `Array<T>`, the compiler-recognized `Slice(r: Range<int>): owned Array<T>` form (stdlib §4.4); **not** the indexer row above. The container is owned by the caller and discharged under the standard rules; class-typed elements are borrows copied as borrows, their sources unchanged. |
| Property access `obj.P` (instance getter) | Borrowed (source: `obj`). Getters are borrow-producing positions — a getter may not return a fresh owned value ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)). |
| Static property access `T.P` (class-typed result) | Borrowed (source: the declaring type's static storage — [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source: process-lived, so every intra-program liveness constraint is satisfied; static state is disposed only at program exit, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)). |
| Static field access `T.f` — or the bare in-scope spelling `f` of the declaring type's own static field — with class- or interface-typed result | Borrowed (source: the declaring type's static storage — [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source, exactly as the `T.P` row above). The field's form — `owned`, `readonly` without `owned` ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)), or an admitted mutable static ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2) — does not change the classification: every admissible form keeps its referents alive to process exit ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); §22.12 rule 2's overwrite-never-disposes store semantics). |
| Invocation of a **function value** whose declared return slot (nullability stripped) is a **concrete class or interface type** — not `owned` (the ordinary transferring return, [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)), not a `Task`-family type (claimed by the exception above: an owned mint), not a bare type parameter (claimed by the rule above), and not one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable/enumerator interfaces or a lazy query (frame ownership at a function-value invocation is an open question, deliberately unclassified here; a reference over a **static iterable factory** must not reach a slot this row claims — direct formation bridging is rejected at [§27.6](#sec-method-references) below, and the two remaining routes — retyping a *formed* iterable-returning function value across the boundary through a typed intermediate, and a bare-parameter slot at an iterable substitution ([§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s narrowed residual) — are a recorded seam: each launders the iterator convention's caller-owned frame into this row's borrow classification, a leak until that issue classifies or fences it) | Borrowed — carrying the **union of the function value itself and every plain (non-`owned`) reference-typed argument** ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)'s lending default with [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)'s site-level re-establishment). The function value contributes its captured borrows' sources transitively (the capture-set contribution, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); the plain arguments cover the adapter-formed references that route a receiver through a parameter ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)'s instance property reference) and parameter-sourced lambda returns; `owned` arguments are never sources; value-typed, runtime-managed, and `null`-literal arguments contribute nothing. The result is never owned, and the factory rule never classifies a function-value invocation. Callee side: the *Concrete-slot function bodies* rule below — the admissible inhabitants supply only sources this classification re-establishes. |
| `move coll[i]` where `coll` is an owning collection that admits slot-move (heap: `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningBuffer<T>` for class-typed T, or a `Span<T>` view into a class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`; inline: `[N owned]T?`, `[N owned]T`) | Owned. Slot is left in moved-from state and must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression), [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). For `OwningBuffer<T>` / `Span<T>` with value-typed T, `move coll[i]` is not admitted (values have no ownership to transfer). `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `ArraySpan<T>`, `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`, and `ReadOnlyStringSpan` do not admit `move` for any T (`ReadOnlySpan<T>` and the string-backed `ReadOnlyStringSpan` have no writable indexer; the `Array<T>`-backed spans have borrowed slots with no ownership to transfer). |
| Local-variable read `x` where `x` is owned (a class-typed owned local, or a local of move-only value type per [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) | Classified by the position the read appears in (see *Consuming positions for an owned-local read*, following this table). In an **owned-consuming position**, the read transfers ownership out of `x` and `x` becomes moved-from (see *Move semantics*). In a **borrow-consuming position**, `x` retains ownership and the value is borrowed for the consuming operation. |
| Local-variable read `x` where `x` is borrowed | Borrowed (source: same as `x`'s source) |
| Parameter `p` declared `owned p: T` | Owned |
| Parameter `p` (no modifier) | Borrowed (source: caller) |
| `this` | Borrowed (source: caller) |
| Function call producing an ordinary value type, `string`, or runtime-managed type | Not applicable ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) |
| Function call producing a move-only value type (an owning inline array `[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`, or an owning-classified choice — [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification), including a case construction) | Owned. The result is a move-only value ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)); the caller takes ownership and must discharge by binding into a local (auto-disposed at scope end via the move-only-local rule), into an owning-inline-array slot, into a class field of move-only type, or — for a choice — by a consuming match ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)). |
| `x as T` | Borrowed (source: same as `x`'s source if `x` is borrowed; `x` itself if `x` is owned). The cast does not move from `x`; `x` retains its ownership state. The result is nullable. See [§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators) for the rationale. |
| `a ?? b` (null-coalescing, [§7.7](#sec-null-coalescing-and-=)) | The **meet** of the ownership states of `a` and `b` per [K7](#sec-kernel-k7) — the same two-branch merge as the control-flow join above: owned ⊓ owned = **owned** (exactly one of the two owned values is produced at runtime and is discharged once — no leak, no double-free), borrowed ⊓ borrowed = **borrowed** carrying the union of both arms' source sets, and a mixed owned/borrowed arm pair is **rejected** — equalize the arms first ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) two-branch patterns). A **named owned binding** written as an arm is an *unmarked read* and therefore a **borrow** arm, per the local-variable-read row above (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register), narrowed — the transfer marker is rejected in `??`-operand position): `a ?? b` over two named owned locals is a borrowed ⊓ borrowed merge and consumes neither binding; to coalesce two named owned bindings into one owned result, use the marked arm transfer — `var r := (if a <> null then move a else move b);` ([K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)) — or equalize by statement, which keeps the no-silent-consume rule of *Move semantics* uniform. A `null`-literal or bottom-typed (`throw`) arm absorbs to the other arm's state (K7.5), legitimizing the `x ?? throw …` shape ([§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)). The compound form `a ??= b` assigns into `a` and follows the same meet rule for the assigned-into location. |
| `(if c then v1 else v2)` ([§20](#sec-the-if-expression)); the result of an expression-position `case`/`when` ([§19.1](#sec-forms), [§19.2](#sec-arms)) | The **meet** of the arms' ownership states, identically to the `a ?? b` row above ([K7](#sec-kernel-k7) at expression joins): owned ⊓ owned = **owned** — exactly one arm's value is produced at runtime and is discharged once; borrowed ⊓ borrowed = **borrowed**, carrying the union of the arms' source sets; a mixed owned/borrowed arm set is **rejected** — equalize the arms. An **unmarked** read of a named owned binding written as an arm is a **borrow** arm (K3.13 — no silent consume); the **marked arm** `move x` — admitted in if-expression branches and expression-`case`/`when` arm results — is an **owned** producer, a [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3) transfer consuming on the path where its arm is selected, the binding joining per [K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7) after the construct (in `??`-operand position the marker is rejected — axiom A7); a `throw` arm is bottom-typed and a `null`-literal arm absorbs to the other arms' state (K7.5; [§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression)). For `case`/`when` the meet ranges over every arm's result expression. |
| The binding atom `(var x := E; body)` ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) | The **body's** classification, transparently — the atom is not a join (clauses and body evaluate unconditionally; no meet arises). Each clause is a *binding form*: its binding classifies per this table applied to its initializer — a borrow initializer yields a borrow binding carrying the initializer's sources; `var y := move x;` is [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked binding transfer; an owned production yields a **named unbound owned temporary bounded by the atom** ([K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8)), disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged. A borrow sourced by an atom binding may not escape the atom ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8) at the atom boundary) — in particular, a body whose value borrows an owned binding of the atom is rejected. The body is not a [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3) marked-transfer position (no `move x` body in this revision). |
| Captured borrow inside a closure | Borrowed (source: same as the captured local's source). The closure value itself is runtime-managed; the captured borrow's lifetime is tracked separately. |
| Captured owned local inside a closure | Borrowed (source: the local's enclosing scope). Capturing does not transfer ownership; the closure cannot outlive the local's scope. See [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types). |

**Consuming positions for an owned-local read.** The owned local-variable-read row above classifies the read by the position it appears in. The **owned-consuming positions** — the read consumes `x`, leaving it moved-from (or explicitly-disposed for the disposing kills, and with reassignment consuming the *displaced* value) — are [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s enumeration (K3.1–K3.12); which of them carry the explicit transfer marker and which are announced by the target or keyword is K3.13's announcement rule (*Move semantics for owned locals* below).

The **borrow-consuming positions** — `x` retains ownership, and the value is borrowed for the consuming operation — are:

- a non-`owned` argument;
- an indexer or property access;
- an operand of a null-coalescing expression (`a ?? b` — the table's `??` row then sees a borrow arm; the marker is rejected in that position, axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)), or an **unmarked** if-expression branch or expression-`case`/`when` arm result (the arm-meet row sees a borrow arm; the *marked* form `move x` in those positions is instead the K3.4 arm transfer);
- the operand of a `yield return` in a borrowing iterator (a re-borrow, source the binding itself — [§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership));
- an **unmarked** local binding or assignment RHS — `var y := x;`, `y := x;`: a plain alias binding is a borrow of `x`, source `x` itself;
- for move-only locals, a borrow of the value through indexing or equality comparison.

<a id="sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns"></a>
#### Factory methods and sourceless returns

A **static** method call has no structural borrow source: there is no receiver, and a static method may not re-expose static storage through a non-`owned` return (the property-getter-only admission, *Borrow lifetime rules* above). A non-`owned` class- or interface-typed static return therefore names no one responsible for the result, and the signature is **rejected at the declaration** (retiring the treated-owned-with-a-warning classification):

A `static` method or `operator` declaration — wherever it occurs: a class, a `static` class ([§11.7](#sec-static-classes)), a record, an enum, or an interface's static member set ([§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)) — whose declared return type, nullability stripped, is a class or interface type is a **compile error** unless one of the following holds:

- the return type carries `owned` — the ordinary ownership-transferring return ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer));
- the declared type is a `Task`-family type (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`) — unmarked, it is itself container-ownership-transferring (*Task-family calls produce owned frames* above);
- the declared type is one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interfaces (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, and the four `IOwning*` forms) — the iterator convention: the unmarked type announces a caller-owned frame carrying parameter-sourced borrows (*Returning a deferred-activation frame*);
- the declared type is a **bare type parameter** with a **non-empty** potential source set (*Bare-type-parameter returns* below) — the announced argument-sourced borrow. An **empty-set** bare-type-parameter return is rejected exactly as a concrete class type is: spell `owned T`, admissible over every constraint domain under [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s per-instantiation erasure. A returned parameter whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions (`where T: value`) is outside this rule entirely — no disposal obligation can arise at any admissible substitution, and §28.1 rejects the marker on such a declaration.

Every admissible static signature is therefore **announced**: the caller-side classification of a static call is read off the declared return type with no heuristic, and the producers-table row above never classifies a static call. The caller of an `owned`-returning static factory discharges the obligation under the standard rules (store in an `owned` field, bind with `using var`, transfer, consume as an unbound owned temporary, or explicitly dispose).

Instance methods are untouched by this rule. A non-`owned` class-typed instance return remains a borrow whose source is the receiver, and an instance method that produces a fresh value must declare `owned` — [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) rejects a freshly-produced owned value returned through a non-`owned` return. Documentation phrases like "returns a fresh instance" carry no weight in any classification; the qualifier in the signature is the only transfer signal. *(Derivation — [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2): every admissible static signature announces its result's classification, and the callee-side borrow-return prohibition below rejects the unannounceable bodies; the two rules are opposite sides of one boundary and are enforced together.)*

**Task-family calls produce owned frames (derives: [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6) — the family keying is axiom A2).** The instance-method borrow classification above has one type-keyed exception: a **call** whose declared return type — read from the signature *before* generic substitution, with nullability stripped (`Task?`, `Task<T>?` qualify) — is a `Task`-family type (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`) produces an **owned** task at the call site, whatever the callee kind: instance, static, extension, interface-dispatched, or an invocation through a function value. No factory warning is emitted — the declared type is the announcement, exactly as the iterator convention below. The receiver is no borrow source for the task container: a task-returning callee mints a fresh frame at every call (an `async` body's state machine, [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) or forwards one, `async` itself is an implementation-side modifier no signature or interface can expose ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)), and §30's disposal story — `using var task := client.GetAsync(url);` ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)), abandoning an unconsumed `OwningTask<T>` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) — requires the caller to hold the container obligation. The caller discharges it under the standard rules: bind it (a `using var` over a task call **assumes the disposal obligation** — an owned right-hand side, not a [§28.10](#sec-using-var-initialized-from-a-borrow) pin), transfer it, or consume it as an unbound owned temporary (*Unbound owned temporaries* below — the dominant `await Producer()` shape). Orthogonally, the produced frame still *carries* the call's receiver's and plain arguments' borrows until settlement — the deferred-activation classification (*Deferred-activation callees* below) and [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s settlement obligation are unchanged. **Callee side:** an unmarked `Task`-family return type is itself ownership-transferring for the task container — the same announcement-by-declared-type logic as an `owned` return — so every return path of a non-`async` method or lambda with such a return type must supply an owned task (an `async` body satisfies this automatically — its return *is* its own fresh frame) — any source an `owned` return admits: a forwarded task-returning call result (except the invocation of a **call-bounded** plain function-typed parameter: its task inherits the call bound and must be awaited to settlement within the callee, and in a non-`async` body the invocation is itself rejected — [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); declare the parameter `scoped` or make the callee `async`), a completed-task factory result ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)), an owned task local or `owned` parameter, or a `move`d owned task field; for a *nullable* `Task`-family return type, `null` remains admissible on any path (the caller's owned binding is then owned-currently-null — the producers-table null row). Returning a **borrow** — a bare task field or property read, a plain parameter, a captured binding — is a compile error: a *stored* task is re-exposed through a **property, field, or collection slot**, whose reads are borrows of their storage ([§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet)'s source-owns-task rule; [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)(b)'s cache read as `_cfg!`), never through a non-`owned` method return. Two scope notes keep the rule sound at its edges: a generic method whose declared return type is a bare type parameter (`First<T>(): T`) is **not** classified by this rule at any instantiation — it is classified by *Bare-type-parameter returns* below, whose receiver-and-argument-sourced borrow is exactly the classification element and cache accessors over collections of tasks keep, and task-valued storage is awaited through [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s admitted borrow positions instead; and an explicit `owned` on a `Task`-family return remains admissible with identical semantics (`Domain.Spawn(...): owned Task`, stdlib §6.8, is the same contract made explicit).

<a id="sec-bare-type-parameter-returns"></a>
**Bare-type-parameter returns (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2); empty source set → rejected at the declaration — *Factory methods* below).** A **call** whose declared return type — read from the signature *before* generic substitution, with nullability stripped (`T?` qualifies; an `owned T` return is not bare — it is the ordinary ownership-transferring return, [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)) — is a **bare type parameter** in scope at the callee's declaration (a method-, type-, or extension-block-level parameter) is classified by this rule at every call site and every instantiation, whatever the callee kind: instance, static, extension, interface-dispatched, or an invocation through a function value whose declared return slot is such a parameter. The keying is pre-substitution, exactly as the `Task`-family rule above — no type-keyed classification (that rule, or any future one) applies to such a call at any instantiation. The classification is **inherited by implementations and overrides**: a method implementing or overriding a generic declaration whose return type is a bare type parameter carries this classification at every call site, direct or dispatched, exactly as the declaration's constraints are inherited ([§14.2](#sec-constraints-on-overrides)) — dispatch flows through the generic signature, so its classification is the only one call sites can be checked against; the potential source set is read from the **generic declaration's** signature, its source parameters identified positionally through the substitution (an implementing signature's own concrete types mention no type parameter, and a coincidentally same-typed non-source parameter is not a source); and the callee-side check below is inherited the same way — an implementing or overriding body is checked under the same return-path admission, against the positionally corresponding source parameters and its own receiver. A returned parameter whose constraints exclude class and interface substitutions (`where T: value`) is outside this rule on both sides. The signature's **potential source set** is the call's receiver (for an extension method, the receiver; for a function-value invocation, the function value), if any, together with every **plain** (non-`owned`) parameter whose declared type mentions the returned type parameter; `owned` parameters are never sources — they are consumed into the callee and die there.

**Caller side.** With a **non-empty** potential source set, at a class or interface instantiation of the returned parameter the call produces a **borrow** carrying the **union of the source-liveness constraints** of the receiver and of every argument bound to a source parameter — the join machinery of the merge rules above: the result is usable only where every contributing source is still live. `Math.Max(a, b)` (stdlib §2.2) yields a borrow with sources `{a, b}` — the returned value *is* one of the caller's arguments, and neither side acquires a disposal obligation. No factory warning is emitted — the declared bare-type-parameter return is the announcement, exactly as the iterator convention below and the `Task`-family rule above. (The stdlib [§5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-linq) class-element terminal accessors are this classification at its highest-traffic site; where such a result's receiver provenance roots at a same-unit fresh-yield iterator, the borrow is dead on arrival and the call draws [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)'s terminal-accessor provenance warning.) A borrowed argument contributes its own carried constraints transitively; an argument that is an **unbound owned temporary** (a fresh producer, a `move` result — `Math.Max(move box.f, b)`) bounds the result borrow to the same full expression, and a binding, store, return, or other escape of the result past that expression is rejected ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s reject-not-extend posture — the remedy names the source first); a null-literal argument, and any argument or receiver whose substituted type is a value or runtime-managed type, contributes no constraint (a call all of whose contributing sources are null literals carries no constraint — any non-null value such a call can return must come from the callee's static-storage paths, which are process-lived). The result composes with the ordinary machinery unchanged: consuming a contributing source while the result borrow is live is rejected by the consume-site freeze below; an explicit `Dispose()` of a source remains the announced kill with the checked-mode backstop ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)); every borrow-lifetime and escape rule applies. At a value or runtime-managed instantiation the result is not a borrow and no constraint attaches ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
