With an **empty** potential source set — no receiver and no plain source parameter (`static method Create<T>(): T where T: new()`) — the call has no structural source at any call site and the signature is **rejected at the declaration** (*Factory methods and sourceless returns* below) — spell `owned T`, the form the standard library itself uses for fresh-producing generic signatures — `OwningSet<T>.Take(query: T): owned T` (stdlib §4.10, under `where T: class`) and, now that the marker is admissible over domains admitting value substitutions ([§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s per-instantiation erasure), the stdlib §2.19 producer members (`Zero(): owned T`, `Parse(s: string): owned T`).

**Callee side.** The check is signature-keyed and decidable, and is enforced **per instantiation category** — the [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2 pattern that [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)'s generic-field admissibility already uses: at value and runtime-managed substitutions of the returned parameter it is vacuous (returning a parameter copies the value — or moves it, for a move-only inline-array substitution, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) under [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s instantiation-time move discipline); at class and interface substitutions the return-path admission is enforced, the diagnostic naming the instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 4). With a **non-empty** potential source set, every return path must supply `null` or a borrow whose sources outlive the call: the receiver (directly or through the receiver's fields and indexers — [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s receiver-sourced notion; an **iteration-variable** borrow is admissible only where its derived source chain reaches the receiver under [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s desugaring and [§29.1](#sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators)'s `Current` semantics at the loop source's static type — a collection-backed source re-borrows (the chain runs element slot → collection → receiver), an enumerator-owned yield does not — and at an interface-typed enumeration source the backing is unprovable, so the variable's source is conservatively the loop's implicit enumerator, a scope-bound local, and returning it is rejected; the index-based spelling `this[i]`, on a receiver that declares an indexer, is receiver-sourced and admissible — v0.235, #1666), a plain source parameter (directly, a borrow reached through it, or the result of invoking a function-typed source parameter — itself classified by this rule), or static storage (a bare read of a `static` class- or interface-typed field, `owned` or non-`owned` in the admissible forms — process-lived, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order); admitted from these method bodies even though the concrete-typed admission below is property-getter-only, because this rule's non-empty-set caller side classifies the result as a borrow, never as owned — no second owner can arise). The declared bare-type-parameter return is the signature-level announcement of the argument-sourced classification, exactly as the deferred-activation kinds announce theirs ([*Returning a deferred-activation frame*](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)); the parameter-sourced prohibition of the borrow-lifetime rules — unchanged for concrete-typed static returns, whose `static method Pick(a: Res, b: Res): Res return a;` remains rejected — is lifted here **because every caller re-establishes the borrow against its own receiver and arguments**. A fresh owned value, or a borrow of an owned local, a `using var`, an `owned` parameter, or a temporary, is rejected at the return site — the value would die with the callee or escape unowned; a generic body that produces fresh values declares `owned T` and transfers. With an **empty** potential source set the factory regime governs the body instead: return paths supply fresh or owned values; parameter-sourced borrows remain rejected exactly as for concrete types; and a **static-storage-sourced borrow return is likewise rejected** under an empty-set bare-type-parameter signature: this rule's caller side classifies the empty-set result as owned, so a static-storage borrow would acquire a second owner — the two-owners defect this rule exists to close. Expose a cached instance through a **static property** instead; the *Static property access `T.P`* producers row is that shape's sound caller-side classification, the same property-face resolution as the `Task`-family carve and the concrete-typed static-method rejection in the borrow-lifetime bullet below. (The concrete-typed case is treated identically: the static-storage admission below is property-getter-only, so a concrete-typed static method returning static storage is rejected callee-side and factory-classified caller-side exactly as here.) *(Resolved: the accumulator shape of [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members)'s `Sum<T>` — an empty-set factory call combined with operator results through `INumber<T>` — is well-formed at every substitution: stdlib §2.19's producer members and `Sum`'s own return are spelled `owned T`, admissible over the mixed numeric domain under [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)'s per-instantiation erasure — the results transfer at class and interface substitutions and are plain values elsewhere.)* **Calls-mint substitutions are excluded from bare-parameter function slots (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) under axiom [A2](#sec-axiom-register)'s family keying).** The pre-substitution keying that makes this rule and the `Task`-family rule sound cannot see through a function slot, and post-substitution keying remains the recorded decline. The seam is closed instead by admissibility, completing the marker fence (`owned`-return function slots are already type-excluded from bare-parameter slots — [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear), [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)) for the one family whose calls mint without the marker: a member whose declared type or signature contains, anywhere within a parameter's declared type, a function type whose **return slot is a bare type parameter** (nullability stripped) is **inadmissible at an instantiation substituting a `Task`-family type** for that parameter — the calls-mint family, today `Task`/`Task<T>`/`OwningTask<T>` (axiom A2; a future ruling extending the family extends this exclusion with it). The use is rejected at the instantiation under [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rules 2/4's per-instantiation pattern, the diagnostic naming the instantiation and the sound spellings: declare the slot with a `Task`-family return (`f: () -> Task<T>` — pre-substitution mint-classified) or a concrete function type, or build the task collection by statement (`tasks.Add(FetchAsync(x))`). Every non-mint substitution is untouched; a bare parameter in a function type's *parameter* slots, or as a plain parameter type (`Pick<T>(a: T, b: T): T` at `T = Task<int>` — a sound argument-sourced lend), is outside this rule. With this exclusion, [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)'s family boundary (below), and the concrete-slot callee-side admission on lambda and body return paths ([§28.3](#sec-producers) *Concrete-slot function bodies* — the fence that catches a minting lambda inhabitant the first two cannot see: `Wrap<Object>(lambda() => Work())` substitutes no family type and retypes no formed value), no **`Task`-family** value whose invocations mint can inhabit a slot whose invocations this rule classifies as lends — the `Task`-family arm of the residual is discharged.

*(One narrowed residual stays recorded: a function value over a **static iterable factory** — a callee whose direct call mints a caller-owned frame under the iterator convention's announced carve ([§28.3](#sec-producers) *Iterator and iterable returns*: "callers must discharge the ownership obligation"), a mint that exists via the factory rule, outside axiom [A2](#sec-axiom-register)'s calls-mint family — inhabiting a bare-parameter function slot at an iterable-interface substitution (`Wrap<IEnumerable<int>>(Nums)` with a yield-based `static Nums(): IEnumerable<int>`), or a concrete slot via retyping (the producers row's recorded seam; the direct formation route is fenced there). The invocation classifies as a borrow of the function value and the minted frame leaks — resource-bearing when the factory's frame holds `using var` state disposed only at frame teardown ([§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)). The family-keyed exclusion above never captures this inhabitant precisely because A2 keeps iterables outside calls-mint (the stored-collection-view idiom is legitimate and common); frame ownership for iterable call results is the residual that inherits this explicitly and closes it by classifying the slot, fencing the substitution, or extending the family, whereupon this exclusion extends with it.)*

**Concrete-slot function bodies (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — the row's announcement has a callee side, as every announced classification in this section does).** A lambda checked against a function-type target whose return slot — after the inference or substitution that types the lambda at its check site, nullability stripped — is a **concrete class or interface type** (not `owned`; not `Task`-family, whose callee side is the rule above; not one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable/enumerator interfaces or a lazy query) admits on each return path exactly the sources the producers row's callers re-establish: `null` (for a nullable slot), a capture-sourced borrow, a plain-parameter-sourced borrow, or static storage — the bare-T non-empty-set admission read against the target's own slots. A **fresh owned value** — a constructor result, a `move` result, a factory-call result, a `Task`-family call result, or any other owned production — is rejected at the return path ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention): the row classifies every invocation as a borrow, so no caller would ever dispose it); spell the slot's return `owned` to transfer (the stdlib's own generic-factory convention, `init: (int) -> owned T`, stdlib §4.14). At value and runtime-managed check-site types the admission is vacuous ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's per-instantiation-category pattern, exactly as the bare-T callee side; the lazy-operator selector rules' stricter per-element treatment of runtime-managed mints in lazy positions, is unaffected). A lambda checked against a slot whose return is a still-unsubstituted bare type parameter takes the same admission under the bare-T rule above. Method references need no new clause: a method's own body is already checked against its declared signature, and [§27.1.1](#sec-function-type-assignability)/[§27.6](#sec-method-references) admit only compatible faces into the slot.

Implementations are encouraged to add `owned` annotations to static factory methods proactively.

**Iterator and iterable returns are outside the static-return error above** (derives: [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6) — the declared iterable interface is the announcement; the carve is type-keyed, so a composed-frame static like `static method Evens(xs: Array<int>): IEnumerable<int> => xs.Where(IsEven);` is admitted by the same clause). A method whose body uses `yield return` or `yield break` (synchronous or async, returning `IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, or `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>` per [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) is a factory by construction — its return is the freshly-constructed state machine — and the natural return type is the iterable interface, not `owned IEnumerable<T>` (or `owned IOwningEnumerable<T>`). The factory rule applies to iterator-method return values exactly as it does to other sourceless static returns: callers must discharge the ownership obligation (typically via the for-loop's implicit `using var __source` binding). Requiring `owned` on every iterator return type would be redundant noise over an announced transfer — the recorded reason the announced set exists. The standard library's iterator-returning methods (`IEnumerable<T>` extensions like `Where`, `Select`, etc., and the owning-collection `Drain()` methods returning `IOwningEnumerable<T>`) follow this convention.

<a id="sec-iterable-instance-returns"></a>
**Iterable-interface returns at instance and extension callees (derives: K1.5 + K2.4 + K3.2 + K1.7/K2.3; the calls-mint family keying of axiom A2 is unchanged, and the owning-head rejection is preserved).** The iterator convention above is the *static* face: a static callee has no receiver and cannot re-expose stored state through a method return ([§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)), so its declared iterable type alone announces a caller-owned frame. An **instance or extension** callee's iterable-interface return announces with the `owned` marker instead, because at the **non-owning heads** (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`) the unmarked spelling already has a meaning the type cannot override — the stored-collection view: **unmarked**, the call result is a **borrow** (source: the receiver, or the extension's receiver parameter — the producers-table row above), carrying no disposal obligation, and the body may return only receiver-sourced (receiver-parameter-sourced) borrows or, under a nullable declared type, `null` — a bare collection-field read upcast to the interface being the canonical form ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); **marked `owned`**, the call result is a caller-owned frame under the ordinary owned-return row, discharged by the standard rules (the `for` desugaring's `using var __source` assumes the obligation, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)). The **owning heads** (`IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`) have **no unmarked instance or extension spelling**: a borrowed view is non-consuming ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s read-or-iterate-but-not-drain contract), while an owning head's static type keys the *consuming* desugaring ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) — a "borrowed owning view" would drain receiver-owned elements through a result carrying no obligation, and under interface dispatch its classification double-frees — so an unmarked instance or extension return typed at an owning head is **rejected at the declaration**: expose the stored view at the concrete collection type or the non-owning interface (the [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) bullet), or declare the return `owned` to transfer. A **freshly-produced frame** — an iterator-method body's state machine, a composed deferred-operator result, a fresh or owned enumerable — returned through an *unmarked* instance or extension iterable return is a compile error (the [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) fresh-value rule; the diagnostic names the remedy: declare the return `owned`); an instance or extension **iterator method** therefore declares `owned IEnumerable<T>` (or the enumerator/owning/async forms). This is the protocol's own spelling generalized — `GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>` ([§29.1](#sec-iterator-protocol)) is exactly an instance fresh-frame face, marked on the interface itself. Frame carriage is orthogonal and unchanged: the declared iterable type keys the carried-source classification on both spellings ([K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6); *Returning a deferred-activation frame* below, whose owning-head borrow-carriage rejection this paragraph's declaration-site reject subsumes for instance and extension callees). The standard library's deferred-operator results (`Where`, `Select`, …), `Drain()`, and `ReceiveAll()` are outside this paragraph: they are the provenance-tracked affine lazy values of [§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration), whose obligation is discharged at the single consumption point (`Drain()` — an instance owning-head return — lives in that recorded carve).

<a id="sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals"></a>
#### Move semantics for owned locals

Reading an owned local `x` in one of [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s owned-consuming positions **transfers ownership out of `x`**: afterward `x` is in the **moved-from** state — it may not be read again until reassigned, and it has no disposal obligation. Reading an owned local in a position that accepts a borrow leaves `x` unchanged, and an **unmarked** read of a named owned binding in a local binding/assignment position is a **borrow** — the aliasing idiom `var b := a;` never silently consumes `a` ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)). Where the transfer must be spelled and where the target announces it is K3.13's announcement rule: the marker at the call site — `M(move x)` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — and in **local binding and assignment positions** — `var y := move x;`, `y := move x;`, `using var y := move x;` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var) adoption); no marker at announced targets — an **`owned` field or owning-collection slot**, `return` under an `owned` return type or (non-`async` bodies) an unmarked `Task`-family return type, or a user-declared `set(owned)` property or indexer ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties): `cache.Current := c;` consumes without a call-site marker, exactly as at the stdlib owning-collection indexer-set, whose setters are themselves declared `set(owned)`) — and none anywhere for a fresh producer (no live binding is invalidated). Writing the marker on a **borrow or fresh-producer right-hand side** is an error, as is a marked reassignment into a **borrowed-state** LHS (the state-match rule above) — mirroring the call-site marker's rules — and so is the marker **at an announced target**: `return move x;` under an `owned` return, `throw move x`, `_ := move x;`, an owned-field or `set(owned)` store spelled `sink._f := move x;`, a Pattern B `await move t` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)), an owning iterator's `yield return move x;` — one spelling per site; the announcement is the spelling there, and the diagnostic names it. A fresh declaration (`var y := move x;`, `using var y := move x;`) or a **polymorphic-null** LHS (`var best: Res? := null; … best := move cur;` — the null-literal producers row) adopts owned state from the marked transfer, exactly as it would from a fresh producer.

The marked assignment form is what makes the loop-accumulator pattern expressible — keep the best, dispose the rest:

```bezel
var best: Res? := null;
for var i in 0..<count do
    var cur := new Res(i);
    if best = null or cur.Score() > best!.Score() then
        best := move cur;          // transfer; the displaced best is disposed (§28.7)
    else
        cur.Dispose();             // or let cur auto-drop with the must-use warning
    end;
    // after the if: cur is moved-from on the taken path, disposed on the other —
    // the §28.3 join rules (maybe-consumed) forbid reading it; scope-end disposal is per-path.
end;
// best: owned; discharge or auto-drop per the standard rules.
```

```bezel
public method Wrap(s: Stream): owned Wrapper
  using var copy := s.Clone();      // copy is owned + scope-bound
  return new Wrapper(copy);          // ERROR: copy is using-var, cannot move out
end Wrap;

public method Wrap2(owned s: Stream): owned Wrapper
  return new Wrapper(s);             // OK: s is moved into Wrapper's constructor
                                     // s is now in moved-from state
end Wrap2;
```

A `using var` is owned but is additionally bound to its scope: it cannot be moved out of, only borrowed from. To transfer a `using var`'s value out, the programmer must either reassign the contents (via an owning method that `take`s the underlying object and replaces the `using var`'s contents — not provided in this version) or restructure to introduce the value as a non-`using var` owned local.

<a id="sec-captured-owned-bindings"></a>
**Captured owned bindings (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)).** Inside a closure, a captured owned binding — an owned local or `owned` parameter of the enclosing body — is uniformly in **borrow state**: reads borrow (the producers rows above), and assignment to it, a marked transfer from it, an explicit `Dispose()` or discard of it, and every other owned-consuming use of it are compile errors — a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding (a closure-side consume would be a kill no body-local liveness can see — K5.5's decidability bound; the move-only closure rule of [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types), "the closure does not own the array", is the same principle). Mutation of captured **plain** (borrowed- or value-state) locals is unaffected ([§27.5](#sec-closures)). A callback that must genuinely consume a value takes an `owned` parameter and is invoked with the value transferred from outside ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).

<a id="sec-borrow-lifetime-rules"></a>
#### Borrow lifetime rules

A borrowed value's lifetime is the lifetime of its *source* ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)). The compiler enforces, as instances of [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)'s bounded-escape rule:

- A borrowed local may not be returned from a method whose return type is `owned`.
- A borrowed local may not be returned from a method at all unless the return is a borrow with a clearly-defined source that outlives the call (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — only sources every caller can re-establish against its own actuals; the sourceless static case is rejected at the declaration) — in this version: a **receiver-sourced** borrow from an instance method (a bare owned-field read — not of a `Task`-family-typed field ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)) — `this`, or a borrow reached through the receiver's fields and indexers, [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)), or the receiver-parameter borrow of an extension method ([§26.7](#sec-ownership-in-extensions)), or a **static-storage-sourced** borrow: a bare read of a `static` **class- or interface-typed field** — `owned`, `readonly` without `owned` ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s exemption: the referent is process-lived and never disposed), or a [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2 admitted mutable static (whose stores never dispose a displaced referent, so every referent it has ever held stays alive to process exit) — from a **static property getter**, returned through a non-`owned` return type — its source is the declaring type's static storage, [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)): every admissible static field form keeps its referents alive to process exit, which is exactly what the always-live claim requires. This is the callee-side form of the *Static property access `T.P`* and *Static field access `T.f`* producers rows above (the stdlib §6.5 event pattern's static idiom and the stdlib §3.2 `Encoding` singletons are the motivating cases). A static **method** may not return such a read: nothing signature-visible distinguishes a storage-returning static method from a factory, so the signature itself is rejected as the sourceless-factory case (*Factory methods* above); were it admitted, every caller would mint a second owner for the borrowed-out storage — the two-owners pairing the empty-set carve closes for bare-type-parameter signatures, closed here for concrete ones; re-expose the field through a static property (whose `T.P` read is the sound caller-side dual) or transfer with an `owned` return. A borrowed *local or parameter* with **no** source that outlives the call — e.g. a static method returning one of its parameters, `static method Pick(a: Res, b: Res): Res return a;` — may **not** be returned; this callee-side prohibition and the declaration-site static-return rule (*Factory methods* above) are one boundary seen from two sides. (Value-typed and runtime-managed returns are not borrows and are outside this rule. A return whose declared type is a deferred-activation kind — an iterable/enumerator interface, a lazy query, a `Task`-family type — is exempted for parameter-/receiver-sourced frames: *Returning a deferred-activation frame*, [§28.3](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame). A return whose declared type is a **bare type parameter** — or that implements or overrides a generic declaration whose declared return type is one — is governed by *Bare-type-parameter returns* ([§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)): with a non-empty potential source set it admits plain-parameter- and receiver-sourced borrow returns — every caller re-establishes them against its own receiver and arguments — and with an empty set the signature is rejected at the declaration exactly as a concrete-typed one is — spell `owned T` (admissible over every domain under §28.1's erasure), or re-expose storage through a static property, the sound spelling.)
- A method's return type that names an **owning-collection or owning-wrapper type** (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `Shared<T>`, `Weak<T>`, and the other owning collection and wrapper types — **not** `OwningTask<T>`: `Task`-family returns are governed by *Task-family calls produce owned frames* above, a call minting a caller-owned frame, a stored task re-exposed only through property/field/slot borrows) follows the *same* owned-vs-borrow rule as any other reference return (the *Producers* table above): declared `owned`, the caller takes ownership; declared **without** `owned`, the result is a **borrow** with a documented source (the `Owning*` type name denotes *element* ownership, orthogonal to the container ownership the `owned` qualifier governs — [§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections)). The borrow-return restrictions then apply unchanged: a bare owning-collection *field* read may be returned (its source is the receiver, [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); a borrowed *local* or *parameter* with no source that outlives the call may **not** be returned; a `move`d field or a freshly-produced owning value must be returned through an `owned` return type. A borrow returned this way carries the capability restriction of [§28.6](#sec-borrowed-owning-collections) — the caller may not `Dispose` it (the owner does); it may otherwise be read and mutated like any borrowed collection.
- A borrow may be stored in a field of an object only if the borrow's source provably outlives that object. A borrowed scope-bound *local* never satisfies this — it is disposed at the end of its scope, which a field of the object outlives — so a borrowed local may not be assigned to any field. A borrow whose source *does* outlive the object **is** admissible: the idiomatic form binds it through a constructor parameter into a non-owned class-typed field (the `_owner: Customer` back-reference of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), where the caller-side source outlives the constructed object. Such a **borrowing class-typed field** — a non-owning class-typed field whose target is owned elsewhere — is the back-edge that serialization synthesis treats specially ([§9.8](#sec-serialization-synthesis)). The field stores a plain reference. **The assignment-site check is structural and decidable** — parameter-sourced and receiver-sourced borrows are admissible; scope-bound locals and temporaries are rejected. **The residual is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause:** whether the caller-side source actually outlives the object is the programmer's obligation, not a compile-time guarantee, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net. The caller-side obligation includes **not transferring the source's object to another domain** — and, its extension, **not consuming it into a construction that makes it reachable from other domains**: `FrozenArray<T>.From(move …)` (stdlib §4.19), a `Shared<T>`/`Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` constructor whose result is then shared across domains ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership), [§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)), or a store into an admitted static ([§22.12](#sec-static-members)); such a consume is not itself a domain transfer, but it creates or publishes an object other domains may reach while the pre-consume borrow still aliases its storage, and every statement below about the transfer case applies to it verbatim. A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below (the freeze sees only local borrows of the consumed binding — [K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5)) and is **not** caught by checked disposal mode (the object stays alive in the receiving domain, so no disposed flag is ever set); it is a data race. The same domain clause attaches to **every** residual-trust borrow admission: collection-held borrows ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule) and borrows held by a **pending async frame** ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods) — an unsettled task's receiver and plain reference-typed arguments live in the state machine, in no local borrow binding the freeze can see; §30.1's settlement obligation carries the clause explicitly). These residuals are the honest limit of the static rule ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)). A class- or interface-typed `scoped` parameter ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) upgrades this residual-trust admission to a fully static bound at participating call sites.
- A borrow may not be assigned to a local whose scope strictly encloses the borrow's source's scope — including flowing into a loop-carried binding along a back edge when the source is declared inside the loop body (`prev := cur;` where `cur` is per-iteration). The scope comparison is structural and decidable; the diagnostic is the standard *"Borrow held by `x` would outlive its source `y`."*
- A borrowed local may not be captured by a closure that may outlive the borrow's source. Capture is permitted for closures that are immediately invoked, closures bound to a `using var` local of function type, and closures passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter — where the callee's use is bounded by its signature: a plain parameter is **call-bounded** (the callee may not retain the callback past the call — for a deferred-activation callee, past the returned frame's life ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters), *Call-bounded × deferred activation*); compiler-verified for user-authored callees, [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)), and a `scoped` parameter stores under [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s storage-bounded admission, which checks the captures against the bounding object. *(An extension method's parameter is an ordinary plain parameter — every plain parameter admits capture-bearing arguments on the caller side. The standard library's lazy query operators, whose returned query values retain the callback until enumeration, are the normative instance of the deferred-activation frame-residence rule ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)): the retention is bounded by the query value, whose carried sources include the callback's captures ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — no `scoped` marking and no certification are involved (stdlib §5).)*
- The same capture-and-escape rule applies to **method references** ([§27.6](#sec-method-references)) that bind an instance receiver: `obj.Method` produces a function value whose captured environment includes `obj`. If `obj` is a borrow, the resulting function value is subject to the closure-escape rules above as if `obj` had been captured by an explicit lambda. The function value's runtime-managed status ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) governs the *function value's own* lifetime; it does not relax the lifetime constraints on borrows captured by the function value.

A borrowed value may be passed as a non-`owned` argument to another call: the callee further borrows for the duration of the call.

<a id="sec-consume-site-freeze"></a>
#### The consume-site freeze

Consuming an owned **binding** — a local or an `owned` parameter — while a **live local borrow of its current value** exists is a compile error ([K5](#sec-kernel-k5)). The consume sites are [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s owned-consuming positions — including an `owned` argument's `Domain.Spawn` and channel `Send` instances ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)/[§30.15](#sec-channels)) and **reassignment** of the binding itself ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) — drop-on-overwrite is a consume of the displaced value). A borrow is *live* at a consume site when some path from the site reaches a later use of it — directly, through a `using var` pin ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), or through a closure value that is itself still live. A live local of **borrow-bearing record** type ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — a span is the canonical case — counts as a live local borrow of every carried borrow's source (stated explicitly, because stdlib §4.19's construction-time soundness is load-bearing on it, making normative what §9.7's subjection of record values to this section's borrow rules already implies): `var s := buf.AsSpan();` freezes `buf` against `FrozenArray<T>.From(move buf)` — and every other consume — for as long as `s` is live. Liveness is the backward dataflow the borrow rules already compute; the check is decidable and local to the method body ([K5.5](#sec-kernel-k5)). The diagnostic names the consumed binding, the borrow, and the borrow's surviving use.

**The explicit-`Dispose()` boundary (recorded).** Which consumes are frozen is [K5](#sec-kernel-k5)'s criterion — *unfrozen ⟺ the kill is announced at the site ∧ flag-backstopped* (rationale [§5.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-not-borrows)): the transferring kills and drop-on-overwrite are **frozen** ([K5.1](#sec-kernel-k5)–[K5.2](#sec-kernel-k5), which state the placements); the [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) announced kills are **unfrozen** ([K5.3](#sec-kernel-k5) — the closed set and each kill's disposal moment are stated once, at K4.2); and a Pattern A chaining `return await x` is unfrozen by [K5.4](#sec-kernel-k5)'s one recorded structural override — vacuity: the chained task moves alive into the outer task, which cannot dispose it before the body, `finally` blocks included, completes ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)). **Unborrowed reassignment stays legal** — only the silent kill under a live borrow is rejected. The one idiom this rejects — borrow, transfer the source into a longer-lived owner, keep using the pre-transfer borrow — has a mechanical rewrite: transfer first, then re-borrow from the new owner (`pool.Add(move item); var b := pool[pool.Count - 1]; b.Configure();`).

**Scope of the freeze.** The [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) admission freeze on captured sources is the storage-bounded form of this rule, strengthened per [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5) to cover the announced kills as well ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)). Fields and collection slots are **not** frozen ([K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5)): a borrow of `obj.f`'s or `coll[i]`'s current value is invalidated by an overwrite or mutation of the slot under the runtime-checked posture ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)); a slot kill *by move* — `move box.f` into a transfer, a spawn argument, or one of the domain-reachable constructions of the domain clause — disposes nothing and sets no flag, and is governed by the borrow lifetime rules' extended domain clause above ([K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)), a recorded obligation, not by this exemption.

<a id="sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement"></a>
#### Owned-local discharge requirement

An owned local is disposed exactly once on every control-flow path. The program may *discharge* the obligation explicitly — transferring it elsewhere or disposing it by hand — at any of [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s owned-consuming positions (K3.1–K3.12; an **unmarked** binding `var y := x;` is a borrow of `x` and discharges nothing, K3.13; after a discard `_ := x;` the binding is left **explicitly-disposed** and after `throw x` **moved-from**, [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)). If it does not, the compiler disposes the value at the end of its scope:

**Auto-drop (affine)** (derives: [K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)). When an owned local — or an `owned` parameter — reaches a *normal-exit* scope end without having reached a discharge point, and is not in moved-from state, it is **disposed implicitly at that scope end** (for an `owned` parameter, at the end of the method) — the same implicit disposal that the *Exception-path discharge* below performs on the unwinding edge, now applied to the normal-exit edge as well. Bezel is therefore **affine**: every owned value is disposed exactly once on every path — explicitly where the program discharges it, implicitly at scope end otherwise — and the move analysis ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) leaves a transferred value in moved-from state so the scope-end disposal skips it; nothing is disposed twice. This makes a plain `var` owned local (and an undischarged `owned` parameter) behave, on a path that never moves it out, like a `using var`: the value is reclaimed when its scope ends.

**Must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)'s lint).** Because a plain `var` (or an undischarged `owned` parameter) that is implicitly dropped is indistinguishable in *effect* from a `using var`, the compiler emits a **warning** (not an error) at the implicit-drop site of a plain-`var` owned local or `owned` parameter, to surface a drop that may have been unintended. The warning names the local and lists the explicit alternatives: declare it `using var` (scope-bound disposal — the value may not then be moved out), `move`/return it (transfer the obligation), or dispose it explicitly with `.Dispose()` or discard it with `_ := …` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). The warning is **suppressed** when the local is declared `using var` (the scope-bound intent is then explicit), when it is explicitly disposed or discarded — including through the null-conditional and null-forgiving spellings `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()`, required for nullable owned locals — and when it is moved or returned (no implicit drop occurs). The warning is a lint over a sound program — it changes no semantics, only flags the implicit drop — so a project may tune or silence it; the auto-drop runs regardless. The rule is uniform across body kinds: for an `owned` parameter of an **iterator or async method**, whose undischarged value is disposed by the frame at teardown ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) rather than at a lexical scope end, the warning attaches at the parameter's declaration; the adoption idiom `using var r := move reader;` suppresses it exactly as `using var` suppresses the local form.

The obligation is always satisfied — by the program or by the compiler — and the lint, not an error, marks the implicit case.

**Exception-path discharge** (derives: [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3) — edge parity). Owned locals and owned parameters that are live when an exception propagates out of their enclosing block are disposed implicitly during stack unwinding. The compiler treats every owned local and owned parameter as if it were wrapped in an implicit `try`/`finally` whose `finally` disposes the value if it is still owned (i.e., not already moved-from and not already explicitly disposed). This guarantees that exceptions do not produce leaks even though the user wrote a plain `var` rather than `using var`, or accepted an `owned` parameter rather than re-binding it; the only difference between the edges is the lint — a plain-`var` implicit drop on the *normal-exit* edge carries the must-use warning above, while the (non-local) exception edge does not.

This rule is what makes plain `var` owned locals safely usable as accumulators that are eventually moved out by `return` or by an `owned` argument. The intent of a plain `var` is "I will discharge this explicitly somewhere"; the intent of a `using var` is "auto-dispose at scope end, never move out." The distinction matters only on normal-exit paths: `using var` is non-movable; plain `var` is movable, and on any normal-exit path where it has not reached a discharge point it is auto-dropped with the must-use warning.

The implicit cleanup ordering follows reverse declaration order across multiple owned locals in the same scope, mirroring the destructor's field-disposal rule ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)). When the exception passes through nested scopes, the inner scope's locals are disposed before the outer scope's, in the same way `using var` cleanups nest.

The implicit cleanup does **not** apply to:
- Locals that are already in moved-from state at the point the exception unwinds past them.
- Locals that were already explicitly disposed before the throwing operation.
- Borrows (locals not in the owned state); these have no disposal obligation.
- Value-typed and runtime-managed-typed locals; these have no `Dispose` to call.

A user who wants to perform additional cleanup on the exception path (logging the partial result, performing a partial-state recovery) writes an explicit `try`/`finally` or `try`/`catch`/`throw` around the relevant operations. The implicit auto-dispose composes with explicit `finally` blocks on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack of [§28.10](#sec-using-var): an owned local's implicit disposal is established at its declaration — exactly as if it were a `using var` — so a `finally` established *after* the declaration runs before the disposal (with the local still in scope), and one established *before* it runs after. Undischarged `owned` parameters' implicit disposals are established at entry to the body, and an expression's unbound owned temporaries at their production (see *Unbound owned temporaries* below).

<a id="sec-unbound-owned-temporaries"></a>
#### Unbound owned temporaries

The discharge requirement above governs *named* owned values — locals, fields, and parameters. An owned value may also be produced as an **unbound temporary**: the result of an `owned`-returning call (or other owned producer) that is not bound to any name, not `move`d, and not returned, but used only by *borrowing* operations within the expression — as the receiver of a further call, as a non-`owned` argument, as a member or index access, or as the scrutinee of a `case` (whose boundary extension is defined below). Such a temporary is disposed at the **end of the full expression** in which it is produced, after every use of it within that expression has completed (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3) + [K8](#sec-kernel-k8)). A **trivial-dispose** temporary is freed at the same K8 boundary as a non-trivial one is disposed — the compiler-inserted, flag-setting free of [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)/[§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), identical timing, no user code. The borrowing uses include serving as the operand of a Pattern A `await` or `.Result` read whose borrowed result is itself confined to the same full expression ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal), [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)) — for such an operand the disposal is deferred to the end of the full expression rather than performed at the await, so the borrowed result outlives its uses.

**The full expression boundary.** The disposal boundary above — and the boundary wherever this specification uses the term for value lifetime — is [K8](#sec-kernel-k8)'s **full expression**: a maximal expression at K8's enumerated positions, which include desugared bindings such as [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)'s `__source` (in an expression statement, "end of the full expression" and "end of the statement" coincide, [§21.9](#sec-statement-form-of-expressions)). Each **evaluation** of a condition, `when` arm condition, or pattern guard is its own boundary (K8.2), so condition temporaries are disposed per evaluation and never accumulate across iterations. (Distinguish the grammar-level use of the phrase — "the scrutinee is a full Expression", [§19.1](#sec-forms) — which is about parse precedence, not this lifetime boundary.)

**`case` scrutinees extend the boundary.** For a `case` whose scrutinee produces an unbound owned temporary, the boundary is [K8.3](#sec-kernel-k8)'s: the **whole `case` construct**, in statement position exactly as in expression position, which is what keeps [§19.3](#sec-patterns)'s pattern bindings — borrows whose source is the scrutinee — alive through the arm body: in `case pool.PopFirst() of var f: FastConnection => f.Warm(), _ => () end;` the binding `f` reads a temporary that is disposed after the selected arm finishes, never before it. (The reject-instead posture of [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal) was considered and declined here: it would have to reject the long-admitted expression-position form too.)

**Binding-atom bindings are named temporaries.** A binding atom's clause whose initializer is an owned production ([§17.15](#sec-the-binding-atom)) produces a **named** unbound owned temporary: within the atom the binding is an ordinary named owned binding — [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s consuming positions discharge it, and a consumed binding is not disposed by the boundary pass — but its boundary is the **atom itself** ([K8.5](#sec-kernel-k8)), tighter than the enclosing full expression: undischarged at the atom's completion, it is disposed there, after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order, before the enclosing expression continues; the exception edge discharges it during unwinding on the same establishment-ordered cleanup stack. No must-use warning attaches (the binding names a temporary; its disposal is the language's job). The escape rule is [K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8) applied at the atom boundary: a borrow or frame whose source set includes an atom binding may not leave the atom — not in the body's value, not by store, not by capture in an escaping closure — and is rejected, never lifetime-extended; the remedy is a statement-level `using var` ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)).

When the full expression is instead exited by an **exception** — an operand or argument evaluated later throws before the temporary's transfer or consumption point — every already-produced, not-yet-consumed unbound owned temporary is disposed during unwinding by the same implicit `try`/`finally` mechanism as named locals (*Exception-path discharge* above; [K3.15](#sec-kernel-k3)/[K8.1](#sec-kernel-k8)): each temporary's disposal is established at its production, so the pass runs in reverse order of production on the establishment-ordered cleanup stack ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), under [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s multi-value supersession discipline. A temporary that had already transferred — into an `owned` parameter, a binding, an owned slot, or a return — is not disposed by this pass (its new owner's rules govern), and a temporary whose producing subexpression never ran was never produced. Exceptions therefore do not leak mid-expression producers: in `Combine(new Connection("a"), Fail())` where `Fail()` throws, the already-produced `Connection` — evaluated first under [§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s call-site textual order, and not yet transferred because the call to `Combine` never began — is disposed during the unwind.

This is the unnamed-temporary counterpart of the discard contract ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) and the discharge requirement above: a *named* owned value reaches a discharge point — an owned slot, a `using var`, a marked transfer, an explicit `Dispose()`, or the discard `_ := x;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — or is auto-dropped at scope end with the must-use warning; an *unnamed* owned temporary — which no named form can reach — is reclaimed automatically once the expression that produced it is finished with it. A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice).

For example, in `Folded(src).Sorted()` where `Folded(src): owned Array<T>` and `Sorted` borrows its receiver, the `Folded(src)` temporary is borrowed by `Sorted`, then disposed once the statement completes — exactly once, with no leak and no double-free. Disposal runs *after* the borrowing use, so the receiver is live for the duration of the call.

This rule is uniform across the source of the temporary: it applies identically to a user method declared `owned` and to the standard-library materializers, which are themselves declared `owned` — `ToArray(): owned Array<T>`, `Sorted()`, `Reversed()`, `ToSet(): owned Set<T>`, `ToDictionary(...): owned Dictionary<K, V>` ([§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections); these own the *container*, borrowing the elements). An unbound materializer result in a chain — `items.Where(p).ToArray().Length`, `xs.ToSet().Count()` — is the same kind of unbound owned temporary and is reclaimed at end-of-statement by the same rule. The `owned` return qualifier is the single signal that drives the reclaim; there is no special-cased list of method names.

**Deferred-activation callees (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6](#sec-kernel-k6)).** A call can defer its use of a borrowed argument past the full expression: an iterator or async-iterator factory ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) captures its plain reference-typed arguments into a state machine that runs later, and a lazy query operator ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)) retains its source until enumeration. The returned **deferred-activation frame carries its arguments' borrows**: it is treated as a borrow-carrying value whose sources are the call's receiver, its plain reference-typed arguments, and the **capture-set contribution** of each plain function-typed argument (below), and the ordinary rule that a borrow may not outlive its source applies to it. **The capture-set contribution.** A function value is runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) and is itself no borrow — but the borrows its closure captures are, and they ride the frame exactly as long as the callback does ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s frame residence): a plain function-typed argument contributes its captured borrows' **sources** to the frame's source set, **transitively** — a captured value that is itself a function value or a deferred-activation frame contributes *its* sources by this same rule — the tracing the consume-site freeze (above) already performs through "a closure value that is itself still live", and the transitive judgment the [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) sink checks already apply. The contribution is computed from the argument's statically-known value provenance: a lambda literal — or a local the flow analysis traces to lambda literals, method references, or plain function-typed parameters of the enclosing body, in any mix (a join contributes the union of the traced forms' contributions per this table) — contributes its captured borrows' sources (a value-typed capture contributes nothing, living in its heap capture cell; a runtime-managed capture contributes only what this rule assigns it — a `string` nothing, a function value or frame its sources); a method reference contributes its receiver's source (a static method reference, nothing); a plain function-typed **parameter** of the enclosing body — the one statically opaque form that can carry borrow captures — contributes **itself** as a carried source, and every caller re-establishes the contribution against its own actual argument by this same rule, the signature-level re-establishment this classification already uses for receivers and arguments. A function value read from anywhere else — a field, a collection element, a call result — contributes nothing, and soundly so: the closure-escape rules (the *Borrow lifetime rules* above) admit a borrow-capturing closure into none of those locations, so such values are borrow-free by construction. The one storing location that does hold capture-bearing callbacks — a `scoped` field ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)) — is no counterexample, because its value cannot reach this position at all: passing a `scoped` field's value to a deferred-activation callee's plain function-typed parameter would let the stored callback ride a frame beyond the bounding object's control, and is rejected as exactly the escaping read-out [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) bars (frame residence announces retention for call-site arguments; it opens no read-out for stored callbacks). And a `scoped` parameter has no admitted path into a plain function-typed argument position either ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s callee-side rights — `scoped`-field store, same-bound `scoped` forwarding, invocation — include none). In particular, an unbound owned temporary passed as a plain argument to such a callee — or reached through a plain function-typed argument's capture-set contribution (a method reference over a fresh receiver) — is admissible only when the returned frame is itself fully consumed **within the same full expression**; where the frame outlives the expression — bound to a name, returned, stored, or used as a `for`/`await for` source (whose desugaring binds it, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) — the program is rejected, the same reject-not-extend posture as [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule for records. The remedy names the source first: `var src := Source(3); await for var line in Shout(src) do … end;`. The callee classification is signature-level and decidable: a callee whose return type is one of the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable or enumerator interfaces, or a lazy query — or a **`Task`-family type** (`Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`): an async callee's state-machine frame holds its plain reference-typed arguments' borrows until *settlement* ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)), so an unbound owned temporary argument is admissible only when the returned task is consumed to settlement within the same full expression — awaited there, or blocked on outside a domain ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)). A task that instead escapes the full expression (bound — `using var t := SumAsync(Nums(3));` — returned, stored, or passed to `Task.FireAndForget`) is rejected: the temporary dies at the full expression's end, so the violation of [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation is statically certain, and the reject posture — not [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s trust posture, which covers only sources whose lifetimes the checker cannot compare — applies. The classification is deliberately conservative: it is by declared return type, so a callee returning an already-materialized collection typed as `IEnumerable<T>`, or an async callee that happens to complete before returning, is treated as borrow-carrying/escaping all the same; the remedy is always the same one line — bind the source first.

<a id="sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame"></a>
**Returning a deferred-activation frame (derives: [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2)).** The callee-side borrow-return prohibition (*Borrow lifetime rules* above) does not apply to a return whose declared type is one of the deferred-activation kinds — the [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)/[§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators) iterable and enumerator interfaces, a lazy query, or a `Task`-family type: the declared return type itself announces the borrow-carrying classification, and every caller re-establishes the returned frame's constraints against **its own** receiver and arguments by the signature-level rule above. A non-iterator method may therefore compose and return such a frame — `public static method Evens(xs: Array<int>): IEnumerable<int> => xs.Where(IsEven);` (an instance or extension callee spells the same contract `owned IEnumerable<int>` — the container half, *Iterable-interface returns at instance and extension callees* above) — provided every borrow the returned frame carries is sourced from the method's own parameters or receiver (directly or through the receiver's fields, the receiver-sourced notion of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)); an iterator method is the canonical instance, its returned state machine carrying exactly its parameters' borrows ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)). A returned frame carrying a borrow of anything else — a scope-bound local, a `using var`, a temporary — is rejected at the return site, since the frame would outlive the source; the remedy is to materialize instead (return an `owned` collection — the materializers above). The callee-side check is structural over the returned expression's construction: the frame's carried sources are the receivers, the plain reference-typed arguments, and the plain function-typed arguments' capture-set contributions (*Deferred-activation callees* above) of the deferred-activation calls that built it, followed transitively through intermediate frames. A returned frame whose capture-set contribution reaches a scope-bound local, a `using var`, or a temporary is rejected at the return site exactly as a directly-carried borrow of one is — `return Doubled(nums, lambda(x) => scale.Apply(x));` over a `using var scale` is the canonical reject: the consumer would enumerate into a closure over a disposed object. A contribution that is the method's own plain function-typed parameter, or a capture sourced from its parameters or receiver, is admitted under the same parameter-/receiver-sourced admission as any other carried borrow. The classification stays deliberately by declared return type: a method returning an already-materialized collection typed as `IEnumerable<T>` is treated as borrow-carrying all the same — sound and conservative (the caller over-constrains its own arguments); declare the return `owned Array<T>` to advertise the stronger contract. This exception lifts only the borrow-return prohibition, and for a `Task`-family method or lambda return it governs the *carried* borrows only: the task container itself transfers under *Task-family calls produce owned frames* above — fresh or owned on every return path, a borrowed container rejected. For the iterable and lazy-query kinds the owned-escape rules of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) are unaffected — a freshly-produced owned value (a materialized collection, a `move` result) still requires an `owned` return type, whatever the declared interface type.

<a id="sec-diagnostics"></a>
#### Diagnostics

The compiler must produce error messages that name the variable, its current ownership state, and the rule violated. Recommended messages:

- *"Owned value in `x` would be dropped here without disposal."* (When an owned local goes out of scope undisposed — [K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3).)
- *"Borrow held by `x` would outlive its source `y`."* (When a borrow escapes — [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)/[K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2).)
- *"Owned value in `x` was already moved out at line N."* (When a moved-from local is read — [K1](#sec-kernel-k1)'s moved-from state.)
- *"Cannot move out of `using var` `x`; `using var` is scope-bound."* (When a `using var` is moved — axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register).)
- *"Cannot consume `x` here: the borrow held by `b` (declared at line N) is still live."* (The consume-site freeze — [K5](#sec-kernel-k5).)

These rules ensure that every owned class instance is disposed **exactly once** at runtime and that no owned reference is silently leaked (with drop-on-overwrite, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), the claim has one recorded carve-out: whole-value reassignment of a **move-only inline array** does not dispose the displaced slots — [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)'s warning-backed manual discipline, deferred). Borrow **liveness** is enforced statically for locals, returns, and captures *up to explicit disposal*: the consume-site freeze rejects a move, transfer, or reassignment of a borrowed-from binding, and the scope rules reject every escape past the source's scope — but an **explicit `Dispose()`** of a borrowed-from source is deliberately not statically tracked (rationale [§5.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-not-borrows)'s recorded trade-off; the one exception is a source frozen by a [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) storage admission, whose disposal *is* statically rejected for the bound's extent): use through a surviving borrow raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and is undefined behavior unchecked. For *field-held* and *collection-held* borrows ([§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule), liveness holds up to the caller-side lifetime obligations of the bullets above, backstopped by checked disposal mode.

<a id="sec-choosing-a-disposal-form"></a>
#### Choosing a disposal form (recap)

One mechanism, two specializations, one lint. Every owned local (and undischarged `owned` parameter) is disposed exactly once on every path by the affine auto-drop above — the exception-path discharge being the same mechanism on the unwinding edge. `using var` and an explicit `Dispose()` therefore never add *safety*; they add **declared intent** and **timing**:

| Form | Disposes at | Movable out? | Diagnostic | Exception edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `using var x := …` | scope end, every exit path | no — scope pin ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)) | none (intent declared) | same disposal, same point |
| plain `var x := …`, undischarged | scope end (auto-drop) | yes | **must-use warning** at the implicit drop | disposed silently during unwinding |
| plain `var` + explicit `x.Dispose();` | at the call; the scope-end pass skips the disposed value | yes, until disposed | none | a throw *before* the call is covered by the unwind — the pattern is exception-safe |
| `_ := expr;` (discard, [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) | end of the discard statement | — (unnamed) | none (the discard is the announcement) | unbound-temporary rules above |
| `_ := x;` on a named owned binding | end of the discard statement; `x` left explicitly-disposed | — | none | as explicit dispose |
| unbound owned temporary | end of the full expression; during unwinding if the expression is exited by an exception | — | none | disposed during unwinding, reverse order of production |

*(Two carve-outs live outside this table: `Task`/`Task<T>` may not be discarded — `_ := …;` is rejected, use `Task.FireAndForget` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — and whole-value reassignment of a move-only inline array does not dispose the displaced slots ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)).)*

Doctrine (non-normative): reach for **`using var`** when the value lives and dies here — the default. Use **plain `var`** when ownership will move on (factory results being returned, accumulators, the loop-carried best) — the must-use warning then marks any path where it silently doesn't. Use an **explicit `.Dispose()`** only for an *early or conditional* release point inside a scope — and prefer a `do … end` block around a `using var` where the release point is really a scope. Use **`_ := expr;`** to dispose an unwanted owned result immediately. **Auto-drop is the safety net, not a style.** Unlike in C#, a trailing `x.Dispose();` is *not* an exception-safety bug — the unwinding edge always discharges live owned locals (Exception-path discharge above; rationale [§5.23](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-the-affine-model)) — so an explicit `Dispose()` in Bezel signals only an early release point, never `try`/`finally` plumbing.

<a id="sec-the-destructor"></a>
### 28.4 The `destructor`

A class may declare at most one destructor. Its body runs exactly once, the first time `Dispose()` is called.

```bezel
class FileStream
  private _handle: IntPtr;

  public constructor(path: string)
    using var cpath := CString.From(path);
    _handle := NativeOpen(cpath);
  end constructor;

  destructor
    if _handle <> IntPtr.Zero then
      NativeClose(_handle);
      _handle := IntPtr.Zero;
    end;
  end destructor;
end FileStream;
```

The compiler generates a public, idempotent `Dispose()` that:

1. Runs the destructor body, if any.
2. Disposes all owned-bearing fields in reverse declaration order. This covers fields marked `owned` (class- or interface-typed; the field's value's `Dispose()` is called) and fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`; each non-null slot's `Dispose()` is called per [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)). Inline-array fields without `owned` slots, value-typed fields, and runtime-managed fields require no disposal.
3. Chains to the base class's `Dispose()`.

After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)). Memory reclamation is not part of the user-observable `Dispose()` contract — programs cannot rely on the precise moment at which an object's storage becomes available for reuse.

Destructors run in subclass-to-base order. `Dispose()` cannot be overridden; the customization point is `destructor`.

There is no `disposing` parameter, no manual `_disposed` flag, no `base.Dispose()` call.

**Destructors should not throw; defined behavior when one does (the rule [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) has cited, now stated).** A destructor body (and hence the disposal it customizes) is expected not to throw. When one does, behavior is defined, not undefined:

- The exception propagates from the **disposal point** — the explicit `Dispose()` call, the `using var`/auto-drop scope-end site, the drop-on-overwrite site ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)), the owning container's cascade, or an unbound owned temporary's end-of-full-expression (or unwind) disposal ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)).
- Before it propagates, the **remaining steps of the generated `Dispose()` still run**: the remaining owned-field disposals (reverse declaration order) and the base-class chain complete, and physical reclamation still occurs — a cleanup fault never leaks the object ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s posture, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s exactly-once invariant).
- In a **multi-value cleanup pass** (scope-end disposal of several locals, an owning collection's element cascade, the exception-path discharge — including the unwind disposal of an expression's produced temporaries, [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a throwing disposer does not skip the remaining values: every remaining disposal still runs. If a later disposal in the same pass also throws, the later exception **supersedes** the earlier one — the [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally) `finally`-supersession discipline — and the superseded exception is disposed (the two owner-owned instances excepted, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).

<a id="sec-owned-fields"></a>
### 28.5 Owned fields

A field marked `owned` belongs to the containing object exclusively:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private owned _transactions: Array<Transaction>;       // non-nullable, owned
  private owned _cache: TransactionCache?;               // nullable, owned
  private _owner: Customer;                              // back-reference, not owned
end BankAccount;
```

The `owned` modifier:

1. **Auto-disposes** the field when the containing object is disposed (after the destructor body runs, in reverse declaration order; a nullable field is null-checked before disposal, and a null field disposes nothing).
2. **Prevents leaks** by rejecting code that would let an owned reference escape the containing object.

Restrictions (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1); the generic-argument position's absence is axiom [A14](#sec-axiom-register)):

- Only fields whose type is a **class type or an interface type** may be `owned`. Interface-typed owned fields are admitted because runtime dispatch resolves disposal to the underlying class's `Dispose()`; an `owned IConnection` field disposes whichever class implementation it currently holds.
- `string` fields may not be `owned`. String memory is runtime-managed.
- Function-typed fields may not be `owned`. Function values are runtime-managed ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
- Inline-array fields (`[N]T`, `[N]T?`) without the `owned` slot marker may not be `owned`. The array's slots hold borrows (or value-typed copies); there is no per-slot ownership to manage.
- Inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (`[N owned]T`, `[N owned]T?`) are move-only value types that carry owned slots ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). They are admissible as class fields *without* a separate `owned` modifier on the field; the inline array's own `owned` slot marker already signals that the class's destructor must dispose each non-null slot. Writing `private owned slots: [16 owned]Connection?;` is rejected as a double-marking error — the field modifier is omitted because the type-level marker already conveys the obligation.
- Local variables are not marked `owned`; use `using var`.
- Records may not have `owned` fields, and may not have inline-array fields with the `owned` slot marker (records support only copy semantics, not move semantics; see [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)).

**Generic class fields** (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1), checked per instantiation). When a generic class declares `private owned _slot: T` (where T is a type parameter), the restriction "only fields of class or interface types may be `owned`" is checked at *instantiation*. A `where T: class` constraint admits classes, interfaces, `string`, and function types ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)) — broader than what `owned` fields admit. Instantiating the generic with a type that satisfies `where T: class` but is neither a class nor an interface (`string`, function types) is a compile error at the instantiation site, with a message naming the rejected type. The generic body itself type-checks under the assumption that T is a class-or-interface type; programmers writing such generics should use `where T: class` and document that runtime-managed reference types are not admitted, or use a more specific constraint like `where T: IDisposable` (which automatically excludes records and runtime-managed types per [§14.2](#sec-constraints)'s interface-conformance rule).

A class with only owned-bearing fields (`owned` class/interface fields and/or owning-inline-array fields) and no native resources needs no destructor — the compiler-generated cleanup is sufficient.

<a id="sec-leak-prevention"></a>
### 28.6 Leak prevention

The compiler enforces:

- A *bare read* of an owned field lends ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)) and may be returned through a **non-`owned`** return type as a **borrow** of the field — its source is the receiver, exactly as for `return this` (*Methods returning `this`* below); for a **static** field read — `owned`, or non-`owned` in either admissible form ([§22.13](#sec-static-class-typed-fields-without-owned)'s exempt `readonly` fields and [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2's admitted mutable statics) — returned from a **static property getter**, the source is the declaring type's static storage — process-lived, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) (the callee-side form of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s static-property and static-field producers rows; narrows the admission to the getter — a static **method** returning such a read is rejected whatever the field's form, because its callers classify the call as the sourceless-factory case and would mint a second owner: re-expose the field through a static property or transfer with an `owned` return). The caller receives a borrow it may not dispose (the receiver rule below, [Who may call `Dispose()`](#sec-who-may-dispose)), may not store in an `owned` location, and may not use past the receiver's lifetime; the field's owner (the receiver's destructor) still disposes it. This is leak-free and double-free-free, and applies uniformly to a class-typed owned field and to an owning-collection field (`owned _items: OwningArray<T>`) — but **not**, for a method return, to a `Task`-family-typed field: an unmarked `Task`-family method return type is container-ownership-transferring ([§28.3](#sec-producers), *Task-family calls produce owned frames*), so a stored task is re-exposed through a property, field, or collection slot — a static property getter's bare read of a `Task`-family-typed static `owned` field remains the sanctioned static face ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — never a method return. The same method-return exclusion applies to a field typed at an **owning iterable-interface head** (`IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`): an unmarked instance or extension method return typed at an owning head is rejected at the declaration ([§28.3](#sec-iterable-instance-returns) — a borrowed view must be non-consuming, and an owning head's static type keys the consuming desugaring, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)); re-expose the stored view at the concrete collection type or the non-owning interface (this bullet's admission), or transfer with an `owned` return.
- **Transferring** an owned field's value out — a `move` expression ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)), the only owned read ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)) — is the only way to hand ownership onward: to a *callee* when consumed in place by an `owned` parameter, to the *caller* only as `return move _f;` through an `owned` return type, and a `move`d owned field returned through a non-`owned` return is an **error** (derives: [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) — the moved value would escape with no owner). A freshly-produced owning value (`return new OwningArray<T>(...)`) returned through a non-`owned` return is likewise an error unless the return type is `owned`. (For the `Task` family the unmarked return type itself announces the transfer — a fresh **or owned** task, a `move`d owned task field included, is returnable, indeed required, through an unmarked `Task`-family return; [§28.3](#sec-producers).)
- An owned field's value reaches a non-owned class-typed field of another object only as a **borrow**, governed by [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field store rule (derives: [K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)/[K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9) + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) — the bare read lends a borrow sourced at the field's holder, and [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s structural site check then classifies by that holder's kind: receiver- and parameter-rooted paths are admissible, scope-bound-local- and temporary-rooted paths are rejected; each admissible store carries the same [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause and [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) backstop as every field-held borrow). The recorded obligation is correspondingly precise: the storing side vouches for the field's **current value** — which [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) drop-on-overwrite or a [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) `move` may end before the holder's own life ends — not merely for the holder. It never reaches one as an owned value: a bare read cannot transfer ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)), and a freshly-produced or `move`d owned value stored into a non-owned field is the error of the fresh-store bullet below.
- A **freshly-produced owned value** — a `new` expression, a call returning `owned T`, a `move` expression, or an owned operator result — stored into a non-`owned` (borrow) field is an **error** (derives: K1.7 + K2.3): the field does not own its referent, so the fresh value would be left with no owner and leak. Declare the field `owned` (the containing object then disposes it, [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)), or hand the value to a method that takes it `owned`. This is the storing-side counterpart of the non-`owned`-return rule above.
- A **property or indexer getter** may not return a freshly-produced owned value (axiom [A4](#sec-axiom-register)). A getter is a borrow-producing position — properties and indexers do not carry `owned` ([§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers); the `owned` modifier applies only to fields), so its return is always a borrow — and a fresh owned value returned through it would escape with no owner and leak. Expose the factory as a **method returning `owned T`** instead, which can hand the caller ownership.

These rules apply to **trivial-dispose** class types unchanged ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) — the classification is carried and the ceremony exemption waives warnings, never escape checks): a fresh trivial-dispose value stored into a non-`owned` field is the fresh-store error above — declare the field `owned`, which, when the field's declared type is itself trivial-dispose, does not flip the containing class's classification ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)); a getter returning a fresh trivial-dispose value (`get => new Random();`) is the A4 error above — the fresh value's owner would be a call-bounded temporary the caller's borrow outlives; and a fresh trivial-dispose value returned through a non-`owned` **instance** return is rejected exactly as any fresh value is (static signatures already announce, per the static-return rule of [§28.3](#sec-factory-methods-and-sourceless-returns)).

```bezel
public method GetTransactions(): OwningArray<Transaction>
  return _transactions;     // OK: borrows the field — the caller may
                            //   read/iterate it but not dispose or drain it.
end GetTransactions;

public method TakeTransactions(): owned OwningArray<Transaction>
  var fresh := new OwningArray<Transaction>();  // build the replacement first (§28.8.1)
  var taken := move _transactions;              // take: the field is now moved-from
  _transactions := fresh;                       // restore — required on every exit path (§28.8.1)
  return taken;                                 // transfer: the caller owns the taken array
end TakeTransactions;

public method LeakTransactions(): OwningArray<Transaction>
  return move _transactions;  // ERROR: a `move`d field through a non-`owned`
                              //   return escapes with no owner.
end LeakTransactions;
```

The same no-escape principle governs storing into a field and returning from a getter:

```bezel
class Handle
  private _c: Cell;            // borrow field (no `owned`)
  public constructor()
    _c := new Cell();          // ERROR: a fresh owned value stored into a
  end constructor;             //   non-`owned` field has no owner — declare `owned _c`.

  public property Item: Cell
    get => new Cell();         // ERROR: a getter may not return a fresh owned
  end Item;                    //   value — use `method MakeItem(): owned Cell`.
end Handle;
```
