Passing an owned field as a plain argument is permitted; the callee receives a parameter-sourced borrow under [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s ordinary rules — the callee further borrows for the duration of the call, and may store the borrow into a non-owned class-typed field only where [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field store rule admits it (the [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields) back-reference idiom), in which case the [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) trust obligation rests on the caller's choice of argument exactly as it rests on the constructor caller in that idiom. Handing the callee *ownership* takes the explicit [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) forms: an `owned` parameter fed by a `move` of the field.

<a id="sec-who-may-dispose"></a>
#### Who may call `Dispose()`

Explicit disposal — `x.Dispose()`, the `x?.Dispose()` / `x!.Dispose()` spellings, and the discard of a named owned binding ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.10](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type — which admits the [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) dispose-then-assign legacy and the destructor idioms of [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)/[§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) unchanged. (The field admission is by **declaring type**, matching [§13.1](#sec-levels)'s class-level privacy: code of class C may dispose an `owned` field of any C instance it can reach — the same access symmetry as any private-member touch; a receiver-instance-only restriction would introduce an access category the language does not otherwise draw.)

`Dispose()` through a **borrow** is a compile error: a borrowed local or parameter (including `this` — an object may not dispose itself out from under its owner; a Close()-style method that wants disposal semantics lets the owner dispose, or puts the work in the class's `destructor`), a non-`owned` field read, an owned-field read outside the declaring class, a getter or other non-`owned` call result (a `Task`-family call result is an owned temporary — [§28.3](#sec-producers) — and is not in this list), a `catch`-arm binding ([§31.1](#sec-exception-ownership)), a pattern binding ([§19.3](#sec-patterns)), a captured owned binding inside a closure ([§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), and an element borrow of an **owning** collection (`pool[i].Dispose()` — use `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, the indexer-set, or `move coll[i]`, whose forms keep the slot state coherent, [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). The check is structural and decidable — it reads the receiver expression's ownership classification, which [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) already computes at every call site.

**No element-borrow disposal.** An element borrow obtained from a **borrowing-family** collection — an indexer-get, a default-iteration variable, the entry fields of dictionary iteration — is a borrow like any other: disposing it is a compile error, with no exception. The owned-receiver rule is exception-free: **only owners dispose.** Elements a holder semantically owns belong in owning locations — an owning-family collection ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)), whose `Dispose()` cascades; selective or interleaved cleanup takes the elements *out* first (`Drain()`, `move coll[i]`, the `Pop*` family) into owned bindings and disposes those. The same rule was always in force for `IEnumerable<T>`-, enumerator-, and lazy-query-typed sources (tracked borrows; an iterator's yields are enumerator-owned, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)): `for var x in xs.Where(p) do x.Dispose(); end;` is rejected.

This rule states who may *invoke* disposal; it changes nothing about what disposal does. [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence stands (the dispose-then-scope-end-no-op shapes of [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) have owned receivers and are unaffected), and it is distinct from the consume-site freeze's recorded boundary ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)): that boundary governs disposing an **owned** binding while borrows *of it* are live (legal — the announced kill with a runtime backstop); this rule governs whether the receiver expression is owned at all.

<a id="sec-borrowed-owning-collections"></a>
#### Borrowed owning collections

A borrow of an owning collection — produced by returning a bare owning-collection field (above), or by any borrow-producing read of one — may not be **disposed**. `Dispose()` on a borrow is a compile error: the borrower does not own the container, and the actual owner (the `using var`, the owned local, or the object whose field this is) disposes the container and cascades to its elements at scope/destructor end. The restriction is owner-liveness, not memory safety: under [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence the owner's later disposal would simply no-op — but the owner and every other borrower still treat the container and its elements as live, and a borrower's `Dispose()` would destroy value the owner relies on (every later use then faults in checked disposal mode). This is the general receiver rule above ([Who may call `Dispose()`](#sec-who-may-dispose)) at its most consequential instance, since the container's `Dispose()` cascades through every element.

Every *other* operation remains available, exactly as on any borrowed collection. The mutation and ownership-transfer operations — the owning `Add` / `Insert`, the ownership-taking indexer-set, `Remove*`, `Clear`, `Drain`, `Pop*` / `Dequeue` — are **memory-safe on a borrow**: each preserves the dispose-exactly-once invariant (an element transferred out is owned by its new holder; the owner then disposes a smaller or empty container), and Bezel already admits them on a borrowed collection — the idiomatic *pass-and-fill* pattern `method Fill(a: OwningArray<T>) a.Add(…)` takes a borrowed `OwningArray<T>` and adds to it ([§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)). The read operations (indexer-get, `Count` / `Length`, `Contains`, iteration, the borrowing LINQ queries) are likewise available. The owning collection types deliberately have **no** value-copy materializers (`ToArray` / `Sorted` / `Reversed` / `ToSet` / `ToDictionary`) at all — uniquely-owned elements cannot be copied out of the container without double-owning or draining them (stdlib [§4.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ownedarrayt)) — so those operations are not part of the surface on a borrow or otherwise. Only `Dispose` is restricted. An *owned* owning collection (a `using var`, an owned field accessed by its owner, a `move`d value) additionally admits `Dispose`.

This is narrower than a full read-only restriction, and deliberately so: Bezel's borrowed collections are already mutable (pass-and-fill is a core idiom), so the only operation a borrow-return newly makes unsound is the container `Dispose` — which is the one this rule forbids.

<a id="sec-methods-returning-this"></a>
#### Methods returning `this`

A method that returns `this` returns a borrow of the receiver ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)'s calls-lend default) — the return type is the class type, not `owned`. The caller receives a reference whose lifetime is bounded by the receiver's lifetime. This enables method chaining:

```bezel
using var sb := new StringBuilder();
sb.Append("hello").Append(" ").Append("world");    // each Append returns a borrow of sb
```

The chained calls all operate on the same object. The returned borrow may not be assigned to an `owned` field or returned as `owned` — it is the receiver under a different name. The compiler infers the borrow from the method's non-`owned` return type.

When a chain originates from a `new` expression — `new StringBuilder().Append("a").Append("b")` — the owned value produced by `new` is the root of the chain. The compiler treats the overall chain expression as owned (its root is a `new`). The borrow-returning intermediate calls do not lose the root's ownership; the chain as a whole must reach an owned location or `using var`, just as any other `new` expression must.

<a id="sec-reassigning-owned-fields"></a>
### 28.7 Reassigning owned fields and locals — drop-on-overwrite

**Assignment to an owned field or owned local disposes the displaced value (derives: [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)).** The right-hand side is evaluated first; then, if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from — the per-slot tracking [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s indexer-set rule already defines), it is disposed; then the new value is stored. The disposal is null-guarded and dynamic-dispatched, exactly the machinery scope-end disposal already uses. With overwrite covered, the §28.3 claim — *every owned value is disposed exactly once on every path* — holds with a single recorded carve-out (axiom [A13](#sec-axiom-register)): move-only inline-array *whole-value* reassignment ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) remains a plain store whose non-empty slots leak with a warning, keeping §15.3's manual discipline for this revision; the slot-wise disposal interacts with the open inline-array-disposal design and is deferred. Owning-classified **choices** ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) deliberately do *not* share the carve-out: a choice has no partial states, so its whole-value reassignment takes this rule's automatic drop-on-overwrite.

```bezel
public method Resize(newSize: int)
  _buffer := new Array<byte>(newSize, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4); previous _buffer disposed here, implicitly
end Resize;
```

An explicit `field.Dispose();` before the assignment remains legal and behavior-preserving — `Dispose` is idempotent ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), so the implicit disposal of an already-disposed value is a no-op.

**Overwrite while borrowed.** Reassigning a plain-`var` owned **local** while a live local borrow of its current value exists is rejected by the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze); [K5.2](#sec-kernel-k5)) — the implicit disposal would silently invalidate the borrow. Reassigning an owned **field or collection slot** is not statically frozen ([K5.6](#sec-kernel-k5)); a borrow of the displaced value is invalidated at the overwrite, caught as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode and undefined unchecked — the same runtime-checked posture as explicit `Dispose()` (rationale [§5.1](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owned-not-borrows)).

**Ordering and exceptions** ([K9.5](#sec-kernel-k9)). Because the RHS is evaluated *before* the displaced value is disposed, a throwing RHS leaves the field/local untouched and still-owned (disposed later by the normal unwinding rules) — the implicit path has no exception-unsafe window — the manual `Dispose-then-assign` pattern's hazard of a disposed field holding a dangling reference while the constructor throws cannot arise. Disposers themselves are still expected not to throw ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)); a throwing disposer during overwrite propagates after the store is abandoned, leaving the new value an unbound owned temporary disposed by [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-temporary rule — on this exception edge, during the unwind.

**Moved-from and null.** Overwriting a moved-from field/local ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) or a null-valued nullable stores without disposal — this is precisely how the field-restoration rule's `move`-then-reassign idiom stays single-disposal. `using var` locals are not reassignable at all ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)); this section covers `owned` fields and plain-`var` owned locals.

<a id="sec-ownership-transfer"></a>
### 28.8 Ownership transfer

`owned` may appear on a parameter or return type to mark ownership transfer across method boundaries:

```bezel
public method TakeOwnership(owned resource: Stream)
  _resource := resource;     // moves into owned field; the previous
                             // _resource is disposed by the assignment (§28.7)
end TakeOwnership;

public static method NewBuffer(size: int): owned Array<byte>
  return new Array<byte>(size, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4); owned by virtue of new, returned as owned
end NewBuffer;
```

When a parameter is `owned`, the caller relinquishes ownership and may not use the argument after the call ([K3.3](#sec-kernel-k3)). When a return type is `owned`, the caller receives ownership and is responsible for disposal ([K3.2](#sec-kernel-k3)).

The owned-field assignment in `TakeOwnership` drop-on-overwrites the displaced value ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)): a replacement method needs no explicit dispose-first step — the assignment alone suffices:

```bezel
public method ReplaceResource(owned resource: Stream)
  _resource := resource;   // previous _resource disposed here, implicitly (§28.7)
end ReplaceResource;
```

Moving an owned field's contents *out* of the field uses the `move` expression form ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression); [K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)–[K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9): the field is left *moved-from* and must be reassigned on every path to the method's exit). The pattern for "atomically take this field's contents and return them as owned" is:

```bezel
public method ReplaceAndReturn(): owned Stream
  var fresh := new Stream();         // build replacement first
  var old := move _resource;          // take from field
  _resource := fresh;                  // restore field
  return old;                          // return the taken value
end ReplaceAndReturn;
```

A `new` expression produces an owned value ([K1.5](#sec-kernel-k1)). Its result either reaches an owned location (`owned` field, `using var`, `owned` parameter, `owned` return) or is explicitly disposed within the same method, or — if bound to a plain `var` that is neither moved nor disposed — is **auto-dropped at the end of its scope** with the plain-`var` must-use warning ([K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3); [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)). The obligation is satisfied on every path; the warning, not a hard error, marks an implicit drop.

Implicit boxing ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) is **not** subject to this rule. When a value type is boxed to be used where `Object` or an interface is expected, the boxed wrapper is a runtime-managed value ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types); [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1)), not an owned `new`-result. The boxing itself is not a `new` expression and produces no disposal obligation; `Console.WriteLine(42)` does not need to discharge anything.

<a id="sec-the-move-expression"></a>
### 28.8.1 The `move` expression

`move x.f` is the one owned read of an owned field ([K9.1](#sec-kernel-k9)): it transfers ownership to the read site and leaves the field in *moved-from* state. `move coll[i]` is the analogous form for an owned-element collection slot ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)); the rules below are written for the field case and apply to the collection-slot case with "field" read as "slot." The identifier-operand form `move x` — `x` a named local binding or `owned` parameter — is the same verb at a named binding: [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)'s marked transfer (*Move semantics for owned locals*, [§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)), admitted positionally — the RHS root of a binding or assignment, an argument ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)), a `case` scrutinee ([§35.5](#sec-owning-match)), an if-expression branch, an expression-`case`/`when` arm result — and rejected elsewhere (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)) and at announced targets ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)). The restoration machinery below is specific to fields and slots: a moved-from *binding* is simply unreadable until reassigned, with no restoration obligation. Static fields are not eligible ([K9.4](#sec-kernel-k9)).

The `move` expression's static type is the slot's element type (the `T` in `owned T`); the result is owned and is subject to the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules like any other owned value.

<a id="sec-the-field-restoration-rule"></a>
#### The field-restoration rule

The rule is [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s restoration rule: every control-flow path from the move site to the method's exit must execute an assignment `x.f := value;` between the move and the exit, statically enforced — failure is a compile error. The exit paths considered include normal return, fall-through (for `()`-returning methods), `throw`, `yield break` (in iterator methods), and any other transfer of control that leaves the method body. The rule applies to every reachable exit; an unreachable exit (one the compiler proves cannot occur) does not contribute an obligation. In particular there is no terminal-move dispensation: a **terminal move** — `return move x.f;`, or any return whose operand evaluation performs the move with no restoring assignment before the exit — is rejected, the return edge being itself an unrestored exit. Restoration precedes the return (*build before take* — the `ReplaceAndReturn` shape of [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer)), or the field is declared nullable and restored to `null` (*Detaching via a nullable field*, below); only a destructor body is exempt ([K9.3](#sec-kernel-k9)).

The error message identifies the move site, the unrestored exit path, and the three standard remedies: assign a value on the offending path; move the move into the branch where reassignment is reachable; or, if the field should sometimes hold no value, declare it nullable and assign `null` after the move.

```bezel
// ERROR: field _resource was moved at line 2 and not reassigned
//        on the path through the false branch of `if replace` (line 3).
public method Wrong(replace: bool): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  if replace then
    _resource := new Stream();
  end;
  return old;
end Wrong;
```

The fix is to reassign on every path:

```bezel
public method Right(replace: bool): owned Stream
  var fresh := new Stream();
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end Right;
```

Or to scope the move to the branch where reassignment is mandatory:

```bezel
public method Right2(replace: bool): owned Stream?
  if not replace then return null; end;
  var fresh := new Stream();
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end Right2;
```

<a id="sec-exception-paths-are-not-exempt"></a>
#### Exception paths are not exempt

[K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9)'s path set includes exception edges: a throwable expression between the move and the reassignment introduces an exit path on which the reassignment has not run, and if the destructor on `this` is reached via that path, it would observe the field in moved-from state — the hole a destructor must never observe:

```bezel
// ERROR: if DangerousFactory throws, _resource is moved but never reassigned;
//        the exception edge is an unrestored exit.
public method WrongOrder(): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  var fresh := DangerousFactory();
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end WrongOrder;
```

The fix is to perform any throwable construction *before* the move, leaving only non-throwable assignments and the return between the move and the exits:

```bezel
public method RightOrder(): owned Stream
  var fresh := DangerousFactory();   // may throw — but no move yet
  var old := move _resource;          // cannot throw
  _resource := fresh;                  // cannot throw (assignment, not call)
  return old;                          // cannot throw
end RightOrder;
```

The general rule — *build before take* — is the resource-management discipline this rule encodes. It is the same discipline that motivates strong exception-safety guarantees in C++ RAII code and that drives the "build a complete replacement, then commit it" pattern in transactional code.

For the purpose of the analysis (derives: [K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9) + [K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)), the following expressions are non-throwable:

- assignments (including compound assignments) where neither the LHS nor the RHS is a throwable expression **and** the assignment performs no drop-on-overwrite of a possibly-live value: a store into an `owned` field, a plain-`var` owned local, or an owning-collection slot that may hold a live (non-null, not moved-from) value is **throwable** — the implicit [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) disposal runs the displaced value's destructor, which may throw with defined behavior ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)), propagating from the drop-on-overwrite site. Stores into provably moved-from or null locations, and stores into borrow-state or value-typed locations, remain non-throwable — which is why this section's restoration idioms are unaffected (`_resource := fresh;` after a `move` targets a moved-from slot).
- field reads
- local-variable reads
- literals
- `move x.f` itself (the move is a state transition, not a runtime check)
- `null`-coalescing where neither operand is throwable

Method calls; indexer accesses (on inline arrays `[N]T`, on resizable collection classes such as `Array<T>` whose indexer can throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` or `KeyNotFoundException`, and on any user-declared indexer); division and modulo (which can throw `DivideByZeroException`); arithmetic on overflow-checked types; explicit casts in function-call form (e.g., `short(x)` and `int(d)`, which can throw `OverflowException` for numeric narrowing per [§5.2](#sec-explicit-conversions) or `NullReferenceException` for nullable-to-non-nullable casts per [§5.3](#sec-nullable-casts)); explicit enum casts from integer values (which throw `OverflowException` for values equal to no declared constant per [§5.4](#sec-enum-casts)); shifts whose count is not a compile-time constant (an out-of-domain count raises `OverflowException` per [§6.5](#sec-bitwise-operations)); a range expression with a computed step ([§16.4](#sec-stride)); and `await` are throwable. The `!` null-forgiving operator is throwable when the target is null.

The `as` operator is **not** throwable: a failed `as` cast returns `null` rather than raising ([§12.7](#sec-type-tests-is-is-not-as), [§17.4](#sec-the-is-is-not-and-as-operators)). Code that uses `as` between a move and the field-restoration point does not introduce an unrestored exception edge.

<a id="sec-loops-and-conditional-control-flow"></a>
#### Loops and conditional control flow

Loops that may execute zero times do not satisfy the rule:

```bezel
// ERROR: the while loop may run zero times, leaving _resource moved
//        but unreassigned.
public method WrongLoop(): owned Stream
  var old := move _resource;
  while SomeCondition() do
    _resource := MakeStream();
    break;
  end;
  return old;
end WrongLoop;
```

The fix is the same as the conditional case: ensure the reassignment is unconditional. Restructure so the reassignment dominates the exits:

```bezel
public method RightLoop(): owned Stream
  var fresh := MakeStream();
  while SomeCondition() do
    fresh := MakeStream();   // refine fresh in the loop
  end;
  var old := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;
  return old;
end RightLoop;
```

The analysis reuses the control-flow graph and dominance frontiers that the existing definite-assignment analysis builds for non-nullable locals ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)); no new machinery is required.

<a id="sec-constructors-and-destructors"></a>
#### Constructors and destructors

Both bodies are [K9.3](#sec-kernel-k9)'s cases. Inside a constructor body, the field has no value to move until it has been assigned: a `move x.f` before the field's first assignment is a definite-assignment violation, the same rule as for any other read of an unassigned non-nullable slot ([§7.9](#sec-definite-assignment-for-non-nullable-fields)). After the first assignment, `move` is permitted, with the same field-restoration rule applying to constructor exit paths.

Inside a destructor body, the field is being read for final disposal. `move x.f` inside a destructor takes the field's value out, which causes the compiler-generated auto-dispose pass for that field to skip it (the field is in moved-from state and has nothing to dispose). The taken value must still be discharged through one of the standard mechanisms — assigned to a local with `using var`, passed as `owned` to a helper, or explicitly disposed. The destructor's exit obligation is satisfied if the moved value reaches a discharge point; the field-restoration rule does *not* require reassignment inside a destructor (K9.3 — teardown, no future read).

<a id="sec-interaction-with-using-var"></a>
#### Interaction with `using var`

`using var u := move x.f;` is the canonical pattern for "take the field's value out and consume it scope-bound." The `using var` discharges the moved value at scope end; the field-restoration rule still applies at the surrounding method's exits.

```bezel
public method ProcessAndReplace()
  var fresh := new Stream();
  using var old := move _resource;        // moved into using var; disposed at scope end
  _resource := fresh;                      // restore
  // ... use old ...
  // at scope end: old.Dispose()
end ProcessAndReplace;
```

The using-var consumes the moved value; the explicit reassignment satisfies the field-restoration rule. No swap helper is needed.

<a id="sec-detaching-via-a-nullable-field"></a>
#### Detaching via a nullable field

A class that wants "take the resource away and leave the field empty" declares the field nullable and assigns `null` after the move:

```bezel
private owned _resource: Stream?;        // nullable

public method Detach(): owned Stream?
  if _resource = null then return null; end;
  var taken := move _resource!;          // move out the non-null contents
  _resource := null;                      // restore (to null)
  return taken;
end Detach;
```

The reassignment to `null` satisfies the field-restoration rule; the destructor's auto-dispose pass treats the null field correctly per [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields).

For non-nullable owned fields, "leave the field empty" is not expressible — by design, a non-nullable field's type contract says a value is always present. Code that needs sometimes-empty semantics declares the field nullable.

<a id="sec-interaction-with-overload-resolution-and-parameter-passing"></a>
#### Interaction with overload resolution and parameter passing

`move x.f` produces an owned value and is type-suitable as the argument to an `owned` parameter — but the exception-edge rule above applies with full force: a method call is throwable, so an argument-position move whose restoration follows the call is rejected on the call's exception edge (the compiling form is `TransferToHelperSafe` below):

```bezel
// ERROR: TakeOwnership may throw (method calls are throwable, above) — on that
//        edge _resource is moved but never reassigned: the WrongOrder shape.
public method TransferToHelper()
  var fresh := new Stream();
  TakeOwnership(move _resource);          // owned argument; helper consumes
  _resource := fresh;                      // restores the normal edge only
end TransferToHelper;
```

The argument expression `move _resource` runs as part of argument evaluation. The field is moved-from from the moment of the move expression's evaluation; the reassignment to `_resource` after the call would satisfy the rule on the **normal** edge only. Because `TakeOwnership` itself may throw — leaving the field moved but not reassigned — the exception edge is an unrestored exit, and the shape above is a **compile error** exactly as `WrongOrder` is. As with all exception-path concerns, the fix is to construct the replacement and reassign before the call:

```bezel
public method TransferToHelperSafe()
  var fresh := new Stream();
  var taken := move _resource;
  _resource := fresh;                      // restore before the call that may throw
  TakeOwnership(move taken);               // owned argument (call-site marker, §22.3), no field state at risk
end TransferToHelperSafe;
```

This is the same "build then take then restore" discipline, with the call moved to after the restore.

<a id="sec-runtime-managed-types"></a>
### 28.9 Runtime-managed types

The following types are exempt from manual disposal ([K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1)'s runtime-managed exemption). Their `Dispose()` is a no-op (or, for types that are not classes and therefore have no `Dispose()` at all, the type's lifetime is managed by the runtime without user involvement).

- `string` — pervasive; created by literals, interpolation, concatenation, and library methods.
- Boxed value types — created implicitly when a value type is used where `Object` (or an interface) is expected.
- **Function-typed values** — values of any function type `(T1, ..., Tn) -> R`, regardless of whether they capture. This includes lambda closures (capturing or not), method references (`obj.Method` and `Type.StaticMethod`), and any value whose static type is a function type. Function-typed fields, parameters, and locals are not subject to `owned` annotations and carry no disposal obligation; a `using var` local of function type is nonetheless permitted (disposal at scope end is a no-op) and serves only the [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) capture-scoping and non-reassignability roles.

  Runtime management governs the *function value itself* — the heap-allocated closure object that backs the function value. It does not relax the lifetime rules on values the closure captures. A lambda or method reference that captures a borrowed class reference is subject to the borrow-escape rules in [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows): the function value may be runtime-managed, but if it outlives the captured borrow's source, the program is rejected. The compiler tracks captured borrows separately from the function value's own lifetime.

  Capturing an *owned* class-typed local does **not** transfer ownership into the closure. Instead, the capture is treated as a borrow whose source is the local's enclosing scope; the closure may not outlive that scope. The capture is borrow-state throughout: the closure may not assign to, transfer from, or dispose the captured binding ([§28.3](#sec-captured-owned-bindings)). The original `using var` (or other owned location) retains the disposal obligation. This rule is what makes function-typed values runtime-managed without contradicting the no-GC promise: a closure cannot extend the lifetime of an owned class instance, so reclaiming the closure never leaves a destructor un-run. Programs that genuinely need to extend an owned class's lifetime past a closure boundary should restructure to keep the owned location in scope (for example, by storing the value in an owned field of a longer-lived object) or use `Task.FireAndForget` for the specific case of fire-and-forget tasks.

  Capturing a *move-only* local (an owning inline array, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) follows the same rule: the closure captures a borrow of the move-only value whose source is the local's enclosing scope. The closure may not outlive that scope. A move-only capture cannot be a copy (copying is forbidden for move-only types) and cannot be a move (the local is still in scope and accessible via its name; moving into the closure would leave the local in moved-from state in surprising ways). The borrow form is the only consistent option. Reads of slots through the captured borrow are admitted; `move arr[i]` through the captured borrow is not (the closure does not own the array). Programs that need to consume slot contents through a closure must arrange for the closure to take an owned-parameter argument and invoke it with `move`d slots from outside.

Note that **inline arrays** `[N]T` (see [§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) are not on this list. Inline arrays are value types, stored inline in their enclosing context; they have no separate allocation to reclaim and no disposal contract independent of their host. Inline arrays with owned slots (`[N owned]T?`) are move-only value types ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) that participate in the ownership system as part of their host's lifecycle. There is no separate runtime-managed fixed-size-array form; fixed-size arrays are inline arrays ([§15.1](#sec-inline-arrays)) and the heap arrays `Array<T>` / `OwningArray<T>` ([§15.2](#sec-heap-arrays)).

The compiler does not warn about undisposed runtime-managed values and does not require them to appear in `using var` or `owned` declarations.

The implementation of runtime-managed types' lifecycle (reference counting, region allocation, or other) is not part of this specification.

**Accessor faces are uniform across type kinds.** A property or indexer **read** is a lend for every declared type — the [A4](#sec-axiom-register)/[§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) rule for class and interface types, and the same face for runtime-managed types: a getter never transfers a reclamation obligation to its reader, and the two accessor body spellings of [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties) (`get => e` and `get => do … end`) are semantically indistinguishable at every read site. A getter body whose result is a fresh runtime-managed production (an interpolation, a concatenation, a library call) remains admissible — runtime-managed values are exempt from the ceremony — and the implementation reclaims the production; **how** is not specified, per the lifecycle carve above.

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-classes"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose classes

A class whose disposal **provably runs no user code and releases only memory** — it has no destructor, no `owned` fields of non-trivial-dispose type, no fields of owning-inline-array type (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`, [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)), and its base class (if any, other than `Object`) is itself trivial-dispose — is a **trivial-dispose class** (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1) — empty *user-visible* obligation content). The check is recursive and, for generics, per-instantiation ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2; the next subsection): an `owned` field whose declared type is itself trivial-dispose does **not** disqualify the holder — the synthesized disposal cascade over such fields frees memory and runs no user code, which is exactly what the property asserts. Mutually-recursive `owned` trivial-dispose references are admitted; the property is evaluated coinductively (assume the types under test trivial-dispose, then check the rules) — the same convention sendability states for its own recursive `owned` references ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)). *Provably runs no user code and releases only memory* means the generated `Dispose()` performs no user-authored work: it releases the instance's own allocation (including the intrinsic backing storage of the compiler-known borrowing collections, part of the instance's single allocation — [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)) and the trivial-dispose trees under its `owned` trivial-dispose fields; storage released by a declared destructor is not in that category (`OwningBuffer<T>`, below). Trivial-dispose classes are tracked like every other class — references to them are classified, source-bounded, and escape-checked by the letter of this chapter's rules. The exemption's principle: the ceremony announces observable disposal *effects*, and a trivial-dispose class's disposal has none to announce — which is why the exemption's boundary is exactly this section's runs-no-user-code line, and why it extends no further (Design Rationale [§5.28](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-silent-tracking)). They are exempt from the **ceremony** only:

- A `new` expression of a trivial-dispose class type whose result is not stored in an `owned` location or `using var` does *not* produce the standard ownership-discharge warning. (The obligation's user-visible content is empty: the compiler frees the undischarged value at its owner's release point, [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1).) The one adjacent diagnostic is [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s store-position lint — a distinct warning with its own trigger, not this exemption's.
- The discard statement `_ := expr;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) is legal for a trivial-dispose class: the value is freed at end of statement, no user code running — the same timing as for a non-trivial-dispose class ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); the difference is only whether the discard does cleanup work.
- Every trivial-dispose instance has exactly one statically-known owner at every point — the [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) classification it carries ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — and the compiler inserts a **free** at that owner's release point: scope end for locals and `using var` ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)); the K8 boundary for unbound temporaries ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); drop-on-overwrite for reassignment ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)); the containing object's teardown for `owned` fields ([§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)); process exit for statics ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)); after the matching catch arm for throw operands ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)); frame teardown for frame-held values ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)); and the aggregate owner's release point for literal-tree nodes ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)). The free is logical disposal followed by reclamation — it sets the per-instance disposed flag and runs no user code ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) — so checked disposal mode backstops a surviving borrow of a freed trivial-dispose instance exactly as for any other class.

`using var` on a trivial-dispose class is permitted; it names the owner explicitly and has no observable effect other than scope limitation (the free at scope end runs no user code).

Standard library classes that are trivial-dispose include `Random` ([§2.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-random) of the standard library) and the singleton `Encoding` subclass instances ([§3.2](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-encoding) of the standard library). User-defined classes with no destructor, no owned fields of non-trivial-dispose type, and no owning-inline-array fields are automatically trivial-dispose.

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-for-generic-class-instantiations"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose for generic class instantiations

For a generic class `C<T>` (or `C<T1, T2, ...>`), the trivial-dispose check is performed on the **instantiation** rather than on the generic declaration (derives: [K1.6](#sec-kernel-k1), computed per instantiation). The compiler substitutes the actual type arguments and applies the rules above to the resulting concrete class.

```bezel
public class Box<T>(value: T)
  public Value: T := value;
  // No destructor, no owned fields. Box<T> is trivial-dispose for any T.
end Box;

public class OwningBox<T>(owned value: T) where T: class
  public owned Value: T := value;
  // Has an owned field of T. OwningBox<T> is trivial-dispose exactly when the
  // substituted T is (§3.6 rule 2): the synthesized cascade over an owned
  // trivial-dispose field runs no user code.
end OwningBox;

using var m := new MyClass();
_ := new Box<int>(0);                          // OK (trivial-dispose)
_ := new Box<MyClass>(m);                      // OK (trivial-dispose; Box doesn't own its T — it borrows m)
_ := new OwningBox<MyClass>(new MyClass());    // OK (disposes the owned T field at end of statement, §17.13)
```

Per-instantiation analysis means trivial-dispose status is computed *after* type substitution — for an `owned` field of a substituted type, from whether the substituted type is itself trivial-dispose (the recursive clause of the definition above). The standard collection types — `Array<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>` — are trivial-dispose for every non-owned choice of type argument because they do not own their elements ([§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements)). A program that holds `Array<MyClass>` may discard the array (the elements remain owned by their original sources, unaffected by the array's free, which releases the array's own allocation only); a program that holds `OwningBox<MyClass>` may also discard it, but the discard *disposes* the box — its `owned` T field is disposed at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) — rather than merely releasing an empty shell.

The owned-element variants of the standard collection types — `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, etc. — are **not** trivial-dispose at any instantiation: they own their elements, disposal cascades through to the elements, and their storage primitive declares a destructor (below). A program that holds `OwningArray<MyClass>` carries the ordinary discharge obligations — the ceremony exemption does not apply, because element disposal needs to run. `OwningBuffer<T>` is similarly non-trivial-dispose for **both** element kinds: for class-typed T its destructor cascades through every non-null slot; for value-typed T the cascade is empty, but the type still declares a destructor over its manually-managed backing allocation (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)) — it is the user-expressible storage primitive, and destructor-released storage is exactly what the trivial-dispose definition excludes; the resizable owning collections compose over it through `owned` fields of that non-trivial type ([§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)), which is what keeps the owning family non-trivial at every instantiation. The contrast with `Array<T>` is the defining line: a borrowing collection's backing storage is an intrinsic part of the instance's single allocation, released by the instance's one compiler-inserted free with no user code running, so its `Dispose()` provably runs no user code and releases only memory.

The rule does not require the generic to be parameterized only by type arguments that are *themselves* trivial-dispose. `Array<MyClass>` is trivial-dispose even if `MyClass` is not, because the array's own surface contains nothing that needs disposal — `MyClass` instances are owned elsewhere, and the array's free doesn't dispose them. The key question is **does the generic class itself need to do disposal work**, not whether its element type does; a type argument's own trivial-dispose status enters the computation only where the class holds it through an `owned` field (the recursive clause above).

Per-instantiation status arises in practice through `owned` fields of substituted type: `OwningBox<T>` above is trivial-dispose at trivial-dispose substitutions and non-trivial-dispose elsewhere, with [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties) rule 2's instantiation-site machinery carrying the verdict. What the language does not admit is *conditionally-declared structure* — an `OwnedIfClass<T>` that has an `owned T` field only when T is a class type cannot be written (the `owned` modifier requires its field's type to be a class or interface, expressed at declaration time, not conditionally on the substitution).

<a id="sec-trivial-dispose-classification-is-part-of-the-api-surface"></a>
#### Trivial-dispose classification is part of the API surface

Adding a destructor, an `owned` field of non-trivial-dispose type, or an owning-inline-array field to a class promotes it from trivial-dispose to non-trivial-dispose — as does an existing `owned` field's declared type itself flipping non-trivial-dispose (the recursive clause above: the flip propagates through owned-field types, across modules). The flip changes **ceremony, never tracking** — both sides are tracked, and the free-or-dispose point is the owner's release point either way — but it can still be **source-affecting**: a `_ := new ThatClass();` discard that ran no user code now runs the destructor at end of statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)); an unused instance that was freed silently now draws the must-use auto-drop warning ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)); and a fresh instance admitted as a literal-tree node ([§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)) or as a plain-parameter default ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)) is rejected there after the upgrade, so code relying on those admissions may fail to compile.

API authors should:

- Treat the trivial-dispose status of public classes as part of their published contract.
- Document trivial-dispose status in the class's API documentation.
- Avoid adding a destructor to a previously-trivial class without bumping the major version of the containing module.

When the addition is necessary (the class genuinely now owns a resource), the standard migration-guide pattern applies: list the affected discard sites and direct callers to `using var _ := …`, an explicit `.Dispose()`, or `Task.FireAndForget` (for tasks).

<a id="sec-using-var"></a>
### 28.10 `using var`

*(The non-owned single-assignment counterpart is the runtime `const` local, [§21.1](#sec-variable-declarations): `using var` binds owned values with declared scope-end disposal; `const` binds values and borrows that carry no obligation.)*

`using var` declares a local that is disposed when the enclosing block ends:

```bezel
public method ProcessFile(filename: string)
  using var fs := new FileStream(filename, FileMode.Open);
  using var buffer := new Array<byte>(4096, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4)
  var data := fs.ReadAll();
  // fs and buffer disposed here in reverse order
end ProcessFile;
```

Disposal happens on every exit path: normal completion, `break`, `return`, or exception. **Cleanup ordering is uniform across exit edges:** `using var` compiles to `try`/`finally` ([§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally)), so `using var` disposals and explicit `finally` clauses form one establishment-ordered stack — on *every* exit edge (normal, `return`, `break`/`continue`, exception, and an iterator's early disposal, [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)), pending cleanups run in reverse order of establishment. No edge runs the two kinds in separate category-ordered phases. A `try` statement's own `finally` is **established at entry to the protected block** — before any establishment the block itself performs. Consequently, on every exit edge, an owned local or `using var` declared **inside** the protected block (established later) is disposed **before** the `finally` runs, exactly as the desugared nested `try`/`finally` of this section and [§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally) would dispose it; cleanups established **before** the `try` run after the `finally`, as before ([§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)).

An expression whose arm-meet is **owned** — a `??`, an `if` expression, or an expression-position `case`/`when` over owned producers (the [K7](#sec-kernel-k7) meet; [§28.3](#sec-producers)) — is an owned producer for this section's admission: `using var x := (if useFresh then new Buffer() else source.CloneBuffer());` — where `CloneBuffer` is declared `CloneBuffer(): owned Buffer`, making both arms fresh producers — binds `x` owned and disposes it at scope end. (An arm that is an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding is a borrow arm per the producers table — the whole expression is then a borrow and the `using var` a borrow-pin; a **marked** arm `move cached` is an owned arm.)

`using var` is a scope pin (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)): it is implicitly non-reassignable, and reassigning a `using var` variable is a compile error. To use a different resource later in the method, introduce a new `do ... end` block.

**Adopting a named owned binding (derives: [K3.4](#sec-kernel-k3)).** `using var y := move x;` transfers a named owned local or `owned` parameter into a scope-bound binding: `y` takes over the disposal obligation and `x` is left moved-from — the binding-position form of the [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers) transfer marker ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)). An **unmarked** `using var y := x;` where `x` is a named owned binding does *not* adopt: it is a borrow, pinned per the subsection below, and `x` retains the obligation.

**The anonymous binding.** `using var _ := expression;` (and `await using var _ := …;`, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)) is the **anonymous owning binding** ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)): the same scope-end disposal, non-reassignability, admission rules, and borrow-pin case as a named `using var` — with no name bound. `_` is not in scope after the declaration, and nothing can read the value; the form is the sanctioned spelling for holding a value to scope end without naming it (`using var _ := mutex.Acquire();`). Adoption composes: `using var _ := move x;` consumes `x` into the anonymous binding exactly as the named form would.

`using var` accepts a value-type or runtime-managed right-hand side. For ordinary value types and runtime-managed types, the disposal at scope end is a no-op (these types do not require disposal per [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), and the only effect is the reassignability restriction. For move-only inline arrays (`[N owned]…`, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), the local's owned slots are auto-disposed at scope end regardless of whether `using var` is used; the only additional effect of `using var` on a move-only local is the reassignability restriction. The uniform admissibility of `using var` across value-typed, runtime-managed, and move-only RHSes makes it safe to use uniformly in generic code or in compiler-generated desugarings (such as the for-loop body of [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) without inspecting the underlying type kind.

To dispose before the enclosing method returns, nest in a `do ... end`:

```bezel
public method Process()
  var result := 0;
  do
    using var fs := new FileStream("data.txt", FileMode.Open);
    using var buffer := new Array<byte>(4096, 0);   // sized ctor (stdlib §4.4)
    result := fs.Read(buffer, 0, buffer.Count);     // bytes read (stdlib §7.1)
  end;     // fs and buffer disposed here
  Console.WriteLine($"count = {result}");
end Process;
```

<a id="sec-using-var-initialized-from-a-borrow"></a>
#### `using var` initialized from a borrow

When the right-hand side of a `using var` declaration is a borrow rather than an owned value (a method call without an `owned` return — unless its declared return type is a `Task`-family type, an owned production per [§28.3](#sec-producers) — an indexer access, a field read, or an *unmarked* read of a named owned binding), the `using var` does **not** assume a disposal obligation (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) — no obligation can be assumed from a borrow): at scope end, no `Dispose()` is called, because the value is not owned by this scope. The `using var` still **pins** the borrow's source for the duration of the scope — meaning the borrow lifetime rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) treat the source as in-scope for the using-var's entire lexical extent. Concretely: the source must remain live (not moved, not disposed) until the using-var's scope ends, exactly as if the borrow were used at every point up to the end of the scope. Pinning is a compile-time constraint, not a runtime mechanism; the compiler enforces it by extending the source's required-liveness range to cover the using-var's scope.

This case is what allows the for-loop desugaring ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for)) to wrap an arbitrary source in `using var __source := source` without taking ownership when `source` is borrowed; programmers also encounter it directly when using `using var` for scope-pinning of a borrowed iterable.

<a id="sec-collections-do-not-own-elements"></a>
<a id="sec-collection-element-ownership"></a>
### 28.11 Collection element ownership

Bezel has two families of collection types (axiom [A9](#sec-axiom-register)):

- **Borrowing collections** (`Array<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>`) store references that the caller continues to own. The collection's `Dispose()` is a no-op — borrowing collections are trivial-dispose ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), their backing storage part of the instance's single allocation and released with it by the instance's one free — and elements are **not** disposed. Element disposal is the arrangement of whoever owns the elements — owned bindings, owned fields, or an owning-family collection; it never happens through the borrowing collection ([§28.6](#sec-who-may-dispose)).

- **Owning collections** (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningSet<T>`, `OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`) own their elements. The collection's `Dispose()` cascades through every element. Every owned-ingress member takes ownership — `Add`/`Insert` on the `IOwningCollection<T>` conformers, `Push`/`Enqueue` on `OwningStack<T>`/`OwningQueue<T>` (the order-disciplined pair declares no `Add`/`Remove`/`RemoveAt`; its egress is `Pop`/`Dequeue`/`Try*`/`Drain`); the indexer setter disposes the previous slot value before installing the new one; `Remove`/`RemoveAt`/`Clear` dispose the affected elements on the types that declare them. Owning collections require `where T: class` (and, for `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `where V: class`) — owning makes sense only for class-typed values.

The two families are declared separately in the standard library ([§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)). A program chooses the form that matches the intended ownership semantics. There is no implicit conversion between the two families; an `OwningArray<Connection>` is not an `Array<Connection>` and vice versa.

<a id="sec-element-slot-policy"></a>
#### The element slot policy

Every standard collection's element semantics follow from one classification, not from per-collection rules (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) per slot + [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)/[K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) for stored borrows). A collection's slots are classified by the collection's family and the element type's *element category* — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)):

| Element category | Borrowing family slots | Owning family slots |
|---|---|---|
| value type (non-move-only) | copies | *(rejected at instantiation)* |
| runtime-managed reference (`string`, function types, boxed values; [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) | shared references | *(rejected at instantiation)* |
| class / interface type | borrows | owned |
| move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — owning inline arrays and owning-classified choices, [§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) | *(rejected at instantiation)* | *(rejected at instantiation)* |

(The owning family admits only class/interface element types; see the instantiation-site restriction in [§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument). Move-only element types are deferred for both families — see stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans) and the rationale.) For dictionaries the classification applies independently to the key slots and the value slots: an owning dictionary owns its *values*; its keys are value-like and classified per the borrowing column (stdlib [§4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)).

The slot kind alone determines what every element operation does:

| Operation | copy slots | shared-reference slots | borrow slots | owned slots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| store (`Add`, `Insert`, indexer-set) | copies the value in (a **borrow-bearing record** value carries [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s lifetime obligation: every carried source must provably outlive the collection — statically checked) | stores the reference | stores the borrow; the element's source must outlive the collection's use of it (enforced per the store rule under *Borrowing collections* below) | takes `owned`; indexer-set disposes the previous value first (skipped for a moved-from slot) |
| `Remove` / `RemoveAt` | drops the copy | drops the reference | drops the borrow; the caller's ownership is unaffected | **disposes** the removed element |
| `Clear()` | drops all | drops all | drops all | **disposes** every element |
| `Dispose()` of the collection | no user-visible work (the backing storage is part of the instance's allocation, released with it — [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) | no user-visible work (as previous column) | no user-visible work; elements untouched | **disposes** every live element — reverse-insertion order for ordered collections, implementation-defined order for unordered — then releases storage |
| indexer-get / default iteration | copy out | reference out | borrow out (source: the element's original owner; the collection is a transit point) | borrow out (source: the collection) |
| ownership out | *(none — nothing owned)* | *(none)* | *(none)* | `move coll[i]`, the `Pop*` family, `Drain()` |

The per-collection clauses in the remainder of this section and in the standard library document ([§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic)) are presentations of this table for each concrete type; they do not introduce element semantics of their own, and a per-collection statement that diverges from the table is a defect in this specification. The storage embodiment of the owning column is `OwningBuffer<T>` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), the primitive over which the resizable owning collections compose; the borrowing family's storage remains a compiler intrinsic in this revision, because a user-expressible borrow-storing primitive needs its own borrow-lifetime rules (storing borrows in fields is otherwise rejected, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — that design is deferred, recorded in the rationale.

<a id="sec-borrowing-collections"></a>
#### Borrowing collections

For a borrowing collection type (`Array<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, etc.), the standard operations are:

- **`Dispose()`** is a no-op ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types); the backing storage is part of the instance's single allocation and is released by the instance's free). Elements are **not** disposed.
- **`Clear()`** removes all elements without disposing them.
- **`Add(item: T)`**, **`Insert(index, item: T)`**, **indexer-set** `coll[i] := value` accept borrowed references and store them.
- **`Remove(item)`** removes the first equal element (by `Equals`) and returns `bool`. **`RemoveAt(index)`** removes the element at the given index and returns `()`. Neither method disposes the removed element on a borrowing collection — the caller continues to own it (if it had ownership) or it goes out of scope (if it was borrowed transit). The **indexer-get** `coll[i]` produces a borrowed reference whose source is whichever owner the borrow originally came from. The collection is a transit point, not a source.

**Storing a borrow (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)).** Storing a class-typed borrow into a borrowing collection follows the same shape as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field rule. The store-site check is structural and decidable: parameter-, receiver-, and field-sourced borrows are admitted; a borrow of a **scope-bound local** stored into a collection that provably outlives that scope — the collection is a field, is reachable from one, escapes the method, or is a local of strictly wider scope — is **rejected** at the store site. The residual is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause: whether each admitted element's source actually outlives the collection's use of it is the programmer's obligation, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net; the obligation includes **not transferring an admitted element's source object to another domain** — nor consuming it into a domain-reachable construction ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s domain-clause extension) — while the collection retains the borrow — that violation has no runtime backstop (the object stays alive; [§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains), the same domain clause as the borrowed-field rule). A **fresh unbound owned temporary** of class type passed to `Add`/`Insert`/indexer-set is not a borrow of any named source but a temporary that dies at its K8 boundary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): the store is admitted under [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s recorded literal-only-rejection asymmetry and draws that section's fresh-store warning — since v0.243 over the full class-typed set, trivial-dispose, `Task`-family, and other non-trivial-dispose arguments alike, the hazard stated per family there — the retained reference dangles at the boundary, and a later use through it faults in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)).

A holding class that semantically owns its elements declares an owning-family collection — the type states the intent and `Dispose()` cascades. (A `DisposeElements()` escape hatch let a borrowing collection's holder dispose elements en masse; it is retired with axiom A8 — the vouch it required is exactly what the owning family expresses structurally.)

The recommended pattern when a class semantically owns a collection-of-resources but uses a borrowing collection type:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private owned _transactions: OwningArray<Transaction>;

  public constructor()
    _transactions := new OwningArray<Transaction>();
  end constructor;
end BankAccount;
```

`owned` on the field handles container disposal, and the owning collection's cascade disposes every element — no destructor is needed. A class wanting *selective or interleaved* cleanup takes elements out first — `Drain()` in a loop, `move _transactions[i]`, or the `Pop*` family — into owned bindings whose disposal it controls.

A dictionary whose holder owns the **values** (keys value-like or shared) is `OwningDictionary<K, V>`'s shape by construction — it owns its values, keys are value-like, and `Dispose()` cascades over the values ([stdlib §4.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owneddictionaryk-v)); no manual pass exists or is needed. The reverse asymmetry (owned keys, borrowed values) has no collection form and no recorded client; a holder with that shape keeps the keys in an owning collection of their own. For collections where ownership of values *is* the natural model, the owning form (next subsection) is preferred.

<a id="sec-owning-collections"></a>
#### Owning collections

An owning collection (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `OwningStack<T>`, etc.) owns its elements. The standard library [§4](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-generic) declares the owning-collection family. Not every owning collection declares every member below: `OwningStack<T>`/`OwningQueue<T>` declare none of `Add`/`Insert`/`Remove`/`RemoveAt` and have no indexer — their owned ingress is `Push`/`Enqueue`, their ownership egress `Pop`/`Dequeue`/`Try*`/`Drain` — while `Clear`, `Dispose`, and `Drain` are family-wide. The signature changes that distinguish owning from borrowing collections are:

- **`Add(owned item: T)`** accepts an owned argument. The caller transfers ownership to the collection.
- **`Insert(index: int, owned item: T)`** likewise.
- **Indexer set** `coll[i] := value` requires `value` to be owned. The previous value at that slot is disposed before the assignment installs the new one (drop-on-overwrite — the paragraph below).
- **`Remove(item: T)`** and **`RemoveAt(index: int)`** dispose the removed element.
- **`Clear()`** disposes every element.
- **`Dispose()`** disposes every element, then frees the backing storage.
- **Indexer get** `coll[i]` produces a borrow of the slot's value, exactly as for borrowing collections. Reading does not transfer ownership; `move coll[i]` is the explicit-take form ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) — see below for the collection-slot extension).

The "indexer-set disposes the previous value" rule is the same drop-on-overwrite discipline [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields) applies to owned-field and owned-local assignment ([K3.11](#sec-kernel-k3)): in both forms the compiler disposes the displaced live value before installing the new one, so neither requires an explicit `Dispose()` at the assignment site. For a slot already in moved-from state (after `move coll[i]`), the setter detects the empty slot at runtime and skips the disposal step before installing the new value — the same live-value guard §28.7 applies to a moved-from field or local.

A user-written *property setter* over an owned field declares an **owned-taking accessor** and contains an ordinary owned-field assignment in its body (`set(owned)` with body `=> _cache := value;`, [§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties) — the default borrow-taking `value` cannot be assigned to an owned field per [§28.3](#sec-ownership-state-of-locals)'s state-match rule), which drop-on-overwrites the displaced value per [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields): the setter needs no explicit `Dispose()`. Writing one anyway (`set(owned) => do _cache.Dispose(); _cache := value; end;`) is legal but redundant — the explicit disposal makes the assignment's implicit drop-on-overwrite an idempotent no-op, [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s blessed dispose-then-assign legacy shape. The auto-disposal is a property of the owned-field *assignment*, not of the setter wrapper; the compiler-synthesized indexer setter on owning collections uses the same discipline.

In addition, owning collections expose **drain methods** that transfer ownership of elements out of the collection:

- **`PopAt(index: int): owned T`** removes the element at the given index and returns it as owned. The slot is closed (subsequent indices shift down for sequence types; the dictionary entry is removed for `OwningDictionary`).
- **`PopFirst(): owned T`** and **`PopLast(): owned T`** for the common cases on `OwningArray`, `OwningLinkedList`. `OwningStack.Pop` and `OwningQueue.Dequeue` are the equivalent operations for those types, returning `owned T`.
- **`Drain(): IOwningEnumerable<T>`** returns an iterable that drains the source as it is iterated. After full iteration, the source collection is empty. Partial iteration drains only the elements yielded; the rest remain. The user iterates with `for var item in coll.Drain() do ... end;`, where `item` is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules apply in the loop body (`using var u := move item;` is the typical form — marker; an undischarged item auto-drops at body end with the must-use warning).

Owning collections need no explicit element pass: disposing the collection already disposes the elements — the cascade is the type's contract.

Default iteration `for var item in coll do ... end` (where `coll` has static type `OwningArray<T>`, etc.) produces *borrows* of each element via the collection's `IEnumerable<T>` conformance. The collection still owns its elements after iteration. To consume, iterate over `coll.Drain()`, which has static type `IOwningEnumerable<T>` and yields owned values.

```bezel
public method UseEach()
  using var pool := new OwningArray<Connection>();
  pool.Add(Connect("primary"));      // ownership transfers in
  pool.Add(Connect("secondary"));     // ownership transfers in

  // Default iteration: each conn is a borrow
  for var conn in pool do
    conn.Ping();                      // pool still owns conn afterward
  end;

  // Drain iteration: each conn is owned
  for var conn in pool.Drain() do
    using var c := move conn;         // discharge each owned element
    c.SendShutdown();
  end;
  // pool is now empty; using var on pool disposes the (empty) array
end UseEach;
```

When an owning collection is itself disposed (whether at the end of a `using var` scope, in a destructor's auto-dispose pass, or at static-program-exit for a static `owned` field), every element it still holds is disposed first, then the backing storage is freed. The element-disposal order is implementation-defined for unordered collections (`OwningDictionary`, `OwningSet`), and is reverse-insertion-order for ordered collections (`OwningArray`, `OwningLinkedList`, `OwningStack`, `OwningQueue`).

<a id="sec-move-on-a-collection-slot"></a>
#### `move` on a collection slot

The `move` expression form ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) extends to owning-collection slots. `move coll[i]` reads the i-th element of an owning collection as an owned value, leaving the slot in moved-from state.

The `move coll[i]` form is admitted on:

- Owning heap collections that support indexer syntax — `OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, and `OwningBuffer<T>` for class-typed T (the dynamic-size owning storage primitive, stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)). `OwningBuffer<T>` for value-typed T does *not* admit `move` — values have no ownership to transfer; the plain indexer-get suffices.
- `Span<T>` for class-typed T (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), which delegates to the underlying `OwningBuffer<T>`. `move span[i]` is equivalent to `move span.Buffer[span.Start + i]` — it takes ownership of the slot's value and leaves the slot in moved-from state in the *underlying buffer*, not in the span (the span is a stateless view; it carries no slot state of its own). `move span[i]` bounds-checks against `span.Length` before delegating; if `i < 0` or `i >= span.Length`, `IndexOutOfRangeException` is thrown and no slot is moved-from. This matches the bounds-check behavior of the span's plain indexer-get and indexer-set. The field-restoration rule applies to the buffer slot in the usual way; the natural restoration is `span[i] := null`. `Span<T>` for value-typed T does not admit `move` (mirroring the underlying buffer). `ReadOnlySpan<T>` does not admit `move` for any T (it exposes no writable indexer and no take operation).
- Owning inline arrays — both `[N owned]T?` and `[N owned]T` (see [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays)).

`Array<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, and the other borrowing collections do not admit `move coll[i]` — their slots hold borrows, not owned values; there is no ownership to transfer. The same applies to `ArraySpan<T>` and `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)), which view into a borrowing `Array<T>` source: `move arrSpan[i]` is rejected at compile time. The string-backed read-only span type `ReadOnlyStringSpan` (stdlib [§3.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-readonlystringspan)) also does not admit `move` — strings are immutable and their character data is reference-shared; no ownership transfer applies. The plain indexer-get is the only read form for all these types.

`OwningStack<T>`, `OwningQueue<T>`, `OwningLinkedList<T>`, and `OwningSet<T>` do not have indexers (`stack[i]`, `linkedList[i]`, etc. do not parse), so `move` cannot syntactically apply to their slots. These structured-or-unordered collection types provide their own ownership-out methods (`Pop`, `Dequeue`, `Take`, etc.) that perform the equivalent take-and-discharge in a single call.

The field-restoration rule applies ([K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9), with per-slot tracking): the slot must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits. For nullable element types (`OwningArray<T>` internally storing `T?`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, `[N owned]T?`, `OwningBuffer<T>` for class-typed T which stores `T?`), assigning `null` to a moved-from slot satisfies the rule. For non-nullable element types (`[N owned]T`), restoration requires assigning a fresh owned T value — a constructor call, another moved value, or a borrow promoted to ownership. Code that needs "leave the slot empty after take" must use the nullable form. (For value-typed `OwningBuffer<T>` the rule is moot — `move buf[i]` is not admitted, so no restoration obligation arises.)

**Indexer setter on a moved-from slot.** When the slot is in moved-from state, assigning to it through the indexer setter does *not* trigger the owned-setter's "dispose previous value" semantics — the previous value was already taken out by `move`, so there is no previous value to dispose. The slot transitions directly from moved-from to holding the new value. This matches owned-field/local reassignment ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)): a moved-from location accepts the new value with nothing to dispose. The compiler's per-slot moved-from tracking is what makes this distinguishable from a non-moved-from slot, where the setter does dispose the previous value.

The compiler tracks moved-from state per slot when the index is a compile-time constant or a local read. For variable indices that the compiler cannot prove are constant within the method, the analysis is conservative: after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state. The admissible restoration operations depend on the collection kind:

- For heap owning collections (`OwningArray<T>`, `OwningDictionary<K, V>`, and class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`): `coll[j] := value` for any `j` (treated as restoration of one slot if `j` matches the moved index, or as unrelated reassignment otherwise), `coll.Clear()` for those that provide it, or `coll.Dispose()` (which dispose the entire collection, satisfying the obligation by destruction). `OwningBuffer<T>` does not provide `Clear()` directly; the equivalent is a loop assigning `null` to every slot or simply disposing the buffer.
- For inline owning arrays (`[N owned]T?` or `[N owned]T`): `arr[j] := value` for any `j` (for nullable forms, `arr[j] := null` is also a valid restoration that marks slots empty). Inline arrays have no `Clear()` or `Dispose()` method (they are value types, not classes); restoration is per-slot assignment only.

The `PopAt` family of methods covers the common case where the user wants to take an element out and let the collection close the gap; `move coll[i]` is the building block for advanced cases where the slot is taken and immediately reassigned to a new value:

```bezel
public method ReplaceAt(index: int, owned newValue: T)
  var old := move pool[index];      // take from slot
  pool[index] := newValue;           // restore slot with new value
  old.Dispose();                     // dispose the old value
  // (or `using var taken := move pool[index];` for scope-bound disposal)
end ReplaceAt;
```

The same exception-safety rules apply: any throwable expression between the move and the reassignment must be an exit path on which the slot has been restored. The "build before take" discipline from [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) carries over directly.

<a id="sec-compatibility-between-borrowing-and-owning-forms"></a>
#### Compatibility between borrowing and owning forms

`Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` are distinct, unrelated types. There is no implicit conversion between them in either direction. A program that has an `OwningArray<T>` and needs to expose it as a borrowing surface (`Array<T>`) must drain the owning array (consuming each owned element) and rebuild a borrowing array of borrows; the spec provides no shorthand for this because the operation always loses information (the original owner of each element is the caller's responsibility once drained).

The most common case where this conversion is *not* what the programmer wants: passing an `OwningArray<T>` to a method expecting `Array<T>`. The intent is usually "let the callee read the elements" — for which the answer is to expose `IEnumerable<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, or `IReadOnlyList<T>` (the borrowing views). Both `Array<T>` and `OwningArray<T>` implement these read-only iteration interfaces, so a consumer signature using one of them accepts either source:

```bezel
public method ReportEach(items: IEnumerable<Connection>)
  for var c in items do Console.WriteLine(c.Name); end;
end ReportEach;

public method UseOwnedPool()
  using var pool := new OwningArray<Connection>();
  pool.Add(Connect("a"));
  pool.Add(Connect("b"));
  ReportEach(pool);     // OK: OwningArray<Connection> implements IEnumerable<Connection>
                        //     iteration yields borrows
end UseOwnedPool;
```

A generic helper works the same way:

```bezel
public method ReportEachGeneric<T>(items: IEnumerable<T>) where T: class
  for var c in items do Console.WriteLine(c.ToString()); end;   // Object's surface only under `where T: class` (§14.2)
end ReportEachGeneric;

// Call with Array<Connection>: T inferred as Connection.
// Call with OwningArray<Connection>: T inferred as Connection.
// Same generic instantiation for both source forms.
```

The borrowing-iteration interfaces (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`) are the shared abstractions between the two collection families. The mutating interfaces (`ICollection<T>`/`IList<T>` for borrowing; `IOwningCollection<T>`/`IOwningList<T>` for owning) are separate hierarchies, intentionally so — `Add` has different semantics in each (borrow-taking vs. owned-taking). Code that abstracts over mutation must pick one hierarchy.

<a id="sec-asynchronous-disposal"></a>
### 28.12 Asynchronous disposal

For resources requiring asynchronous cleanup, classes may implement `IAsyncDisposable`:

```bezel
interface IAsyncDisposable
  method DisposeAsync(): Task;
end IAsyncDisposable;
```

`DisposeAsync` is declared without an `async` modifier on the interface; `async` is an implementation-side modifier and never appears on interface method declarations. Implementations add `async` to the matching method and use `await` freely.

A class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` also has its compiler-generated synchronous `Dispose`. The two are distinct phases of the disposal lifecycle:

1. **Logical disposal** runs once. For `await using`, the awaited `DisposeAsync()` performs whatever asynchronous cleanup the class defines; the destructor body (if any) is **not** also run, because `DisposeAsync` supersedes it. For plain `using` (or a synchronous `Dispose()` call) on a class that implements both, the destructor body runs synchronously and `DisposeAsync` is **not** invoked — the class's two cleanup paths are alternatives, not a sequence. A user-written `DisposeAsync` should not call `Dispose` itself.
2. **Physical reclamation** runs once, after logical disposal has completed: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, the base class's reclamation chains, and the heap block is released. This phase is the same regardless of which logical-disposal path ran. For `await using`, the runtime invokes physical reclamation as the second step of the implicit `Dispose()` it issues after `DisposeAsync` returns; the destructor body that would normally run in the synchronous path is skipped. The rule is object-central: physical reclamation runs **exactly once, immediately after whichever logical-disposal path completes** — a synchronous `Dispose()`, `await using`'s implicit sequence, or a **direct `DisposeAsync()` call** awaited outside `await using` (legal; the awaited task's completion is logical-disposal completion, and reclamation follows exactly as if `await using` had issued it). This includes the fault edge: when `DisposeAsync` completes **by throwing**, logical disposal is over — the runtime performs physical reclamation, then the exception propagates from the await.
