A `DisposeAsync()` task that is itself abandoned without an await (e.g. `using var t := obj.DisposeAsync();` dropped) still runs to its terminal state ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)); logical disposal completes at that terminal state and reclamation follows there — abandonment delays reclamation, it never skips it. Cleanup faults never leak the object ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s exactly-once invariant; the §22.9 exception-safety posture).

**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown ([§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement), [§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields), [§28.11](#sec-collections-do-not-own-elements), [§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) — always take the synchronous `Dispose()` path, on every edge and in every context including `async` bodies: an implicit disposal point never awaits. Asynchronous cleanup runs only where the program wrote `await using` (whose implicit `finally` awaits `DisposeAsync` on both the normal and exception edges of an async body, with [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous fallback on early iterator abandonment) or awaited a direct `DisposeAsync()` call. A class whose async cleanup must run therefore needs an `await using var` binding — the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning on an implicitly-dropped value is the nudge — and the no-destructor warning below covers the class side.

A class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` and has resources requiring cleanup **should** also declare a `destructor` that performs the synchronous fallback of the same cleanup. If a class implements `IAsyncDisposable` but has no destructor, synchronous `Dispose()` performs only physical reclamation (owned-field disposal and base chaining) — any cleanup that `DisposeAsync` would have performed is skipped. The compiler emits a warning when a class implements `IAsyncDisposable` without a destructor: *"Class implements IAsyncDisposable but has no destructor; synchronous Dispose() will skip async cleanup."*

A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has run is a no-op ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence rule). The runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method.

The compiler-inserted free of a **trivial-dispose** instance ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) is this same two-phase lifecycle in degenerate form: logical disposal sets the per-instance flag and runs no user code, and physical reclamation follows — immediately in unchecked builds, deferrable under checked mode's quarantine latitude ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) so the flag stays readable behind surviving borrows.

`await using` is the async counterpart of `using var`:

```bezel
public async method ProcessAsync(): Task
  // ConnectAsync and SendAsync are illustrative: the standard library's
  // System.Net module is deferred to a future revision (std lib §11).
  await using var connection := await ConnectAsync(url);
  await connection.SendAsync(data);
  // connection.DisposeAsync() awaited at scope end
end ProcessAsync;
```

`await using` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda.

When a class implements both `IDisposable` and `IAsyncDisposable`, prefer `await using` in async contexts.

<a id="sec-shared-ownership"></a>
### 28.13 Shared ownership: `Shared<T>` and `Weak<T>`

The ownership model is single-owner: every disposal obligation has exactly one holder. `Shared<T>` (stdlib [§2.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-shared-and-weak)) is the scoped exception — a compiler-known class whose instances (*handles*) jointly own one underlying value; the value is disposed exactly once, when the last handle is disposed. Shared ownership is opt-in, visible at every site (`Clone()` is an explicit call), and **domain-local except for synchronized `T`** (see the sendability rule below; [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)).

```bezel
using var primary := new Shared<Connection>(Connect("db"));   // consumes the owned Connection; count = 1
using var second  := primary.Clone();                          // count = 2; an independent owned handle
second.Get().Ping();                                           // borrow of the underlying Connection
// scope end: second disposed (count 1), then primary disposed (count 0) → Connection disposed
```

The semantics, stated against the existing model:

- **Handles are ordinary owned class instances.** Every rule of this chapter applies to a handle unchanged: it is produced owned (by `new Shared<T>(...)` or `Clone()`), discharged by `using var`, an `owned` field, an `owned` parameter or return, `move`, or explicit `Dispose()`; branch joins, exception-path discharge, and the leak-prevention rules of [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention) see nothing new. A handle may be stored in owning collections (`OwningArray<Shared<T>>`) like any class instance. The *only* novel behavior is inside the compiler-known type: the shared count, and last-one-disposes.
- **`new Shared<T>(owned value: T)`** consumes an owned T — the constructor is an owned-consuming position like any other ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); after construction the handle's disposal obligation *is* the value's. `T` must be a proper class type; runtime-managed and value types are rejected at instantiation ([§14.4](#sec-owned-as-a-generic-argument) pattern — they have no disposal obligation to share).
- **`Clone(): owned Shared<T>`** produces a new handle and increments the count. Cost and intent are visible at the call site; there is no implicit handle duplication anywhere in the language (assigning a handle moves or borrows it per the ordinary rules — it never silently clones).
- **`Get(): T`** produces a *borrow of the underlying value whose source is the handle*, valid while that handle lives — the same shape as the owning-collection indexer-get ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy) owned column: borrow out, source: the collection). The borrow does not extend the value's lifetime; the handle does. [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s owned-field-return rule is not violated: `Get()` is the compiler-known accessor dispensation that owning-collection reads already have.
- **Disposal.** Disposing a handle decrements the count; disposing the last live handle disposes the underlying value (running its destructor cascade normally). Handle disposal is idempotent per [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract). The exactly-once invariant of [Appendix C](#sec-appendix-c) is preserved: the value's `Dispose()` runs once, from the last handle.
- **Cycles leak.** A value that (transitively, through owned fields) holds a `Shared<T>` handle participating in its own ownership keeps its count above zero forever — the standard reference-counting hazard. The compiler does not detect ownership cycles through `Shared<T>`. Break cycles with `Weak<T>`.
- **`Weak<T>`** (stdlib [§2.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-shared-and-weak)) is a non-owning observer minted from a handle (`shared.Downgrade(): owned Weak<T>`). A weak handle does not keep the underlying value alive; **`TryUpgrade(): owned Shared<T>?`** atomically produces a new strong handle if the value is still alive, and `null` otherwise (Try shape (b), stdlib §1 — the handle is a proper class type at every instantiation, so null alone carries the signal; `using var` + null test at the call site, the `Mutex.TryAcquire` idiom). Weak handles are themselves ordinary owned class instances and are disposed like any other.
- **Aliasing.** Multiple handles give multiple borrows of one mutable value within a domain. This is serial-execution-safe ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)) and carries the same *logical* aliasing hazards as any other long-lived borrow; nothing about `Shared<T>` relaxes use-after-dispose ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) for borrows taken from a handle that is then disposed.
- **Sendability.** `Shared<T>` is sendable **iff `T` is in the `Shared`-payload synchronized set**: the derived set of every type declaring the **synchronized** or the **immutable** fact and not the **self-distributing** fact (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-statics-and-sharing-facts)'s statics-and-sharing facts — the formula is normative, and each grant's grounds live on the type's own fact line; derived membership (shared-payload), informative — currently `Mutex`, `Atomic<T>`, `AtomicInteger<T>`, `Semaphore`, `Locked<T>`, `RwLocked<T>`, and `FrozenArray<T>` — stdlib §4.19, and stdlib §6.2–§6.4, §6.11; machine-checked, `scripts/check_docs.sh` 3b). The **synchronized** disjunct admits real synchronization machinery — for the data-owning locks, interior sendable by instantiation ([§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)); the **immutable** disjunct is sound with no machinery at all: no writer can exist after construction (stdlib §4.19's recorded construction obligations, for the disjunct's first member `FrozenArray<T>` — **deep immutability** rather than machinery), and the reclamation synchronization that sharing needs is carried by `Shared<T>`'s own synchronized handle count together with the string-precedent storage tolerance ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)). The **self-distributing** exclusion keeps out `ChannelSender<T>` and `SharedEventSource<T>`, though both are internally synchronized: each already has its own sanctioned distribution channel — senders are minted per producer from the channel ([§30.15](#sec-channels)); static reachability is the shared source's ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 5, stdlib §6.5) — and `Shared<T>` wrapping would add a second (the grounds at each fact line). Growth is governed by stdlib §1's fact discipline: a derived set grows only by a **fact ruling**, which states the facts it grants and confronts each derived-set consequence in its record — the divergence protections the former per-set clause carried (form-(i) membership never implying membership here, and vice versa) are now structural, held by the **self-distributing** and **displacement-unbounded** facts, the two recorded reasons the sets ever diverged. For such `T`, a cloned handle may move to another domain (as a spawn argument or through a channel), and the handle count is maintained with synchronized operations; the underlying value is still disposed exactly once, by whichever domain drops the last handle. For every other `T`, `Shared<T>` remains domain-local and not sendable — the count synchronization alone would not make an unsynchronized `T` safe to reach from two domains. This realizes §6.2's "reached by multiple domains simultaneously" for mutexes: `Shared<Mutex>` is the cross-domain sharing idiom (clone, move the clone, both domains `Get().AcquireAsync()` — the blocking `Acquire()` is barred inside domain continuations, [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization)).

---

<a id="sec-scoped-callback-parameters"></a>
### 28.14 Scoped callback parameters: storage-bounded capture

The closure-capture rules ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) admit three escape forms — immediate invocation, a `using var` local of function type, and a closure passed as an argument to a function-typed parameter — all bounded by the borrow's source. This section defines the last form's two variants, whose bound is carried by the parameter's signature: a plain parameter is **call-bounded** (the callback is scoped to the call), and a `scoped` parameter is **storage-bounded** — **a stored callback whose lifetime is bounded by the object that stores it** (derives: [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5), under axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)'s forms).

**The `scoped` modifier.** A function-typed parameter may be declared `scoped`: `method Spawn(scoped body: () -> Task)`. The declaration is a two-sided contract:

- **The callee may store the callback**, but only in `scoped` fields **of the bounding object itself** (below), or forward it to another `scoped` parameter whose bounding object is the same object; it may invoke it. It may not return it, move it into non-`scoped` storage, or store it in any other object. A `scoped` **field** holds such a callback: it may be invoked, overwritten, or cleared, but never read out as an escaping value — including into a deferred-activation call: passing a `scoped` field's value to a plain function-typed parameter whose call mints a deferred-activation frame (below) is such an escaping read-out and is rejected, since the frame would retain the stored callback independently of the bounding object and beyond severance's reach; the capture-set contribution ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) soundly assigns storage reads nothing only because this read-out is barred. *(Liftable: a future revision may instead admit the read with the field's owner as the contributed source, bounding the frame by the bounding object.)* These obligations are compiler-verified for user-authored callees. *(v1 deliberately excludes storage reached through owned fields of the bounding object: an owned child holding the callback could be moved out (§28.8.1), extending the callback past its bound. Direct fields only.)* A `scoped` parameter on a **static** method is admitted only when the method's return is `owned`, so that a call site can resolve bounding form 2 or 3; declaring `scoped` on a static method with no `owned` return is a compile error — there is no receiver, no constructed object, and no instance to hold the stored value, so nothing could ever bound the storage.
- **The caller's captures are storage-bounded.** At the call site the compiler resolves the **bounding object** (axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)):
  1. a constructor call → the constructed object;
  2. a call whose return is `owned` **and** is the initializer of a `using var`/`await using var` local → the returned object;
  3. a call whose return is `owned` **and** is directly assigned to (or initializes) an **`owned` field of `this`** → `this`;
  4. a call whose receiver is a **member chain** rooted at `this` or a local binding in which every hop is an **`owned` field** — → the **chain head**: `this` for `this._clicked.Add(h)` (and the bare `_clicked += h` spelling — the stdlib §6.5 event pattern), the local `pub` for `pub._clicked.Add(h)` (cross-instance `private` access is class-keyed, [§13.1](#sec-levels)). A chain containing a non-owned (borrow) field hop, an indexer, a getter, or an intervening call resolves **no** bounding object (capture-free callbacks only): across a borrow hop the storing object is externally owned and may outlive the chain head, so the head's teardown would not sever the registration (*liftable*: a future revision may admit *transparent getters* — an expression-bodied getter whose body is a bare read of an `owned` field of its receiver, exactly the stdlib §6.5 event pattern's property — restoring chain-hop resolution through such properties; recorded, not shipped);
  5. otherwise → the receiver.

  The forms are tested **in order; the first that resolves determines the bounding object** — `using var sub := pub.Clicked.Subscribe(h)` bounds by `sub` (form 2, the tightest bound; `Clicked` being the stdlib §6.5 pattern's getter-faced property, no later form would resolve a bound at all — an off-idiom discharge of the `Subscription` admits capture-free handlers only, with the `using var`/owned-field discharges of forms 2/3 as the admitted capture-bearing spellings).

  A closure argument capturing locals or parameters is admitted **iff** the bounding object resolves to one of:
  - a `using var`/`await using var` local `L` (directly, through the initializer resolution of forms 1/2, or as the chain head / receiver of forms 4/5), where every captured **local** source is declared **before** `L` in the same or an enclosing scope (`this` and the enclosing method's parameters count as declared before every local), **or is `L` itself, or is a value whose borrow provably originates from `L`** (self-capture: `scope.Spawn(lambda() => Work(scope.Token))` and the bound intermediate `var tok := scope.Token;` are both admitted; `L` outlives every invocation of what it stores, and the quiescence rule below plus [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s logical-before-physical ordering guarantee no stored callback observes a reclaimed `L`); or
  - **`this`** (per forms 3/4), where every captured source is `this` itself or a value whose borrow provably originates from `this` — the only things the stored callback can dangle on are then the very object whose teardown bounds the storage.

  Until `L`'s scope exits, the captured local sources are **frozen** (derives: [K5.7](#sec-kernel-k5)): they may not be moved from, reassigned, or disposed — the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) **plus explicit disposal**. The storage freeze is deliberately *stronger* than the consume-site rule it extends — K5.7's strengthening: a stored callback's later invocation is invisible at a `Dispose()` site, and this admission promises a fully static bound, so §28.3's announced-kill carve-out does not apply to admitted captures. A bounding object that is none of the admitted resolutions — a plain expression, a parameter, a returned value that reaches no admitted slot — admits **no** capture-bearing arguments (capture-free callbacks are always admitted).

  **The registration-lifetime residual.** Forms 3 and 4 bound invocations by an object whose teardown must sever the storage: for form 4 the storing member is reached through the bounding instance's **owned** fields (the chain-hop restriction above) and is therefore disposed with it; for form 3 the returned handle (e.g. a `Subscription`, stdlib [§6.5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-events-ievent-eventsource)) held in the `owned` field severs the registration when `this` is disposed — logical disposal precedes physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)), so severance completes before any capture dangles. The admission therefore carries one obligation the checker does not close: **the registration must not be extended past the bounding object** — `move`-ing the handle-holding `owned` field (or a storing owned child) out into longer-lived storage re-opens the invocation window. This is deliberately the same recorded residual-trust shape as the quiescence rule ([K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)) below — structural checks decidable, the temporal guarantee the programmer's, `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode the deterministic backstop — and it deliberately re-opens a corner of the owned-field-extraction closure recorded here: the alternative (freezing such fields against `move`) would require flow-marking fields by what initialized them, a per-value property a field declaration does not carry. Recorded, not silent.

**Quiescence.** Disposal of the bounding object must guarantee that no stored callback is invoked after disposal completes (by draining in-flight work or severing registrations before teardown). For compiler-known types the guarantee is stated normatively in the standard library (`TaskScope`, the stdlib §6.5 event types, the task-completion sources). For user-authored types the obligation is the recorded residual of [K2.3](#sec-kernel-k2)'s admission posture: the storage-site checks are structural and decidable; the temporal guarantee is the author's, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). A callback that runs *during* the drain may touch the bounding object soundly: logical disposal precedes physical reclamation ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)).

**The call-bounded default (derives: [K2.4](#sec-kernel-k2) — a plain signature carries no capture set, so no retention can be announced).** A function-typed parameter declared *without* `scoped` is **call-bounded**: the callee receives the callback for the duration of the call only — or, when the call mints a deferred-activation frame, for the duration of that frame's life (*Call-bounded × deferred activation* below). Within the callee the callback may be invoked, bound to locals, and passed on as an argument to another call-bounded parameter (a deferred-activation callee's included — the retention that creates rides the returned frame, judged below); it may **not** be stored in a field of any object, stored into any collection that is itself reachable beyond the call (a parameter, a borrow, or a field — a purely local collection is a local binding), returned, captured by a closure that itself escapes the callee (judged by these same rules, applied transitively), or forwarded into a `scoped` parameter position. The last restriction is load-bearing: the callee cannot see its argument's capture set, so it cannot vouch for the [§28.14 admission](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters); a callee that needs to register a callback it received must itself declare the parameter `scoped` (the forwarding rule above then requires the same bounding object). These obligations are compiler-verified for user-authored callees — structural and decidable, the same sink checks [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) applies to frame-bounded borrows.

The caller side is correspondingly unrestricted: **any** closure — capture-bearing or not — may be passed to a call-bounded parameter, since every captured source trivially outlives the call (for a deferred-activation callee the admission is re-keyed to the returned frame — *Call-bounded × deferred activation* below). (The default completes the lattice: plain = call-bounded, `scoped` = storage-bounded.)

**The stdlib retention register.** Standard-library callees state their retention in their signatures:

- `scoped` where they store (stdlib §6.5's `Subscribe`/`Add` positions — including `EventSource<T>.Add`/`AsyncEventSource<T>.Add` — and stdlib §6.10);
- the [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet) task-completion-source admission as the legacy statement until those signatures migrate;
- the lazy query operators, whose retention is the frame residence of *Call-bounded × deferred activation* below — a normative consequence of their deferred-activation signatures, not a certification;
- the asynchronous spawn positions of [§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains) (`Domain.Spawn`'s capture-free entries and the `Parallel` combinator bodies, [§30.14](#sec-data-parallel-combinators)/stdlib §6.12) under §30's capture and sendability rules rather than this section;
- the register's first **interface-declared** positions: the shared-event handler positions of stdlib §6.5 — any call that resolves to a subscribe position **declared on** `ISharedEvent<T>` or `SharedEventSource<T>` (`Subscribe`/`Add` — whether the receiver's static type is the pair itself or a generic parameter constrained to it) admits only **capture-free** handler arguments, a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference; user implementations of `ISharedEvent<T>` gain no retention right and are verified under the ordinary call-bounded regime above.

**The method-reference formation bar (protects the position-keyed register admissions — axioms [A10](#sec-axiom-register)/[A11](#sec-axiom-register)).** Register positions are stated at the callee, not marked in the parameter's function type, so — to keep the admission alias-proof — **forming a method reference over a capture-free-register position is a compile error** (covering every register entry: `Domain.Spawn`'s and the shared-event positions): the formed value's plain function type would erase the admission, and a call through it would reach the trusted storing implementation under the call-bounded default's caller side above, which admits any closure. (`scoped`-marked positions need no such bar: `scoped` is part of function-type identity, [§27.1](#sec-function-types), and survives formation.)

**Call-bounded × deferred activation (unified across the deferred-activation kinds).** Two shapes are defined. (1) **Frame residence** (derives: [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K6.2](#sec-kernel-k6)). A callee whose call mints a deferred-activation frame (the kinds of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries) *Deferred-activation callees*: an `async` callee — the returned task; an iterator or async-iterator callee — the returned enumerable or enumerator frame ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)); a lazy query operator — the returned query value, stdlib §5) holds a plain function-typed parameter in that frame: the callback runs after the constructing call has returned, and frame residence is **not** an escape sink — the deferred-activation return type is the signature-level announcement of the retention (K6.2), exactly as it announces the frame's carried borrows ([§28.3](#sec-returning-a-deferred-activation-frame)). The bound is the **frame's life** (K6.1): a task's settlement ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)); an iterator frame's completion or disposal ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation), [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators) — the `for` desugaring's `using var` bounds both, [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for); `await for`'s, [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)); a lazy query's single-consumption point ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration); the retention transfers into the consuming frames by the transitive rule of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)). The caller-side admission above ("every captured source trivially outlives the call") is correspondingly re-keyed to the returned frame: the callback's captured borrows' sources are **carried sources of the frame** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s capture-set contribution), bounded by the ordinary borrow machinery — the scope and store rules and the frame-return check — and, for a task, by [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation where lifetimes cannot be statically compared, discharged by awaiting before the captured sources' scopes exit; the abandonment idioms carry the residual exactly as they do for object borrows ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)). Callee-side, the sink checks above still govern the body's own uses of the parameter, and they extend transitively to the frame: a call-bounded callback **forwarded** to a plain function-typed parameter of another deferred-activation call rides that call's frame — admitted when the frame is consumed within the callee or returned under a deferred-activation return type (the announcement composes: the outer caller re-establishes against its own arguments); a frame that carries the callback and escapes any other way — stored in a field or an escaping collection, captured by an escaping closure — is an escape of the callback itself, rejected by these same rules applied transitively. No `scoped` spelling is involved: `scoped` states open-ended storage in an object under the storage-bounded admission above, while frame residence is bounded by a value the caller's own flow analysis tracks — the lazy query operators' plain signatures are this shape's normative instance (stdlib §5), and an iterator callee that needs owned state alongside a callback declares an `owned` parameter beside it ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)). (2) A callee — synchronous or async — that **invokes** a call-bounded callback whose invocation returns a task must treat that returned task as inheriting the call bound: it must `await` it to settlement before returning. Returning it, storing it, passing it to `Task.FireAndForget`, or binding it and dropping it undisposed-to-settlement (`using var t := cb();` with no await) lets the callback's caller-sourced environment outlive the call through the still-running frame ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) and is an **escape sink**, rejected by the same structural verification as the other sinks above. In a **synchronous** callee the invocation itself is rejected (derives: [K6.3](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) — the minted task inherits the call bound, and a non-`async` body has no consuming position for it): a non-`async` body cannot await the returned task at all (and blocking on it is barred inside continuations, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)), so invoking a plain function-typed parameter whose invocation yields a `Task`-family value is a compile error there — declare the parameter `scoped` (shifting the admission to the caller under the storage-bounded rules above) or make the callee `async`. The await-to-settlement requirement is per-path and admits **fan-out**: the returned tasks may be accumulated in a purely-local collection (the purely-local exemption above, applied to the tasks) provided every one of them is awaited to settlement before the callee returns on every path — awaiting an aggregation helper over that collection (`await Task.WhenAll(pending)`, [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)) discharges all of its inputs, since the aggregate completes only after every input settles.

**Class- and interface-typed `scoped` parameters: scoped construction.** The `scoped` modifier extends beyond function types: a class- or interface-typed parameter may be declared `scoped` — `constructor(scoped stream: Stream)` — applying the same two-sided contract to a **passive borrow** instead of a callback:

- **Callee side:** the callee may store the borrow in a direct non-owned field of the bounding object — the ordinary back-reference field of [§28.5](#sec-owned-fields)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) — and may forward it only to another `scoped` parameter with the same bounding object. It may not return it or store it anywhere else. No new field kind is introduced: `scoped` on the *parameter* **upgrades** [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s residual-trust back-reference admission to a static bound at the participating call sites; a plain (non-`scoped`) borrow parameter stored per §28.3 remains legal with the trust residual.
- **Caller side:** the argument carries the call-site marker — `new StreamReader(scoped stream)` ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) — and is admitted under the bounding-object forms above with *the argument's borrow source* in place of a closure's capture set: the source must satisfy the same declared-before/self/`this`-derived tests, and it is **frozen** until the bound's scope exits. A **fresh producer** argument is rejected (`new StreamReader(scoped new FileStream(...))` — the unbound owned temporary dies at the end of the full expression; [§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)'s no-temporary-source rule, identical remedy: bind the source first).
- **No quiescence obligation arises:** a stored borrow is passive data — it never fires. With declared-before admission, the freeze, and reverse-declaration-order disposal ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)), the source provably outlives the bounding object *including its destructor*; the guarantee is fully static with **no residual trust** — strictly stronger than the callback case. The [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal) backstop remains defense-in-depth only.

Note the deliberate asymmetry with ordinary borrows: a parameter-sourced *object* borrow may be stored into a field under §28.3's borrowed-field rule — a structural check whose residual is the caller's trust — but a call-bounded *function* value may not be stored at all — frame residence (*Call-bounded × deferred activation* above) is not a store but the retention the deferred-activation return type itself announces. A closure's true bound is its capture set, which a plain signature does not carry, so neither party is positioned to accept the trust; `scoped` is exactly the signature-carried form of it, and the deferred-activation case needs neither: there the capture set rides the frame as carried sources ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), visible to the caller's own flow analysis.

*Known v1 limitation:* combinators that compose received callbacks into a returned **function value** (`Compose(f, g)` returning `lambda(x) => g(f(x))`) are not expressible over call-bounded parameters — the returned closure would capture them beyond the call, and no bounding frame exists. The missing third tier is an *unbounded* marker (admitting only capture-free or transitively unbounded arguments, which the callee may then retain freely); it is deferred until evidence demands it. Combinators that compose received callbacks into a returned **deferred-activation frame** — an iterator method over a callback parameter, a body returning `xs.Where(f)` — are the expressible neighbors: there the frame bounds the retention (*Call-bounded × deferred activation* above).

**v1 admission bounds (ratified; axiom [A11](#sec-axiom-register)).** The implementation chose conservatively at eight corners the original text left silent; those choices are **normative**. Bounds marked *liftable* may be widened by a future revision with more analysis; the rest are settled. (The first recorded choice — self-capture of the bounding local — is promoted into the admission text above rather than listed here.)

1. **Value-typed captures are exempt from the declared-before test**: a captured value-typed local lives in its heap capture cell, which the closure keeps alive — no lifetime hazard; only class/interface-reference captures are order-checked.
2. **Freeze granularity**: (a) the freeze persists to the end of the enclosing method body, not merely to the bound's scope exit (conservative — may over-reject mutation after an inner block closes); (b) enforcement is source-order gated, so a reassignment lexically *before* the admission that re-executes on a loop back edge escapes the semantic freeze — a known **non-hole** (the reassignment writes the shared capture cell, never a memory-safety violation; back-edge moves and disposes are caught by the general moved-from/disposed rules); (c) `Dispose()` counts as moved-from for the freeze.
3. **Unverifiable argument forms are rejected** (*liftable*): a function-typed local, a non-`scoped` function-typed parameter, a field read, or a call result cannot have its capture set verified at the scoped call site. The verified forms are lambda literals and method references (whose capture is the receiver); the diagnostic directs to them or to a capture-free function.
4. **Form-2 exact-initializer**: the owned-return call must itself be the `using var` initializer node; `await`-wrapped or otherwise nested forms resolve no bounding object (capture-free only).
5. **Scoped-field right-hand sides** (*liftable*): only a `scoped` parameter of the enclosing callable, or `null`; a capture-free lambda literal is not admitted as a `scoped`-field RHS in v1.
6. **Callee-side uses inside a nested closure are escaping uses** (*liftable*): invoking a scoped parameter through a locally-invoked closure could be admitted with more analysis; v1 rejects it.
7. **`TaskScope` missing-`Join` provable subset** (stdlib §6.10): the compile error fires iff no `await L.Join()` appears anywhere in the method *and* `L` is never delegated (bare argument or closure capture). A method whose only exit is a throw between `Spawn` and an unreachable `Join` is still flagged — conservative, recorded.

**Interaction with the type system.** `scoped` participates in function-signature identity like `ref`/`out` ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)): a `scoped` parameter and a plain function-typed parameter are distinct signatures, and a function value does not convert between them. `scoped` is **illegal on `extern` declarations** ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)): neither the storage obligations nor quiescence can be verified across the FFI boundary. A plain function-typed `extern` parameter is this section's call-bounded default at the boundary: caller-side admission per [§32.8](#sec-callbacks) (capture-admitting only under the `env` pairing there), callee-side obligations carried by [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)'s documented-trust contract in place of the compiler verification a Bezel callee gets.

**Relation to §30.11.** The [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet) task-completion-source callback admission is a **derived instance** of this section: the source is the bounding object, settlement is its quiescence point. §30.11's four-condition text remains as the legacy statement until the standard library's signatures migrate to `scoped`; no new hard-coded patterns will be added.


<a id="sec-iteration-2"></a>
## 29. Iteration

`for` operates on any value whose type implements `IEnumerable<T>`. The protocol is interface-based; there is no duck-typing fallback.

<a id="sec-the-protocol"></a>
<a id="sec-iterator-protocol"></a>
### 29.1 The protocol

```bezel
interface IEnumerable<out T>
  method GetEnumerator(): owned IEnumerator<T>;
end IEnumerable;

interface IEnumerator<out T>: IDisposable
  method MoveNext(): bool;
  readonly property Current: T;
end IEnumerator;
```

Calling `GetEnumerator()` produces a fresh enumerator positioned just before the first element. `MoveNext()` advances the cursor and returns `true` if a new element became available, `false` if the sequence is exhausted. `Current` returns the element at the current position. Reading `Current` before the first successful `MoveNext` or after `MoveNext` returns `false` raises **`InvalidOperationException`** (normative for standard-library enumerators and compiler-generated iterators; contractual for user implementations, the same shape as [§29.12](#sec-mutation-during-iteration)'s mutation rule).

`IEnumerator<T>` extends `IDisposable`. An enumerator with no resources to release simply has an empty `Dispose` body; the compiler generates one if the implementor writes none.

`GetEnumerator()` returns `owned IEnumerator<T>`: the caller takes ownership of the enumerator and must dispose it. The standard `for` and `await for` desugarings ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) wrap the enumerator in a `using var` (or `await using var`) automatically, so loop forms satisfy the obligation without the user writing the disposal explicitly. Code that calls `GetEnumerator()` manually — outside a loop form — obtains an owned enumerator subject to the standard [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) discharge rules; the `using var x := source.GetEnumerator();` shape is recommended (scope-bound disposal, no must-use warning), though a plain `var` binding is also legal and auto-drops at scope end with the must-use warning.

<a id="sec-current-on-owned-element-enumerators"></a>
<a id="sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators"></a>
#### `Current` semantics on borrowing and owning enumerators

`IEnumerator<T>` and `IOwningEnumerator<T>` (declared in stdlib [§4.12](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-borrowing-enumeration-interfaces), [§4.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-enumeration-interfaces)) are distinct interfaces with different `Current` semantics:

- **`IEnumerator<T>.Current`** is **non-destructive**: it returns a borrow of the most-recently-yielded value, which the enumerator continues to own (if it has ownership of the source) or re-borrow (if the source is borrow-based). Multiple reads between `MoveNext` calls produce additional borrows of the same value. The async variant `IAsyncEnumerator<T>.Current` has the same non-destructive semantics relative to `MoveNextAsync`.

- **`IOwningEnumerator<T>.TakeCurrent()`** is an ordinary **owned-returning method**: after a successful `MoveNext`, `TakeCurrent()` transfers ownership of the most-recently-yielded value to the caller, leaving the enumerator's internal slot empty; the result follows the standard [§28.1](#sec-where-the-owned-modifier-can-appear)/[§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) owned-return rules (discharge or auto-drop-with-warning — no special carve-out needed). A second take without an intervening advance, or a take before the first advance / after exhaustion, raises **`InvalidOperationException`**. A *destructive property getter* is thereby avoided — a getter that moved out of a field would violate [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention), and [§23](#sec-properties-and-indexers) itself prescribes "an explicit method that returns the owned value" for transfer-out semantics. The async variant is `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>.TakeCurrent()` relative to `MoveNextAsync`.

`IOwningEnumerator<T>` is reached via:
- `IOwningEnumerable<T>.GetOwningEnumerator()` — typically called by the for-loop desugaring when the source is `IOwningEnumerable<T>`.
- Drain methods on owning collections (`OwningArray<T>.Drain()` etc.) — their return type is `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, and the resulting enumerator is `IOwningEnumerator<T>`.
- Iterator methods using `yield return` whose declared return type is `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (or async equivalents).

Default iteration over an owning collection (`for var x in coll do ... end` where `coll: OwningArray<C>`) uses the collection's `IEnumerable<C>` conformance — the borrowing path — and produces borrows of C. To opt into owned-transferring iteration, call `coll.Drain()` (which returns `IOwningEnumerable<C>`) and iterate over the result. The for-loop desugaring at [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) picks based on the static type of the source expression: a source typed `IEnumerable<T>` desugars via `IEnumerator<T>` (non-destructive); a source typed `IOwningEnumerable<T>` desugars via `IOwningEnumerator<T>` (destructive).

The for-loop desugaring calls `__enumerator.TakeCurrent()` exactly once per iteration on the owning path (and reads the non-destructive `__enumerator.Current` on the borrowing path). The ownership transfer is invisible to user code that uses `for` or `await for` loops — the loop body sees `var x := __enumerator.TakeCurrent()` (or its `for var x in ...` equivalent), and `x` is owned and subject to the standard discharge rules. Users who call `MoveNext`/`MoveNextAsync` and take the current value manually (outside a loop form) need to be aware that `TakeCurrent()` transfers ownership and may be called at most once per advance for the owning variant.

Implementations of `IOwningEnumerator<T>` or `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>` may choose either of two storage strategies for the most-recently-yielded value: store it in a private owned field that `TakeCurrent()` moves out (using the [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) `move` form internally), or maintain the value in transient state that exists only between the advance call and the next `TakeCurrent()` call. Both strategies satisfy the contract; the choice is implementation-detail — with one observable requirement the freedom does not cover: under either strategy the enumerator **owns** the pending value from a successful advance until `TakeCurrent()` transfers it, and a `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()` after an advance whose value was never taken **disposes the pending value**. An advanced-but-untaken element neither leaks nor reaches the consumer — the dispose-exactly-once contract ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract), Appendix C.3) holds through manual-protocol abandonment.

<a id="sec-desugaring-of-for"></a>
### 29.2 Desugaring of `for`

```bezel
for var x in source do
  // body
end;
```

When `source` is typed as `IEnumerable<T>` (or implements `IEnumerable<T>` through inheritance), the desugaring is:

```bezel
do
  using var __source := source;
  using var __enumerator := __source.GetEnumerator();
  while __enumerator.MoveNext() do
    var x := __enumerator.Current;
    // body
  end;
end;
```

When `source` is typed as `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (or implements it), the desugaring uses the owning-enumerator path:

```bezel
do
  using var __source := source;
  using var __enumerator := __source.GetOwningEnumerator();
  while __enumerator.MoveNext() do
    var x := __enumerator.TakeCurrent();     // x is owned; §28.3 rules apply
                                              //   on every body-exit edge
    // body
  end;
end;
```

The iteration variable `x` is a **plain owned local**, not a `using var`. This is intentional: the user must be able to discharge `x` by moving it into another owned slot (e.g., `dest.Add(move x)`, `using var c := move x` for scope-bound adoption — the binding-position marker, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) — or `return x`), and `using var` would forbid the move. The compiler applies the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) owned-local discharge rule to the iteration variable on the loop body's every exit edge (fall-through to the next iteration, `break`, `continue`, `return`, `throw`): on each normal-exit edge `x` is either discharged by the program or auto-dropped with the must-use warning, and the "fall-through to the next iteration" edge is checked the same way as the body's end. The compiler-generated check is identical to the [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) owned-local discharge rule applied to the iteration variable.

The choice is made by the static type of `source`. If `source`'s static type implements both `IEnumerable<T>` and `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (as `OwningArray<T>` does), the desugaring uses the `IEnumerable<T>` path — default iteration is borrowing. To opt into the owning path, the source must be expressed at static type `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, typically by calling `.Drain()` on an owning collection.

Both `__source` and `__enumerator` are disposed on every exit path. The loop variable is freshly bound each iteration. `break` exits the surrounding `do ... end`, triggering disposal of both. `continue` jumps to the next `MoveNext` call. A loop label carries onto the generated `while` — not onto the wrapper block — so `break name;` exits the labeled `while` and then the wrapper, disposing both bindings, and `continue name;` targets the labeled loop's advance: the next `MoveNext()`/`MoveNextAsync()` on the enumerator paths, and the index/step **increment** (then the bound check) on the direct-indexed and counted forms — targeting the bare condition would skip an advance and diverge from the enumerator desugaring. A labeled `break`/`continue` is a body-exit edge **for every loop body it exits** ([§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue)): each exited body's iteration variable is discharged or auto-dropped at the jump exactly as at an unlabeled `break` of that body.

When `source` is a value-type expression, a runtime-managed expression (e.g. a string), or a borrowed local of class type, the `using var __source := source;` is a no-op (per [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types) for runtime-managed cases; per [§28.10](#sec-using-var) a `using var` initialized from a borrow does not assume a disposal obligation but does pin the source for the loop's duration). When `source` is a fresh class-typed expression — a call announced as producing a caller-owned frame (a static iterable-interface-returning call, or an `owned`-marked instance or extension one — [§28.3](#sec-iterable-instance-returns)), a stdlib deferred producer ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)), or a `new` expression — the wrapping `using var` assumes the disposal obligation and ensures the iterable is disposed when the loop ends. This closes the leak that would arise from `for var x in GetThings() do ... end` when `GetThings()` returns a heap-allocated state-machine iterable.

When `source` is itself an owned local — including a `using var` of class type or any other owned class-typed local — the desugaring is adjusted: `using var __source := source;` is replaced by a borrow that pins `source` for the loop's duration without assuming the disposal obligation. This case mirrors the borrowed-local case above; the obligation stays with the original owner. In particular, `for var line in stream do ... end` where `stream` is a `using var` does not move out of `stream` (which would be a [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) violation) and does not double-dispose at the for-loop's end.

When `source` is a `Range<T>` value ([§16.3](#sec-the-ranget-type)), the compiler may replace the entire desugaring above with a direct counted loop, provided the observable behavior is identical. For range literals with constant endpoints, this avoids heap-allocating an enumerator. See [§16.5](#sec-iteration) for details.

When `source` has inline-array type (`[N]T`, including the borrow-bearing and owning slot-marker forms), the desugaring is a direct indexed loop over the array's slots — inline arrays do not implement `IEnumerable<T>` and the enumerator path of [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) does not apply ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)). The iteration variable's type and ownership state follow the slot kind: a copy for value-typed slots, a borrow for class-typed slots (whether the slot marker is `owned` or not — for owning slots the array retains ownership, and the loop body sees a borrow that does not consume the slot). Direct `move arr[i]` inside the loop body is admitted, but the field-restoration rule ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) applies: every moved-from slot must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits. Iterating an `[N owned]T` non-nullable owning array and moving from every slot without restoration is therefore rejected; the typical pattern for "consume every slot" uses `[N owned]T?` and assigns `null` after each move.

When `source` has type `Span<T>` or `ReadOnlySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), the desugaring is also a direct indexed loop over the span's range, parallel to the inline-array case. Spans do not implement the enumeration protocol (`IEnumerable<T?>` for class-typed T, `IEnumerable<T>` otherwise) — the enumerator the protocol would return is an ordinary class instance that would need to hold a borrow of the underlying buffer across its own lifetime, which the borrow tracker cannot bound through the enumerator interface — so the enumerator path of this section does not apply. The iteration variable's type follows the span's slot type: `T?` for class-typed T (the loop body sees a borrow of each slot's value, possibly null) and `T` for value-typed T (the loop body sees a borrow of the slot — effectively a value copy for primitive T). The borrow's source is the underlying `OwningBuffer<T>`, reached transitively through the span's `Buffer` field. Direct `move span[i]` inside the loop body is admitted for class-typed `Span<T>` (not for value-typed `Span<T>`, not for any `ReadOnlySpan<T>`); the same field-restoration rule applies to the underlying buffer slot, and the typical restoration is `span[i] := null`.

When `source` has type `OwningBuffer<T>` for value-typed T (stdlib [§4.14](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owned-buffers-and-spans)), the desugaring is a direct indexed loop, parallel to the span case. The iteration variable's type is T and the loop body sees a borrow of each slot's value. (For class-typed `OwningBuffer<T>`, the type implements `IEnumerable<T?>` and the standard enumerator path applies, with the optimization-elision rule above; the observable result is the same as a direct-indexed loop.)

When `source` has type `ReadOnlyStringSpan` (stdlib [§3.3](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-readonlystringspan)), the desugaring is a direct indexed loop, parallel to the `ReadOnlySpan<T>` case. `ReadOnlyStringSpan` does not implement `IEnumerable<char>` — the enumerator returned by `IEnumerable<T>.GetEnumerator()` is an ordinary class instance that would need to hold the span (or its borrow of the source string) across its own lifetime, and the borrow tracker cannot bound that lifetime through the enumerator interface. The iteration variable's type is `char` and the loop body sees a copy of each code point (chars are value-typed primitives). The borrow's source is the underlying `string`, reached through the span's `Source` field.

When `source` has type `ArraySpan<T>` or `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` (stdlib [§4.15](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-arrayspant-readonlyarrayspant)), the desugaring is a direct indexed loop, parallel to the `Span<T>` / `ReadOnlySpan<T>` case. Neither type implements `IEnumerable<T>` — the same enumerator-escape reasoning given for `ReadOnlyStringSpan` above applies. The iteration variable's type is T and the loop body sees a borrow of each slot (the borrow's source is the underlying `Array<T>`, reached through the span's `Source` field). The iteration-variable type follows the array's element type directly — `T` is whatever the array was instantiated with (no `T?` wrapping, unlike the OwningBuffer-backed span case for class T, because `Array<T>` slots store borrows rather than owned nullable references). `move arrSpan[i]` is not admitted in the loop body for any T, since `Array<T>` slots are borrows with no ownership to transfer.

When `source` has type `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>` (stdlib [§4.16](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-ireadonlyspan)), the desugaring is a direct indexed loop over `0..<source.Length`, accessing each element via `source[i]`. The iteration variable's type is `TElement`. Indexer and `Length` access through the interface are virtual dispatches (vtable lookup, indirect call); the iteration is correspondingly slower than iterating a concrete span type. Authors writing inner loops should iterate over concrete span types where peak per-element throughput matters; the interface-typed for-loop is the convenient form for code where breadth across span sources is more important than performance. The lifetime constraint is the standard one: the `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>` value (a boxed borrow-bearing record per the rule of [§8.6](#sec-boxing-of-borrow-bearing-records)) may not outlive the source of the underlying span's borrow, which the compiler tracks through the boxed-value lifetime constraint.

More generally, the compiler may elide the `IEnumerable`/`IEnumerator` protocol and the associated heap allocation whenever it can prove that the observable behavior is identical to the desugared form. For heap arrays (`Array<T>`, `OwningArray<T>`) and strings, the compiler is expected to emit direct indexed loops as an optimization (these types do implement `IEnumerable<T>`, but the protocol is elided when the compiler can see the type concretely). Inside a `pure` body this elision is **normative** for the concretely-typed sources, per [§22.15](#sec-pure-body-rules) rule 5. For inline arrays (`[N]T`), the direct indexed loop is mandatory rather than optimizational — inline arrays are not class types and do not implement `IEnumerable<T>` at all ([§15.1.2](#sec-inline-array-members)). For range literals with constant endpoints, the compiler emits tight counted loops with no allocation. These optimizations ensure that the common `for` patterns — iterating an array, a string, or a numeric range — incur no disposal overhead from `IEnumerator<T>: IDisposable`.

<a id="sec-iterator-yield-ownership"></a>
#### Iterator yield ownership

(This subsection covers `yield return` semantics; the yield construct itself is introduced in [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods). The placement here keeps it close to the for-loop desugaring with which it interacts most directly.)

The behavior of `yield return expression;` depends on the static type of the yielded expression *and* on the iterator method's declared return type. Under the marker discipline the operand read of a **named owned binding** is classified by the return type: in an iterator returning an **owning** enumeration interface the read is an owned-consuming position — the declared return type is the announcement, exactly as for `return` under an `owned` return type ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)); in an iterator returning a **borrowing** enumeration interface the unmarked read is a **borrow** (nothing announces a kill), falling under the borrowed-expression bullet below. There is no yield-position transfer marker — the same recorded, liftable bound as `??`-operand position (axiom [A7](#sec-axiom-register)). The cases:

- **Owned class-typed expression — a fresh producer (a `new` expression, an `owned`-returning call, any unbound owned temporary) or a `move` result; *not* an unmarked read of a named owned binding, which is a borrow (preamble above) — yielded from an iterator returning `IEnumerable<T>` or `IEnumerator<T>`.** The yield transfers ownership to the iterator's enumerator. The enumerator owns the most-recently-yielded value; the next `MoveNext()` (or `MoveNextAsync()`) call disposes the previous value before producing the next. The consumer's iteration variable in `for var x in src do ... end` is a **borrow** of the enumerator's owned slot, valid until the iteration body completes one full pass and `MoveNext` is called again. Disposing the enumerator (`break`, exhaustion, or explicit `Dispose()`) disposes any outstanding yielded value the iterator still owns. A borrow of the enumerator's owned slot may therefore never escape the enumerator's lifetime — and, within that lifetime, it is invalidated by the next advance (above): the loop desugaring's wrapper block bounds any escape of the iteration variable (return, store, capture) by the ordinary borrow-lifetime rules, and [§28.3](#sec-bare-type-parameter-returns)'s callee-side admission applies exactly this at interface-typed loop sources (v0.235, #1666).

  This is the established rule. It is the appropriate model for iterators whose consumers borrow each value briefly and discard it: filtering, formatting, dispatching to handlers. To hand the enumerator a value already bound to a named owned local, yield a producer expression instead, or adopt-then-yield — `using var l := move line; yield return l;` — which pins the value in the frame and yields a warning-free borrow; the named binding's yield is deliberately not a silent consume.

- **Owned class-typed expression yielded from an iterator returning `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, or `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`.** The yield transfers ownership *through* the enumerator to the consumer on each `MoveNext()` (or `MoveNextAsync()` for the async case). The enumerator does not retain ownership between yields — the value is handed off as part of the advance boundary (`MoveNext()` through `TakeCurrent()`: until the take completes, the pending value is held — and on abandonment disposed — by the enumerator, [§29.1](#sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators)). The consumer's iteration variable in `for var x in src do ... end` (or `await for var x in src do ... end` for the async case) is **owned**; the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) discharge rules apply in the loop body on every body-exit edge. Falling off the body still owning the value auto-drops it at the body's end for that iteration, with the must-use warning identifying the iteration variable and pointing at the standard remedies (`using var u := move x;` for scope-bound adoption (marker), an `owned`-consuming method call, an explicit `x.Dispose()`, or `_ := x;`).

  This is the model for iterators whose consumers take ownership of each value: drain operations on owning collections (synchronous), async iterators producing owned resources (async pipelines such as `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<FileStream>`).

  A **named owned binding** as the yield operand is **consumed** here: the operand read is an owned-consuming position announced by the declared owning return type — no marker, the same announcement family as `return` under an `owned` return type ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — and the binding is moved-from when the yield resumes. Because the transfer hands the value **alive** to the enumerator and consumer — no disposed flag is set at the transfer, and the consumer may dispose the value before the iterator body resumes — the consume **joins the consume-site freeze** ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)): a `yield return x;` while a live local borrow of `x`'s current value exists is a compile error, like any other transfer.

  The [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules apply on every *normal-exit* edge from the loop body. The iteration variable is a local of the body's scope, and the standard owned-local rules — including the auto-drop with the must-use warning — apply to it directly: `break`, `continue`, `return`, `yield break`, and fall-through to the next iteration all count as normal-exit edges; on each, the iteration variable is either discharged by the program or auto-dropped with the warning. The same rule applies inside an `await for` body. On *exception* edges — whether from an explicit `throw` or from a method call that propagates an exception out of the body — the iteration variable is auto-disposed by the implicit `try`/`finally` rule of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) "Exception-path discharge"; no user-written discharge is required for the exception case. Code that conditionally `break`s before the natural discharge point must move the discharge before the conditional, typically by binding the iteration variable to a `using var` immediately on entry to the body:

  ```bezel
  for var conn in pool.Drain() do
    using var c := move conn;   // discharge on entry — covers all exit edges
    if c.IsExpired() then
      break;                     // c disposed by using-var on the way out
    end;
    c.Use();
  end;
  ```

  The shape `using var c := move <iteration variable>` is the standard way to convert the iteration variable's "must discharge on every edge" obligation into the simpler "scope-bound disposal" obligation (the `move` marker is the binding-position transfer spelling, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows); an unmarked `using var c := x` would merely borrow-pin `x`, [§28.10](#sec-using-var)). The marked move from the iteration variable into the using-var is a single discharge that the compiler can verify dominates every exit; subsequent `break`/`continue`/`return`/exception edges are then clean.

  On `break`, on an exception thrown from the body, or on any other early exit from the for-loop, the enumerator's `Dispose()` runs. The enumerator at that point is between yields (it has produced values, the consumer has taken ownership of them, and the consumer's per-iteration discharge has either run or not). The enumerator has no per-yield ownership to release on this path — under the loop desugaring every advance is immediately paired with `TakeCurrent()`, so every produced value either reached the consumer's owned slot (where the standard discharge rules apply) or was never produced. (Outside the loop forms — the manual protocol — a third state exists: an **advanced-but-untaken** pending value is still owned by the enumerator and is disposed by its `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()`, [§29.1](#sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators).) The enumerator's `Dispose()` runs only the per-iterator cleanup (closing files, releasing source resources) defined by the iterator method's body.

  When the iterator method's body sources the yielded values from an owning collection (the typical implementation of `Drain()`), it does so via the collection's removal operations — `PopFirst()`, `PopAt(i)`, `Pop()`, `Dequeue()`, etc. These operations remove and return the owned element in a single step, leaving the collection in a consistent post-call state without invoking the field-restoration rule. A naïve implementation using `move coll[i]` per slot without reassignment would *not* compile: each `move` leaves the slot in moved-from state, and the field-restoration rule ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) requires reassignment before the iterator method exits. The `Pop`-style operations sidestep the issue by removing the slot rather than emptying it. If the iterator is disposed before exhaustion — `break`, exception, manual `Dispose()` — the source collection's state is "consumed elements gone, remaining elements intact," consistent with the prefix actually iterated.

- **Borrowed class-typed expression.** The yield is a re-borrow whose source is the original borrow's source. The lifetime constraint propagates: the iterator's enumerator may not outlive the source. The compiler enforces this by attaching the borrow source to the enumerator's lifetime, just as for any other borrow-bearing structure. This case applies regardless of whether the iterator's return type is `IEnumerable<T>` or `IOwningEnumerable<T>` — but the latter is unusual; an iterator declared to yield owned T but yielding borrows would have to source the ownership from somewhere, typically by wrapping each borrow in a fresh allocation, which is rarely the intent.

  An **unmarked read of a named owned binding** in the yield position of a *borrowing* iterator is such a borrowed expression: the yield re-borrows the binding, whose source is the binding itself — a frame-resident local of the iterator's own heap frame ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)), so the enumerator-outlives-source constraint is satisfied structurally. The binding stays owned in the frame and is discharged by the ordinary [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) rules — auto-dropped at its scope end with the must-use warning if never discharged, and on early abandonment disposed by [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s pass, which runs the frame's scope exits exactly as if the body had exited at the suspension point; the adopt-then-yield spelling above is the warning-free form. In an *owning* iterator the same read is a consume (previous bullet).

- **Value-typed, `string`-typed, or runtime-managed expression.** No ownership transfers. The yield is a copy (for value types) or a shared reference (for `string` and other runtime-managed types). The enumerator does not dispose anything for these yield types; the next `MoveNext` simply produces the next value. The consumer's iteration variable is a copy (value types) or shared reference (runtime-managed) by the standard rules of those type kinds. The iterator's return type for these cases is `IEnumerable<T>`; the `IOwningEnumerable<T>` form is not available because `IOwningEnumerable<T>` requires `T: class` (stdlib [§4.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-enumeration-interfaces)). The class-only requirement is uniform across the owning collection family — owning makes sense only for class-typed values.

When the body holds a borrow across a `MoveNext` (or `MoveNextAsync`) boundary — for example, by stashing the iteration variable in an outer field — the borrow becomes invalid as soon as the next advance runs. This is the standard borrow-lifetime rule ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) applied to iterator-yielded values. To retain a yielded value across iterations, the consumer must materialize it explicitly: dispose-and-replace into an owned slot if the producer documents the yield as transferable, or copy if the value is a record. This rule applies to the *first* of the owned-class-typed cases above (iterator returns `IEnumerable<T>` or `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` and yields owned values); for iterators returning `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerator<T>`, `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, or `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`, the iteration variable is owned and the consumer is responsible for it for the body's duration regardless of advance timing — the value's lifetime is bounded by the consumer's discharge, not by the enumerator's next call.

Disposing the enumerator (`break` from a `for` or `await for` loop, exhaustion, or `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()` on a manually-held enumerator) disposes any outstanding yielded value the iterator owns. For yield types that the iterator does not own (value types, `string`, runtime-managed types, or any case where ownership transfers to the consumer per the rules above), there is nothing for the enumerator to dispose.

<a id="sec-iterator-methods"></a>
### 29.3 Iterator methods

A method that uses `yield return` or `yield break` is an **iterator method**. The compiler translates the body into the equivalent state-machine implementation of `IEnumerator<T>`. An iterator method declared as an **instance or extension** member marks its return type `owned` (`owned IEnumerable<T>`, `owned IOwningEnumerable<T>`, and the enumerator/async forms) — the container announcement of [§28.3](#sec-iterable-instance-returns); static iterator methods keep the unmarked convention, whose declared type already announces the caller-owned frame.

```bezel
public static method Squares(n: int): IEnumerable<int>
  for var i in 0..<n do
    yield return i * i;
  end;
end Squares;

public static method TakeWhilePositive(numbers: IEnumerable<int>): IEnumerable<int>
  for var n in numbers do
    if n <= 0 then
      yield break;
    end;
    yield return n;
  end;
end TakeWhilePositive;
```

`yield return expression;` produces the next value and suspends. `yield break;` terminates iteration. Falling off the end of the method has the same effect as `yield break`.

An iterator method's return type is `IEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable: each call to `GetEnumerator()` runs the body again from the start), `IEnumerator<T>` (single-use: the call returns the enumerator directly), or one of the owning forms `IOwningEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable) / `IOwningEnumerator<T>` (single-use), whose yielded values transfer ownership to the consumer ([§29.1](#sec-current-semantics-on-borrowing-and-owning-enumerators)). An **async** iterator method (one declared `async` that uses `yield`; `await` is permitted but not required) has return type `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable) or `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` (single-use), or the owning forms `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` / `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>`, the async counterparts of the synchronous forms ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)).

An iterator method may not declare `ref` or `out` parameters: its arguments are captured into a heap state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call, and a caller-stack-slot reference cannot be — the same rule and reasoning as [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s, stated there. `owned` parameters remain admitted ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)).

<a id="sec-lazy-evaluation"></a>
### 29.4 Lazy evaluation

An iterator method's body does not run when the method is called. Calling produces an `IEnumerable<T>` (or `IEnumerator<T>`); the body runs incrementally as the consumer calls `MoveNext()`. The returned state machine holds the factory's plain reference-typed arguments as borrows until it completes or is disposed — and its plain **function-typed** arguments for the same extent: the callback resides in the frame, its retention bounded by the frame's life ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) *Call-bounded × deferred activation*), and its captured borrows' sources are carried sources of the returned frame ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s capture-set contribution); see [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries) "Deferred-activation callees" for the rule on temporary-sourced arguments. A **borrow-bearing record local** ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) whose live range crosses a `yield return` is subject to the same frame-resident-source rule as [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s across-suspension rule: the iterator's heap frame outlives the producing call, and the consumer may dispose caller-side sources between `MoveNext` calls, so every borrow the local carries must have a source the frame itself owns — an owned local, a `using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the iterator body ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)); stdlib-certified records ([§30.8](#sec-cancellation)) are exempt as there.

<a id="sec-return-not-allowed-in-iterator-methods"></a>
### 29.5 `return` not allowed in iterator methods

A method that uses `yield` cannot use plain `return`, including `return;`. Use `yield break` to exit early. This rule applies equally to synchronous iterators (returning `IEnumerable<T>`) and async iterators (declared `async`, returning `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`). Although async methods normally use `return` to complete a task, an async iterator is first and foremost an iterator — `yield` controls the flow, and `yield break` terminates it.

<a id="sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally"></a>
### 29.6 Restrictions inside `try`/`catch`/`finally`

- `yield return` or `yield break` inside a `try` block whose surrounding statement has a `catch`: forbidden.
- `yield return` or `yield break` inside a `try` block whose surrounding statement has only a `finally`: allowed.
- `yield` inside a catch arm's body or a `finally` block: forbidden.

`using var` compiles to `try`/`finally` (no `catch`), so it is the preferred resource-management mechanism inside iterators.

<a id="sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators"></a>
### 29.7 Disposal of partially-consumed iterators

When a consumer stops iterating early — `break`, exception, or `using var` ending before exhaustion — the iterator is disposed. The state machine:

- Runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension — `using var` disposals (including, via [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path, `await using var` disposals) and `finally` clauses — **in reverse order of establishment, exactly as if the body had exited at the suspension point**. This is the single reverse-nesting rule that already governs every other exit edge ([§28.10](#sec-using-var), [§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally)'s `using var` ≡ `try`/`finally` equivalence): an inner `finally` established after an outer `using var` runs *before* that `using var`'s disposal, and vice versa.
- Transitions to a completed state; subsequent `MoveNext()` returns `false`; second `Dispose()` is a no-op.

<a id="sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters"></a>
### 29.8 Iterators with `owned` parameters

An iterator method may take `owned` parameters. The state machine takes ownership at construction time. When the iterator is disposed, the state machine disposes any `owned` parameter that has not been moved out of by the body.

The body may treat the `owned` parameter as it would in any other method. The example below uses `using var … := move …` — the binding-position transfer marker ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)) — to make scope-bounded disposal explicit; the marked transfer moves ownership from the parameter to the local, after which the parameter is in moved-from state and the state machine's auto-dispose does not run for it (the local's `using var` does the work; an *unmarked* `using var r := reader;` would merely borrow-pin the parameter, [§28.10](#sec-using-var)):

*(`StreamReader`, `AtEnd`, and `ReadLine(): string` are illustrative — the example shows the owned-parameter shape, not a reader API in the standard library; within the illustration `ReadLine()` returns a non-nullable `string`.)*

```bezel
public method ReadAndClose(owned reader: StreamReader): owned IEnumerable<string>
  using var r := move reader;             // ownership moves: parameter → local
  while not r.AtEnd do
    yield return r.ReadLine();
  end;
  // r disposed by using var when the iterator completes or is disposed early.
end ReadAndClose;
```

If the body does not move ownership out, the state machine disposes the parameter at iterator disposal — after `using var` cleanups within the body and after `finally` clauses. The order across multiple owned parameters is reverse declaration order, mirroring [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s destructor rule. This implicit frame disposal carries the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning, attached at the parameter declaration; the `using var … := move …` adoption above is the warning-free spelling.

The same machinery handles iterator parameters of move-only value type (owning inline arrays, [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). The parameter is moved into the state machine at construction time; the body sees a move-only local; at iterator disposal, the state machine auto-disposes the array's remaining non-moved-from slots in the same pass that handles owned class-typed parameters. Slots the body moved out of (via `move arr[i]` and onward transfer) are not in the state machine's responsibility set; the field-restoration rule of [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) governs the body's discipline.

*(Same illustrative reader API as above.)*

```bezel
public method Echo(owned source: StreamReader): owned IEnumerable<string>
  while not source.AtEnd do
    yield return source.ReadLine();
  end;
  // No using var: source is disposed by the iterator state machine when the
  // consumer disposes the enumerator. Legal, and carries the §28.3 must-use
  // warning — ReadAndClose above is the warning-free spelling.
end Echo;
```

Moving the parameter out of the iterator (via an `owned` argument call or a `using var` re-bind) puts the parameter in the moved-from state, and the state machine's auto-dispose for that parameter does not run.

<a id="sec-yield-not-allowed-in-lambdas"></a>
### 29.9 `yield` not allowed in lambdas

`yield` is a method-level construct only.

<a id="sec-empty-iterators"></a>
### 29.10 Empty iterators

An iterator method with only `yield break;` is the canonical empty iterator. An empty body (no `yield`) is not an iterator method.

```bezel
public static method Empty<T>(): IEnumerable<T>
  yield break;
end Empty;
```

<a id="sec-multiple-enumeration"></a>
### 29.11 Multiple enumeration

Each `GetEnumerator()` call produces an independent enumerator. Iterating the same source twice with two `for` loops works as expected for collection types.

A **lazy query** — a value produced by a deferred LINQ operator ([stdlib §5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-linq), e.g. `var q := xs.Where(...)`) — is **single-consumption**. It may be enumerated **at most once**: the first enumeration (a `for` loop, or a terminal operator such as `Count`, `First`, or `ToArray`) **consumes** it, exactly as `move` consumes an owned value. A second enumeration, or any other use after the first, is a compile error where the flow analysis can see it statically (the diagnostic points to `.ToArray()`); where a re-enumeration is reachable only at runtime, it raises `InvalidOperationException` (the same loud-failure discipline as mutation-during-iteration, [§29.12](#sec-mutation-during-iteration)). To enumerate the results more than once, materialize first: `var ys := xs.Where(...).ToArray();` produces an owned `Array<T>`, which — like any collection — may be enumerated any number of times. This is stricter than the C# precedent, which silently re-executes a deferred query on each enumeration; Bezel makes the re-execution explicit (it interacts with the borrow lifetime of the query's source) rather than implicit. (A lazy or single-pass source whose backing is itself external, such as a streaming reader, follows the same single-consumption rule.)

**Consumption points (normative list).** A *bound* lazy query is consumed by exactly these uses:

1. **Enumeration or a terminal operator** (`for`, `Count`, `First`, `ToArray`, …) — the case above.
2. **Applying a further deferred operator**: `var q2 := q.Select(f);` consumes the binding `q` — the at-most-once obligation transfers into the composed query (using `q` afterwards is a static error where visible, mirroring move-into-constructor).
3. **Passing the query as an `IEnumerable<T>` argument**: the caller's binding is consumed and the single-enumeration right transfers to the callee.
