Inside a callee, a plain `IEnumerable<T>` parameter is **statically untracked** — the affine tracking is by provenance, not by type — so a violation there is enforced only by the runtime `InvalidOperationException` guard. The diagnostic for every static consumption error names the consumed binding, the consuming use, and the `.ToArray()` materialization remedy.

**The terminal-accessor provenance warning (v0.243, #3047).** A call to a stdlib [§5](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-system-collections-linq) class-element terminal accessor or no-selector aggregation — `First`/`Last`/`Single`/`ElementAt` with the `*OrNull` and predicate forms, `Min()`/`Max()`, and `Aggregate(seed, fold)` on its receiver leg (the seed-leg qualifier at this paragraph's end): the compiler-known members whose result at a class or interface element type is a borrow of the element — **must draw a warning** iff the receiver's statically-tracked provenance — the same flow tracing this section performs for single-consumption, followed through the deferred lazy operators, callback-free and callback-taking alike — roots at a **directly-called iterator method, compiled in the same compilation unit, at least one of whose reachable `yield return` sites classifies as an enumerator-owned fresh yield** ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership)'s first owned-class-typed bullet: a fresh producer or `move` result yielded from a borrowing iterator). Such a borrow is dead on arrival: the element is owned by the terminal's internal enumerator, which the terminal disposes before returning ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership)), so a later use faults deterministically in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal); undefined behavior unchecked). When every reachable yield of the traced iterator is fresh, the diagnostic states the fault as certain; when yields are mixed (some re-borrows of parameter-sourced collections, some fresh), it states that the element may not survive the call. The remedies are stdlib §5's own: materialize first (`ToArray()`), build the elements into an owning collection, or consume the producer through the owning path (`IOwningEnumerable<T>` and owning iteration, stdlib [§4.13](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-owning-enumeration-interfaces)). Every other root stays **silent**: a concrete collection type; a materializer result (`ToArray()`/`ToSet()`/`ToDictionary(…)` — owned collections, collection-backed by construction; a materializer is a terminal, not a deferred operator, so the trace stops at its owned result); an interface-typed parameter, an interface-typed field read, or a call result the trace cannot resolve to a same-unit iterator (statically untracked — this section's stated parameter boundary and its analogues at fields and opaque producers, the runtime backstop remaining the guard); a **cross-module iterator** (the same-unit bound is a **chosen under-approximation**, not a forced one: the artifact interface carries no yield-classification fact, and although [§2.8.2](#sec-artifact-interface)'s definition-site clause does carry exported generic bodies — a public generic iterator's yields are in principle visible there — v0.243 does not read them; carrying the classification as an interface fact is the recorded liftable, not taken at v0.243); and any receiver whose element type is value, `string`, or runtime-managed (no borrow is produced). For `Aggregate(seed, fold)` at a class accumulator only the receiver leg participates, under the same predicate — the seed leg is caller-supplied and sound. The warning changes no acceptance: stdlib §5's admission and the checked-mode backstop are unchanged.

<a id="sec-mutation-during-iteration"></a>
<a id="sec-concurrent-modification"></a>
### 29.12 Mutation during iteration

Modifying a collection while iterating it invalidates the active enumerator. Standard collections detect this and throw `InvalidOperationException` on the next `MoveNext()` (or `MoveNextAsync()`).

**What counts as modification.** *Structural* modification invalidates: any operation that adds, removes, or repositions entries or reallocates storage — `Add`, `AddRange`, `Insert`, `Remove`, `RemoveAt`, `Clear`, `Push`/`Pop`, `Enqueue`/`Dequeue`, a dictionary indexer-set that *inserts* a new key, and the in-place `Sort()`/`Reverse()` (they reposition), together with their owning-collection counterparts. An **element-level write that changes no structure** does not invalidate: assigning through the indexer to an existing position (`arr[i] := v`; `dict[existingKey] := v` updating a present key) leaves the enumerator valid, and a later visit of that position observes the new value — for an owning collection such a set still disposes the displaced element per [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy), which invalidates *borrows of that element*, not the enumerator. The [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) protocol-elision optimization must preserve these faults: a `for` loop the compiler lowers to direct indexing still raises `InvalidOperationException` at the iteration boundary following a structural modification, exactly as the enumerator path would.

The standard pattern for removing during iteration:

```bezel
var toRemove := new Array<Transaction>();
for var t in transactions do
  if t.IsExpired then toRemove.Add(t); end;
end;
for var t in toRemove do
  transactions.Remove(t);
end;
```

<a id="sec-async-iterators"></a>
### 29.13 Async iterators

`await for` iterates `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (borrowing) and `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` (owning) sources. See [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators).

---

<a id="sec-asynchronous-programming"></a>
## 30. Asynchronous Programming

Asynchronous methods run within an *execution domain* — a unit of serial execution scheduled by the runtime ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)). The compiler transforms an async method's body into a state machine that suspends and resumes at each `await`.

<a id="sec-async-methods"></a>
### 30.1 `async` methods

*(`requires` clauses on an `async` method evaluate in the synchronous prefix — a violation surfaces at the call expression, on the caller's stack, before any suspension; `ensures` on `async` methods is not admitted in this revision — [§22.16](#sec-contract-scope).)*

A method declared `async` may use `await`. The return type must be one of:

- `Task` — no result value.
- `Task<T>` for some type T admitted by [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s producer taxonomy (a move-only value T is admitted by neither container) — a result of type T, with no transferable ownership obligation on the awaiter.
- `OwningTask<T>` for some class type T — a result whose ownership transfers to the awaiter ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)).
- `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` — for re-iterable async iterators that contain `yield return` ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)). The yielded values are borrowed by the consumer.
- `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` — for single-use async iterators with borrowed-by-consumer values.
- `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` for class T — for async iterators that yield owned values; each consumer iteration variable is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules (auto-drop with the must-use warning) apply in the loop body.
- `IOwningAsyncEnumerator<T>` for class T — single-use owned-yielding async iterator.

```bezel
public async method DownloadAsync(url: string): Task<string>
  using var client := new HttpClient();
  using var task := client.GetAsync(url);
  return await task;
end DownloadAsync;
```

Calling an async method begins execution synchronously on the calling thread until the first `await` of an incomplete task, at which point the method suspends and returns its `Task` to the caller. If the method completes before encountering an incomplete `await`, the returned task is already in a completed state.

The returned task is a **fresh, caller-owned** value at every call site — the `Task`-family production rule of [§28.3](#sec-producers), keyed on the declared return type, so it holds through interfaces and function values and for instance methods exactly as for static ones (`async` itself is invisible in signatures, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)). This is what entitles `DownloadAsync`'s body above to bind `client.GetAsync(url)` with an obligation-assuming `using var`, and `DownloadAsync`'s own caller to do the same with its result. The signature carries no `owned` marker; the `Task`-family return type is the announcement.

`async` may appear on instance methods, static methods, and lambdas. It may not appear on constructors, destructors, or property/indexer accessors.

Modifier order: `visibility static async ... method ...`.

**Borrow-bearing parameters and results are forbidden (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) — a frame outlives the synchronous call; stack slots cannot enter it).** An `async` method, `async` lambda, or async iterator may not declare a parameter whose type is a borrow-bearing record ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — a span (stdlib §4.14, §4.15) or any record carrying a non-runtime-managed borrow — nor a result/element type that is such a record; for a generic async method the check is re-applied after substitution, so an instantiation whose type argument makes a parameter borrow-bearing is rejected at the instantiation site. The reason is structural: an ordinary borrow is bounded by the synchronous call frame that receives it and is unwound at return ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), [§8.6](#sec-boxing)), but an async method captures its parameters into a heap-allocated state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call and lives until the task settles — a moment the caller does not lexically bound, since the task is an ordinary heap value that may be stored, moved, awaited elsewhere, or fire-and-forgotten ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)). A borrow captured into that frame from a caller-side source therefore has no stack frame whose unwinding bounds it, and [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s frame-local borrow-lifetime rules cannot establish that the source outlives the frame. The **one exception** is a borrow-bearing record the standard library certifies with a normatively-stated source-outlives-task obligation backstopped by checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)): currently only `CancellationToken` ([§30.8](#sec-cancellation); axiom [A10](#sec-axiom-register)), whose borrowed source is a disposal-tracked `CancellationTokenSource` and whose default argument is the null-source sentinel `CancellationToken.None` ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) — the [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) residual-trust shape, on the same stdlib-certified footing as [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet). Records whose only borrows are runtime-managed (`string`-backed spans such as `ReadOnlyStringSpan`, function types, boxed values) are not borrow-bearing ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) and are unaffected. Where a buffer must cross an `await`, pass a heap-owned window — an `Array<T>` with explicit `offset`/`count`, or an owned result type.

**`ref` and `out` parameters are forbidden (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6)).** An `async` method, `async` lambda, or iterator method — synchronous or async ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods)) — may not declare a `ref` or `out` parameter; a compile error at the declaration. The grammar admits the modifiers through the shared `Param` production and the rejection is semantic — the same over-admit-and-reject pattern as [§22.10](#sec-methods-and-constructors-primary-constructors)'s primary constructors and [§23.4](#sec-indexers)'s indexer parameter lists. The reason is the same structural one as the borrow-bearing rule above: a `ref`/`out` argument is a reference to a caller stack slot, bounded by the synchronous call — but these bodies capture their parameters into a heap-allocated state-machine frame that outlives the synchronous call, so the captured slot reference dangles the moment the method returns its task or enumerable at the first suspension; and [§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)'s `out` contract ("must assign every `out` parameter on every exit path") has no coherent exit for a body whose synchronous exit *is* that early return. The rule extends to conversions: an `async` lambda may not be assigned to a function type ([§27.1](#sec-function-types)) whose parameter list carries a `ref`/`out` slot. Non-`async` methods that merely *return* `Task`-family types are unaffected (no state machine — the out-contract completes synchronously), as are `owned` parameters ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters), above); other parameter modifiers' admissibility is governed by their own sections ([§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) for `scoped`). (The alternative — requiring every `out` assigned before the first suspension point — was considered and declined: it is coherent for `out` only and unsound for `ref` (the callee can *read* the dead slot after resumption, not just write it), fragile (inserting an `await` above the assignment breaks callers), and has no known use case; C# rejects both, for both method kinds.)

**Borrow-bearing record locals across suspension (derives: [K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6.1](#sec-kernel-k6) — frame-resident sources).** A local of borrow-bearing record type whose live range crosses a suspension point (`await`, `await using`, `await for`, or — in an async iterator — `yield return`, which suspends the frame while the consumer runs arbitrary code between `MoveNextAsync` calls, [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods), [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) is captured into the state-machine frame together with the borrows it carries. It is admitted across the suspension **iff every borrow it carries has a frame-resident source**: an owned local, a `using var`/`await using var`, or an `owned` parameter of the same async body — locations the frame itself owns (below), which therefore provably survive every suspension. A borrow whose source is caller-side — a plain parameter, `this`, a field reached through `this`, or a capture from an enclosing scope — does not qualify: the source's owner may dispose it while the frame is suspended, and, as with the parameter rule above, a raw span window has no disposal-tracked object through which checked mode could catch the dangle. The program is rejected at the suspension point, naming the local, the non-resident source, and the remedy: re-derive the record after the `await`, or copy the borrowed data into frame-owned storage before it. Values of a stdlib-certified borrow-bearing record (currently only `CancellationToken`) are exempt however obtained — they carry the certified source-outlives-settlement obligation of [§30.8](#sec-cancellation) instead. (A **synchronous** iterator's `yield return` is subject to the same rule — its heap frame has the same shape; see [§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation).)

**`owned` parameters transfer into the frame (derives: [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) with the frame as scope).** An async method's `owned` parameters transfer into the state-machine frame at call time, exactly as an iterator's do ([§29.8](#sec-iterators-with-owned-parameters)). The body may move them out under the ordinary rules — chaining one with `return await <param>` moves it into the outer task's chained slot ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) and counts as such a move-out, so the outer task's teardown, not this rule, disposes it; any `owned` parameter never moved out is disposed by the frame when the task reaches its terminal state — on every completion path (success, fault, and cancellation), after the body's `using var` cleanups and `finally` clauses, in reverse declaration order ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s ordering). Parameters of move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) ride the same machinery. An `owned` parameter never discharged by the body carries the [§28.3](#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement) must-use warning at its declaration; `using var c := move conn;` on entry is the warning-free way to declare frame-lifetime intent. Disposing a not-yet-settled task does not cut this short: the underlying operation runs to its terminal state ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)), and the frame's parameters are disposed then.

**Borrowed parameters, `this`, and captures are held until settlement (derives: [K6.4](#sec-kernel-k6) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)).** An async method's plain (non-`owned`) parameters of class or interface type ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrow vocabulary), its `this` receiver, and an `async` lambda's captures are borrows captured into the state-machine frame — held not for the duration of the synchronous call but until the task **settles**. The call-site admission is unchanged (any borrow admissible as an argument remains admissible, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), with the statically-certain exceptions of [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s deferred-activation rules: an unbound owned temporary may not source a borrow into a frame — iterator or task — that escapes the full expression, and a callback argument's capture-set contribution is rejected by the ordinary scope, store, and frame-return rules where the frame provably escapes a contributed source's lifetime); what the frame adds is a temporal obligation on the **caller**: *every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task, and the borrowed object must not be transferred to another domain — nor consumed into a domain-reachable construction ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s domain-clause extension) — before that settlement.* The domain clause is stated here because a frame-held borrow is invisible to the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze) — it lives in the state machine, in no local borrow binding), and its violation has no runtime backstop of any kind: the transferred object stays alive in the receiving domain, so no disposed flag is ever set ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)). The obligation is a [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)-recorded trust clause: the structural checks are decidable, the temporal guarantee is the programmer's, with [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop as the named safety net — a violation is a deterministic `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and undefined behavior in unchecked mode. The obligation is discharged trivially by the dominant shape — awaiting the task before any source's scope exits — and structurally by `TaskScope` ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers); stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope)), whose disposal quiesces its children before the enclosing scope unwinds. The shapes that carry a live residual are the abandonment idioms — `using var t := call();` dropped without an await, and `Task.FireAndForget(call())` — where an argument's or the receiver's owner can dispose it while the frame is suspended ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) names the hazard). Abandon only tasks whose inputs are owned (transferred in), sendable-copied, `string`/value-typed, or otherwise guaranteed to outlive the operation; supervise everything else to settlement.

An async method's `return expression;` completes the task with the value. `return;` (in `Task`-returning forms) completes the task with no value. Falling off the end of a `Task`-returning async method is equivalent to `return;`. A `Task<T>`-returning async method must `return` a value on every path.

<a id="sec-await"></a>
### 30.2 `await`

`await` suspends the current async method until a task completes:

```bezel
var result := await someTask;
```

The shape above is the simple case — appropriate when `someTask` returns a value type, `string`, or `Task` (no value). When the task's result type is a class, one of the patterns in [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) applies; the bare assignment shown here is rejected.

Behavior:

- If the task is already completed, `await` returns the result synchronously.
- If the task is faulted, `await` re-raises the exception.
- If the task was cancelled, `await` raises `OperationCanceledException`.
- If the task is running, the async method suspends; when the task completes, the continuation is queued to its domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)).

`await` is valid only inside an `async` method or `async` lambda.

<a id="sec-the-task-and-taskt-types"></a>
<a id="sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types"></a>
### 30.3 The `Task`, `Task<T>`, and `OwningTask<T>` types

```bezel
public class Task
  public readonly property IsCompleted: bool;
  public readonly property IsFaulted: bool;
  public readonly property IsCancelled: bool;

  public method Wait();

  destructor;       // runs continuation cleanup and disposes any
                    //   unconsumed `owned` result. Task is non-trivial-
                    //   dispose, which is why discard `_ := someAsyncCall();`
                    //   is rejected ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)).
end Task;

public class Task<T>: Task
  public readonly property Result: T;
end Task;

public class OwningTask<T>: Task where T: class
  // Owning task: result transfers ownership to the awaiter (Pattern B).
  // Single-consumer by type.
  public readonly property Result: T;
                    // reading Result on a COMPLETED OwningTask
                    // in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership
                    // exactly like `await` (the result buffer is consumed;
                    // a second read/await raises InvalidOperationException).
                    // Subject to the same §30.3 blocking rules as Task<T>.Result:
                    // legal on an incomplete task only outside domains.
end OwningTask;
```

`Wait()` and `Result` are synchronous escape hatches for **code running outside any domain** — in practice, the synchronous portion of program startup: a non-`async` `Main`, and code it calls directly on the main thread. There, they block the calling thread until the task completes; the pool's workers drain the task's domain concurrently, so completion makes progress (this is the same mechanism by which the runtime itself drives an `async Main`, [§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)).

**Inside a domain continuation — equivalently, anywhere `await` is available or the caller was reached from one — a blocking wait on an incomplete task is an error.** A domain executes its continuations serially to completion ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)); a continuation blocked in `Wait()`/`Result` freezes its domain, and any awaited chain whose completion routes through that domain can never finish: a deterministic deadlock, not a hazard. The compiler rejects `Wait()` and `Result` lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (there, `await` is strictly superior and always available). Where static rejection cannot see the call (a non-`async` helper invoked from a continuation), the runtime raises `InvalidOperationException` at the call site instead of parking: *"blocking wait inside a domain continuation; the domain can never advance — await the task, or query IsCompleted."* Reading `Result` on a **completed** task is always legal and non-blocking: on a faulted task it re-raises the exception; on a cancelled task it raises `OperationCanceledException`.

Reading `Result` on a completed `Task<T>` whose `T` is a **class** type (Pattern A) is additionally subject to the same owning-source rule as `await` ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) consumer-side rules; unified with [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s temporary machinery in): the read produces a **borrow whose source is the task expression's location** — a named owning position bounds the borrow by that location's lifetime, and an unbound owned temporary (`SomeProducer().Result`) is admitted when the borrow is confined to the same full expression, the temporary being disposed at the expression's end exactly as for the corresponding `await`. A form whose borrow escapes a temporary read's full expression remains a compile error, exactly as the corresponding `await` is.

`OwningTask<T>` exposes `Result`: reading it on a **completed** task in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership of the result to the reader exactly as `await` does — the result buffer is consumed, and a second read or `await` raises `InvalidOperationException`. The same blocking-wait rules as `Task<T>.Result` apply (legal on an incomplete task only outside a domain). Awaiting an `OwningTask<T>` in an owned-consuming position remains the normal way to obtain the result (see [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) Pattern B).

`Task`, `Task<T>`, and `OwningTask<T>` are classes — they require disposal, with the patterns described in [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal). Listing `IDisposable` explicitly in the inheritance clause would be redundant since every class implicitly implements it ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)). The `destructor;` form above follows the standard library documentation-shorthand convention (stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-conventions)); the actual destructor body is provided by the runtime and runs the continuation-cleanup logic described in [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) (the `FireAndForget` and `using var`-disposal-without-await cases).

<a id="sec-multiple-awaiters"></a>
### 30.4 Multiple awaiters

A `Task` or `Task<T>` may be awaited from multiple places, sequentially or concurrently. Every awaiter sees the same eventual state. The underlying computation runs once. Continuations resume in unspecified order, but never concurrently with one another within a domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)).

`OwningTask<T>` is single-consumer per the Pattern B rules in [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal): **the first await spends the task regardless of outcome** (success, fault, or cancellation), and a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`. (The "awaiting a faulted task re-raises" rule of [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods) applies to `Task`/`Task<T>` and to the *first* await of an `OwningTask<T>` only.) Sharing an `OwningTask<T>` across multiple potential awaiters is not the intended pattern. For fan-out with a class-typed result, use `Task<T>` (Pattern A); for single-consumer ownership-transferring resource production, use `OwningTask<T>` (Pattern B).

<a id="sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal"></a>
### 30.5 Result lifetime and task disposal

The task owns any class-typed result it produces; the task *itself* is owned by the caller of the call that produced it ([§28.3](#sec-producers)'s `Task`-family production rule — the patterns below govern the *result*; the container obligation is the caller's from the call site on). The pattern by which a result is consumed is selected by the producer's return type — there is no syntactic peeking at `await`'s context.

<a id="sec-producer-side-return-type-rules"></a>
#### Producer-side return-type rules

(axiom [A3](#sec-axiom-register) — the two-container design: `Task<T>` for class T carries shared borrows, `OwningTask<T>` a single owned transfer; the kernel checks both patterns' flows, forces neither.)

- `Task` and `Task<T>` for **copyable** value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), `string`, or runtime-managed T: produced as today; no ownership obligation crosses the await boundary.
- `Task<T>` for **class** T: the task may be awaited from multiple places. Every awaiter receives a borrow of the same underlying result. The result's lifetime is tied to the task — disposing the task disposes the result. This is **Pattern A**.

  **Pattern A result slots are of three kinds (scope-bound chaining; borrowed-source chains).** What the outer task's result slot records — and what its teardown disposes — is determined by what the async body produced:

  1. **A fresh owned value** (a `return` of an owned expression): the task **owns the result** and its destructor disposes it directly (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1)).

  2. **`return await` over an owned Pattern A source — the chained slot** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K6](#sec-kernel-k6) — the task cannot own what it borrowed, so the container moves into a chained slot; exactly-once transitively). The result is a *borrow through the source task*: ownership of the **source task** transfers into the outer task's state (a **chained** slot), and the outer destructor disposes the chained source task, never the borrowed result directly. "Disposing the task disposes the result" thereby holds *transitively*, and every Pattern A borrow has a defined owner at every link of the chain. **Chaining from a scope-bound source.** When the source of `return await <source>` is an `owned` parameter of the enclosing async method, the transfer into the chained slot is an ordinary [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) **move-out** of the parameter: it is thereby moved out, so [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s dispose-at-terminal-state rule for not-moved-out `owned` parameters does not apply to it — the outer task's teardown disposes the chained task instead. When the source is a `using var`/`await using var` local — which [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) forbids moving — no move occurs: the source's slot already lives in the enclosing state-machine frame, and the chained-slot arrangement **defers its disposal** from the frame's scope end to the outer task's teardown; a disposal-*timing* dispensation of the same kind as the await-consumes-operand rule below, not an exception to the `using var` no-move rule (axiom [A12](#sec-axiom-register)). On both paths the source task is disposed exactly once — by the outer task's destructor, transitively.

  3. **`return await` over a borrowed source** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4) — no transfer possible; teardown disposes nothing; the residual discharges trivially for process-lived statics)**.** When the source is a **borrow** — an admitted static task field or property ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)(b)'s cache is the canonical case), an `owned` field of `this` read without `move`, an owning-collection slot, a borrowing-iteration variable, or any other admitted borrowed operand — no ownership transfers: the outer task's result slot records a **borrow through the source task**, and the outer task's teardown disposes **nothing** on that link. Transfer is impossible for a borrowed source and would be unsound (a static cache disposed at some caller's teardown while every other caller still awaits it; an owned field moved without `move`); the borrowed-source chain is the only coherent third kind.

  Soundness of the borrowed-source chain (kind 3) rides on the source outliving the outer task's result uses — a caller-side residual of [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)'s recorded family, backstopped per [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4) (the task and its result are disposal-tracked, so a violated bound faults as `DisposedAccessException`, [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) — and it is discharged **trivially for process-lived static storage**: an admitted static task field lives for the duration of the program and is never disposed before exit ([§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)), and even overwriting the mutable cache never disposes the displaced referent (same section), so a chained borrow of it cannot dangle. The chained move-out of an **owned** source (an `owned` parameter or a plain owned local — kind 2 above; a `using var` source is not moved, only disposal-deferred) is announced by the Pattern A `return await` form itself and joins no consume-site freeze list, for a structural reason: its new owner is the outer task, which cannot dispose the chained task before this body — including its `finally` blocks — completes ([K5.4](#sec-kernel-k5)'s recorded vacuity override; [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)).
- `OwningTask<T>` for **class** T: the task produces a single owned result. Awaiting transfers ownership to the awaiter. The task may be awaited at most once for a successful (non-faulted, non-cancelled) result. This is **Pattern B**.
- `OwningTask<T>` for **copyable** value type, `string`, or runtime-managed T: a compile error. `owned` on such a result is meaningless.
- A **move-only value T** ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types) — an owning-classified choice instantiation ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification) rule 1) or an owning inline array ([§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays))) is admitted by **no row**: declaring `Task<T>` or `OwningTask<T>` over such a T is a **compile error at the declaration** — [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)'s multi-award rule would hand the same must-move-exactly-once value to every awaiter, and `OwningTask<T>` admits class T only. For a generic declaration whose result classification depends on a type parameter (`Task<Result<T, E>>`), the check is re-applied after substitution — an instantiation whose type arguments make the result move-only is rejected at the instantiation site, as for the borrow-bearing rejection ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)) and per [§35.11](#sec-choice-generics)'s instantiation-site enforcement.

`OwningTask<T>` is the right choice for resource acquisition — operations whose entire purpose is to produce a fresh, single-consumer resource (a connection, a lock token, a parsed document). `Task<T>` is the right choice for fan-out: multiple subscribers reading the same eventual result.

<a id="sec-consumer-side-rules"></a>
#### Consumer-side rules

For `await someTask`, the consumer's obligations are determined by the task's static return type:

**Copyable value type, `string`, or runtime-managed result:** any form is permitted. The result is a value or shared-immutable reference.

```bezel
var n := await CountBytesAsync(url);     // result is int
var s := await FetchStringAsync(url);    // result is string
```

For these forms, the awaited task expression may be a bare producer call (as above); the await operator is **owned-consuming with respect to its operand** when the operand is an **unbound owned temporary** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — a bare producer call or other unnamed owned task expression. The implicit task-disposal performed by the runtime as part of the await satisfies the discharge requirement on the temporary — the user does not write a separate `using var` for the task. A **named** operand — a `using var` or plain owned local, an `owned` parameter, an `owned` field — is **borrow-awaited**: the await neither consumes nor disposes it, multiple awaits are permitted per [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters), and an owned local operand keeps its ordinary [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge (auto-drop at scope end). Named-operand consumption is the **Pattern B (`OwningTask<T>`) rule only** (below); it does not apply to `Task`/`Task<T>`.

**`Task<T>` for class T (Pattern A)** (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) — the admission is [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s ordinary borrow machinery applied to the awaited operand)**:** the borrow produced by the await must have a source whose lifetime the compiler can bound, and that source is the awaited task expression's **own location** — the operand kinds are [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s. A *reference to* a **named location** whose lifetime is visible at the await site bounds the borrow by that location's scope ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)); for a plain borrowed operand, the binding's own borrow chain carries the true-task-outlives-the-use residual ([K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4)), and a borrowed alias of an admitted operand inherits the admission. An **unbound owned temporary** ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) — a bare producer call or other unnamed owned task expression — bounds the borrow by its [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) full-expression boundary, *provided the borrowed result is used only within that expression*: the temporary is then disposed at the expression's end, after every use of the borrow, and disposing the task disposes the borrowed result with it. A producer call whose result is directly consumed by a Pattern A return in the enclosing async method is the **chained slot** (kind 2 above; [K6](#sec-kernel-k6)) — a task *move*, not a borrow escape. A borrow that would **escape** the full expression of an unbound-temporary await — a `var` binding, a store, a non-chained return — has no source that survives the expression, and the await is a compile error ([K8.4](#sec-kernel-k8): rejected, never lifetime-extended); bind the task to a `using var` first.

The principle resolves into the following examples of admitted task-expression positions — each an instance of one of [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s source kinds, the first eight named locations of the several kinds, the ninth the frame case; the list is not exhaustive but illustrates the rule, and its closure is [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s named-location taxonomy: a task-typed storage read through any field path rooted at a live object, and a borrowed alias of any admitted operand, are admitted with the source set the path derives:

- **A reference to a `using var` or `await using var`-bound local** of static type `Task<T>`. The canonical form. The await produces a borrow whose source is the local; the borrow is valid within the local's scope.
- **A reference to an `owned` parameter** of the enclosing method, of static type `Task<T>`. The parameter's lifetime spans the method body; the borrow is valid within the body.
- **A reference to a plain owned local** of static type `Task<T>`. The local's scope bounds the borrow — the named-location principle applied to the movable binding; consuming or reassigning the binding while the borrow lives is rejected by the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)), and an explicit `Dispose()` remains the announced kill with the checked-mode backstop. `using var` stays the canonical form (the pin makes the bound obvious).
- **A reference to a plain (non-`owned`) local or parameter** of static type `Task<T>`. The everyday helper shape — `public async method Report(t: Task<Data>): Task` awaiting `t` — is admitted: the parameter is a named binding whose scope bounds the result borrow, the caller's own obligations ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods) settlement, [§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters) fan-out) keep the underlying task alive around the callee's use, and ownership of the location was never the admission's real criterion (the owned-field, static-field, and iteration-variable positions below are themselves borrow reads).
- **A reference to a task-typed field path rooted at a live object** — an `owned` field of `this` (`await _t`; the field's lifetime spans `this`'s, and the borrow is valid within method calls on `this`), an `owned` field of any other live root (`await b._t` where `b` is a borrowed local or parameter — the [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) named location "a field path rooted at a live object"), or a plain task-typed borrow field, whose held borrow's own chain joins the set. The borrow's source set is the path ([K2.1](#sec-kernel-k2)/[K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2)): bounded by the root's scope, carrying the root's true-task-outlives-the-use residual exactly as the principle paragraph above records for a plain borrowed operand ([K2.2](#sec-kernel-k2) + [K4.3](#sec-kernel-k4), backstopped per [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)).
- **A reference to an admitted static field** of static type `Task<T>` — a `static readonly` task field, or a mutable static admitted by [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2(ii) (the [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)(b) lazy cache, read as `_cfg!`). The storage is process-lived and never disposed before exit, so the borrow is valid everywhere. The class-typed result reached through such a chain is process-shared across every domain that awaits the cached task; [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's confine-or-synchronize obligation applies to it unchanged.
- **An indexer access on an owning collection** whose static type is `OwningArray<Task<T>>` (or analogous), where the collection itself occupies an owning location. The await produces a borrow whose source is the collection; the borrow is valid within the collection's lifetime. The same applies to dictionary indexer access into `OwningDictionary<K, Task<T>>`.
- **An iteration variable** in `for var task in tasks do ... end` where `tasks` is `Array<Task<T>>` or `OwningArray<Task<T>>` (borrowing iteration, not Drain). Each `task` is a borrow whose source is `tasks`; the await within the loop body produces a borrow valid for the loop body.
- **A producer call directly inside `return` of an async method whose return type is `Task<U>` for class U** (Pattern A) — i.e., `return await Producer();`. The producer's task is owned by the enclosing state machine; the borrow flows into the outer Pattern A task's result slot, whose lifetime is bounded by the outer task.

`Process(await Producer())` is therefore **admitted**: the producer's task is an unbound owned temporary, its borrowed result is consumed by `Process` within the same full expression, and the task — and with it the result — is disposed at the end of the statement ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)); the disposal runs after the borrowing use, so the result is live for the call, exactly as in the `Folded(src).Sorted()` example there. What the principle rejects is a borrow that **outlives** an unbound temporary: `var x := await Producer();` binds the borrow to a local that survives the expression while the task that sources it dies with the expression. The fix is to bind the producer's result to a `using var` first:

```bezel
using var task := Producer();
Process(await task);
```

The borrow produced by `await task` (where `task` occupies one of the admitted positions) may flow to:

- A `var` binding: `var r := await task;` — `r` is a non-owned local with the same source as `task`.
- A non-owned argument: `Process(await task);`.
- A `return` expression whose return type accepts a borrow with the same source (e.g., `return await task;` from an async method returning Pattern A `Task<T>`).

The borrow may **not** flow to (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) state-match — a borrow cannot assume an obligation):

- A `using var` binding: `using var r := await task;` is rejected — `using var` requires an owned right-hand side, but the await produced a borrow.
- An assignment to an `owned` field or owned-element collection slot — would manufacture ownership the source did not grant.
- An `owned` parameter argument.
- A `return` expression whose return type is `owned T` or carries ownership.

```bezel
using var task := FetchAsync(url);
var response := await task;              // borrowed reference, OK
ProcessResponse(response);
// At end of scope: task is disposed; response disposed with it.
```

A bare `var x := await someTask;` where `someTask` is not in one of the admitted positions is a compile error. The error message identifies the offending await and references the principle above; the typical fix is to introduce a `using var task := Producer(); var x := await task;` pair.

**`OwningTask<T>` for class T (Pattern B)** (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) + [K3](#sec-kernel-k3) — the await mints an owned result, which must reach a discharging position)**:** the await must appear in an **owned-consuming context**. The contexts are [K3](#sec-kernel-k3)'s owned-consuming positions — among them the store into an owned-element collection slot or `owned` field (`coll[i] := await ...`; `field := await ...` restoring a moved-from field, [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)), the argument bound to an `owned` parameter, the `return` under `owned T` or a return type that wraps it (such as `OwningTask<T>`), and the owning iterator's `yield return`, whose transfer flows through the enumerator to the consumer per [§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) "Iterator yield ownership" — together with the owned binding forms: `using var x := await ...` (the canonical form; `await using var x := await ...` for an asynchronously-disposable result) and `var x := await ...`, which introduces an owned local of class type T under [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s standard discharge rules from the binding point forward — and the discard statement `_ := await ...;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_), [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)), which disposes the awaited result at the end of the statement as an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)): the end-of-statement counterpart of `using var _ := await ...;`.

The task is disposed implicitly without disposing its result; it cannot be awaited again, and a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`.

The await operator on a `OwningTask<T>` for class T is itself **owned-consuming with respect to its operand** (derives: [K3.5](#sec-kernel-k3) + [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4)): when the awaited expression is an owned task value (a plain owned local of `OwningTask<T>` — not a `using var` binding: a `using var` cannot be moved out of ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), so a read of it is a borrow and such an await is the borrowed-operand case below — an iteration variable from draining an `OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>`, an `owned` parameter, or any other owned-typed expression of `OwningTask<T>`), the await consumes the task as part of the operation and satisfies the discharge requirement on the operand — **on all outgoing edges of the await, including the fault/cancel (exception) edge**: after a faulted first await, an owned operand is moved-from per [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows), and a retry requires binding a fresh task. The implicit task-disposal that the runtime performs is the same operation that satisfies the type system's discharge rule; one is the runtime view, the other is the static-analysis view of the same event.

Like `throw x` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and the discard `_ := x;` ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)), this consume is a [K4.2](#sec-kernel-k4) **announced kill** with a runtime backstop: the `await` keyword plus the single-consumer operand type announce the kill at the source, and the await's implicit task disposal sets the disposed flag — a stale borrow of the operand faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)). Pattern B await therefore deliberately joins no consume-site freeze list and takes no operand marker — the `await` keyword plus the single-consumer operand type are themselves the announcement ([K3.13](#sec-kernel-k3)'s announced set), and the transfer marker is not admitted where the target already announces the consume ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)); it is [K3.5](#sec-kernel-k3) in the kernel's owned-consuming enumeration.

In practice this means the natural patterns work without explicit task disposal:

```bezel
// Iteration variable from draining: task is owned, await consumes it
for var task in taskArray.Drain() do
  results.Add(await task);     // task discharged by the await; no further obligation
end;

// Local variable of owned task type
var theTask := SomeFactory();   // theTask: owned OwningTask<T>
using var result := await theTask;  // theTask discharged by the await
```

In neither case does the user need a separate `using var` to discharge the task itself — the await's implicit disposal *is* the discharge.

Pattern B tasks are single-consumer by type — once awaited they are spent, and sharing a `OwningTask<T>` across multiple potential awaiters is not the intended pattern. In the typical case the operand is owned (an owned local, an owned parameter, or an iteration variable from draining an array of tasks), and the discharge rule applies as described above. When the operand is borrowed, the await still disposes the task implicitly per the runtime semantics, but no discharge is owed for it. The `using var task := SomeFactory(); var x := await task;` shape, where `task` is `using var`-bound and then awaited, is one common form; the await's implicit disposal happens first, and the using-var's disposal at scope end is a no-op per the idempotency rule ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)).

```bezel
// Canonical form: using-var binding
using var token := await semaphore.AcquireAsync();
DoCriticalWork();
// At end of scope: token disposed, releasing the semaphore.

// Plain var binding — x is an owned local subject to standard discharge rules
var token := await semaphore.AcquireAsync();
TransferToHelper(move token);     // owned local consumed by owned parameter

// Direct ownership transfer to a method call accepting owned
results.Add(await loadTask);     // results: OwningArray<T>; Add takes owned

// Direct return
public async method Acquire(): OwningTask<Connection>
  return await ConnectAsync(url);     // owned T flows to owned T return
end Acquire;
```

A bare `var x := await someTask;` compiles: `x` is an owned local under the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules; an `x` never discharged auto-drops at scope exit with the must-use warning. `var x := <owned producer>` — a binding whose right-hand side is a fresh owned producer (an await result, a `new` expression, an owned-returning call) — is itself an owned-consuming context. *(scope note: producer right-hand sides only; a read of a named owned binding in a binding position is a borrow unless marked `owned` — [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows). Pattern B awaits are producers and are unaffected.)*

For an asynchronously-disposable owned result, use `await using var`:

```bezel
// ConnectAsync is illustrative; see §28.12 note.
await using var connection := await ConnectAsync(url);
await connection.SendAsync(data);
// At end of scope: connection.DisposeAsync() awaited.
```

For a `OwningTask<T>` not awaited in an owned-consuming context — a bare expression-statement `await t;`, whose minted result would be dropped silently, or an await in a non-owned-consuming expression position (a non-`owned` argument, an operand of a larger expression) — the await is a compile error. The explicit discard `_ := await t;` is **not** such a case: the discard is itself an owned-consuming position (this section's list; [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) and disposes the result. The error message names the owned-consuming positions admitted by the rule above and points to the `using var` form as the canonical choice.

<a id="sec-disposing-an-unconsumed-ownedtaskt"></a>
#### Disposing an unconsumed `OwningTask<T>`

If a `OwningTask<T>` is dropped or disposed before its result has been transferred — for example, by `using var` on the task itself with no await — disposing the task disposes the result if one was produced (derives: [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) cascade + [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)'s non-blocking discipline — the container owns the result until transfer). This makes "fire and forget then drop" safe for owned-result tasks.

```bezel
do
  using var t := semaphore.AcquireAsync();
  // No await; nothing transferred. If t completes before we leave the block,
  // its produced token is disposed (the semaphore is released).
end;
```

When the task has not completed at the point of disposal, the `Dispose()` call attaches a continuation that disposes the produced result whenever it appears, then returns immediately. The dispose call does not block waiting for completion. The underlying operation continues to run; any side effects of the operation still occur, and the result, when produced, is disposed by the continuation. The task transitions to its terminal disposed state immediately for the purposes of any further awaits — any await of an already-disposed task raises `InvalidOperationException`, a never-awaited-then-disposed task's first await included.

A task that has been awaited and faulted, or awaited and cancelled, has no owned result to dispose; disposal is a no-op for the result.

Dropping a not-yet-settled task this way leaves the running frame holding whatever borrows entered it — the receiver and any borrowed arguments — so [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation rests on the caller (in the example above: `semaphore` must outlive the abandoned acquisition's settlement).

<a id="sec-multiple-awaits-on-ownedtaskt"></a>
#### Multiple awaits on `OwningTask<T>`

A `OwningTask<T>` is single-consumer by type (derives: [K2](#sec-kernel-k2) fan-out vs. [K1.7](#sec-kernel-k1) — one obligation moves once; `InvalidOperationException` is its dynamic dual). Awaiting one twice raises `InvalidOperationException` on the second await even when the first await completed successfully — the result has already been moved out.

For a `Task<T>` (no `owned`) for class T, multiple awaits are permitted ([§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)); each receives a borrow.

<a id="sec-constructing-a-completed-task-with-a-class-typed-result"></a>
#### Constructing a completed task with a class-typed result

The factory `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T)` produces a completed task whose result is `value`. It is restricted to non-class T (value types, `string`, runtime-managed reference types); calling it with a class-typed T is a compile error.

For class T, use `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T>` instead (derives: axiom [A3](#sec-axiom-register) + [K1](#sec-kernel-k1) — an externally-supplied owned value transfers into the single-consumer container). The caller transfers ownership of `value` to the task; the produced task is Pattern B (single-consumer, owned result), and consumers await it under the `using var x := await ...` shape:

```bezel
class TaskFactoryDemo
  async method Consume(): Task
    var i := await Task.FromResult(42);                                // T = int, value-typed
    var s := await Task.FromResult("done");                            // T = string, runtime-managed
    using var m := await Task.FromOwnedResult<MyClass>(new MyClass());  // T = MyClass → OwningTask<MyClass>
  end Consume;
end TaskFactoryDemo;
```

The same split applies to `TaskCompletionSource<T>`: the standard form is for non-class T (copyable value, string, runtime-managed) and produces `Task<T>`; `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> where T: class` is the form for class T and produces `OwningTask<T>`. See [§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) and [§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet).

There is no factory for producing a Pattern A `Task<T>` of class T from an externally-supplied owned value; Pattern A class-typed tasks arise from async methods whose body returns a value (the compiler inserts the appropriate ownership transfer into the task's slot) and from awaiting other Pattern A sources. Imperative completion of a Pattern A class-typed task is a future-revision question; the cases that motivate it are uncommon, and the available patterns (writing an async wrapper that awaits an `OwningTaskCompletionSource` and re-publishes the result) cover the practical needs.

<a id="sec-idiom-async-resource-acquisition"></a>
#### Idiom: async resource acquisition

The combination of `OwningTask<T>` and Pattern B is what makes resource-acquisition APIs natural:

```bezel
public class Semaphore
  public async method AcquireAsync(): OwningTask<SemaphoreToken>;
end Semaphore;

// Caller:
using var token := await sem.AcquireAsync();
DoWork();
// token disposed at scope end -> semaphore released.
```

The owned-result task expresses the intent directly; no separate synchronous allocation step is needed.

<a id="sec-async-lambdas"></a>
### 30.6 Async lambdas

```bezel
var fetcher: (string) -> Task<string> := async lambda(url) => do
  using var client := new HttpClient();
  using var task := client.GetAsync(url);
  return await task;
end;

var quick: (string) -> Task<int> := async lambda(url) => await CountBytesAsync(url);

var loader: (string) -> OwningTask<Resource> := async lambda(path) => do
  return await LoadResourceAsync(path);     // Pattern B return; the lambda's
                                             //   state machine forwards the
                                             //   owned Resource through.
end;
```

The function type of an async lambda has a `Task`, `Task<T>`, or `OwningTask<T>` return type. The choice follows the same rules as for async methods ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)): `Task` for void, `Task<T>` for borrowing or value-typed results, `OwningTask<T>` for class-typed results that transfer ownership to the awaiter (Pattern B; see [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)). The parameter slots of an async lambda's function type are plain, `owned`, or `scoped` only: a target type carrying a `ref` or `out` slot is rejected for an `async` lambda ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods)).

<a id="sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators"></a>
### 30.7 Async iterators

An async iterator combines `yield` and `await`. The method is `async` and returns `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` ([§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods) for the `owned` marker on an instance or extension member):

```bezel
public async method ReadLinesAsync(path: string): owned IAsyncEnumerable<string>
  // OpenAsync, ReadLineAsync, and AtEnd are illustrative; the example shows
  // the async-iterator shape, not a stream API in the standard library.
  await using var fs := await OpenAsync(path);
  while not fs.AtEnd do
    yield return await fs.ReadLineAsync();
  end;
end ReadLinesAsync;
```

```bezel
interface IAsyncEnumerable<out T>
  method GetAsyncEnumerator(token: CancellationToken := CancellationToken.None): owned IAsyncEnumerator<T>;
end IAsyncEnumerable;

interface IAsyncEnumerator<out T>: IAsyncDisposable
  method MoveNextAsync(): Task<bool>;
  readonly property Current: T;
end IAsyncEnumerator;
```

Consume with `await for`:

```bezel
public async method ProcessFileAsync(path: string): Task
  await for var line in ReadLinesAsync(path) do
    Process(line);
  end;
end ProcessFileAsync;
```

`await for` is valid only inside an async method or async lambda. It desugars analogously to `for`: it acquires an async enumerator with `await using`, calls `MoveNextAsync()` with `await` in a loop.

<a id="sec-cancellation-in-await-for"></a>
#### Cancellation in `await for`

`await for` accepts an optional `with` clause to pass a `CancellationToken` to the async enumerator:

```bezel
await for var line in ReadLinesAsync(path) with token do
  Process(line);
end;
```

The `with token` clause passes `token` as the argument to `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)`. When omitted, `CancellationToken.None` is passed. The `with` clause is syntactically distinct from the record `with(...)` suffix — it appears after the `in` source expression and before `do`, its content is a single expression of type `CancellationToken`, and it carries no parenthesized assignment list ([§9.5](#sec-non-destructive-update-with)'s header rule: `with` followed by `(` `Identifier` `:=` is the record-update suffix on the source; any other `with` opens this clause).

**Token routing in generated async iterators.** For a compiler-generated async iterator, the enumerator returned by the generated `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)` captures the token, and every `MoveNextAsync()` performs an implicit `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` — on entry, and at each resume from suspension within the advance — so a requested cancellation faults the in-flight `MoveNextAsync` task with `OperationCanceledException` at the next suspension boundary. The iterator body cannot otherwise observe the enumerator's token: there is no implicit binding of it to a body name (a C#-`[EnumeratorCancellation]`-style parameter binding is declined as implicit magic). A body that needs to observe cancellation mid-operation declares its own `CancellationToken` parameter, and the caller passes the same token both ways.

<a id="sec-async-iteration-with-owned-yields"></a>
#### Async iteration with owned yields

For async iterators that produce owned values, declare the return type as `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` (where `T: class`; [§29.3](#sec-iterator-methods) for the `owned` marker on an instance or extension member) and `await for` over the result:

```bezel
public async method OpenFilesAsync(paths: IEnumerable<string>): owned IOwningAsyncEnumerable<FileStream>
  for var path in paths do
    yield return await OpenAsync(path);    // each yielded FileStream is owned
  end;
end OpenFilesAsync;

public async method ProcessAllAsync(paths: IEnumerable<string>): Task
  await for var fs in OpenFilesAsync(paths) do
    using var f := move fs;                 // discharge owned iteration variable
    await ProcessOneAsync(f);
  end;
end ProcessAllAsync;
```

The `await for` desugaring picks `GetOwningAsyncEnumerator()` (and `TakeCurrent()`) when the source has static type `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`. Each iteration variable is owned; the §28.3 discharge rules apply on every exit edge of the loop body — the same rule as for synchronous `for` over `IOwningEnumerable<T>` ([§29.2](#sec-desugaring-of-for) "Iterator yield ownership"). When the source implements both `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` and `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>`, the static type of the source expression selects the desugaring; default iteration uses `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (borrowing), and the owning path requires the source to be typed `IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` explicitly.

The `with token` clause works the same way for owning async iterators — `await for var fs in OpenFilesAsync(paths) with token do ...` passes the token to `GetOwningAsyncEnumerator(token)`.

**`await` inside `finally`.** Inside an async iterator, `await` may not appear in a `finally` block — a compile error. The `yield` placement restrictions of [§29.6](#sec-restrictions-inside-try-catch-finally) apply unchanged; this rule additionally restricts `await`, and only inside async *iterators* (an ordinary `async` method may await in its `finally`, [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)). The reason is disposal: when a consumer abandons iteration early, the iterator's pending `finally` blocks run synchronously inside `Dispose` ([§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)) — there is no async driver at that point, so a suspension inside the `finally` would have nowhere to resume; the continuation would be silently discarded, which is precisely the defined-fault philosophy's forbidden outcome. A `finally` that needs asynchronous cleanup awaits *before* yielding (hoisting the resource acquisition), or the type implements the cleanup in its `Dispose` path. This mirrors the catch-guard rule of [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods): positions evaluated during synchronous unwinding or dispatch are synchronous.

The rule governs **source-written** `finally` blocks only. The implicit finally of an `await using var` in an async iterator is exempt on the normal path: at scope end the generated code awaits `DisposeAsync()` under the ordinary async driver — which is why this section's own `ReadLinesAsync` example is well-formed. On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point: the destructor runs and `DisposeAsync` is skipped ([§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s no-destructor warning covers types whose async cleanup has no synchronous fallback). For a class that implements `IAsyncDisposable` and declares **no destructor** — no synchronous fallback at all, by design (`TaskScope`, stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope), is the standard instance) — that silent skip would void cleanup the type states normatively. An `await using var` whose static type is such a class (or is of **interface** static type — `IAsyncDisposable` or any interface deriving from it: an interface cannot promise a destructor, so the runtime type's fallback posture is statically unknowable and interface-typed bindings are conservatively included; a recorded liftable bound) therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator: a compile error at the yield, naming the binding and the remedies — dispose before the yield, or hoist the work into a non-iterator `async` helper called between yields. The check is static and local: the class-level fact is the one [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s declaration-site warning already keys on, and across-suspension liveness is the analysis [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s borrow-bearing-record rule already runs. For types **with** a destructor, the synchronous-fallback path above remains the defined degraded behavior, unchanged. (Driving `DisposeAsync` from the abandonment pass via an async unwind driver would lift this restriction wholesale; that driver is deferred future work, not foreclosed.)
<a id="sec-cancellation"></a>
### 30.8 Cancellation

Cancellation is cooperative via `CancellationToken`. The standard library defines the surface (the full declaration is in std lib [§6.1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-cancellationtoken-and-cancellationtokensource); the members referenced by the language rules are shown here). Sources compose: a **linked** source — `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinked(a, b)` / `CreateLinkedAll(parents)` — cancels when any parent token cancels, with the parent sources outliving the linked source per the ordinary source-outlives-token rule; linking is intra-domain (cross-domain cancellation remains a channel message, rationale §12.6). Cancel-on-dispose makes `using var` scopes double as cancellation scopes (stdlib §6.1).

```bezel
public record CancellationToken
  public static readonly property None: CancellationToken;
  public readonly property IsCancellationRequested: bool;
  public method ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
  public method Register(scoped callback: () -> ()): owned Subscription;
end CancellationToken;

public class CancellationTokenSource: IDisposable
  public readonly property Token: CancellationToken;
  public readonly property IsCancellationRequested: bool;
  public method Cancel();
  public method CancelAfter(delay: TimeSpan);
end CancellationTokenSource;
```

`CancellationToken` is a record holding a borrowed reference to its source. The token observes the source's state; when `Cancel()` is called on the source, all tokens derived from it report `IsCancellationRequested == true`. Per the record-disposal rules ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), the token does not own the source; the source must outlive any tokens that observe it. For typical short-lived uses (token passed as a parameter to async calls that complete before the source is disposed), this is automatic.

That conditional is load-bearing: passing a token to an `async` method captures it into a state-machine frame that lives until the task settles, and `CancellationToken` is the **single stdlib-certified exception** to [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s borrow-bearing-parameter prohibition. The certification is this normative obligation: **the `CancellationTokenSource` must outlive the settlement of every task observing one of its tokens.** Awaiting the call inside the source's `using var` scope discharges the obligation; abandoning such a task ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers)) transfers it to whatever outlives the task. A token read after its source's disposal raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) and is undefined behavior in unchecked mode — the same residual-trust shape as [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field rule.

Reading `IsCancellationRequested` on a `CancellationToken` involves reading through the borrowed reference to the `CancellationTokenSource`. This read is guaranteed to be atomic and to observe the effect of a `Cancel()` call from another thread without additional synchronization — the runtime ensures the necessary memory ordering. The `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` method is similarly thread-safe.

`CancellationToken` is auto-imported as a language primitive ([§2.3](#sec-always-available-names)). `CancellationTokenSource` and the other threading types live in `System.Threading` and require explicit `import System.Threading;`.

`CancellationToken.None` (a token whose source never cancels) is provided for callers that do not want cancellation.

By convention, async methods that should be cancellable accept a `CancellationToken` parameter and pass it to inner async calls. Cancellation typically happens at `await` points: the inner call observes the request and completes with `OperationCanceledException`.

<a id="sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods"></a>
### 30.9 Exception handling in async methods

- An exception thrown in the synchronous prefix of an async method (before any `await`) faults the returned task, not the immediate caller.
- An exception thrown after an `await` faults the task.
- Awaiting a faulted task re-raises the exception with the original stack trace preserved.
- `try`/`catch` inside an async method catches exceptions normally, including those raised by `await`.

**Fault ownership.** A faulted task **owns its fault exception**. Awaiting a faulted task (or reading a faulted `Result`, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)) re-raises the task-owned instance; the catching arm's binding is a **borrow** of it, exactly as [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching) frames every caught exception — but the instance is **exempt from [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching)'s dispose-after-arm rule** (the [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) `TypeInitializationException` pattern): handling completes without disposing it, which is what makes re-raising the same instance to every awaiter of a multi-awaited `Task`/`Task<T>` ([§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)) sound. The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, when the task is disposed** — with two timing refinements: a task disposed while its own fault exception is in flight defers that disposal until the exception's handling completes (so a `using var`-bound task unwound by its own fault never destroys the exception mid-dispatch), and an await that consumed its operand task ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)) performs the deferred task disposal as its terminal act, after handling completes. Imperative fault paths transfer ownership **in**: `SetException`/`TrySetException` on the task-completion sources and `Task.FromException` take the exception as an `owned` parameter ([§30.11](#sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet), stdlib §6.6/§6.7); a caller holding only a caught *borrow* constructs a fresh exception chaining the cause (`new Exception(ex.Message, ex)`, [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) snapshot chaining) — consistent with [§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching)'s rule that caught instances do not escape their arm. The **aggregation helpers are the one exception to the first sentence** ([§30.10](#sec-standard-library-task-helpers) aggregation contracts): a non-successful `WhenAll`/`WhenAllOwned` owns no fault instance of its own — when the first non-successful input is faulted, awaiting the aggregate re-raises, *as a borrow*, the fault owned by that **input** task (a cancelled first input raises a fresh `OperationCanceledException`, [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)), which keeps every fault single-owned; the input-lifetime consequences are stated with the contracts.

`await` has no syntactic restrictions on its placement inside `try`/`catch`/`finally` *bodies*. The state machine handles suspension across exception-handling boundaries correctly.

Catch **guards** are the one exception: a `when` guard on a catch arm ([§19.4](#sec-guards)) is evaluated synchronously during exception dispatch and may not contain `await` (a compile error, in async and sync methods alike). Exception dispatch — deciding *which* arm handles a raised exception — runs to completion without suspension; permitting a suspension point inside dispatch would leave the exception neither caught nor propagating across the suspension. A guard that needs asynchronous information awaits it *before* the `try`, or catches unconditionally and re-raises (`throw;`, [§21.8](#sec-throw)) after an awaited check in the arm body.

```bezel
public async method WithCleanupAsync(): Task
  try
    await DoWorkAsync();
  catch
    var ex: Exception => do
      await LogErrorAsync(ex);
      throw;
    end
  finally
    await ReleaseResourcesAsync();
  end;
end WithCleanupAsync;
```

The `do ... end` block is required here because the arm body has multiple statements. When the body is just a re-raise, the bare `throw` expression makes the arm a one-liner:

```bezel
catch
  var ex: TransientException => Retry(ex),
  var ex: Exception => throw          // re-raise unrecognized exceptions
end;
```

<a id="sec-standard-library-task-helpers"></a>
### 30.10 Standard library task helpers

The standard library provides:

- `Task.FromResult<T>(value: T): Task<T>` — completed task with a value. Restricted to non-class T (value types, `string`, runtime-managed reference types). For class T, see `Task.FromOwnedResult` below; calling `FromResult` with a class-typed T is a compile error pointing to the owned variant.
- `Task.FromOwnedResult<T>(owned value: T): OwningTask<T> where T: class` — completed Pattern B task whose owned result is `value`. The caller transfers ownership of `value` to the task. Awaiters consume the task under Pattern B ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)): the await must appear in an owned-consuming context (`using var`, an `owned` parameter, an `owned` return, etc.), and ownership transfers to that context. Use this when constructing a completed task from a freshly-acquired or freshly-constructed class instance that the awaiter should own.
- `Task.FromException<T>(owned exception: Exception): Task<T>` and the non-generic `Task` form. The exception parameter is `owned`: the produced task owns its fault exception per [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods).
- `Task.FromCancelled<T>(): Task<T>` and the non-generic form.
- `Task.Delay(milliseconds: int): Task` and `Task.Delay(duration: TimeSpan): Task`, plus overloads of each taking a `CancellationToken`.
- `Task.WhenAll(tasks: Array<Task>): Task` — completes when all tasks complete.
- `Task.WhenAll<T>(tasks: Array<Task<T>>): Task<Array<T>>` — homogeneous result type for non-class T.
- `Task.WhenAllOwned<T>(owned tasks: OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>): OwningTask<OwningArray<T>> where T: class` — Pattern B aggregator. The caller transfers ownership of the array (and its tasks); the result is an owned array of owned elements. Each task is awaited in turn (sequentially in the implementation, but the underlying operations run concurrently because the tasks were started before being passed in). See std lib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers) for a worked example.
- `Task.WhenAny(tasks: Array<Task>): Task<int>` — completes when the first task completes, yielding the **index** of the winner in `tasks` (a `Task<Task>` result would be unconstructible under this section's own rules: no factory produces a Pattern A `Task<T>` of class T from an externally-supplied value, and its destructor semantics would be unsound; the input array is already indexable, so the index identifies the winner with no ownership question).
- `Task.FireAndForget(owned task: Task)` — registers a continuation that logs or handles any exception the task produces, then disposes the task. The calling code relinquishes ownership; the runtime supervises the task's lifecycle. **`Task.FireAndForget` is the only supported way to discard a `Task` value** — the discard form `_ := someAsyncCall();` is rejected at compile time because abandoning a `Task` reference would skip its continuation cleanup — disposing a task abandons a running operation (a semantic, not a leak, restriction; [§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)). The two legal patterns for "I don't want to await this task" are `Task.FireAndForget(call())` (supervised: exceptions thrown by the task are logged) and `using var t := call();` (unsupervised: the task is disposed at scope end without blocking, and any exceptions it raises are silently swallowed — except that in **checked disposal mode** ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)) a `DisposedAccessException` raised in an abandoned continuation is first **reported** through the same implementation-defined diagnostic channel as `FireAndForget`'s logging, then swallowed: the backstop that catches a [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) source-outlives-settlement violation must never itself be invisible; see [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) for the disposal-of-unconsumed-task semantics).

These compose with the rest of the async machinery; awaiting them works like awaiting any other task.

**Aggregation contracts.** `Task.WhenAll` (both forms) completes only after **every** input has settled — it never abandons laggards. If every input succeeded it completes successfully (for the generic form, with the results in input order); otherwise awaiting it re-raises the exception of the **first non-successful input in input order** — a cancelled input counting as `OperationCanceledException` — per the first-fault-no-aggregation posture (stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope), rationale §13.5); the other inputs' faults remain observable on those tasks individually. When that first non-successful input is **faulted**, the re-raise is **by borrow of the input task's owned fault instance** ([§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods) fault ownership) — an aggregate task owns no fault of its own, so every fault keeps a single owner; when it is **cancelled**, the runtime raises a fresh `OperationCanceledException`, exactly as awaiting that input directly would ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)). `WhenAll` of an **empty** array returns an already-completed task. `Task.WhenAny` completes when the first input **settles in any state** (success, fault, or cancellation), yielding its index; awaiting `WhenAny` never re-raises an input's fault — the caller inspects the winner. `WhenAny` of an empty array raises `ArgumentException` **synchronously at the call site**, not as a faulted task (it could never complete, and the misuse is local). `Task.WhenAllOwned` behaves as its stdlib §6.7 sketch shows, now as **contract**: inputs are awaited in input order; on the first non-successful input, results already produced are disposed with their tasks and laggards' eventual results are disposed on production ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) disposal continuations), and awaiting re-raises that first fault — the first non-successful input task itself is **retained by the aggregate and disposed with it**, so the re-raised instance remains owned by its own task, transitively, for the aggregate's lifetime; on all-success the returned array owns every result; `WhenAllOwned` of an empty array returns an already-completed task owning an empty array.
