The borrowing aggregators (`Array<Task>`/`Array<Task<T>>` inputs) hold their inputs as **frame borrows across suspension** — [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s obligation applies, extended through consumption: the input tasks (and the array) must outlive the aggregate task's settlement **and every await or `Result` read of the aggregate** — a faulted aggregate's re-raise borrows an instance an input task owns, so disposing an input after the aggregate settles but before it is consumed would dangle the re-raise.

**Structured fan-out: `TaskScope`.** The default posture for concurrent fan-out is the structured nursery `TaskScope` (stdlib [§6.10](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-taskscope)): children are spawned into a lexically-scoped owner consumed by `await using`; `await Join()` is mandatory on the normal path and is the single re-raise site (first fault wins and cancels siblings via the scope's token); disposal **quiesces** — no child outlives the scope — which is what discharges [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation structurally. The two discard idioms above are the exceptional escape hatches, not the default: `FireAndForget` severs fault propagation (logged only), and the `using var`-drop severs it silently *and* leaves the running frame's borrows unsupervised ([§30.1](#sec-async-methods), [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)); both are appropriate only for genuinely unsupervised work whose inputs the task owns. (Storing a freshly-minted task into a **borrowing** collection slot is not a third idiom: the slot takes no ownership, so the task dies at the statement's [K8](#sec-kernel-k8) boundary — abandoned unsupervised, the slot dangling besides — and the store draws [§15.4](#sec-collection-literals)'s fresh-store warning; hold each task in a named binding, or use `OwningArray<OwningTask<T>>` with `Task.WhenAllOwned` for dynamic fan-in, stdlib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers).)

<a id="sec-taskcompletionsourcet-and-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet"></a>
### 30.11 `TaskCompletionSource<T>` and `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>`

A `TaskCompletionSource<T>` produces a task whose state is controlled imperatively. The standard use is wrapping callback-based or event-based APIs into awaitable form.

The split into two classes — one for non-class T, one for class T with ownership transfer — exists for the same reason as the `FromResult` / `FromOwnedResult` split. For non-class T (copyable value, string, runtime-managed), the produced `Task<T>` carries no ownership across the await boundary; the standard `TaskCompletionSource<T>` is sufficient. For class T, the result must be owned by something — and the natural shape is for the produced task to be Pattern B (`OwningTask<T>`, [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)): the source takes ownership of the result on completion, and the eventual awaiter takes ownership through the `using var x := await ...` shape. `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> where T: class` produces this shape.

<a id="sec-taskcompletionsourcet-—-for-non-class-t"></a>
#### `TaskCompletionSource<T>` — for non-class T

```bezel
public class TaskCompletionSource<T>
  // Intrinsic restriction: T must be a copyable value type, string, or other
  // runtime-managed reference type. Instantiating with a class T is a
  // compile error pointing to OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>; a move-only
  // value T is rejected per §30.5 (its Task<T> is itself ill-formed).
  public constructor();
  public readonly property Task: Task<T>;

  public method SetResult(result: T);
  public method SetException(owned exception: Exception);   // the task owns its fault (§30.9)
  public method SetCancelled();

  public method TrySetResult(result: T): bool;
  public method TrySetException(owned exception: Exception): bool;
  public method TrySetCancelled(): bool;
end TaskCompletionSource;
```

A non-generic `TaskCompletionSource` (for `Task` with no result) has the same shape minus the `result` parameter on `SetResult`/`TrySetResult`.

<a id="sec-ownedtaskcompletionsourcet-—-for-class-t"></a>
#### `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>` — for class T

```bezel
public class OwningTaskCompletionSource<T> where T: class
  public constructor();
  public readonly property Task: OwningTask<T>;

  public method SetResult(owned result: T);
  public method SetException(owned exception: Exception);   // the task owns its fault (§30.9)
  public method SetCancelled();

  public method TrySetResult(owned result: T): bool;
  public method TrySetException(owned exception: Exception): bool;
  public method TrySetCancelled(): bool;
end OwningTaskCompletionSource;
```

The `where T: class` constraint excludes value types, string, and runtime-managed reference types. The caller transfers ownership of `result` to the source via the `owned` parameter; the source forwards ownership into the produced `OwningTask<T>`. The awaiter consumes the task under Pattern B ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)): one consumer takes ownership of the result via `using var x := await source.Task;`. A second await raises `InvalidOperationException`.

If `TrySetResult` returns `false` because the task is already in a terminal state, the implementation disposes `result` before returning. The caller has no further obligation — ownership was transferred at the call, and the implementation is responsible for releasing it on every path. The same applies if `TrySetException` or `TrySetCancelled` returns `false` while a previous `SetResult` already took ownership of a result; the existing result remains owned by the task.

`SetException`/`TrySetException` take the exception **`owned`**: the produced task becomes the single owner of its fault exception ([§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods) fault ownership — awaiters borrow it on re-raise; it is disposed once, at task disposal; a `TrySetException` that returns `false` disposes the passed exception, mirroring the `TrySetResult` rule above). A caller completing a source from a caught exception constructs a fresh cause-chained instance ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)), since the caught binding is a borrow that cannot escape its arm ([§31.1](#sec-throwing-and-catching)).

<a id="sec-common-semantics"></a>
#### Common semantics

The `Task` exposed by either source observes the source's state. The `Set*` methods complete the task; `TrySet*` returns `false` instead of throwing when the task is already in a terminal state.

**Task-object ownership.** The **source owns the task object** its `Task` property exposes. A read of the property is a **borrow** of the task, sourced at the source object's location — the same receiver-sourced notion as an owned-field read ([§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)) — and is admitted wherever [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal) admits a task borrow with that source: for the canonical `using var tcs` shape, the borrow is bounded by `tcs`'s scope, so `return await tcs.Task;` inside the scope (every example below) is well-formed, while returning `tcs.Task` *itself* out of the scope is the return of a borrow sourced at a local with no source that outlives the call — rejected by [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-return rule and [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s receiver-sourced accessor regime. The task never outlives its source, and there is no first-read ownership transfer. **Disposal accounting is by source kind.** For `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>` (Pattern B): an await through the borrow disposes the task per [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s borrowed-operand rule, and the source's own later disposal of it is [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotent no-op. For `TaskCompletionSource<T>` and the non-generic form (Pattern A / no result): awaits neither consume nor dispose the task — multiple awaits remain permitted ([§30.4](#sec-multiple-awaiters)) — and the source's disposal is the task's single disposal. For either kind, a **never-awaited** task is disposed exactly once, by the source at source disposal. A source disposed before completion first faults the task (below) and then disposes it; [§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)'s fault-disposal deferral extends across the resumption of every awaiter registered at the fault — the task's disposal of its fault instance runs after those queued re-raises' handling completes. (An awaiter that outlives the source's scope could only have been registered through a borrow of the task that escaped its source — the escape rejected above; where residual-trust code reaches one anyway, checked disposal mode faults it deterministically, [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract).)

If the source is disposed before the task completes, the task is automatically transitioned to a faulted state with `InvalidOperationException("source disposed before completion")`.

If the source is disposed after `SetResult` was called, results already delivered are unaffected: a `TaskCompletionSource<T>` (non-class T) await delivered the result as a **value copy**, and an `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>`'s single Pattern B await **moved the result out** — it belongs to the awaiter, and disposing the source (and with it the task) does not touch it. A task **never awaited** by the time the source is disposed is disposed with the source — for `OwningTaskCompletionSource<T>` this disposes the still-held produced result too ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal), disposing an unconsumed `OwningTask<T>`); no borrow of the task survives the source (above), so nothing observes the task afterward.

Pattern — wrapping a **one-shot** callback API (the registration invokes the callback at most once; illustrative API):

```bezel
public async method ReadSectorAsync(dev: BlockDevice, lba: long): Task<int>
  using var tcs := new TaskCompletionSource<int>();

  dev.BeginRead(lba, lambda(status) => do        // BeginRead invokes the callback ONCE
    tcs.TrySetResult(status);
  end);

  return await tcs.Task;
end ReadSectorAsync;
```

*(A repeating registration — an event subscription whose handler can fire again after the `using var` scope ends — is outside this exception; see the one-shot requirement.)*

Pattern — wrapping a class-typed result with ownership transfer:

```bezel
public async method LoadResourceAsync(path: string): OwningTask<Resource>
  using var tcs := new OwningTaskCompletionSource<Resource>();

  StartLoadInBackground(path, lambda(owned loaded: Resource) => do
    tcs.TrySetResult(move loaded);                       // ownership moves into tcs's task
  end);

  return await tcs.Task;                            // moves ownership out of tcs's task
                                                    //   and into the outer Pattern B task's
                                                    //   result slot. tcs is then disposed,
                                                    //   but its task already has no result.
end LoadResourceAsync;
```

The outer async method's return type `OwningTask<Resource>` and the inner `OwningTaskCompletionSource<Resource>.Task` (which is `OwningTask<Resource>`) align: the `await` performs the Pattern B move out of the inner task, and the outer `return` moves the same value into the outer task's result slot. A caller of `LoadResourceAsync` then writes:

```bezel
using var r := await LoadResourceAsync("/etc/foo");
Process(r);
// r disposed at scope end
```

**Closure capture and callback lifetime.** The lambda in the example captures `tcs` (an owned local) and is passed to `StartLoadInBackground`. Per the closure-capture rules ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), capturing an owned local treats the capture as a borrow whose source is the enclosing scope; the closure may not outlive that scope. For this pattern to type-check, the compiler must prove that the callback runs (and any references it holds become unreachable) before `tcs`'s scope ends.

The proof is structural: the `await tcs.Task` blocks the enclosing method's continuation until `tcs.TrySetResult` is called from the callback. The enclosing method's `tcs` local stays in scope until the method completes; the await ensures the method does not return until the callback has either completed (running `TrySetResult`) or failed in a way the task observed. By the time `tcs`'s scope ends, the callback has been invoked (or the task is in a terminal state without invocation, in which case the callback may still hold a borrow but `tcs`'s task is already settled and disposal of `tcs` will fault the task safely).

This reasoning is **specific to the TCS callback-registration pattern** and not a general closure-escape exception. **The admitted shape is defined by compiler-checkable conditions:**

1. the captured local is a `using var` of one of the four TaskCompletionSource classes;
2. the lambda is passed **directly** as an argument to exactly one call in the same block (the registration site) and does not otherwise escape — not stored, not returned, not captured again;
3. an `await` of that local's `.Task` post-dominates the registration and dominates every normal exit of the local's scope;
4. the lambda's only use of the capture is invoking TCS members.

A capture meeting all four conditions is admitted; anything else falls to the standard closure-escape rules. **The registration API's callback must be one-shot** — never invoked after its first invocation or after the operation settles. A *repeating* registration (an event subscription, a polling hook) is **outside** this exception: its callback can fire again after the `using var` scope ends, a use-after-dispose the structural proof cannot discharge; wrap repeating sources with an owned subscription object and an explicit lifetime instead. The explicit non-escaping-callback annotation this contract anticipated now exists — [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s `scoped` — and the four-condition shape is the legacy statement retained for the current signatures until the standard library migrates them to `scoped`.

**Re-derivation.** The callback-capture admission above is now a derived instance of [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s storage-bounded capture (the source is the bounding object; settlement is its quiescence point). The four-condition text remains normative for the current signatures and is retired when the standard library migrates them to `scoped`; no further hard-coded capture patterns will be added.

<a id="sec-thread-synchronization"></a>
### 30.12 Thread synchronization

Bezel has no language-level synchronization primitives (no `synchronized` keyword, no `lock` statement). The standard library provides:

- `Mutex` — a mutual-exclusion lock. `Acquire()` returns a `Lock` object; releasing the lock is disposal of the `Lock`.
- `Lock` — a scoped guard implementing `IDisposable`. Integrates with `using var`.
- `Semaphore` — a counting semaphore.
- `Atomic<T>` — atomic operations on primitive types.
- `Locked<T>` / `RwLocked<T>` — **data-owning locks**: the lock owns an interior `T`, reachable only through scoped guards (`LockGuard<T>`; `ReadGuard<T>`/`WriteGuard<T>`). See "Data-owning locks" below; full surface stdlib [§6.11](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-locked-and-rwlocked).

The `Lock` pattern with `using var`:

```bezel
class BankAccount
  private owned _mutex: Mutex := new Mutex();
  private _balance: decimal := 0m;

  public method Deposit(amount: decimal)
    using var guard := _mutex.Acquire();
    _balance := _balance + amount;
  end Deposit;
end BankAccount;
```

Within a single execution domain ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)), continuations never run concurrently, so a program needs no synchronization for state shared between one domain's tasks; interleaving occurs only at suspension points. Nor does spawning additional domains ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)) create synchronization obligations: domains share no mutable state — everything that crosses a boundary is moved or immutable, and the channel types ([§30.15](#sec-channels)) are internally synchronized. The synchronization types above are needed in exactly three places: where foreign threads enter through the FFI ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)); for cross-domain mutual exclusion and shared-state guarding through `Shared<Mutex>`, `Shared<Locked<T>>`, or a `static owned readonly` data-owning lock ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership); [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4); and in code running outside any domain ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types) — the synchronous startup prefix).

**Blocking acquisition follows the [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types) discipline.** `Mutex.Acquire()`/`TryAcquire(timeout)`, `Semaphore.Acquire()`/`TryAcquire(timeout)`, and the data-owning locks' blocking forms — `Locked<T>.Lock()`/`TryLock(timeout)` and `RwLocked<T>.Read()`/`TryRead(timeout)`/`Write()`/`TryWrite(timeout)` — **block the calling thread**. Inside a domain continuation, a blocked thread pins one of the pool's workers and cannot advance its own domain — the pool-starvation cousin of [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)'s deterministic blocking-wait deadlock (the lock's holder may itself need this domain to advance, or the fixed-size pool may have no free worker left to run the releasing continuation). The same two-layer rule therefore applies: the compiler rejects the blocking forms **lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas** (there the async forms are strictly superior — `await m.AcquireAsync()` / `await m.TryAcquireAsync(timeout)`); where static rejection cannot see the call (a non-`async` helper reached from a continuation), the runtime raises `InvalidOperationException` **when the acquisition would actually park a thread inside a domain continuation** — an immediately-available acquisition, and any acquisition on the startup thread or an FFI foreign thread (both outside any domain), proceeds as before. Cross-domain locking from async code uses `Shared<Mutex>` with `Get().AcquireAsync()` ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)). `Mutex` and the data-owning locks are **non-reentrant**: a holder re-acquiring waits on itself, whatever the acquisition form. (`Semaphore` is a counting primitive: a second `Acquire()` by the same holder consumes another permit — not reentrancy, and legal while permits remain.)

<a id="sec-data-owning-locks"></a>
#### Data-owning locks: `Locked<T>` and `RwLocked<T>`

`Locked<T>` and `RwLocked<T>` (stdlib [§6.11](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-locked-and-rwlocked)) are compiler-known locks that **own their interior**: construction consumes an owned `T`; the interior is reachable only through a scoped guard; the lock's destructor disposes the interior. They are the in-language home for structured mutable state reached from more than one domain — the `static owned readonly` registry ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's warning-suppression set: warning-free) and the `Shared<Locked<T>>` handle ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) — replacing the lock-next-to-data convention that rule 4 warns about with a tie the compiler checks.

- **Interior admission.** `T` must be a **sendable class type** ([§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)) — the existing derived property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)), reused; an instantiation whose `T` is not sendable is rejected at the instantiation site with the standard property-naming diagnostic. The reason is reachability: a `Locked<T>` is by design reachable from every domain, so a borrow inside `T`'s state would let a guard-holder in one domain chase a reference into another domain's heap *outside any lock*. A wholly-owned interior makes guard-mediated access the only access. (`Locked<Dictionary<string, Session>>` with class-typed values is rejected — the borrowing slots alias externally-owned state, [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy); `Locked<OwningDictionary<string, Session>>` is the admitted spelling.)
- **Guards.** The acquisition families (`Lock`/`TryLock`/`LockAsync`/`TryLockAsync`; the `Read*` and `Write*` families of `RwLocked<T>`) produce owned guard objects. A guard's `Value` property is a **borrow of the interior whose source is the guard** — the same compiler-known accessor dispensation as `Shared<T>.Get()` ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) — so the borrow rules of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) bound every interior borrow by the guard's life, and the guard's disposal is the release. Because this dispensation promises that the guard's scope *is* the critical section, [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)'s announced-kill carve-out does **not** extend to guards (the same deliberate strengthening as [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters)'s admission freeze, for the same reason: the carve-out is justified by the killed object's own disposed-flag backstop, and killing a guard sets no flag on the *interior* that its surviving borrows reference, while releasing the lock out from under them): an explicit `Dispose()` or discard of a guard binding while any borrow sourced from it is live is a **compile error**, the same body-local liveness dataflow as the consume-site freeze. For the same body-local analysis, a live guard counts as a live local borrow **of the lock binding it was acquired from**: consuming, discarding, or explicitly disposing a lock binding while a guard obtained from it is live is rejected the same way. Guards are domain-bound and **not sendable**, like `Lock` and `SemaphoreToken`.
- **Blocking discipline.** The blocking forms follow this section's two-layer rule verbatim: rejected at compile time lexically inside `async` methods and `async` lambdas (the `Async` forms are strictly superior there); where static rejection cannot see the call, the runtime raises `InvalidOperationException` when the acquisition would actually park a thread inside a domain continuation. The locks are **non-reentrant** (the posture stated above, now covering `Mutex` too): a holder re-acquiring waits on itself — the async forms deadlock at the task level; the blocking forms inside a continuation hit the runtime guard. For `RwLocked<T>` this includes `Write()` while holding *any* guard of the same lock, and — the classic rwlock hazard, stated so programs do not rely on it — a **second `Read()` while already holding a read guard** may also block: fairness and ordering between waiting readers and writers are unspecified, so the second read may queue behind a waiting writer. Nested acquisition of the same lock must not be relied on in any form.
- **Read guards are write-restricted (`RwLocked<T>` only).** Multiple `ReadGuard<T>`s may be live at once, including across domains (that is the read-parallel point of the type), so a mutation through a read guard would be a cross-domain data race between "readers". **Within the body holding the guard**, through a borrow whose source is a `ReadGuard<T>` — the guard's `Value`, or any borrow derived from it through member chains or element reads — the compiler **rejects every store and consuming use**: assignment (plain or compound) to any field, property, or indexer slot reached through it; `move` from it; and passing it, or a location reached through it, as a `ref`/`out` argument. (Explicit `Dispose()` through it is already rejected by [§28.6](#sec-leak-prevention)'s owned-receiver rule.) The check is expression-site and borrow-provenance-keyed — the dispose-through-borrow family — and body-local is all it can be: borrow provenance does not cross call boundaries. What it cannot see is a **recorded programmer obligation** of the same genus as [§30.14](#sec-sendable-types)'s indirect-alias obligations: a **mutating method invoked through the read borrow** (`g.Value.Add(...)` — indistinguishable from a read in a language with no const-method vocabulary, deliberately declined), and **any callee reached with the read borrow (or a location reached through it) as a plain argument** — a borrowed parameter admits stores in the callee, which no caller-side rule can reject without rejecting the pass-and-read idiom wholesale. Reader purity beyond the checked stores is the author's responsibility; a violation is a data race no conformance mode detects. `WriteGuard<T>.Value` and `LockGuard<T>.Value` carry no restriction — those guards are exclusive.
- **Disposing the lock.** The lock's destructor disposes the interior. Where lock and guard are visible in one body, the guard-liveness rule above rejects killing the lock binding under a live guard. Where no body-local rule can see it — a guard still live when the *last* `Shared<Locked<T>>` handle drops in another domain, or a lock reached through storage the body did not bind — destroying a lock while any guard is outstanding has the [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract) posture: in **checked disposal mode** the runtime must detect destruction of a lock with live guards (holders or waiters) and fault deterministically, and subsequent access through a surviving guard's `Value` faults as `DisposedAccessException` off the interior's disposed flag; in unchecked mode it is undefined behavior. The discipline is the ordinary nesting one: `using var` guards inside the scope that owns the lock (reverse-order disposal releases every guard before the lock dies), and for `Shared`-held locks, no domain's guard outlives its handle — the [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership) aliasing bullet's genus.
- **Visibility.** Guard release carries [§30.13](#sec-cross-thread-visibility)'s mutual-exclusion happens-before edge: disposal of a guard happens-before the next acquisition of the same lock. For `RwLocked<T>`: a write guard's release happens-before every subsequent read or write acquisition, and each read guard's release happens-before the next write acquisition.
- **Membership.** Both types are in [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)'s `Shared`-payload synchronized set (`Shared<Locked<T>>`/`Shared<RwLocked<T>>` are sendable) and in [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4's warning-suppression set — a `static owned readonly` lock is the canonical warning-free process-global registry, enrolled in [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s program-exit disposal. They are deliberately **not** in rule 2's form-(i) set: a *mutable* static of a lock type remains rejected — rule 2's overwrite-never-disposes store semantics would leak a displaced lock *plus its whole interior* until process exit, and no use case demands lock-slot reassignment (the interior's mutability lives behind the guards). Each membership, and the form-(i) exclusion, is carried by the types' recorded fact grants — **synchronized** plus **displacement-unbounded** (stdlib §1, v0.245).
- **Guards across `await`.** Holding a guard across a suspension point is legal (the guard is an ordinary owned local) but discouraged; an implementation **should** warn when a guard is live across an `await` (stdlib §6.11 states the lint). Deadlock between two locks (lock ordering) remains out of scope, as everywhere else; the actor idiom ([§30.15](#sec-channels)) is the recommendation when ordering gets complicated.

<a id="sec-runtime-model"></a>
### 30.13 Runtime model

<a id="sec-execution-domains"></a>
#### Execution domains

All **asynchronous** Bezel code executes within an **execution domain**; the synchronous startup prefix runs outside any domain (below). A domain is a unit of *serial* execution: at any instant, at most one continuation belonging to a domain is running, and a continuation, once started, runs without interruption from the domain's other work until it suspends at an `await`, completes, or propagates an exception (*run-to-completion*). Continuations of a domain's tasks therefore interleave only at suspension points and never overlap.

A program begins with a single domain (the *main domain*) plus the **startup thread**, which runs outside any domain: the synchronous portion of program startup — a non-`async` `Main` and the code it calls directly — executes on the startup thread, and it is exactly the code for which [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)'s blocking escape hatches are legal. Asynchronous work started from the startup thread belongs to the main domain, whose continuations the runtime's workers drain concurrently — which is why a blocking wait at the process edge makes progress. An `async` `Main` is driven as the main domain's first continuation, with the startup thread blocked on its task's completion ([§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)). A program that never spawns is a single-domain program. Additional domains are created explicitly with `Domain.Spawn` ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)); data crosses a domain boundary only by ownership transfer or immutable sharing — through spawn arguments, join results, and channels ([§30.15](#sec-channels)) — under the *sendable* discipline of [§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains). Domains share no mutable state.

The guarantees that follow from serial execution within a domain are normative:

- **Memory visibility.** The effects of a continuation are visible to every continuation that subsequently runs in the same domain, without synchronization: each continuation *happens-before* the next continuation in its domain, regardless of which threads the runtime uses to run them.
- **No intra-domain data races.** Two continuations of the same domain never access memory concurrently, so unsynchronized access to state shared between a domain's tasks is well-defined. Interleaving at suspension points can still reorder logical operations — an invariant that must hold across an `await` must be re-established before suspending — but partially-written memory is never observed.
- **Soundness of ownership and borrow checking.** The rules of [§28](#sec-resource-management) assume that between two points of a continuation with no intervening suspension, no other code of the program runs. Within a domain this assumption holds by construction: a borrow's source cannot be disposed mid-use by concurrently-running code, and the disposal obligations of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) are discharged exactly once under every interleaving. The guarantee is scoped to suspension-free spans: **at a suspension point, other continuations of the same domain run and may dispose objects a suspended frame holds borrows of** — not a data race but an interleaving, governed by [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s source-outlives-settlement obligation and caught in checked disposal mode as `DisposedAccessException`.

<a id="sec-cross-thread-visibility"></a>
**Cross-domain and cross-thread visibility.** The model's remaining
synchronization edges are likewise normative — in each, the release side
*happens-before* the matching acquire side, on any hardware, whatever threads
the runtime or the FFI involve:

1. **Mutual exclusion.** The release of a `Mutex`, a `Semaphore`, or a
   data-owning lock (`Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>`) — disposal of the
   `Lock`/`SemaphoreToken` guard (stdlib §6.2/§6.3) or of a
   `LockGuard<T>`/`ReadGuard<T>`/`WriteGuard<T>` (stdlib §6.11; the
   read/write refinement of the edge is stated in
   [§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)) — happens-before the next acquisition
   of the same primitive, through any acquisition form (`Acquire`,
   `TryAcquire`, `AcquireAsync`/`TryAcquireAsync`, and the
   `Lock`/`Read`/`Write` families of [§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)'s
   data-owning locks), from any domain, from code outside any domain, or
   from a foreign thread entered through the FFI — the case
   [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization) prescribes `Mutex` for;
   `Shared<Mutex>` and `Shared<Locked<T>>`/`Shared<RwLocked<T>>`
   ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) carry the same edge. The next holder
   observes every write the previous holder made before releasing.
2. **Channels.** The acceptance of an item by `Send`/`SendAsync` happens-before
   the completion of the `Receive` (or successful `TryReceive`) that delivers
   that item ([§30.15](#sec-channels)): the receiving domain observes every
   write the sending domain made to the transferred ownership tree before the
   send.
3. **Spawn and join.** The `Domain.Spawn` call happens-before the entry's first
   continuation (the entry observes the spawn arguments' transferred trees
   fully written), and the entry task's settlement happens-before the join
   handle's completion as observed in the spawning domain
   ([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)).
4. **Task settlement.** A task's settlement happens-before the resumption of
   each awaiter's continuation, and before the return of a blocking
   `Wait()`/`Result` read outside a domain
   ([§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types)). Within one domain this
   is already implied by the continuation rule above; stated generally it also
   covers the startup thread blocking at the process edge.
5. **Static publication.** A store into an admitted mutable static
   ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 2(ii)) happens-before any read — from
   any domain — that observes the stored reference: the reader sees the
   referenced object's memory as fully written at publication, not merely an
   untorn pointer. Likewise, the completion of a type's static initialization
   happens-before any other domain's use of that type's statics
   ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rules 1 and 4). This is the edge that makes
   [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order) pattern (b)'s cross-domain task
   cache — and [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s
   borrowed-source chain through it — sound on weakly-ordered hardware.

Two object-specific guarantees stated in their own sections complete the set:
a `CancellationToken` read observes a cross-thread `Cancel()` without
additional synchronization — the ordering guarantee
[§30.8](#sec-cancellation) itself states — and each `Shared<T>` handle's drop
happens-before the destruction performed by the *last* drop
([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership) — the synchronized handle count carries the
release/acquire pairing, so the single destructor run observes every
handle-holder's writes). Atomics remain sequentially consistent (stdlib §6.4). Beyond this enumeration there is nothing left to specify, by
construction: no mutable state is ever reachable from two domains
([§30.14](#sec-multiple-domains)), so every cross-thread memory interaction a
Bezel program can express travels through these internally-synchronized
objects, the admitted statics, or the atomics — there is no residual "racy
access" category for the memory model to give semantics to. Memory shared
with foreign threads *outside* these primitives — native memory mutated
across the FFI without a `Mutex` — is outside these guarantees and governed
by the platform ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)).

#### Scheduling

- Calling an async method allocates the state machine and begins execution synchronously, as part of the running continuation, until the first `await` of an incomplete task.
- At an `await` of an incomplete task, the state machine registers a continuation and returns control to the caller.
- When the awaited task completes, the continuation is queued to its domain. The domain runs queued continuations one at a time, in unspecified order.
- A domain is not bound to an OS thread. The runtime may run a domain's successive continuations on different threads — but never on two threads at once — and it preserves the memory-visibility guarantee above across any thread migration. Async methods cannot assume thread affinity; code interacting with thread-affine foreign APIs (UI toolkits) must arrange marshalling explicitly.
- Foreign threads introduced through the FFI ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)) are outside the domain model. Bezel-level state shared with such threads requires the synchronization types of [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization).

The runtime does not provide synchronization contexts in this version.

<a id="sec-determinism"></a>
#### Determinism

A domain's execution is a deterministic function of what its edges deliver. Precisely: fix one executable artifact and its runtime. An **edge** of a domain is one of: a **scheduling decision** of this section (which queued continuation is dispatched next; which item a channel receive delivers, [§30.15](#sec-channels); a grant, completion, or observed result of an operation on a compiler-known internally-synchronized object — the [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization) types, channels, task settlement and join delivery, the [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule-1 first-touch election, the [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership) last-drop election; a timer-driven completion's delivery point); a **runtime-mediated world interaction** (the standard library's clock, entropy, environment and argument, console, and file-system operations — the intercept points the standard library designates, stdlib [§1](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-conventions)); or a **foreign-function boundary event** ([§32](#sec-foreign-function-interface)). Two executions of that artifact in which corresponding edges deliver identical values in identical per-domain order are **observationally identical**: each domain runs the same continuation steps computing the same values, issues the same edge requests with the same request payloads in the same order, produces the same output bytes at each output edge, and the program terminates identically. Exclusions, exactly two: (i) elapsed real time — how long anything takes, and every value derived from an unsubstituted clock; (ii) the contents of foreign memory and every value obtained through it ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)) outside the writebacks the boundary contract names ([§32.5](#sec-ffi-compatible-types), [§32.10](#sec-boundary-contract)) — foreign reads are outside this statement entirely. Memory addresses need no exclusion: no conforming program can observe one ([§32.12](#sec-foreign-memory)'s no-object-address invariant), and identity hash codes are assigned per [§8.3](#sec-identity-hash-assignment), never derived from addresses. Executions that encounter undefined behavior are outside this statement, as they are outside every guarantee. This subsection imposes no new obligation on programs and no new restriction on schedulers — it states the property the preceding rules already establish. It is what makes a recorded execution replayable, and it is checkable against the implementation: any within-domain nondeterminism given fixed edges — an uninitialized read, an unpinned iteration order, an address leak — is an implementation defect, not latitude.

<a id="sec-multiple-domains"></a>
### 30.14 Multiple domains and sendable types

Domains run in parallel: while each domain's continuations are serial ([§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)), continuations of *different* domains may run simultaneously on different threads. The data-race freedom of the single-domain guarantees is preserved across domains by one discipline: **no mutable state is ever reachable from two domains.** Every value that crosses a domain boundary is either *moved* (ownership transfers by the same `move` transfer machinery as [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer); the origin domain loses access **statically at the binding level** — the consumed binding is left moved-from, and the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) rejects the transfer while any local borrow of that binding is live) or *immutable* (`string`, copies of values). The static guarantee is deliberately scoped: an *indirect* pre-transfer alias — a borrow stored in a field of another object or a collection before the transfer, a borrow held by a **pending async frame** (an unsettled task's receiver or plain reference-typed argument, [§30.1](#sec-async-methods) — `var t := c.BumpAsync(); Domain.Spawn(W, move c);` is this shape), or a re-transfer through a different binding (`move box.f` into a spawn argument) — is governed by the caller-side trust obligations of [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s borrowed-field rule, [§28.11](#sec-borrowing-collections)'s store rule, and [§30.1](#sec-async-methods)'s settlement obligation (each carrying the "not transferred to another domain" clause — extended in to consumption into domain-reachable constructions, [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), not by a compile-time check, and checked disposal mode cannot catch a violation (the object stays alive in the receiving domain). Programs that honor those recorded obligations have no mutable state reachable from two domains. The compiler enforces the discipline through the *sendable* property below; the channel types ([§30.15](#sec-channels)) and the other compiler-known internally-synchronized types — together with the deeply-immutable `FrozenArray<T>`, behind `Shared` handles or as a `static readonly` singleton ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership); [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4) — are the only objects two domains may reach simultaneously. **Static state** — process-global and hence reachable from every domain — is constrained to uphold this same invariant by [§22.12](#sec-static-members)'s statics-and-domains rules.

<a id="sec-sendable-types"></a>
#### Sendable types

A type is **sendable** — a derived type property ([§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)) — when a value of the type may cross a domain boundary: as a spawn argument, a spawn result, or a channel element. Sendability is determined by category:

- **Value types** are sendable iff they are not borrow-bearing ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)) and not move-only ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)). All primitives and enums are sendable; a record is sendable per its fields, and a choice per its payloads ([§35.12](#sec-choice-sendability)), transitively (the borrow-bearing computation already supplies the transitivity). A sendable value crosses as a copy.
- **`string`** is sendable; it crosses as a shared reference, which is safe because strings are immutable (implementation note: the runtime's reclamation bookkeeping for strings must tolerate cross-domain sharing). A **boxed value** is sendable iff the boxed value's type is sendable. **Function-typed values are never sendable**: their captures are borrows of the origin domain's scopes ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)).
- **Class types** are sendable iff the class is **transfer-closed**:
  1. The class is `sealed` ([§12.4](#sec-sealing)); or it is `closed` and every class in its module-closed hierarchy is itself transfer-closed (then the whole closed hierarchy is sendable). Open classes are not sendable — an open class's sendable-looking surface could be extended by a subclass holding origin-domain references, and a base-typed owned field could carry that subclass across.
  2. Every instance field, including inherited fields, is: a sendable value type; `string`-typed; an `owned` field whose declared type is a sendable class type; an owning-inline-array field (`[N owned]C` / `[N owned]C?`) whose element class is a sendable class type; or an owning-choice-typed field whose every `owned` payload class is a sendable class type ([§35.12](#sec-choice-sendability)).
  3. The class has no function-typed fields, no `Object`-typed or interface-typed fields (boxed contents and runtime types behind interfaces cannot be statically verified), and no non-`owned` class-typed fields (a back-reference aliases an object owned in the origin domain).
  Mutually-recursive `owned` references among sendable classes are admitted; the property is evaluated coinductively (assume the types under test sendable, then check the rules). A sendable class instance crosses as an **owned transfer** — the entire ownership tree under it moves with it, and rule 2 guarantees that tree contains everything the instance can reach.
- **Interface types** are never sendable (rule 3's reasoning, applied at the root).
- **Compiler-known standard-library types** state their sendability in their stdlib sections, justified by their internal structure: owning collections and `OwningBuffer<T>` are sendable iff their element type is a sendable class type (their state is wholly owned); borrowing collections are sendable iff their element category ([§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)) is sendable-value or `string` (copy and shared-immutable slots; a borrowing collection of class elements carries borrows and is not sendable); `Task`, `Task<T>`, `OwningTask<T>`, enumerators, `EventSource<T>`/`AsyncEventSource<T>`, `CancellationTokenSource`, and `Weak<T>` are domain-local and not sendable; `SharedEventSource<T>` is likewise **not sendable** even though it is internally synchronized and process-reachable as a static ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 5): static reachability, not transfer, is its distribution mechanism; **`Shared<T>` is sendable iff `T` is in the `Shared`-payload synchronized set of [§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)** (wording for the rule — `Shared<Mutex>` is the cross-domain sharing idiom; for every other `T` it remains domain-local); of the [§30.12](#sec-thread-synchronization) types, `Mutex`, `Semaphore`, and the atomics are **sendable** (internally synchronized — stdlib §6.2–§6.4; that is their purpose) while `Lock` guards are domain-bound and not sendable; the data-owning locks `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` are **sendable** (internally synchronized; their interior is a sendable class by instantiation, [§30.12](#sec-data-owning-locks)) while their guards (`LockGuard<T>`, `ReadGuard<T>`, `WriteGuard<T>`) are domain-bound and not sendable, the `Lock` reasoning verbatim; `FrozenArray<T>` (stdlib §4.19) is **sendable** — a wholly-owned, deeply immutable tree that crosses as an owned transfer, readable from many domains at once behind `Shared<FrozenArray<T>>` handles ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership)) or as a `static readonly` singleton ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 4); `Channel<T>` and `ChannelSender<T>` are sendable ([§30.15](#sec-channels)). `CancellationToken` is a borrow-bearing record and therefore not sendable by the value-type rule — cancellation does not cross domains in this revision; the cross-domain cancellation pattern is a message on a channel.

Sendability of a generic instantiation is checked at the instantiation or call site under the rules of [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties); diagnostics name the property ("not sendable"), the offending type, and the failing rule.

**Moved trivial-dispose instances: the free obligation transfers with the move.** Sendability does not key on trivial-dispose — a sealed trivial-dispose class with sendable fields is sendable under the transfer-closed rules above (rule 2's admission of `owned` sendable-class fields composes with [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)'s definition, so a type can be simultaneously trivial-dispose and sendable). When a sendable trivial-dispose instance crosses a domain boundary — a spawn argument, a task result, a channel element — its compiler-inserted free obligation ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)) transfers with the move: the receiving domain's owner — the `owned` entry parameter, the awaited join result, the `Receive` result — frees the instance at that owner's release point, and the origin binding is left moved-from as usual. No cross-domain bookkeeping exists or is needed: the instance has exactly one owner at all times, in whichever domain currently holds it. Pre-transfer aliases of a moved trivial-dispose instance are governed by this section's recorded residual obligations **verbatim** — the field-held, collection-held, and pending-frame borrows of the paragraph above carry the same domain clause at trivial-sourced borrows as at any other. The channel-internal disposal sites ([§30.15](#sec-channels) — undelivered items disposed at the channel's disposal; the item disposed by a faulting send) need no separate clause: disposal of a trivial-dispose item *is* the flag-setting free ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal), [§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)), so those rules already state the free.

<a id="sec-spawning-domains"></a>
#### Spawning

`Domain.Spawn` (stdlib [§6.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-domain)) creates a new domain, runs an entry function as its first continuation, and returns a join handle in the spawning domain:

```bezel
// Representative forms; the stdlib section declares the full set.
Domain.Spawn(entry: () -> ()): owned Task
Domain.Spawn<R>(entry: () -> owned R): owned OwningTask<R>            // R: sendable class
Domain.Spawn<A, R>(entry: (owned A) -> owned R, owned arg: A): owned OwningTask<R>
Domain.Spawn<R>(entry: () -> R): owned Task<R>                       // R: sendable value type

// Async entries: the runtime awaits the returned task inside the
// spawned domain; the join handle tracks that task.
Domain.Spawn(entry: () -> Task): owned Task
Domain.Spawn<R>(entry: () -> OwningTask<R>): owned OwningTask<R>      // R: sendable class
Domain.Spawn<R>(entry: () -> Task<R>): owned Task<R>                  // R: sendable value type
```

The compiler enforces at the call site:

- **The entry must be capture-free**: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference. A capturing lambda or an instance method reference is rejected — captures and receivers are borrows of the origin domain ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)). Data enters the new domain only through the explicit `arg` parameters, which must be of sendable types; class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter.
- **Argument and result types must be sendable**, per the rules above.

**Async entries.** An entry may be an `async` function — a capture-free `async` lambda or a static `async` method reference; its function type is `() -> Task`, `() -> Task<R>`, or `() -> OwningTask<R>` ([§30.6](#sec-async-lambdas)). The runtime runs the entry as the spawned domain's first continuation and **awaits the returned task within that domain** — the exact analog of how the runtime drives an `async` `Main` ([§33.2](#sec-accepted-signatures)). The entry's task object never crosses the boundary: it lives and dies in the spawned domain; for the `OwningTask<R>` form the runtime is its single Pattern B consumer, and only the **sendable** result (or the fault, as `DomainFaultedException`) crosses into the join handle under the unchanged rules. In overload resolution, an entry whose return type is in the `Task` family resolves to the async forms; the synchronous generic forms never bind `R` to a task type (task types are not sendable, so every such binding was already an error — the preference changes no program's meaning).

The join handle is an ordinary task of the spawning domain. Awaiting an `OwningTask<R>` join follows Pattern B ([§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)): single consumer, ownership of the (sendable) result transfers to the awaiter — the existing single-consumer transfer semantics are exactly the cross-domain join semantics, unchanged. `Task`/`Task<R>` joins follow Pattern A.

**Faults.** An exception that propagates out of the entry does not cross the boundary as an object (exception classes are not in general sendable). The join instead raises `DomainFaultedException` (stdlib [§6.8](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-domain)), whose `Message` and `FaultStackTrace` carry copies of the original exception's message and stack-trace text (`string`s — sendable). Programs that need richer fault data return it as a sendable result or send it over a channel.

**Domain completion.** When the entry's task completes — for a synchronous entry, the task wrapping the entry invocation; for an `async` entry, the task the entry **returned** — the join handle completes (with the result or fault). Tasks started within the spawned domain that are still pending continue to run in that domain; their eventual exceptions are handled as `Task.FireAndForget` handles them (logged, not propagated — stdlib [§6.7](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-task-static-helpers)). The domain's resources are reclaimed when its last continuation completes.

<a id="sec-data-parallel-combinators"></a>
#### Data-parallel combinators

`Parallel.Map`, `Parallel.Reduce`, and `Parallel.ForEach` (stdlib
[§6.12](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-parallel)) are compiler-known combinators that run a function over a
collection's elements on a process-wide team of worker domains. They introduce **no new checking rule**: their
function-typed parameters are **spawn positions** — the call-site category this section defines for `Domain.Spawn`
entries, whose stdlib membership [§28.14](#sec-scoped-callback-parameters) names — checked at each call site exactly
as spawn entries are (**capture-free**: a non-capturing lambda or a static method reference; a capturing lambda or
instance method reference is rejected with the spawn-entry diagnostic), and their element and result types cross
between domains under the unchanged sendable rules of this section (value elements as copies, class elements as owned
transfers, results likewise). The bodies never cross as *values* — function-typed values remain never-sendable; the
call site proves they never need to.

Semantics (normative here; the full overload surface is stdlib §6.12):

- **Snapshot-at-call.** For borrowed inputs (`items: Array<A>`) the element chunks are copied **synchronously by the
  call itself**, before the returned task is exposed. [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model)'s run-to-completion makes this a
  real contract: the calling continuation cannot suspend mid-call, so by the first point at which any parent-domain
  code could mutate the source, the workers hold copies — mutation-after-call can never race a worker. For owned
  inputs (`owned items: OwningArray<A>`) the elements are **moved**: partitioned across workers and consumed by the
  call. For `Shared<FrozenArray<A>>` inputs the call clones one handle per participating worker and copies no
  element ([§28.13](#sec-shared-ownership); stdlib §4.19).
- **The team.** A lazy, process-wide team of ordinary [§30.13](#sec-runtime-model) worker domains, created on first
  use, `Parallel.DefaultDegree` wide (the value of `Environment.ProcessorCount` at team creation, fixed per process),
  reused across calls; bodies run as continuations of team domains. Work distribution rides the channel machinery
  ([§30.15](#sec-channels)); no object beyond the compiler-known synchronized types becomes reachable from two
  domains.
- **Results and faults.** `Map` reassembles results in **input order**, regardless of completion order. The first
  body fault cancels remaining work cooperatively (unstarted items are skipped; already-running bodies complete), and
  the returned task faults with `DomainFaultedException` — this section's fault vocabulary, with the no-aggregation
  posture of `TaskScope` (stdlib §6.10); later faults are swallowed. Moved-in items that were never processed are
  disposed by the runtime (the [§30.15](#sec-channels) channel-close precedent). The parent suspends at the `await`;
  it never blocks — no [§30.3](#sec-the-task-taskt-and-ownedtaskt-types) question arises.
- **Visibility.** The `Parallel.*` call happens-before each body invocation, and each body's completion
  happens-before the returned task's settlement — derived from [§30.13](#sec-cross-thread-visibility)'s spawn,
  channel, and settlement edges over the machinery the team rides on; stated so programs may rely on it without
  reasoning about the team's internals.
- **`Reduce` reassociates.** The combiner must be associative and the seed its identity for the serial-fold
  correspondence to hold; each worker folds its chunk from `seed` and the per-worker partials combine in an
  unspecified tree (stdlib §6.12 states the consequences plainly, including for floating-point).

*Recorded, not normative:* the in-place fork-join extension — `Parallel.Join`, a `concurrently-readable`
derived property, `par` fork positions, and provenance-linear disjoint span lending — is a **designed future
extension** whose rulings and soundness analysis are recorded in the design rationale
([rationale §12.9](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-data-parallelism)). Nothing in this revision reserves grammar or
adds checking rules for it; it lands, if it lands, through its own ruling-class revision.

<a id="sec-channels"></a>
### 30.15 Channels

A **channel** carries sendable values from one domain to another with ownership transfer at both ends: `Send` consumes the value in the sending domain; `Receive` produces it owned in the receiving domain. Channels are the only mutable objects reachable from more than one domain; they are compiler-known, internally synchronized, and their element type must be sendable (checked at instantiation per [§3.6](#sec-derived-type-properties)).

The shape is multiple-producer, single-consumer. The `Channel<T>` object is the *receiving* end, owned like any class instance (typically by a `using var` or an `owned` field in the receiving domain). Sender endpoints are minted from it and moved to wherever sending happens:

```bezel
using var inbox := new Channel<Report>();          // unbounded; this domain receives
using var worker := Domain.Spawn(ProcessAll, inbox.NewSender());   // sender moves to the new domain

// in this domain:
using var first := await inbox.Receive();          // ownership of one Report transfers in

// in the spawned domain (static method):
public static method ProcessAll(owned tx: ChannelSender<Report>)
  using var sender := move tx;                     // marker: adopt the owned parameter
  sender.Send(BuildReport(1));                     // ownership of each Report transfers out
  sender.Send(BuildReport(2));
end ProcessAll;                                    // sender disposed: last sender closes the channel
```

Normative semantics (full API: stdlib [§6.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-channel)):

- **`new Channel<T>()`** creates an unbounded channel. **`NewSender(): owned ChannelSender<T>`** mints a sender endpoint; any number may be minted, and each is an independently owned, sendable object. The channel and its senders share an internal core whose synchronization is the implementation's responsibility and invisible to programs.
- **`Send(owned item: T)`** (class-typed T; for sendable value types and `string` the parameter is unmodified) appends the item, transferring ownership into the channel. Unbounded channels never block on send. Sending on a closed channel raises `ChannelClosedException`.
- **`Receive()`** is asynchronous — `OwningTask<T>` for class-typed T (Pattern B: awaiting transfers ownership of the item to the receiver), `Task<T>` otherwise. If the channel is empty and open, the receive completes when an item arrives; if empty and closed, it raises `ChannelClosedException`. **`TryReceive(out owned item: T?): bool`** is the non-blocking form (Try pattern; `out using var` at the call site); it returns `false` when no item is available — consult **`IsClosed`** to distinguish empty-but-open from closed. **Abandoning a pending receive deregisters, never consumes.** Disposing a `Receive` task before an item has been dequeued into it deregisters the waiter; **no message is consumed or lost** — the next item goes to the next receive. An item being handed to the waiter at the instant of disposal is returned to the channel's head (an internal give-back; items remain exactly-once). This is the one place [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s dispose-continuation semantics do not apply to a pending result: the channel's item is given back rather than produced-then-disposed. (A first-class cancellable receive and multi-source select remain deferred to the give-back protocol design — proposal 0060, consolidating stdlib [§6.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-channel)'s deferral list. Until it lands, the sanctioned multi-source shape is to **merge into one channel**: one forwarder task per source, each `Send`ing into a single merged channel, the consumer receiving from that channel only — no task is abandoned mid-receive, and per-sender FIFO is preserved per source.)
- **`ReceiveAll()`** is the non-exceptional drain form: an async enumeration (`IOwningAsyncEnumerable<T>` for class-typed T, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` otherwise — [§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)) that yields each item with `Receive`'s transfer semantics, suspends while the channel is empty and open, and completes **normally** when the channel is drained and closed. At most one consumption may be in progress (the channel is single-consumer; this names the obligation): beginning a `ReceiveAll` while another enumeration is active **or while a `Receive` task is pending**, and calling `Receive`/`TryReceive` while a `ReceiveAll` enumeration is active, raise `InvalidOperationException`. The enumerator is affine ([§29.11](#sec-multiple-enumeration)). Abandoning the enumeration mid-drain deregisters like an abandoned `Receive` (below); no item is consumed or lost. An enumeration ended by a cancellation fault ([§30.7](#sec-asynchronous-programming-async-iterators)'s token routing) deregisters the same way — an item mid-handoff at that instant is returned to the channel's head; items already yielded to the body are the consumer's. The at-most-one-consumption obligation releases when an enumeration ends by any edge — normal completion, fault, or enumerator disposal — after which a `Receive`, `TryReceive`, or fresh `ReceiveAll()` (a new affine enumerable) is admissible.
- **Closing.** Disposing the last `ChannelSender<T>` *closes* the channel: items already sent remain receivable (the channel drains), and after the drain, receives raise `ChannelClosedException`. The receiving end may close first-class: **`Close()`** puts the channel in the same closed state — buffered items remain receivable, subsequent sends fault with `ChannelClosedException` (disposing the offered item, the rule), and a `SendAsync` pending at that instant has its item disposed by the channel and its task faulted with `ChannelClosedException` — with no give-back: the failed-send edge keeps its recorded dispose posture, and the give-back family remains deferred to proposal 0060. `Close()` is idempotent. Disposing the `Channel<T>` itself closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order (the owned column of [§28.11](#sec-element-slot-policy)); subsequent sends raise `ChannelClosedException`.
- **Ordering.** Items from one sender are received in the order sent; items from different senders interleave in an unspecified but consistent total order (each item is received exactly once).

**Bounded channels.** A channel constructed with a capacity bound buffers at most that many items. `SendAsync` awaits capacity (run-to-completion: the awaiting continuation resumes when space frees or the channel closes — closing disposes the pending item and faults the task with `ChannelClosedException`); the synchronous `Send` never blocks on any channel and raises `ChannelFullException` on a full bounded one. Back-pressure therefore composes with the ordinary task machinery and adds no new suspension concept. A send that **faults** disposes its class-typed item before the exception surfaces: `ChannelFullException` from the synchronous `Send` on a full bounded channel, and `ChannelClosedException` from `Send` or `SendAsync` on a closed one, all leave the item disposed — a channel never retains an item it did not accept. This states the composition [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s exception-path discharge already implies for the `owned` parameter; it is stated here because the item's data is unrecoverable on a *retryable* condition — a producer that cannot afford the loss uses `SendAsync` (which awaits capacity), and a give-back failure path remains deferred with the `TrySend` RFC (stdlib [§6.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-channel)'s deferral list). Full surface: stdlib [§6.9](Bezel_Standard_Library.md#sec-channel).

Multi-consumer channels (receiver cloning, which requires shared ownership) are deferred; see the design rationale.

---

<a id="sec-exception-handling"></a>
## 31. Exception Handling

<a id="sec-throwing"></a>
<a id="sec-throwing-and-catching"></a>

### 31.1 Throwing

```bezel
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive.", nameof(amount));
throw;          // re-throw the current exception (in a catch arm body only)
```

The first form constructs and raises an exception. The second form preserves the original stack trace. The bare re-throw is also available as an expression — `throw` without the trailing semicolon — which composes naturally with arm bodies; see [§31.2.4](#sec-bare-re-raise) and [§17.12](#sec-the-throw-expression).

<a id="sec-the-throw-operand"></a>
#### The throw operand

`throw expr` requires `expr` to be an **owned instance of an `Exception`-derived class type**: the operand's static type, nullability not admitted, must be `Exception` or a class deriving from it (v0.243 — the re-ruling that discharges the owner-review flag carried here since v0.182; rationale [§11.7](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-every-throwable-is-an-exception)). Values of primitive, `string`, record, enum, inline-array, unit, or function type cannot be thrown — a compile error at the throw site. An `Object`- or interface-typed operand is likewise rejected (no interface derives from `Exception`, and an `Object` referent may be a boxed value); narrow to the exception class first. The operand is consumed as an owned value under the ownership rules below, so a *borrowed* class reference is not a valid operand: to re-raise the exception being handled, use the bare re-raise ([§31.2.4](#sec-bare-re-raise)); to propagate a caught exception's information, chain a fresh instance through the snapshot constructor ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)). The consume composes with [§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)'s recorded boundary on the **announced** side: `throw x` is a source-visible kill — the keyword is itself the announcement, so the transfer marker is not written here — `throw move x` is rejected at the announced target ([§28.3](#sec-move-semantics-for-owned-locals)) — the same no-marker rule as an `owned` return — and the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)); `throw` therefore deliberately joins no silent-kill freeze list — it has exactly the runtime backstop whose absence forced the freeze for transfers.

Catch dispatch is purely by type ([§31.2.1](#sec-arm-patterns)): a thrown exception is caught by the first arm naming its class or a base of it, and a bare `Exception` arm catches every **catchable** throwable ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types); [§31.2.3](#sec-catch-ordering-and-exhaustiveness) — the catch-all). Every throwable carries the `Exception` reporting surface — `Message`, `StackTrace`, `CauseChain` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) — and participates in the unhandled-exception report.

<a id="sec-exception-ownership"></a>
#### Exception ownership

`new SomeException(...)` produces an owned class instance that the `throw` statement immediately consumes — ownership transfers to the runtime's exception machinery, which disposes the exception after the matching catch arm completes (or after the exception terminates the program if uncaught). Two exemptions to dispose-after-arm exist, both instances owned by a longer-lived object and disposed by it: the cached `TypeInitializationException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) and a faulted task's fault exception ([§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)) — which is what makes re-raising the same instance repeatedly sound in both cases. A borrowing (non-`owned`) class-typed field *inside* a thrown instance follows [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)'s field-held residual-trust regime unchanged: the throw extends the instance's lifetime to the matching handler, so a field borrow whose source is a binding of the throwing frame — or of any frame the exception unwinds past — violates the source-outlives-the-object obligation the moment the unwind disposes the source; the catch-arm access then faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal); undefined behavior unchecked), because the unwind itself set the disposed flag. A same-frame handler whose sources' scopes enclose the `try` remains sound. Exception classes should therefore carry owned or snapshot state — the [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) `CauseChain` snapshot constructor on the base `Exception` type is the design's own precedent.

Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable (`var ex: Exception` in the arm pattern) is a **borrow** of the in-flight exception; its source is the runtime, and its lifetime is the arm body's. The borrow may be passed to other methods (which further borrow for the duration of the call) but may not be assigned to an `owned` field, returned as `owned`, or captured by a closure that may outlive the arm.

To preserve an exception past the arm body — for logging, deferred reporting, or aggregation — copy the relevant data out of it (typically `ex.Message`, `ex.StackTrace` — a `string`, [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types) — the `CauseChain` snapshot, and any domain-specific properties) into separate owned values. Exception instances themselves cannot escape the arm that caught them. The bare re-throw `throw;` (which preserves the original instance) is the one exception to this rule, since it transfers the in-flight exception back to the runtime rather than capturing it.

<a id="sec-try-catch-finally"></a>
### 31.2 `try`/`catch`/`finally`

A `try` statement consists of a protected block, optionally followed by a `catch` block, optionally followed by a `finally` block. At least one of `catch` or `finally` must be present:

```bezel
try
  // protected statements
catch
  // arms (see §31.2.1)
finally
  // cleanup statements
end;
```

The `catch` block contains comma-separated arms whose syntax mirrors `case` arms ([§19](#sec-the-case-construct)). Each arm is a pattern with an optional guard and a body. The arms are tried in order; the first arm whose pattern matches the thrown exception (and whose guard, if any, evaluates to `true`) is selected, its body runs, and exception handling completes. Arms after the matched one are not considered.

If no arm matches, the exception continues propagating to the enclosing handler — exactly as if the `try` statement had not been present for that exception. This is the behavior of an unmatched arm in statement-position pattern dispatch ([§19.6](#sec-exhaustiveness)); `catch` does not warn about non-exhaustiveness because letting non-matching exceptions propagate is the normal case.

`finally` runs whether the protected block completed normally, was exited by an exception (caught or uncaught), or was exited by `return` — or by a `break` or `continue` targeting an enclosing loop. `return` inside a `finally` block is a compile error; so are `break` and `continue` inside a `finally` when their target loop encloses the `finally` (on the exception edge such a jump would silently discard the in-flight exception; a loop wholly inside the `finally` is unaffected, [§21.5](#sec-break-and-continue)). The `finally` is **established at entry to the protected block** ([§28.10](#sec-using-var)): on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack it ranks before anything the block itself establishes, so an owned local or `using var` declared inside the protected block is disposed before the `finally` runs on every exit edge, and cleanups established before the `try` run after it.

**A throw escaping a `finally` supersedes the in-flight exception (the rule §31.2.1 has always cited, now stated here):** when a `finally` entered during exception propagation itself completes by throwing (directly, or via a call that propagates), the new exception replaces the one being handled; the superseded exception is **disposed by the runtime exactly once**, as if its handling had completed — unless it is one of the two [§31.1](#sec-exception-ownership) dispose-after-arm exemptions: a superseded task-owned fault instance ([§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)) or cached `TypeInitializationException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) is dropped from the in-flight slot **undisposed**, its owner's disposal rules unchanged — supersession ends the instance's handling, never its life, so later awaiters of a multi-awaited task and later touches of a failed type still re-raise it live. The superseding exception then propagates from the `try` statement as usual.

If the `try` has only a `finally` (no `catch`), the catch block is omitted entirely:

```bezel
try
  using var fs := new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);
  ProcessFile(fs);
finally
  Log("file processing finished");
end;
```

<a id="sec-arm-patterns"></a>
#### 31.2.1 Arm patterns

A catch arm's pattern is one of:

- A bare type: `IOException`. Matches any thrown exception that is an instance of the type, without binding.
- A binding pattern: `var name: Type`. Matches and binds the exception to `name` for use in the arm's guard and body. The binding is in scope only within the arm.
- A multi-type alternative, with or without binding: `Type1 | Type2 | ...` or `var name: Type1 | Type2 | ...` (the `|` alternatives spelling — the same separator as case-pattern alternatives). Matches if the thrown exception is an instance of any of the listed types. When binding, `name` has the static type of the **nearest common base** of the listed types — the most specific class that is a base of every listed type. Every listed type is `Exception`-derived (the arm-type rule below), so the nearest common base is always `Exception` or a class deriving from it; for alternatives sharing nothing more specific, it is `Exception`. The non-binding form `Type1 | Type2` needs no common type.

**Arm types are `Exception`-family.** Every class type named in an arm pattern — bare, binding, or listed in a multi-type alternative — must be `Exception` or a class deriving from it (an **interface-typed** arm remains admissible — no interface derives from `Exception`, but an `Exception`-derived class may implement one, so the arm matches exactly the throwables whose class implements the interface). With every throwable `Exception`-derived ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) and inheritance single, an arm naming any other class type is **provably dead** — every base of a throwable's class other than `Object` lies on its own chain through `Exception`, so no thrown instance can ever match — and is a **compile error** naming this rule (the same reject-dead-shapes posture as the generic-bound check below); `Object` itself is rejected by the same rule for the opposite reason — as the universal root ([§8.1](#sec-definition)) it matches every throwable, and the spelling for that is the bare `Exception` arm ([§31.2.3](#sec-catch-ordering-and-exhaustiveness)); the remedy is to delete the arm or fix the type.

A **generic type parameter** is admissible as an arm's type: in a generic method or type, `var ex: TEx` (or bare `TEx`) matches exactly as the **substituted** type argument would — binding is fixed per instantiation, the [§11.8](#sec-static-interface-members) resolution vocabulary — so an `Assert.Throws<TEx>`-style helper matches the concrete exception type, subtypes included. The parameter must carry an **`Exception`-derived class bound** (`where TEx: Exception`, or a class deriving from it — the formerly idiomatic form is, since v0.243, the required one) so that every substitution is a throwable class ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)); a parameter that is unconstrained, value-constrained, bounded only by `where TEx: class` (which admits `string` and function types), or bounded by a class outside the `Exception` family is a compile error at the arm, **checked at the generic declaration** — whether the parameter carries such a bound is decidable from the enclosing declaration's constraint set alone, including through `where TEx: U` chains ([§14.2](#sec-constraints)), so the arm's well-formedness never depends on an instantiation; only the *matching* is per instantiation, against the substituted type.

Each pattern may be followed by an optional `when Expression` guard. The guard is evaluated only if the pattern matches; if the guard returns `false`, the arm is skipped and the next arm is considered. Inside the guard, the bound variable (if any) is in scope. The guard runs while the matched exception is in flight, but it evaluates as ordinary code — allocations, calls, and any other operations behave exactly as they would outside dispatch; the in-flight exception does not interfere with them. If the guard itself **throws**, that new exception *supersedes* the in-flight one — the superseded exception is **disposed by the runtime exactly once**, as if its handling had completed (the two owner-owned instances excepted, [§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)) — and propagates to the enclosing handler — it is not caught by a later arm of the same `try` and does not resume guard evaluation. This mirrors the rule for a `throw` in a `finally` ([§31.2](#sec-try-catch-finally)): an exception raised in a non-normal position replaces the one already propagating.

Arms are evaluated in textual order. Within a pattern, type alternatives are tested in declaration order, but this is not observable when types are disjoint; for non-disjoint alternatives (a base type listed alongside a derived type), the first matching type-arm wins, and the binding's static type is determined statically by the rule above, not by which alternative matched at runtime.

<a id="sec-arm-bodies"></a>
#### 31.2.2 Arm bodies

A catch arm's body uses the same shape as a `case` arm body ([§19.2](#sec-arms)). Three forms are valid (catch arms are always statement-position, so all three apply):

- **An expression**: `=> SomeMethod(args)`. The expression's result is discarded.
- **A single statement**: `=> Log(ex); ` ends with the statement's `;`. The convenient form for the common one-line arm body that is a statement (assignment, `return`, `throw`, etc.).
- **A `do ... end` block**: `=> do statements end`. Used when the body contains multiple statements.

The arm separator is `,`. A trailing comma after the last arm is permitted.

```bezel
try
  DoWork();
catch
  var ex: ArgumentException when ex.ParamName = "amount" => Console.WriteLine("Invalid amount"),
  InvalidOperationException => Console.WriteLine("Invalid state"),
  var ex: IOException | TimeoutException => Retry(ex),
  var ex: Exception => do
    Log(ex);
    throw;
  end
end;
```

The example demonstrates: a binding arm with a guard, a no-binding arm, a multi-type arm with binding (the `ex` parameter has type `Exception`, the nearest common base of `IOException` and `TimeoutException`, and is passed to a method accepting `Exception`), and a final binding arm whose body re-raises after logging.

<a id="sec-catch-ordering-and-exhaustiveness"></a>
#### 31.2.3 Catch ordering and exhaustiveness

Arms are tried in order; the first match wins. The most specific exception types should appear first. A bare `Exception` arm at the end **is the catch-all**: every throwable derives from `Exception` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)), so such an arm captures any thrown exception (the sole exception is `StackOverflowException`, which no arm matches — [§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)).

```bezel
try
  DoWork();
catch
  var ex: TimeoutException => RetryWithBackoff(ex),
  var ex: Exception => do          // the catch-all (§31.2.3)
    Log(ex);
    throw;
  end
end;
```
